issues.title: typing docs: Use soft deprecation
issues.author: JelleZijlstra
issues.bodyHTML:
A while ago we introduced the concept of "soft deprecation" in PEP 387 (https://peps.python.org/pep-0387/#soft-deprecation): for things that we no longer recommend using, but which we aren't planning to remove in the near future.

The typing docs already list four classes of objects that are deprecated without a scheduled removal (https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/typing.html#deprecation-timeline-of-major-features):

  • Pre-PEP-585 generic aliases (e.g. List)
  • Text
  • Hashable and Sized
  • TypeAlias

I'd like to also soft-deprecate the following:

  • Optional (obviated by PEP-604)
  • NoReturn (prefer Never)
  • typing.ForwardRef (deprecated alias for annotationlib.ForwardRef)
  • types.UnionType (deprecated alias for typing.Union)
  • Creating a Union using subscripting (Union[A, B] instead of A | B) (PEP-604)
  • Creating a TypeVar, ParamSpec, or TypeVarTuple using the constructor directly (PEP-695)
  • Directly inheriting from Generic (PEP-695)

None of those will be removable for many years if ever, but I think it's useful to have a clear statement in the docs that the newer syntax is preferred.

Linked PRs

  • gh-154480

thread.author: AA-Turner
thread.html:
types.UnionType (deprecated alias for typing.Union)

I had assumed that merging the two types would mean the types name becomes preferred (as it's an interpreter type). I agree it would be useful to clarify which (or both) of the names to use. I've very likely missed prior discussion on this, though!

A

thread.author: JelleZijlstra
thread.html: In general I see types as the place for interpreter types that don't have a better home. Other typing-related interpreter types (TypeVar, ParamSpec, TypeVarTuple, TypeAliasType) also live in typing not types.

thread.author: srittau
thread.html: I'm generally in favor, except for blanket deprecating NoReturn. This should stay non-deprecated for return types, similar to what is currently suggested by the Modernizing Superseded Typing Features document (written by me, so not a third opinion). I see no reason to deprecate NoReturn in this case, especially as I find it more readable. I don't have a very strong opinion on this, though.

thread.author: sobolevn
thread.html: I would like to soft deprecate NoReturn, because right now it is easy for me to explain the difference like: "NoReturn is just an old deprecated name for Never". It would be much harder to explain if there are any nuances.

thread.author: AlexWaygood
thread.html:
I have no strong opinion on NoReturn. To me it reads slightly better than Never in return annotations. But I can also see the arguments that it's better to have only one preferred way of doing things. I also understand the argument that it's confusing to beginners who think that functions which have no return statements in them "never return", not realising that None is a more appropriate annotation for these functions.

The other proposed soft deprecations all sound reasonable to me. I'm not wild about using the term "soft deprecation" in documentation, as I don't think it's self-evident to users what it means for something to be "soft-deprecated": you almost always need some explanation of what some specific soft deprecation actually means, practically, if you want users to have clarity about what API is good to use and what isn't. (The existing soft deprecations in typing have slightly different policies laid out in the docs to other soft deprecations in the stdlib!)

But that's just about how we describe the soft deprecations in the docs, not about whether we do them or not.

thread.author: carljm
thread.html: FWIW I agree with soft-deprecating NoReturn and recommending Never in all cases. I don't think NoReturn has any advantage in readability that justifies two aliases for the same thing.

thread.author: srittau
thread.html:
Linking a few related issues and PRs for posterity:

  • PyCQA/flake8-pyi#551
  • python/typeshed#13891
  • python/typing#2322

thread.author: cdce8p
thread.html:
While I think that the soft-deprecations are helpful, I'd like to suggest to exclude the explicit constructor calls for TypeVar, etc and inheriting from Generic at least for now. AFAIK PEP 695 is not a full replacement for these. I've come across at least one case which isn't possible to express with 695 due to the automatic variance inference. If the generic isn't referenced in any method but should be invariant, the TypeVar needs to be constructed using the "old" style. An example from Home Assistant: https://github.com/home-assistant/core/blob/2026.7.4/homeassistant/util/hass_dict.pyi#L12

_T = TypeVar("_T")  # needs to be invariant

class _Key(Generic[_T]):  # noqa: UP046
    """Base class for Hass key types. At runtime delegated to str."""

    def __init__(self, value: str, /) -> None: ...
    ...

issues.title: Metaclasses with type annotated attributes do not add `__annotations__ = {}` to derived classes.
issues.author: matthewwardrop
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

This can cause odd behaviour for subclasses which then propagate their parent's annotations rather than their own.

class MyType(type):
    METACLASS_VAR: int = 1

class A(metaclass=MyType):
    value: str = "HI"

class B(A):
    pass

B.__annotations__  # {"value": str} instead of {}; but if you remove the type annotation in `MyType`, you get {}

This issue only seems to affect versions prior to 3.14

CPython versions tested on:

3.10, 3.13, 3.14

Operating systems tested on:

Linux

thread.author: JelleZijlstra
thread.html: This is discussed in https://peps.python.org/pep-0749/#pre-existing-bugs and fixed in 3.14 (unless you use from __future__ import annotations).

thread.author: matthewwardrop
thread.html: Oh... just noted that as I did a quick test on Python 3.14. I tried search for this in Google, but didn't find it (probably had the wrong keywords). Thanks for linking me on @JelleZijlstra . Feel free to close this issue if this is considered a non-issue going forward.

thread.author: DavidCEllis
thread.html:
It is somewhat of an obscure place for this to be documented but it is also probably a fairly rare thing to come across? I think technically this was supposed to be fixed in 3.10 where it was fixed for classes without the metaclass.

Whether or not this is considered worth fixing for __future__ annotations or as a bugfix on 3.13, perhaps it may be worth putting something in the annotations best practices page about this? Currently it indicates that in 3.10 and newer you can use getattr if you can't use inspect.get_annotations which would lead you to this bug.

thread.author: JelleZijlstra
thread.html:
I wouldn't mind documenting this in the best practices doc.

We could also fix this (in 3.13, and in 3.14+ when from __future__ import annotations is involved), but I suspect any fix will also break some other ways of using annotations and it's better left alone.

thread.author: Taeknology
thread.html:
I took a look at this issue and noticed that the custom-metaclass behavior already appears to be documented in the __annotations__ quirks section of the Annotations Best Practices HOWTO.

That section links to the PEP 749 metaclass examples and recommends using annotationlib.get_annotations() on Python 3.14+, inspect.get_annotations() on Python 3.10+, or reading the class's own __dict__ on earlier versions. The paragraph was added in gh-119180 / PR #122235.

On current main, I can still reproduce the direct-access behavior with from __future__ import annotations:

from __future__ import annotations
from annotationlib import get_annotations

class Meta(type):
    value: int

class Base(metaclass=Meta):
    field: str

class Derived(Base):
    pass

print(Derived.__annotations__)   # {'field': 'str'}
print(get_annotations(Derived))  # {}

Is the existing HOWTO guidance sufficient to resolve this issue, or would it be useful to add a more prominent caveat near the earlier statement that direct __annotations__ access works on classes in Python 3.10 and newer?

issues.title: PEP696 + PEP749: Defer evaluation of defaults when parametrizing
issues.author: randolf-scholz
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

With PEP 696 + PEP 749, the following works just fine:

class Scalar[CompatT, TruthT = BoolScalar]: ...
class BoolScalar(Scalar): ...
class IntScalar(Scalar[int]): ...  # OK ✅️

However, if we switch around the order of definition, the code breaks:

class Scalar[CompatT, TruthT = BoolScalar]: ...
class IntScalar(Scalar[int]): ...  # ❌️ NameError: name 'BoolScalar' is not defined
class BoolScalar(Scalar): ...

I guess since the default gets evaluated here. Not sure whether this is a bug or feature request, but it would be nice if the evaluation of the default could be deferred in is case as well.

CPython versions tested on:

3.14

Operating systems tested on:

Linux

Linked PRs

  • gh-152208

thread.author: sabasiddique1
thread.html:
Hi! I’d like to work on this issue and share the direction I’m considering.

It appears that the default type parameter is evaluated eagerly during specialization (e.g. Scalar[int]), which raises NameError if the default (BoolScalar) isn’t defined yet. Since annotation evaluation already supports deferred forward‑reference handling, it seems reasonable for type parameter defaults to follow the same mechanism.

Proposed approach:

  • In typevar_default_for_subst, evaluate the default using annotationlib.call_evaluate_function(..., Format.FORWARDREF) instead of direct evaluation.
  • This should allow forward references in defaults to resolve correctly while preserving the existing caching behavior of __default__.

Regression test:

class Scalar[CompatT, TruthT = BoolScalar]: ...
class IntScalar(Scalar[int]): ...  # should work
class BoolScalar(Scalar): ...

If this aligns with the intended semantics of PEP 696/749, I’d be happy to prepare a PR.

T = TypeVar("T")
ListDefaultT = TypeVar("ListDefaultT", default=list[T])

class Bar(Generic[T, ListDefaultT]):

issues.title: Make abstract/dunder methods positional-only.
issues.author: randolf-scholz
issues.bodyHTML:
Feature or enhancement

It would be nice if certain abstract methods / dunder methods would be defined with positional-only arguments, so that when one subclasses them an appropriate name can be chosen, or they can be defined positional-only in the subclass.1

Code sample in pyright playground1

from typing import overload
from collections.abc import Sequence

class MySequence[T](Sequence[T]):
    def __len__(self): return 0
    @overload
    def __getitem__(self, idx: int, /) -> T: ...
    @overload
    def __getitem__(self, idx: slice, /) -> Sequence[T]: ...
    def __getitem__(self, idx: int | slice, /) -> T | Sequence[T]:  # ❌ override
        return MySequence[T]()

In some cases, the stubs already fake that the argument is positional-only, such as for Container.__contains__:

  • def __contains__(self, x: object, /) -> bool: ... in typeshed/stdlib/typing.pyi
  • def __contains__(self, x): in cpython/Lib/_collections_abc.py

Personally, I think only changing the stubs would be a pragmatic choice, but I was told by the maintainers that they believe this change should be done in Cpython first.

Backward Compatibility

  1. Changing non-abstract methods can potentially break user code. For example, this is currently legal code at runtime

    from collections.abc import Container.
Container.__subclasshook__(C=list)  # True

  2. Changing the signature of abstract methods can introduce type-checker errors Code sample in pyright playground1

    from collections.abc import Sequence
def get(x: Sequence[float], index: int) -> float:
    return x.__getitem__(index=index)

With this in mind, I believe changing abstrac dunder methods to use positional only arguments should be relatively safe, as calling them directly with keyword is very uncommon, and at worst it will introduce type errors.

Personally, I'd also like so see methods like Container.__subclasshook__ use positional-only arguments, but I also understand if this is not feasible due to bc-conerns.

Has this already been discussed elsewhere?

python/typeshed#14071

Linked PRs

  • gh-136324

Footnotes

  1. Note that mypy special cases certain dunder methods, and yields different results than pyright on these examples ↩ ↩2 ↩3

thread.author: JelleZijlstra
thread.html:
Let's make the parameters positional-only on all the dunder methods and on all the abstract non-dunder methods.

If I was creating these from scratch, in your list above I think I'd only allow keyword arguments for the default= arguments on Mapping/MutableMapping methods, but there's a few others we probably need to maintain as positional-or-keyword for compatibility.

thread.author: randolf-scholz
thread.html:
@JelleZijlstra I opened a PR (#136324) for collections.abc

What about other builtin libraries? For example, abc.ABCMeta.__isinstancecheck__.

thread.author: rhettinger
thread.html:
In general, you can't add any constraints to existing methods without possibly breaking some code that currently works.

And while dunder methods are normally called indirectly from operators, keywords, and builtin functions, they can be called directly.

If I was creating these from scratch ...

There's the rub. We're not creating these from scratch. They have been in the wild for a very long time.

thread.author: JelleZijlstra
thread.html: Making the parameters positional-only doesn't add constraints; it removes them. For example, Sequence.__getitem__ is currently declared as def __getitem__(self, index):, which seems to imply that any conforming implementation must accept index as a keyword argument. Yet list (probably the most prominent Sequence) does not accept keyword arguments in its __getitem__ implementation. If we make the parameter to __getitem__ (an abstract method) positional-only, we fix this small wart.

thread.author: rhettinger
thread.html:
Making the parameters positional-only doesn't add constraints; it removes them. For example, Sequence.getitem is currently declared as def getitem(self, index):, which seems to imply that any conforming implementation must accept index as a keyword argument.

Yes, I get why this makes sense from the point of view of typing and from a specification point of view. For the abstract methods, I don't see any harm.

However, the PR also changes concrete methods which can currently be called with keywords. That part of the PR is a breaking change.

This snippet is based on an example in the docs (though that one uses an operator and not a dunder method call with a keyword argument).

import collections.abc

class ListBasedSet(collections.abc.Set):
    ''' Alternate set implementation favoring space over speed
        and not requiring the set elements to be hashable. '''
    def __init__(self, iterable):
        self.elements = lst = []
        for value in iterable:
            if value not in lst:
                lst.append(value)

    def __iter__(self):
        return iter(self.elements)

    def __contains__(self, value):
        return value in self.elements

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.elements)

s1 = ListBasedSet('abcdef')
s2 = ListBasedSet('defghi')
overlap = s1.__and__(other=s2)   # <-- This currently works
print(vars(overlap))

Stylistically, that call is unattractive, but it does currently work and would be broken.

Every single class that has ever been written that uses these concrete mixin methods is vulnerable to being broken by the PR. The person writing ListBasedSet isn't the one who would be affected. Instead, it would be all of the users of that class who have relied on the public API which has been stable for a very long time.

thread.author: serhiy-storchaka
thread.html:
This is not documented behavior, and not what we want to encoruage. The name "other" is an implementation detail.

On other hand, if leave support of keyword arguments, it will make list not conforming the Sequence protocol.

thread.author: randolf-scholz
thread.html: I completely get that there is BC-issue; hence why I pointed it already out in the OP. But do we even have a single, meaningful example where this happens? I did a lot of regex-based searches on GitHub in my comment #135312 (comment), which already shows that dunder usage with keyword arguments is very rare. Randomly inspecting some of the search results, I did not find a single case where the class in question inherited from collections.abc.

thread.author: randolf-scholz
thread.html: mypy-primer did not find any violations either. python/typeshed#14380 (comment)

thread.author: JoBeGaming
thread.html:
Perhaps we should first make all methods (dunder and normal) have a temporary different name for value..., and an optional argument (kw only) with that name, which is transformed to the original one, but throws a warning.

def m(self, arg): 
    ...

will be

def m(self, _arg=_sentinel, /, *, arg=_sentinel):
    if arg is not _sentinel:
        warnings.warn("Using arg as a positional argument is deprecated and will be removed in ...", DeprecationWarning)
    elif _arg is _sentinel:
        raise TypeError("m() missing 1 required positional argument: 'arg'")
    ... # Update code var names

thread.author: randolf-scholz
thread.html:
OK, so at least in typeshed we now mark these methods as positional-only, even if the collections.abc member technically accepts keyword arguments, to avoid bad scenarios like

from collections.abc import Sequence

def null_count(seq: Sequence[int | None]) -> int:
    return seq.count(value=None)

null_count([1, None, 2])  # TypeError at runtime. (false negative)

I think @JoBeGaming 's proposal is quite reasonable and maybe could be done over the course of 2 versions, but maybe this would require a PEP?

thread.author: serhiy-storchaka
thread.html:
As a first step, we could make abstract dunder methods positional-only. There should not be any objections.

@randolf-scholz, could you please create a new PR for methods which are both abstract and dunder? There are many such methods not only in _collections_abc.py, but also in abc.py, numbers.py, os.py...

thread.author: JoBeGaming
thread.html: @serhiy-storchaka perhaps i could try and make a PR, at least for some of the mentioned modules (e.g. _collections_abc and abc). I'll try and work on this today, maybe I could send in a PR (partially) fixing this for some modules by tomorrow.

thread.author: serhiy-storchaka
thread.html: I could do this myself, but since @randolf-scholz already worked on this, and he is currently active, it is more polity to ask him first. I also prefer to see all non-controversial changes in a single PR.

thread.author: JoBeGaming
thread.html: @serhiy-storchaka I guess that makes sense, so we'll have to see what he thinks about this I guess.

thread.author: randolf-scholz
thread.html: @JoBeGaming Feel free to go right ahead.

issues.title: get_type_hints() fails on TypedDict inheriting from a generic TypedDict under PEP 563
issues.author: JelleZijlstra
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

This fails:

from __future__ import annotations
import typing
class TD1[T](typing.TypedDict):
    a: T

class TD2(TD1):
    pass

print(typing.get_type_hints(TD2))
$ uv run --python=3.13 sample3.py 
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/Users/jelle/py/cpython/sample3.py", line 9, in <module>
    print(typing.get_type_hints(TD2))
          ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^
  File "/opt/homebrew/Cellar/python@3.13/3.13.7/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.13/lib/python3.13/typing.py", line 2461, in get_type_hints
    value = _eval_type(value, base_globals, base_locals, base.__type_params__)
  File "/opt/homebrew/Cellar/python@3.13/3.13.7/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.13/lib/python3.13/typing.py", line 474, in _eval_type
    return t._evaluate(globalns, localns, type_params, recursive_guard=recursive_guard)
           ~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/opt/homebrew/Cellar/python@3.13/3.13.7/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.13/lib/python3.13/typing.py", line 1081, in _evaluate
    eval(self.__forward_code__, globalns, localns),
    ~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
NameError: name 'T' is not defined

Also reproduces on 3.12 and on the latest RC of 3.14.

(Got here while investigating #137226 (comment), but since this variant is a longstanding bug we don't need to fix it for 3.14.0. I want to record and eventually fix it though.)

CPython versions tested on:

CPython main branch, 3.15, 3.14, 3.13, 3.12

Operating systems tested on:

macOS

Linked PRs

  • gh-150762

thread.author: wiomoc
thread.html:
I was able to reproduce this error in a smaller MRE - subclassing TD1 isn't even necessary:

from __future__ import annotations
import typing

class TD1[T](typing.TypedDict):
    a: T


print(typing.get_type_hints(TD1))

thread.author: JelleZijlstra
thread.html: @wiomoc that one works in 3.13 and 3.12, and I'll have a PR up soon fixing it for 3.14+.

thread.author: sobolevn
thread.html:
The root cause of this bug is that __type_params__ of TD1 is not inherited by TD2:

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import get_type_hints, TypedDict

class TD1[T](TypedDict):
    a: T

class TD2(TD1):
    b: int

print(TD1.__required_keys__)
print(TD1.__type_params__)
print(TD1.__annotations__)
print('--')
print(TD2.__required_keys__)
print(TD2.__type_params__)
print(TD2.__annotations__)
print('--')

Will produce:

frozenset({'a'})
(T,)
{'a': ForwardRef('T', module='__main__', owner=<class '__main__.TD1'>)}
--
frozenset({'b', 'a'})
()
{'a': ForwardRef('T', module='__main__', owner=<class '__main__.TD1'>), 'b': ForwardRef('int', module='__main__', owner=<class '__main__.TD2'>)}
--

When we try to resolve the ForwardRef which is ForwardRef('T', module='__main__', owner=<class '__main__.TD1'>), but we don't have TD2.__type_params__ set. And we fail with a NameError as shown.

Possible options:

  1. We can populate "child" typed dicts with type params from the base ones. It seems kinda expected, since we "inherit" all the keys? But, this can produce unknown side effects for libs like msgspec and pydantic, etc. This would also make TD2 implicitly generic, which is kinda strange?
  2. We can create a new attribute called __parent_typed_dict_type_params__, where we can copy parameters from parent typed dicts. This feels like a hack, but it more safe in terms of generic, probably?

Which way do you prefer? Any other ideas?

thread.author: JelleZijlstra
thread.html: The root cause is that we made the questionable decision to copy over base class annotations into child TypedDict classes. Every annotation needs to be evaluated in the context of the class where it is defined, and the way TypedDict currently works at runtime makes that difficult. Unfortunately, it's probably too late to fix that completely. However, the bases are still accessible in __orig_bases__, so maybe we can reconstruct the right class to use in get_type_hints().

In this python-ideas thread it was suggested to create a public API for typing._eval_type in order to be able to create custom versions of get_type_hints. Specifically a version that allows to specify an upper boundary in the MRO when retrieving type hints for a class object.

issues.title: Type annotations in `exec`d code do not resolve as expected
issues.author: vfazio
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

We've counted on the ability to exec code to test that various type annotations lead to the correct success/error scenarios

@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "annotation, value, raises, match",
    [
        pytest.param("Annotated[int, at.Gt(1)]", "0", True, "0 is not greater than 1", id="Gt fail"),

A smaller repro is

I believe this has to do with exec interactions with import and global/local scopes. Looking at bytecode of the generated __annotate__ function, the problem is Literal is loaded with LOAD_GLOBAL, but inside exec the import goes to locals if one is passed in. And as the docs for exec mention

For OP, if you remove the explicit locals dictionary (or make it the same as globals to mimic module level behavior), the tests should pass (of course you may want to make a copy to prevent pollution).

Maybe this is inline with the documentation you mentioned:

Remember that at the module level, globals and locals are the same dictionary.

and maybe this:

Note: When exec gets two separate objects as globals and locals, the code will be executed as if it were embedded in a class definition. This means functions and classes defined in the executed code will not be able to access variables assigned at the top level (as the “top level” variables are treated as class variables in a class definition).

thread.author: inventshah
thread.html:
Reading the execution model docs, I believe there is likely a bug. When globals is not locals in exec, the statements are executed in a class definition, which I think would look something like this:

class _TempExec:
    from typing import Literal
    def test(x: Literal[1]): ...

Then in 3.14+, if we manually do what the compiler might generate:

class _TempExec:
    from typing import Literal
    def test(x): ...
    test.__annotate__ = lambda s: {"x": Literal[1]}

In that way, it's clear why the annotation fails. As the name binding docs say,

The scope of names defined in a class block is limited to the class block; it does not extend to the code blocks of methods.

However, this transformation is not exact, and as the next sentence says

This includes comprehensions and generator expressions, but it does not include annotation scopes, which have access to their enclosing class scopes.

Which suggests that the compiler generated __annotate__ function should get access to the imports.

I'll wait for @JelleZijlstra to chime in with more context before continuing. I suspect there is an issue somewhere in the annotation scope codegen.

For @vfazio, I think if your goal is to mimic what happens at module level, passing the same dict for globals and locals seems like the most correct path forward, regardless of the outcome here.

issues.title: `NamedTuple` can't inherit from another class
issues.author: Conchylicultor
issues.bodyHTML:
Feature or enhancement

Proposal:

Currently this code is failing:

class A:
  pass

class B(A, typing.NamedTuple):
  x: int

Raising:

TypeError: can only inherit from a NamedTuple type and Generic

But this code is not:

class A:
  pass

class _B(typing.NamedTuple):
  x: int

class B(A, _B):
  pass

B(x=1)

I believe those 2 snippets are mostly equivalent (the final B class behave the same), so it's confusing and force boilerplate that class B(A, typing.NamedTuple): fail.

Has this already been discussed elsewhere?

This is a minor feature, which does not need previous discussion elsewhere

Links to previous discussion of this feature:

No response

Linked PRs

  • gh-31781

thread.author: serhiy-storchaka
thread.html: If they support indirect multiple inheritance with subclasses of NamedTuple (see #116241 (comment)), they should not have problems with supporting more direct multiple inheritance. Do they?

thread.author: AlexWaygood
thread.html:
I feel that NamedTuple is special to type checkers -- and in fact it was originally introduced as something you could put in a .pyi file to create a properly typed collections.namedtuple.

I could make the same argument about PEP-585 subscriptions, which were a typing-specific feature introduced specifically for typing purposes, but allow many things at runtime that type checkers will complain about:

>>> dict[int, str, bool, bytes]
dict[int, str, bool, bytes]
>>> list[42]
list[42]

If they support indirect multiple inheritance with subclasses of NamedTuple (see #116241 (comment)), they should not have problems with supporting more direct multiple inheritance. Do they?

Both mypy and pyright accept indirect multiple inheritance but reject direct multiple inheritance:

  • Mypy demo: https://mypy-play.net/?mypy=latest&python=3.12&gist=8b684c2b4a28944cab638c9a3f246233
  • Pyright demo: https://pyright-play.net/?pythonVersion=3.12&strict=true&code=GYJw9gtgBALgngBwJYDsDmUkQWEMoByAhhAKYAmAKgK4IA2pAsAFAsDGdRAzl1AEJEQALigJuXFu048oAMTBgAFMTJVaDADT9BASiEsohqAA8RqGJOYdx2gF7KSFGvVJ6DR05hQXWV6bwBlMQhFAVstARA9UXEgA

So yes, they would both require at least some modifications in order to support this. I don't know whether that's as simple as just removing a few lines of code that are there to make sure that they complain about the thing that fails at runtime, though, or whether it would require them to rewrite some fundamental assumptions about how NamedTuples work.

thread.author: erictraut
thread.html:
In the case of pyright, this change would be easy to support. Just a few lines of code to make the current check conditional on the python version. I'm guessing this is true of other type checkers as well.

Edit: This would require a small change to the typing spec, which currently states:

NamedTuple does not support multiple inheritance. Type checkers should enforce this limitation.

thread.author: gvanrossum
thread.html:
I could make the same argument about PEP-585 subscriptions, which were a typing-specific feature introduced specifically for typing purposes, but allow many things at runtime that type checkers will complain about: [...]

That seems to be a wrong analogy (maybe just a strawman?). What you want to do with multiple inheritance here is useful at runtime; the examples you quoted are useless, and we don't promise that those incorrect usages won't become errors at runtime too (they're the result of an implementation shortcut).

But given other feedback I think this is fine, and I will approve the PR next.

thread.author: AlexWaygood
thread.html:
What you want to do with multiple inheritance here is useful at runtime; the examples you quoted are useless, and we don't promise that those incorrect usages won't become errors at runtime too (they're the result of an implementation shortcut)

That's a fair point. (Though I'm quite confident there are other examples I could come up with using the typing-module internals of "useful" things that are allowed at runtime but disallowed by the typing spec and type checkers :-)

thread.author: gvanrossum
thread.html: I cringe every time I see code that uses undocumented parts of typing.py — they are risking breakage but also constraining what we can do.

thread.author: AlexWaygood
thread.html:
I cringe every time I see code that uses undocumented parts of typing.py — they are risking breakage but also constraining what we can do.

So do I; I fully agree. That wasn't what I meant (I should have been clearer; apologies). I was thinking more about the fact, for example, that ClassVars subscripted by type variables are allowed at runtime despite the spec explicitly prohbiting them; or the fact that Literal[int] has no meaning to type checkers currently (though it could plausibly be used to mean "exactly the int class, and not a subclass"), but is allowed. These and other things are things which are allowed at runtime, which could plausibly be useful, and which users might reasonably expect type checkers to support (but which they don't).

>>> from typing import *
>>> T = TypeVar("T")
>>> class Foo(Generic[T]):
...     x: ClassVar[T]
...     
>>> Foo.__annotations__
{'x': typing.ClassVar[~T]}
>>> Literal[str]
typing.Literal[str]
>>> Literal[int]
typing.Literal[int]

Anyway, this is a pretty minor point. I agree that none of these are an exact analogy to NamedTuple, where the runtime is already strict and we are considering loosening it.

thread.author: JukkaL
thread.html:
I don't see this as something that is important to change, though the implementation in type checkers is probably not very hard. My reasoning is that it adds ambiguity about inherited attributes (would they be settable?) and I'm a little worried that there may be additional edge cases that we haven't thought of yet.

Basically I see this as only slightly useful (it hasn't been requested much even though NamedTuple was added years ago), but it makes things more complicated, with a small risk of some tricky or confusing edge cases. If there are some unclear edge cases, we'd probably need to document them as well, and write conformance tests, etc. Then every new user who learns about NamedTuple may have to deal with all these, at least when reading the documentation. I prefer to keep it simple unless there is a compelling reason not to.

thread.author: CoolCat467
thread.html: I feel that this is important to change. There are only four lines of code stopping multiple base inheritance at runtime, and while I understand removing the current limitation could make type checkers need to do a bit more work, I think that's better than leading people like myself to having to make a copy implementation of NamedTupleMeta without those four lines or jump through other hoops to achieve the desired result. It encourages bad practices if someone is determined. I understand from reading here that the limitation was imposed at the time NamedTuple was introduced to adhere to exactly what the specs say, but that's just because no one thought of a reason to allow that at the time. Allowing multiple base classes means if you want some sort of shared functionality between multiple objects, that's now possible, just like other built-in python objects. It feels a bit arbitrary that NamedTuple doesn't share this feature.

thread.author: JukkaL
thread.html: Even if a typing-related change looks small, the effort quickly adds up. There are at least 6 type checkers which could want to implement support for it, since they probably try to follow standards. A small change might take 4 hours to implement (implementation, writing tests, documentation, code review) per type checker. So it could take 24 hours of effort overall, as a very rough approximation. If there are tricky edge cases, it may be much more that this.

thread.author: gvanrossum
thread.html: Couldn’t we try to phase out NamedTuple in favor of data classes with slots? I still think that NamedTuple should only exist as a quick typed version of collections.namedtuple, not as a feature in itself.

thread.author: sveinugu
thread.html:
Ran into this issue. I have a hard time understanding the hostility towards NamedTuple. When I write a function that returns more than one type of value, I often turn to NamedTuple for a self-documenting data type that easily unpacks. This is especially useful for tests, e.g.:

from typing import NamedTuple

class TestCase(NamedTuple):
    name: str
    age: int

def my_test_cases() -> tuple[TestCase, ...]:
    return (TestCase(name='Jane Doe', age=33), TestCase(name='John Doe', age=32))

def test_something():
    for name, age in my_test_cases():
        print(f'{name=}, {age=}')
        ...

The need for generic NamedTuples will often arise naturally in slightly more complex tests. That this is not yet supported is surprising to me.

Please ignore, I see now that support was added to 3.11 (still using 3.10 for main dev) in #92027

thread.author: serhiy-storchaka
thread.html: Is there any progress in mypy and pyright? I suspect that they reject direct multiple inheritance because it is forbidden in Python.

thread.author: CoolCat467
thread.html: As far as I am aware no, no changes have been made in typecheckers to support this use case as of writing

thread.author: serhiy-storchaka
thread.html:
@johnslavik drew my attention to one case, when the class is inherited from other named tuple and NamedTuple:

>>> from typing import *
>>> class A(NamedTuple):
...     x: int
...     
>>> class B(A, NamedTuple):
...     y: int
...     
>>> B(1)
B(y=1)

Now it will be accepted, but it will work in an unexpected way. The subclass will ignore the fields of the superclass, replacing them with the fields defined in its body. I think the expected behavior is to extend the named tuple with additional fields. If it does not work that way, it should be error. This is a showstopper to me.

For now, I switched the PR to draft. If it turns out that such a case is easy to turn into an error again, or to implement an extension of named tuples (I think that would be comparable in complexity), we will have something to talk about again. If it turns out to be more complicated, I give up.

issues.title: Protocol named "Protocol" or "Generic" has no members.
issues.author: danielknell
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

If a protocol is named Protocol or Generic then it will ignore any defined members.

when you get lazy with naming in your unit tests this makes for quite a head scratcher...

Minimal Reproduction

import typing


class Protocol(typing.Protocol):
    a: int


members = typing.get_protocol_members(Protocol)

assert members == {"a"}, f"Expected members to be {{'a'}}, got {members}"

Output:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../test_protocol.py", line 10, in <module>
    assert members == {"a"}, f"Expected members to be {{'a'}}, got {members}"
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AssertionError: Expected members to be {'a'}, got frozenset()

Expected Output:

Nothing, script should succeed without error.

Investigation

The problem appears to stem from the _get_protocol_attrs function used by _ProtocolMeta which is defined as follows:

cpython/Lib/typing.py

Lines 1879 to 1899 in 171133a

def _get_protocol_attrs(cls):
"""Collect protocol members from a protocol class objects.
This includes names actually defined in the class dictionary, as well
as names that appear in annotations. Special names (above) are skipped.
"""
attrs = set()
for base in cls.__mro__[:-1]: # without object
if base.__name__ in {'Protocol', 'Generic'}:
continue
try:
annotations = base.__annotations__
except Exception:
# Only go through annotationlib to handle deferred annotations if we need to
annotations = _lazy_annotationlib.get_annotations(
base, format=_lazy_annotationlib.Format.FORWARDREF
)
for attr in (*base.__dict__, *annotations):
if not attr.startswith('_abc_') and attr not in EXCLUDED_ATTRIBUTES:
attrs.add(attr)
return attrs

The if statement on line 1887 is too loose in what it matches.

Possibile Fix

The check for base needs to be more specific, either using the instance itself:

if base in {Protocol, Generic}:
    continue

or checking the module too, in order to ensure its the correct class being excluded:

if base.__name__ in {'Protocol', 'Generic'} and base.__module__ == 'typing':
    continue

CPython versions tested on:

3.14

Operating systems tested on:

macOS

Linked PRs

  • gh-145724

thread.author: mvanhorn
thread.html: I've submitted a fix for this in PR #145724. Changed the name-based check to also verify base.__module__ == 'typing' so user-defined Protocol subclasses named "Protocol" or "Generic" are no longer skipped.

issues.title: Dataclasses fields should evaluate their annotations
issues.author: Zaharid
issues.bodyHTML:
Feature or enhancement

Proposal:

In Python 3.14 (a5), I was surprised that while

import dataclasses

@dataclasses.dataclass
class X:
    a: X | None

print(X.__annotations__)

works as expected and prints,

{'a': __main__.X | None}

if one tries to look at the type of the field using the dataclasses.fields interface:

print(dataclasses.fields(X)[0].type)

then this instead results in a ForwardRef

ForwardRef('X | None')

Surely, someone trying to inspect the field would want the value version, consistent with the new default functionality of __annotations__ rather than trying to figure out how to evaluate the ForwardRef precisely.

The current behaviour was introduced in

7b7b90d#diff-44ce2dc1c4922b2f5cf7631d8f86cc569a4c25eb003aaecdc2bc22eb9163d5f5R986

where the dataclasses fields are constructed by reading the ForwardRef mode of annotationlib.

I believe this would be backwards in that the type value had to exists without from __future__ import annotations and would be a string with it.

Has this already been discussed elsewhere?

This is a minor feature, which does not need previous discussion elsewhere

Links to previous discussion of this feature:

No response

thread.author: ericvsmith
thread.html: X does not exist when @dataclass runs and evaluates the annotations, so I don't think anything can be done about this. But I'm open to suggestions.

thread.author: JelleZijlstra
thread.html:
We considered and rejected this in PEP 749: https://peps.python.org/pep-0749/#behavior-of-dataclass-field-types .

Surely, someone trying to inspect the field would want the value version, consistent with the new default functionality of annotations rather than trying to figure out how to evaluate the ForwardRef precisely.

Using .evaluate() is a pretty good bet.

thread.author: Zaharid
thread.html:
I suppose this is a request to add the functionality hinted in PEP 749 to evaluate the types. On the grounds that I can't think of a case where such functionality is not required when purposefully inspecting the types. (As an aside, I am also confused how the argument about executing arbitrary code is different between the .type of Field and the __annotations__ descriptor of the class).

Meanwhile PEP 749 states that documentation will be added to the dataclasses module explaining how to evaluate the type. Could it be added here https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/dataclasses.html#module-contents ?

For example it is unclear to me if .evaluate() without arguments would always resolve in the same way as accessing __annotations__, and I was not able to intermediately answer that from going over the documentation or PEP 749 (e.g. when do I need to pass an owner?). I would argue this is the kind of difficulty that could be handled by the dataclasses module.

thread.author: ericvsmith
thread.html:
I suppose this is a request to add the functionality hinted in PEP 749 to evaluate the types. On the grounds that I can't think of a case where such functionality is not required when purposefully inspecting the types.

Is your suggestion to automatically call .evaluate() when .type is referenced? Presumably this would use ForwardRef.VALUE, which could raise NameError. That doesn't seem like useful behavior. Dataclasses itself definitely needs the ForwardRef values, so I'm not sure where the existing behavior could be improved.

thread.author: Zaharid
thread.html:
Given

>>> import dataclasses
>>> @dataclasses.dataclass
... class C:
...     f: NonExisting
...

This raises a NameError in Python 3.13 at the time the class is defined.

It does not immediately raise an error on Python 3.14, however the following does

>>> C.__annotations__
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-8>", line 1, in <module>
    C.__annotations__
  File "<python-input-4>", line 3, in __annotate__
    f: NonExisting
       ^^^^^^^^^^^
NameError: name 'NonExisting' is not defined

(or equivalently, with annotationlib.get_annotations(C)).

I believe I would always use __annotations__ to get the types of the fields (thereby getting the name error there) and would never use field.type.

With field.type one gets something that is sometimes the annotation and sometimes a ForwardRef which would fail in an unrelated part of the code when trying to use it (e.g. using it in an isinstance check elsewhere). That error is hard to debug due to the action at a distance (indeed it took me a bit to see where the ForwardRefs where coming from in my code). The workaround is somewhat awkward: Import annotationlib, check if the .type is a ForwardRef and evaluate it then (potentially getting a NameError anyway). This also requires a much higher understanding of the brand new typing of forward references discussed over multiple PEPs.

This is all to say that I don't see what the downside with evaluating the ForwardRef and potentially raising the same error that further uses of the result would likely get in a more inconvenient place. By querying the type of the field, the user presumably expects to recover the value that was intended in the annotation or an error if that is not well formed. If the issue is specifically with NameError, I suppose it could be re-raised as some other exception (RuntimeError?) although having consistency with __annotations__ seems preferable.

thread.author: Zaharid
thread.html:
The workaround is somewhat awkward: Import annotationlib, check if the .type is a ForwardRef and evaluate it then (potentially getting a NameError anyway).

Thinking about this, isn't it the case that every existing usage of Field.type in current code that intends to deal with arbitrary dataclasses would need to be modified to handle ForwardRefs?

thread.author: ericvsmith
thread.html:
Thinking about this, isn't it the case that every existing usage of Field.type in current code that intends to deal with arbitrary dataclasses would need to be modified to handle ForwardRefs?

Is there a case where, without any code changes, code that worked in 3.13 would suddenly get a ForwardRef in 3.14? I think this would only happen if you're already changing from from __future__ import annotations to PEP 649 annotations. At which point, yes: if you're changing the code to allow FowardRef's, you'll need to deal with the implications of that.

But maybe I've missed a case where existing code would suddenly get a ForwardRef.

I believe I would always use __annotations__ to get the types of the fields (thereby getting the name error there) and would never use field.type.

You might want to use annotationlib.get_annotations() instead, with a different format value, depending on what you're doing.

thread.author: Zaharid
thread.html:
Is there a case where, without any code changes, code that worked in 3.13 would suddenly get a ForwardRef in 3.14?

I believe the answer is no if the code only handles dataclasses that were created in python 3.13 but yes if it is generic code that works with arbitrary classes that might have been written with 3.14 and may involve ForwardRefs. Code that used to handle all the valid cases would fail for some.

Examples include various flavours of json-like structure to dataclasses (example), code that generates user interfaces from dataclasses (example) or similarly code that generates some kind of schema (example).

I think this would only happen if you're already changing from from future import annotations to PEP 649 annotations. At which point, yes: if you're changing the code to allow FowardRef's, you'll need to deal with the implications of that.

Isn't the advantage of PEP 649 is that one can largely ignore that something like

class X:
    a: X | None

involves a forward reference and can be treated the same as other types at runtime? From this perspective, it is not as much changing code to allow ForwardRef as keeping it as it was and reasonably expecting that it works for new cases enabled by the new annotation system.

You might want to use annotationlib.get_annotations() instead, with a different format value, depending on what you're doing.

It is certainly good that one can do that in general. But it seems to me that the VALUE format is the most appropriate generalization for Field.type. I struggle to think of situations where I would be interested if a particular, valid, reference could or could not be resolved at class creation time or where I would want to carry around an invalid reference.

thread.author: ericvsmith
thread.html:
It is certainly good that one can do that in general. But it seems to me that the VALUE format is the most appropriate generalization for Field.type.

The problem is that there's no obvious place (or time) at which Field.type could be set to something where VALUE wouldn't raise an error.

@dataclass
class X:
    a: X

When dataclass is called, X has not been defined, so Field.type must be a ForwardRef (or raise an error). And that's okay with dataclass: it doesn't need to know the actual type, just that it's not ClassVar or InitVar. When could Field.type be set to X?

In any event, if the actual type is important to you, my suggestion is to use annotationlib.get_annotations(), and not use 'Field.type.

thread.author: Zaharid
thread.html:
I see there are three possibilities:

  1. Have Field.type return the value type and accept the possibility that it can raise an error.
  2. Add a separate functionality (maybe a method to field) to field that gets the type (and, maybe, while we are at it, handles things like InitVar).
  3. Do nothing, but hopefully document the situation.

The arguments for 1. have already been made in previous comments and would be my preference: it is consistent with the 3.14 behaviour of __annotations__ and it is the most likely expectation of existing code, which would otherwise run into not-so-obvious errors. I think PEP 749 was hinting at doing 2:

If use cases come up in the future, we could add additional functionality, such as a new method that re-evaluates the annotation from scratch.

thread.html:
As further evidence that the current situation is not satisfactory, dataclasses.fields automatically gives the inherited fields from the parent dataclasses, but get_annotations does not return the types from the field from the parent class.

print('fields', [f.name for f in dataclasses.fields(Child)])

print('annotations', annotationlib.get_annotations(Child).keys())
fields ['base_field', 'child_field']
annotations dict_keys(['child_field'])

so doing this

In any event, if the actual type is important to you, my suggestion is to use annotationlib.get_annotations(), and not use 'Field.type.

is not trivial either.

issues.title: PEP 649: Avoid creation of function objects for `__annotate__`
issues.author: JelleZijlstra
issues.bodyHTML:
Currently, when a class, function, or module has any annotations, we always generate an __annotate__ function object at import time. A function object takes 168 bytes. But in most cases, all of the relevant fields on an __annotate__ function are predictable (there's no docstring and no defaults or kwdefaults, the name is __annotate__, etc.). So we could save significant memory by constructing only a smaller object and constructing the function on demand when somebody asks for it (by accessing __annotate__).

We need the following to create an __annotate__ function object:

  • The code object itself. That's inescapable.
  • The globals dict. For function annotations, we can reuse the function's globals. For module annotations, we can use the module dict. But for classes, the __annotate__ descriptor can't easily get to the globals dict. To do this, we may need a new bytecode that just loads the current globals.
  • The closure tuple. Module annotations never have this, classes always have it (a reference to the classdict), functions often have it (always for methods, never for global functions, often for nested functions).

I am thinking of a format where __annotate__ can be any of the following:

  • A function, like today
  • A bare code object
  • A tuple containing a code object at position 0, optionally a globals dict at position 1, plus any number of cell objects

__annotate__ getters would have to recognize the second and third cases and translate them into function objects on the fly. As a result, users accessing .__annotate__ would never see the tuple, though those who peek directly into a module or class's __dict__ might.

Other related opportunities for optimization:

  • Tools like functools.wraps would unnecessarily force materialization of the __annotate__ function. Not sure there's an elegant solution for this.
  • The function objects created for various PEP 695/696 objects (e.g., TypeVar bounds) work very similarly to annotate functions, and we could apply the same optimization to them.
  • A code object by itself is also pretty big (232 bytes), and many of its fields are not needed for an annotate function that may never get executed. We could internally create a more streamlined "mini-codeobject" and materialize the real code object only when necessary.

thread.html:
We could internally create a more streamlined "mini-codeobject" and materialize the real code object only when necessary

Maybe a variation of this could be that we create a bytestring with the marshalled code object, and unmarshal it only on demand.

issues.title: UAF in GC `visit_generation()`
issues.author: johng
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Similar to #112564 we call GC_NEXT(gc) which is vulnerable to UAF in

cpython/Python/gc.c

Lines 2165 to 2179 in 036d309

visit_generation(gcvisitobjects_t callback, void *arg, struct gc_generation *gen)
{
PyGC_Head *gc_list, *gc;
gc_list = &gen->head;
for (gc = GC_NEXT(gc_list); gc != gc_list; gc = GC_NEXT(gc)) {
PyObject *op = FROM_GC(gc);
Py_INCREF(op);
int res = callback(op, arg);
Py_DECREF(op);
if (!res) {
return -1;
}
}
return 0;
}

Fix could be similar to proposal in #160662

Reproduction, similar to the above bug we are looping through each entity but rely on the entity being alive when calling NEXT in the entity loop

#include <Python.h>

static PyObject *victim;            /* the only reference to the victim */

static int
drop_current(PyObject *op, void *arg)
{
    if (op == victim) {
        Py_CLEAR(victim);           /* the visitor's +1 is now the last ref */
    }
    return 1;
}

static PyObject *
run(PyObject *module, PyObject *unused)
{
    victim = PySet_New(NULL);       /* GC-tracked, and sets have no freelist */
    if (victim == NULL) {
        return NULL;
    }
    PyUnstable_GC_VisitObjects(drop_current, NULL);     /* segfaults */
    Py_RETURN_NONE;
}

static PyMethodDef methods[] = {
    {"run", run, METH_NOARGS, NULL},
    {NULL, NULL, 0, NULL},
};

static struct PyModuleDef module = {
    PyModuleDef_HEAD_INIT, "visitmin", NULL, -1, methods,
};

PyMODINIT_FUNC
PyInit_visitmin(void)
{
    return PyModule_Create(&module);
}

import visitmin
visitmin.run()
print("no crash")

issues.title: Optimize class creation
issues.author: JelleZijlstra
issues.bodyHTML:
Currently, creating an empty class is about 70x slower than creating an empty function in my profiling. Classes are much more complex and it makes sense that they're slower to create, but 70x feels excessive. (Related: #118761.)

I ran some profiling on my Mac with a sample script that just made empty classes in a loop:

A few things stood out:

  • A lot of time is spent updating slot definitions, i.e. filling in all of the tp_*, nb_*, etc. functions in the C struct for the type. We do this by iterating over all the slots, then looking up the function name (e.g., __add__) in the MRO and placing it in the slot for this class.
  • Significant time is spent in resolve_slotdups which has a comment "XXX Maybe this could be optimized more -- but is it worth it?". Sounds promising. It helps deal with cases where one name maps to multiple slots (e.g. __add__ is both nb_add and sq_concat), and does that by iterating over all the slotdefs and finding other slots with the same name. It does that using some scratch space in the interpreter state, which seems not thread-safe. I feel we could precompute the data instead, so we don't have to figure it out at runtime. For example, the slotdef struct could grow a new member to indicate whether or not the name is unique.

Most types will define very few of these slots, so it makes sense to try to look for an approach that does less work for slots without changes. I think something like this should work:

  • First fill in the slots table with all the slots from the first base class.
  • Then collect all slots for which we may need changes: either slots that have a non-NULL value in the second or later base, or slots the name of which appears in the new class's __dict__. For those slots only, perform an update.

This should make it possible to make class creation something like 2x faster. I haven't started working on implementing this and I may not have time to do it; if you see this and are interested, feel free to pick it up!

thread.author: markshannon
thread.html:
I think the whole concept of slots (the tp_... slots, not __slots__ or PyType_Slot) as an optimization is the root of the problem, they slow down class creation and don't help performance as they complicate the real optimizations that we perform.

We should view the tp_slots as doing two distinct things:

  1. Specifying the behavior of operations when the struct _typeobject is passed to PyType_Ready
  2. A backwards compatible way for C extensions to access operations. Eg. iter(i) as Py_TYPE(i)->tp_iter

For pure Python objects, all slots can be filled in with a function that does the dynamic lookup, which should be very quick.
Once resolved, we can overwrite the slot with a more direct version.

For classes defined by struct _typeobject we can just replace the NULLs with the dynamic lookup function.
For classes defined from PyType_Spec we fill in the defined slots and then replace the NULLs with the dynamic lookup function.

Also, see faster-cpython/ideas#146 (comment)

thread.author: markshannon
thread.html:
The bytecode for creating classes is also a bit of a mess. We seem to be creating code objects, just to create functions just to call them, to do things that could easily be done inline.

There is also a fair bit of machinery about finding the metaclass and the base class tuple. We should compute those in the interpreter as pass them into the class creation machinery.

E.g given a BUILD_CLASS instruction that expects name, meta, bases, dict for class C: ... we get:

    LOAD_CONST "C"
    LOAD_CONST object
    LOAD_CONST ()
    // create method dictionary
    BUILD_CLASS

For class C(D): ... we get:

    LOAD_CONST "C"
    LOAD_NAME "D"
    COPY 1
    LOAD_ATTR __class__ # Get the metaclass
    SWAP 2
    BUILD_TUPLE 1
    // create method dictionary
    COPY 2
    LOAD_ATTR "__prepare__"
    SWAP 2 
    CALL 1   # meta.__prepare__(method_dict)

For multiple inheritance LOAD_ATTR __class__ becomes CALL_INSTRINSIC 2 calculate_metaclass and
if metaclass is explicit, metaclass=expr, then COPY 1; LOAD_ATTR __class__ becomes just expr.

I'm missing the code for setting __orig_bases__ and __class__, but I think those come after BUILD_CLASS.

issues.title: CPython crashes on memory-allocation failure (OOM): 35 findings  (4 dups → 31 distinct)
issues.author: devdanzin
issues.bodyHTML:
Crash report

What happened?

Allocation-failure fuzzing of CPython main turned up 35 distinct ways the interpreter
crashes — segfault, failed assert(...), or Py_FatalError — when a memory allocation (4 have since been confirmed as duplicates via rr → 31 distinct; see the dedup comment)
fails part-way through an operation. Each is a separate underlying bug with a minimal,
stdlib-only reproducer, a backtrace, a root-cause analysis, and a suggested fix, published
as a self-contained gist (linked below).

I'm filing them under one umbrella so they can be picked off individually without flooding
the tracker with 35 issues at once. To take one: open a normal CPython issue (or PR) for
it and drop a comment here with the link — I'll mark it in the table. If any turn out to be
duplicates or non-bugs, say so and I'll annotate them.

These were found with fusil's OOM-injection mode
(fusil originally by @vstinner). The reports and reduced reproducers were drafted with
AI assistance (Claude Code) and then reviewed and re-verified by hand — see Disclosure.

Reproducing

  • Found on main (3.16.0a0) at commit 15d7406. These are allocation-path bugs, so they
    are not tied to that exact revision.
  • Every gist ships a minimal OOM-ID-repro.py (standard library only) that drives the failing path
    while _testcapi.set_nomemory(...) forces allocations to fail. Just run python OOM-ID-repro.py — where the exact failing-allocation index is sensitive to the build's
    allocation count, the repro self-sweeps (a fresh subprocess per index) and stops at the
    first crash, so no manual tuning is needed.
  • _testcapi.set_nomemory requires a test/debug interpreter (--with-pydebug exposes it).
  • Build matrix (in each report): many of these are debug-only assertion / Py_FatalError
    failures — the assert(...) is compiled out under -DNDEBUG, so a release build doesn't
    abort. They are still real bugs: on release the same defect is latent undefined behaviour
    (a use-after-free, a Py_DECREF(NULL), or a silently-lost exception). A subset segfault on
    release builds directly; those are called out below.

Highest-confidence starting points

These crash a release build (not just a debug assertion) and have a clean minimal
reproducer — the lowest-effort to confirm and fix:

  • OOM-0034, OOM-0028 — unchecked PyUnicode_AsUTF8 / PyUnicode_EncodeFSDefault
    returning NULL is dereferenced (≈ one-line NULL checks).
  • OOM-0001, OOM-0002, OOM-0014 — Py_DECREF(NULL) on an unchecked-allocation
    error path.
  • OOM-0031 — _interpreters.capture_exception calls _PyXI_FreeExcInfo(NULL) with no
    NULL guard.
  • OOM-0012, OOM-0020 — instrumentation / thread-state corruption under OOM.

Findings

Status: blank = not yet filed · #N = open issue · #N (PR) = open pull request · #N FIXED = filed and fixed (issue closed-completed or PR merged) · 🔁 = confirmed duplicate, folded into another finding — please don't pursue.

Segfaults (7)

OOM-0002 Segfault: Py_DECREF(NULL) in PyContextVar_Set (context.c:367) #151773 FIXED
OOM-0024 Segfault: dealloc of uninitialized iterator in template_iter (templateobject.c:232) #151815
OOM-0028 Segfault: NULL deref in os__path_normpath_impl (posixmodule.c:6149) #152058 FIXED
OOM-0031 Segfault: NULL info deref in _excinfo_clear_type (crossinterp.c:1319) #151842 FIXED

OOM-0029 [SUPERSEDED — duplicate of OOM-0036 / #151818] Abort: negative refcount on a MemoryError (tuple_dealloc, tupleobject.c:277) 🔁 dup of OOM-0036 → #151818
OOM-0030 Abort: Py_DECREF of NULL-data unicode in unicode_subtype_new (unicodeobject.c:13986)
OOM-0032 Abort: pending-exception assert from warn_explicit normalization (_warnings.c:799/806)
OOM-0035 Abort / malformed str: invalid maxchar in _PyUnicode_FromUCS4 (unicodeobject.c:2228)

Fatal Python error (5)

Report Title Status
OOM-0007 Fatal: context_tp_dealloc clears the pending exception (context.c:535) #152083
OOM-0020 Fatal: _PyMem_DebugRawFree: bad ID in free_threadstate (pystate.c:1527)
OOM-0021 Fatal: NULL returned without an exception set in _Py_CheckFunctionResult (call.c:43)
OOM-0022 Fatal: stale MemoryError trips _Py_CheckSlotResult in reload_singlephase_extension (import.c:2011)
OOM-0023 Fatal: dealloc clears the in-flight exception in subtype_dealloc (typeobject.c:2719)

Related groups (one fix may cover several)

  • Dealloc clears the in-flight exception (the gh-89373 _Py_Dealloc invariant): OOM-0007
    (context_tp_dealloc) and OOM-0023 (the generic subtype_dealloc, covering a family of
    pure-Python types) free an object while a MemoryError is pending and don't save/restore it.
  • A pending exception survives into code that asserts there is none (specializer / eval /
    call layers): OOM-0008, 0010, 0015, 0025, 0032 (OOM-0011 was a second detector face of
    OOM-0008 — same frame.f_back swallow — and is folded). Several share the theme that the
    adaptive specializer / call machinery is entered with a MemoryError already pending.
  • Py_DECREF/Py_CLEAR of a NULL or partially-initialized object on the OOM error path:
    OOM-0001, 0002, 0006, 0014, 0024, 0030, 0031 (an allocation fails after a slot is taken
    but before the object is valid, and the error path frees it anyway).
  • Over-decref → negative refcount under OOM (a real memory-safety bug; the assert is the
    debug-build detector): OOM-0019. (rr later showed OOM-0005, OOM-0029 and OOM-0033 are
    all the same _CALL_LIST_APPEND list.append()-under-MemoryError double-free —
    OOM-0036, filed #151818 — and are
    folded; OOM-0019 is a distinct pegen double-free.)
  • Free-threading-specific: OOM-0003 (_co_unique_id), OOM-0017 (cyclic GC),
    OOM-0018 (managed dict), OOM-0020 (thread-state reservation).

Disclosure & caveats

  • The reports and reduced reproducers were drafted with AI assistance (Claude Code); each
    gist carries an explicit disclaimer. The reproducers were re-run on the build matrix and the
    root causes audited against the CPython source before publishing.
  • A few root causes are explicitly marked partial — the trigger is minimal and verified,
    but the exact offending line wasn't pinned (noted in those reports): OOM-0010, 0027, 0035.
  • OOM-0001 is already filed as
    #151673; the other 34 had no matching
    python/cpython issue when checked and appear novel.

Found with fusil (OOM-injection mode; fusil originally
by Victor Stinner). Drafted with Claude Code; reproducers machine-generated and human-verified.

thread.author: zainnadeem786
thread.html:
Hi @devdanzin,

I investigated OOM-0020 and was able to reproduce it on current main in both free-threaded debug and release builds.

From tracing the allocation and cleanup paths, the crash appears to occur because the preallocated initial thread state can enter the cleanup path before its interpreter back-pointer has been initialized. As a result, free_threadstate() fails to recognize it as the embedded initial thread state and incorrectly calls PyMem_RawFree() on memory that is embedded within PyInterpreterState.

The fix appears to be localized, and I'm preparing a focused PR based on this investigation. I'll link it here once it's ready.

I'm also continuing to investigate OOM-0030 separately.

thread.author: zainnadeem786
thread.html:
Hi @devdanzin,

I investigated two additional findings from this umbrella issue and have opened focused PRs for both.

OOM-0020

Opened: GH-#152165

This issue was caused by an early cleanup path in the free-threaded interpreter. During thread state allocation, tstate->base.interp was not initialized before later allocations could fail. If cleanup ran in that window, free_threadstate() could not recognize the embedded initial thread state and attempted to free embedded memory, leading to _PyMem_DebugRawFree: bad ID (debug) or an access violation (release).

The fix initializes the interpreter back-pointer immediately after obtaining the thread state, allowing the existing cleanup logic to correctly identify the embedded initial thread state while leaving the normal successful initialization path unchanged.

OOM-0030

Opened: GH-#152164

This issue occurs during cleanup of a partially constructed non-compact Unicode subtype after an allocation failure. In debug builds, unicode_is_singleton() could attempt to read the first character from an object whose internal data pointer was still NULL, triggering the data != NULL assertion.

The fix adds a narrow guard for this temporary construction state before calling PyUnicode_READ_CHAR(). Fully initialized Unicode objects continue to follow the existing invariants, while failed construction now cleans up without triggering the debug assertion.

Both fixes were reproduced locally, validated after the changes, and submitted as separate focused PRs to keep review straightforward.

Thanks again for collecting and documenting these OOM findings—they've been very helpful to investigate.

thread.author: tonghuaroot
thread.html:
Taking OOM-0033. Reproduced on a current --with-pydebug main build — deterministic _Py_NegativeRefcount abort (the negative refcount surfaces in typeobject.c is_subtype_with_mro during exception/traceback construction).

Ablation root-causes the over-decref producer to the zipimport path hook (zipimporter.__init__) on its OOM error path: running each sys.path_hooks entry in isolation, zipimporter aborts while FileFinder is clean, and removing/replacing the zip hook eliminates the crash. It only triggers on the _path_stat-fails archive-search retry (an already-existing archive is clean), and only with heap-mortal single-character path components (latin-1 1-char strings are immortal, so the extra decref is a no-op there — which is why the reproducer needs a non-ASCII path element).

Pinning the exact unmatched Py_DECREF statement needs an -O0 watchpoint (the optimized build inlines the decref call sites); I'm working on that and will follow up with a PR.

Reproduced and analysis prepared with AI assistance (Claude Code), reviewed and re-verified by hand. Finding credit is @devdanzin's (found with fusil OOM-injection fuzzing).

Update (pinned with an -O0 watchpoint): the double-close is in _CALL_LIST_APPEND (Python/bytecodes.c) — its list-resize MemoryError path uses ERROR_NO_POP() after arg was already consumed by _PyList_AppendTakeRef, so the exception unwind PyStackRef_XCLOSEs it a second time (regression from GH-142711; the sibling ops LIST_APPEND / SET_ADD use ERROR_IF). I see this already has its own issue (gh-151818) and fixes in flight (#151826, #152114) — same root cause, so I'm standing down here, no PR needed. Thanks @devdanzin.

rr dedup pass — 4 of the 35 are confirmed duplicates (please don't pursue these)

Following up on my note above: I went through the over-decref / negative-refcount and stale-MemoryError clusters with rr reverse-execution to pin each crash's producer (for these, the assert/segv site is a detector, not the bug). Four turned out to be duplicates, now folded:

Finding Actually Evidence
OOM-0005 (_PyFrame_ClearLocals over-decref, frame.c:101) OOM-0036 → #151818 rr ledger: the over-decref'd object is freed by _PyList_AppendTakeRefListResize ← _CALL_LIST_APPEND — the list.append()-under-MemoryError double-free. frame.c:101 is just where the reused object is next touched.
OOM-0029 (tuple_dealloc negref, tupleobject.c:277) OOM-0036 → #151818 same double-freed appended item, surfaced at tuple teardown.
OOM-0033 (PyType_IsSubtype over-decref of a sys.path entry) OOM-0036 → #151818 same; sys.path[:]=…; __import__ internally list.appends a second-referenced object under OOM.
OOM-0011 (specialize assert(!PyErr_Occurred()), specialize.c:364) OOM-0008 rr: the stale MemoryError is set by PyFrame_GetBack swallowing it while materializing frame.f_back — exactly OOM-0008, caught at a different !PyErr_Occurred() checkpoint.

So OOM-0036 (#151818) is the canonical bug behind OOM-0005/0029/0033, and OOM-0008 already covers OOM-0011. I've struck those rows in the table above, removed OOM-0033 from the starting-points list, and retitled the corresponding gists [SUPERSEDED — duplicate of …]. Thanks to everyone who looked at these — sorry for the wasted cycles.

(Method, for anyone curious: record the repro under rr, watch the victim's refcount / tstate->current_exception, and reverse-continue to the producing decref / exception-set. For the over-decref family it reliably lands on OOM-0036.)

@devdanzin I was looking into OOM-0023, and while implementing the proposed fix, I ran into another issue that appears to be distinct from OOM-0023. It looks like a separate free-threaded bug that becomes visible once this fix is applied, rather than being introduced by it.

The changes I made are:

 > diff --git a/Objects/typeobject.c b/Objects/typeobject.c
index d52cdedff10..3cf7c7afbd8 100644
--- a/Objects/typeobject.c
+++ b/Objects/typeobject.c
@@ -2833,6 +2833,13 @@ subtype_dealloc(PyObject *self)
        }
    }

+    /* Save the current exception: clear_slots() and the dict/base-dealloc
+         below decref arbitrary attribute values, which may clear
+           tstate->current_exception (gh-89373).  Mirroring slot_tp_finalize(). */
+    PyThreadState *tstate = _PyThreadState_GET();
+     PyObject *exc = _PyErr_GetRaisedException(tstate);   /* preserve in-flight exception */


    /*  Clear slots up to the nearest base with a different tp_dealloc */
    base = type;
    while ((basedealloc = base->tp_dealloc) == subtype_dealloc) {
@@ -2882,6 +2889,9 @@ subtype_dealloc(PyObject *self)
    if (type_needs_decref) {
        _Py_DECREF_TYPE(type);
    }

+    /* Restore the saved exception (see save above). */
+   _PyErr_SetRaisedException(tstate, exc);
}

static PyTypeObject *solid_base(PyTypeObject *type);

After making this change, I consistently hit the following assertion:


python: Objects/dictobject.c:207: set_keys: Assertion `_Py_IsOwnedByCurrentThread((PyObject *)mp) || IS_DICT_SHARED(mp)' failed.
Fatal Python error: Aborted


  Binary file "../cpython/python", at _Py_HandlePending+0x190 [0x56b5e10dde7a]
  Binary file "../cpython/python", at PyObject_Vectorcall+0x27 [0x56b5e0d4fde1]
  Binary file "../cpython/python", at _Py_VectorCall_StackRefSteal+0x11d [0x56b5e1006879]
  <truncated rest of calls>

Extension modules: _testcapi (total: 1)
[1]    465360 IOT instruction (core dumped)  ../cpython/python OOM-0023-repro.py

It seems to me that it aborts on (need to check it very carefully though, since I used Claude Code to debug this):

Objects/dictobject.c:207: set_keys:
  Assertion `_Py_IsOwnedByCurrentThread((PyObject *)mp) || IS_DICT_SHARED(mp)' failed.

Since this assertion originates from a different function/subsystem than OOM-0023, would you prefer that I fold this into the same PR, or track it as a separate issue? I'm happy to do either.

For reference, this was reproduced on the latest main branch.

thread.author: devdanzin
thread.html:
@Abhi210 Thanks for flagging this and sorry for the delay. It is a genuinely distinct, pre-existing bug that your OOM-0023 fix unmasks. Nice catch! I reproduced and root-caused it, here's what I found with help from Claude.

Answer to your question: file it as a separate issue, don't fold it into the OOM-0023 PR. Your exception save/restore is correct and can't touch dict ownership — it's a completely different subsystem, and keeping the PRs separate keeps both reviewable and bisectable.

Root cause. The assertion (set_keys → ASSERT_OWNED_OR_SHARED, Objects/dictobject.c:205) fires from the MemoryError-recovery branch of PyObject_ClearManagedDict:

err = detach_dict_from_object(dict, obj);   // materializes the keys — this ALLOCATES
if (err) {                                   // reached ONLY on MemoryError
    assert(PyErr_Occurred() == PyExc_MemoryError);
    PyErr_FormatUnraisable("Exception ignored while clearing an object managed dict");
    set_keys(dict, Py_EMPTY_KEYS);           // Objects/dictobject.c:7896  ← the assert
    dictkeys_decref(oldkeys, IS_DICT_SHARED(dict));
    ...

When an object with a materialized managed dict (still pointing at its inline values) is reclaimed by the cyclic GC — i.e. it's part of a reference cycle — delete_garbage → subtype_clear → PyObject_ClearManagedDict tries to materialize the keys via detach_dict_from_object(), which allocates and fails under OOM. The recovery path then calls set_keys(dict, Py_EMPTY_KEYS). But mid-collection the free-threaded GC has repurposed the dict's ob_tid to hold gc_refs (it restores ob_tid only for reachable objects — gc_free_threading.c), and a single-threaded program never marks a dict _PyGC_BITS_SHARED (ensure_shared_on_read/ensure_shared_on_resize only fire on cross-thread access). So _Py_IsOwnedByCurrentThread(dict) || IS_DICT_SHARED(dict) is false → abort.

That set_keys line is reachable only when the allocation fails, which is exactly why it needs OOM — a plain garbage-cycle gc.collect() doesn't hit it (the detach succeeds, err == 0).

Minimal reproducer — stdlib + _testcapi only, no argparse/http.server, and (importantly) no OOM-0023 involvement. Reproduces 8/8 on a stock free-threaded debug build (--disable-gil, Py_DEBUG):

import gc
from _testcapi import set_nomemory, remove_mem_hooks

class C:
    pass

def make_cyclic():
    o = C()
    o.__dict__                       # materialize the managed dict (keeps inline values)
    o.a = 1; o.b = 2; o.c = 3
    o.self = o                       # self-cycle → only the cyclic GC can reclaim it

for start in range(300):
    make_cyclic()
    set_nomemory(start, start + 25)  # fail an allocation window during gc.collect()
    try:
        gc.collect()                 # delete_garbage → ClearManagedDict → detach fails → set_keys
    finally:
        remove_mem_hooks()

Scope / severity. Free-threaded Py_DEBUG only: on a release build the assert is compiled out and it's benign (the collection is stop-the-world and this is single-threaded, so the set_keys store is safe); on a GIL build the assertion doesn't exist. So it's a false/over-strict assertion on a legitimate OOM-recovery-during-GC path rather than a memory-safety bug — worth fixing, but lower severity than OOM-0023 itself.

Likely fix direction (for the free-threading / dict folks): the OOM-recovery set_keys / dictkeys_decref in PyObject_ClearManagedDict need to account for running during cyclic-GC clearing (where the dict's ob_tid is gc_refs scratch, not a thread id), or the assertion should exempt the stop-the-world-GC context.

Since you found it, it's yours to file. Feel free to use the repro and analysis above, and tag me on the issue if you'd like a review.

Investigation and draft by Claude Code (Opus 4.8).

thread.html:
Another uninit-dealloc on the OOM path, same pattern as OOM-0024:

odictiter_new, Objects/odictobject.c:1945

PyObject_GC_New succeeds but di->di_odict, di->di_current, and di->kind are uninitialized. The next allocation (di->di_result) fails → Py_DECREF(di) → odictiter_dealloc reads garbage fields → crash.

Reproducer (needs freelist drain — tuple freelist masks index 0):

import _testcapi, collections

live = [tuple([None, None]) for _ in range(4000)]  # drain freelist
od = collections.OrderedDict(a=1)

for start in range(20):
    _testcapi.set_nomemory(start, start + 1)
    try:
        iter(od.items())
    except MemoryError:
        pass
    finally:
        _testcapi.remove_mem_hooks()

Confirmed on main 1a852139408, Linux, Python 3.16.0a0.

issues.title: sqlite3: deadlock when threads share a connection that has Python callbacks
issues.author: gpshead
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

A sqlite3 connection shared between threads (check_same_thread=False, SQLite in serialized mode, sqlite3.threadsafety == 3) deadlocks the whole process if it has a Python callback registered (function, aggregate, collation, authorizer, progress handler or trace callback). SQLite invokes the callback from sqlite3_step() with the connection mutex held, and the callback then waits for the GIL in PyGILState_Ensure(); meanwhile another thread holds the GIL and blocks on the same connection mutex in an SQLite call the module makes without releasing the GIL, for example sqlite3_column_int64() in _pysqlite_fetch_one_row(), sqlite3_bind_*(), sqlite3_errmsg() or sqlite3_set_authorizer().

import sqlite3, threading

cx = sqlite3.connect(":memory:", check_same_thread=False)
cx.create_function("f", 1, lambda x: x)
cx.execute("create table t(x)")
cx.executemany("insert into t values(?)", [(i,) for i in range(1000)])

def work(n):
    # different SQL in each thread, so no cached statement is shared
    for i in range(100):
        cx.execute(f"select f(x) from t limit {n + i}").fetchall()

threads = [threading.Thread(target=work, args=(n,)) for n in (10000, 20000)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()  # never returns

The script should finish; instead it hangs within a second and cannot be interrupted with Ctrl-C. gh-86864 was the same lock inversion in Connection.close(), fixed by releasing the GIL around sqlite3_close_v2().
