issues.title: Crash on concurrent first read of Element.text or Element.tail on the free-threaded build
issues.author: gpshead
issues.bodyHTML:
Crash report

What happened?

On the free-threaded build, two threads doing the first read of Element.text or Element.tail of an element built by the C parser can crash. Text that arrives from expat in several chunks (anything containing an entity such as &, or the whitespace tail in an indented document) is kept as a list and joined on first access; element_get_text() and element_get_tail() in Modules/_elementtree.c do that join without a lock, so both threads join the list and both release the element's only reference to it.

import threading
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

doc = "<root>" + "<item>a & b</item>" * 500 + "</root>"
for _ in range(200):
    root = ET.fromstring(doc)
    barrier = threading.Barrier(8)
    def read():
        barrier.wait()
        for item in root:
            item.text
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=read) for _ in range(8)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()

A debug build aborts with Modules/_elementtree.c:587: _Py_NegativeRefcount: Assertion failed: object has negative ref count or segfaults; concurrent ET.tostring(root) calls hit it the same way. The default build is not affected.

This is a small part of gh-146022. gh-149816 item (87) is about the getter racing the text setter, which is a different race in the same functions.

issues.title: `xml.parsers.expat` crashes when `DefaultHandler` raises on a long non-UTF-8 token
issues.author: gpshead
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

When a DefaultHandler or DefaultHandlerExpand callback raises, pyexpat clears all of the parser's C handlers. For a document that needs encoding conversion (any encoding but UTF-8 or ASCII, including UTF-16), Expat delivers a token longer than 1024 bytes to the default handler in several pieces and re-reads the handler between them, so the next piece is a call through a NULL function pointer.

from xml.parsers.expat import ParserCreate

def default(data):
    if data.startswith("<!--"):
        raise ValueError("comments are not allowed")

p = ParserCreate()
p.DefaultHandler = default
p.Parse(b'<?xml version="1.0" encoding="iso-8859-1"?><a><!--' + b"x" * 2000 + b"--></a>", True)

With encoding="utf-8" this raises ValueError; with iso-8859-1 the interpreter dies with SIGSEGV. Setting p.DefaultHandler = None from inside the callback, or a CharacterDataHandler that raises when buffer_text is flushed before a default-handler call, crashes the same way. The character data handler had the same problem and was fixed in gh-42389 by installing a no-op handler instead of NULL; the default handler was left out.

The default C xml.etree.ElementTree, xml.sax and xml.dom.minidom are not affected; the pure-Python ElementTree parser (used only without _elementtree) is.

issues.title: `TextIOWrapper.tell()` returns a wrong position after `next()` and `flush()`
issues.author: gpshead
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

TextIOWrapper.__next__() stops updating the decoder snapshot that tell() relies on and disables tell() (OSError: telling position disabled by next() call), but flush() re-enables tell() without restoring the snapshot. tell() then computes the position from a stale snapshot and silently returns a wrong cookie.

import io
f = io.TextIOWrapper(io.BytesIO(b"a\n" + b"b" * 10000 + b"\nc\n"),
                     encoding="ascii")
f.readline()
next(f)
f.flush()
pos = f.tell()
print(pos)
f.seek(pos)
print(repr(f.read(3)))

This prints 3624 and 'bbb' instead of 10003 and 'c\n' (or the OSError that tell() raises without the flush() call); _pyio.TextIOWrapper returns 9768, also wrong. If the snapshot was replaced by an earlier seek(), tell() instead raises OSError: can't reconstruct logical file position (before gh-161053 it read past the snapshot).

gh-81217 asks for next() not to disable tell() at all.

thread.author: gpshead
thread.html:
The repro still prints 3624 and 'bbb' on current main (9768 with _pyio). Calling next() as the first read, then flush() and tell(), is another way to trigger the bug.

The PR makes flush() re-enable tell() only when no internal snapshot state or decoded text is pending, so in these cases tell() raises the same OSError as without the flush() call; seek() and reaching the end of iteration still re-enable it.

issues.title: `TextIOWrapper.tell()` reads past the decoder snapshot after `seek()`
issues.author: gpshead
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

TextIOWrapper.tell() guesses where to start re-decoding its decoder snapshot as the bytes-per-character ratio times the number of characters to skip, and bounds that guess only with an assert. After seek() to a cookie that skips characters, the snapshot can be much shorter than the ratio of the previously decoded chunk implies, so the next tell() passes the decoder bytes from past the end of the snapshot.

import io
data = b"+AGEAYg-+" + b"A" * 8183
f = io.TextIOWrapper(io.BytesIO(data), encoding="utf-7")
f.read(1)
f.seek(f.tell())
f.tell()

On a debug build the last line fails with Assertion 'skip_bytes <= PyBytes_GET_SIZE(next_input)' failed. On a release build it reads about 4 KiB past the 8-byte snapshot and raises UnicodeDecodeError for a byte that is not in the input, where it should return the position passed to seek(). Codecs that decode one byte sequence to several characters (utf-7, big5hkscs) and errors="ignore" on mostly undecodable data can over-read by thousands of bytes this way.

Common codecs reach the same assertion in ordinary use, for example a CRLF file opened with newline="" as the csv module requires:

f = io.TextIOWrapper(io.BytesIO(b"a\r\n" * 10), encoding="ascii", newline="")
f.read(29)  # stops between "\r" and "\n"
f.seek(f.tell())
f.readline()
f.tell()    # assertion failure on a debug build

On release builds that case over-reads by one byte, into the bytes object's terminating NUL, so it goes unnoticed there.

gh-141314 fixed another way to fail the same assertion; gh-153662 is a separate open crash in the same cookie handling.

issues.title: `tarfile` writes a member's old pax records after its name or other attributes are changed
issues.author: gpshead
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

A TarInfo read from an archive keeps the member's pax records in pax_headers, and TarInfo.create_pax_header() gives an existing record priority over the attribute. If a program changes name (or linkname, uname, gname, uid, gid, mtime, size) on such a member, by assignment or with TarInfo.replace(), and adds it to a new archive in the default pax format, the new value goes into the ustar header but the old record is written in front of it and wins for every pax reader. Any member with a long or non-ASCII name has a path record, so no unusual input is needed.

import io, tarfile

src = io.BytesIO()
with tarfile.open(fileobj=src, mode="w") as tar:
    tar.addfile(tarfile.TarInfo("d\xe9j\xe0-vu.txt"))       # non-ASCII: gets a pax "path" record
    tar.addfile(tarfile.TarInfo("plain.txt"))

src.seek(0)
dst = io.BytesIO()
with tarfile.open(fileobj=src) as tar, tarfile.open(fileobj=dst, mode="w") as out:
    for member in tar:
        member.name = "prefix/" + member.name.encode("ascii", "replace").decode()
        out.addfile(member)

dst.seek(0)
with tarfile.open(fileobj=dst) as tar:
    print(tar.getnames())

This prints ['déjà-vu.txt', 'prefix/plain.txt']; expected ['prefix/d?j?-vu.txt', 'prefix/plain.txt']. member.replace(name=...) behaves the same, and a GNU.sparse.name record has the same effect as path. USTAR_FORMAT and GNU_FORMAT output is not affected.

issues.title: asyncio: compute the event loop's clock resolution once, in `asyncio.constants`
issues.author: asvetlov
issues.bodyHTML:
Each BaseEventLoop.__init__ calls time.get_clock_info('monotonic').resolution and stores the result in the private attribute self._clock_resolution, which only _run_once reads. The clock resolution belongs to the platform and process, not to a loop, and it never changes at runtime.

I propose computing it once as asyncio.constants.CLOCK_RESOLUTION, next to the other asyncio tuning values. _clock_resolution is private and undocumented, so the public API doesn't change.

issues.title: Speed up tarfile.calc_chksums()
issues.author: turtle-byte-17
issues.bodyHTML:
Feature or enhancement

Proposal:

tarfile.calc_chksums() runs once per header block, every time a header is read
(TarInfo.frombuf) or written (TarInfo._create_header). It currently builds
two 504-element tuples with struct.unpack_from (one unsigned, one signed) and
sums each one in Python:

unsigned_chksum = 256 + sum(struct.unpack_from("148B8x356B", buf))
signed_chksum = 256 + sum(struct.unpack_from("148b8x356b", buf))
return unsigned_chksum, signed_chksum

Both totals can be had from one C-level sum(buf): a byte b >= 128 adds b
to the unsigned sum and b - 256 to the signed one, so
signed == unsigned - 256 * (number of bytes >= 128). Almost every real header
is pure ASCII, in which case the two sums are equal and bytes.isascii()
detects that cheaply. Otherwise the high bytes are counted with
bytes.translate(None, ...).

The patch (+13 lines, no deletions) keeps the original code verbatim as the
fallback, and only takes the fast path when type(buf) is bytes and len(buf) == BLOCKSIZE, which is the only thing tarfile itself ever passes.
Any other input (memoryview, array, bytearray, other lengths) behaves exactly as
before, including raising struct.error below 512 bytes.

+_HIGH_BYTES = bytes(range(128, 256))
+
 def calc_chksums(buf):
     ...
+    if type(buf) is bytes and len(buf) == BLOCKSIZE:
+        # Fast path for the only input tarfile itself passes. The chksum
+        # field (buf[148:156]) counts as eight spaces, i.e. 256. A byte with
+        # the high bit set adds b to the unsigned sum and b - 256 to the
+        # signed one, so signed == unsigned - 256 * (number of such bytes).
+        unsigned_chksum = 256 + sum(buf) - sum(buf[148:156])
+        if buf.isascii():
+            return unsigned_chksum, unsigned_chksum
+        head = buf[:148] + buf[156:]
+        high = BLOCKSIZE - 8 - len(head.translate(None, _HIGH_BYTES))
+        return unsigned_chksum, unsigned_chksum - 256 * high
     unsigned_chksum = 256 + sum(struct.unpack_from("148B8x356B", buf))
     signed_chksum = 256 + sum(struct.unpack_from("148b8x356b", buf))
     return unsigned_chksum, signed_chksum

Benchmarks

The absolute gain per archive is small (milliseconds), so I'm not claiming
this fixes a bottleneck. It is a modest, free speedup on a function called
about once or twice per archive member (PAX archives carry an extra x
header per member).

calc_chksums alone, ASCII header, ns per call (stock / patched):

Python stock patched
3.11.10 4877 1027
3.14.10 3008 826
3.15.2 3474 827

Headers containing high bytes are about 2.6-3.3x faster.

End to end (tarfile.open + iterate + read every member, CPU time via
time.process_time, 25 ABBA-interleaved rounds, geometric mean of the
per-workload median speedups, stock / patched):

Python read list (getmembers) stream (r|) write
3.9 1.35x 1.51x 1.07x 1.40x
3.11 1.52x 1.79x 1.08x 1.63x
3.12 1.34x 1.52x 1.05x 1.38x
3.13 1.36x 1.54x 1.05x 1.38x
3.14 1.32x 1.50x 1.05x 1.33x
3.15 1.40x 1.61x 1.39x 1.38x
3.16.0a1+dev (built from main, 4a9b981) 1.34x 1.55x 1.34x 1.35x

Each cell aggregates 20 synthetic workload/operation rows: many small members,
few large members, ustar/gnu/pax formats, high-bit names, and plain/gz/bz2/xz
variants. No row's 95% bootstrap confidence interval reaches 1.0; the smallest
gain is about 1.02x (bz2 stream, where decompression dominates) and the
largest about 2.0x.

For scale, on a synthetic archive of 20,000 x 100-byte members, reading every
member went from 199 ms to 134 ms on the 3.16 build (1.48x), and getmembers()
from 158 ms to 94 ms. Archives with only a few hundred members save a few
milliseconds. Peak memory (tracemalloc) is unchanged to within 3 KB on 3.11,
3.15 and 3.16.

Verification

  • Exhaustive equivalence against the original function on 1,118,530 headers
    per interpreter (every byte value at every position of 7 base blocks, plus
    random, clustered-high-byte and k-high-byte buffers): 0 mismatches on 3.9,
    3.11, 3.12, 3.13, 3.14 and 3.15.
  • The full test_tarfile suite passes identically with and without the patch
    (3.11.10: 591 tests, 3.12.15: 633, 3.13.16: 666, 3.14.10: 768, and 795 on a
    3.16.0a1+dev build of main, with _lzma and _zstd available). test_shutil
    also passes identically on that build.
  • Differential run of stock vs patched tarfile over about 4.1 million cases
    (about 120 base archives including the test data, ustar/gnu/pax, Sun-style
    signed-checksum headers; every single-bit flip in the first headers,
    truncation at every length, header mutations, r:*, r:, r|,
    gz/bz2/xz, extractall): 0 differences. Archives written by the patched
    tarfile are byte-identical in every format. The corpus exercises the
    unsigned-match, signed-only-match and bad-checksum branches
    (about 2.09M, 3,238 and 200k headers in one run).
  • To check the harness could actually fail, I injected six deliberate bugs
    into the patch (signed == unsigned, checksum field not excluded, off-by-one
    high-byte count, wrong high-byte threshold, wrong head slice, inverted
    isascii); all six were caught.

Hello,

Benchmark scripts and results

All numbers below are for CPython 3.16.0a1+dev built from main at 4a9b98115f (-O3 -DNDEBUG, no PGO/LTO; full configuration below), on an Apple M5 Pro (arm64) macOS laptop that was not isolated (pyperf system tune is Linux-only). "stock" is main's unmodified Lib/tarfile.py; "patched" is the same file with the calc_chksums change from this issue. The archives are all synthetic. Earlier results for 3.9, 3.11-3.15 are in the issue description.

Build configuration

Out-of-tree build of main at 4a9b98115fec4d93c32c554aa541d6c3fc4c3b27, macOS 26.7.1 (arm64, Apple M5 Pro), Apple clang 21.0.0 (CC=gcc is the Apple clang shim on macOS):

mkdir build && cd build
../configure -q \
    LIBLZMA_CFLAGS=-I/opt/homebrew/include 'LIBLZMA_LIBS=-L/opt/homebrew/lib -llzma' \
    LIBZSTD_CFLAGS=-I/opt/homebrew/include 'LIBZSTD_LIBS=-L/opt/homebrew/lib -lzstd'
make

No --enable-optimizations, no --with-lto, no --with-pydebug, so this is a release build without profile-guided or link-time optimization. The LIBLZMA_*/LIBZSTD_* variables are only there because pkg-config is not installed on this machine; without them _lzma and _zstd are not built.

Resulting flags (sysconfig):

CONFIG_ARGS = 'LIBLZMA_CFLAGS=-I/opt/homebrew/include' 'LIBLZMA_LIBS=-L/opt/homebrew/lib -llzma' 'LIBZSTD_CFLAGS=-I/opt/homebrew/include' 'LIBZSTD_LIBS=-L/opt/homebrew/lib -lzstd'
OPT           = -DNDEBUG -g -O3 -Wall
PY_CFLAGS     = -fno-omit-frame-pointer -mno-omit-leaf-frame-pointer -fno-strict-overflow -Wsign-compare -Wunreachable-code -DNDEBUG -g -O3 -Wall

1. calc_chksums microbenchmark

Two versions: a plain time.perf_counter loop and a pyperf one.

bench_calc_chksums.py (median of 15 rounds x 20000 calls):

python 3.16.0a1+dev - ns per call, median of 15 rounds x 20000 calls
ascii header   stock   5820  patched   1676  3.47x

2. End to end (bench_tarfile.py)

CPU time (time.process_time), 25 rounds, stock/patched interleaved ABBA, ratio is the median of the per-round paired ratios, CI is a bootstrap 95% interval on that median. read iterates the archive and reads every regular member, list is getmembers(), stream is the same as read in r| mode, write adds 3000 members.

3. Scripts

Run everything with ./run.sh /path/to/python. It takes tarfile.py from that interpreter's own (unpatched) stdlib, so use a stock interpreter, or edit the build_variants.py call to point at git show main:Lib/tarfile.py. For a quick smoke test: BENCH_ARGS="-n 5 --quick" ./run.sh /path/to/python. The pyperf version needs pyperf installed (python -m pip install pyperf).

run.sh

#!/bin/sh
# Usage: ./run.sh /path/to/python [TAG]
# Builds stock/patched tarfile.py from that interpreter's own (unpatched) tarfile,
# then runs both benchmarks. Set BENCH_ARGS="-n 5 --quick" for a fast smoke test.
PY=${1:?usage: run.sh /path/to/python [TAG]}
cd "$(dirname "$0")"
TAG=${2:-$("$PY" -c 'import sys; print("%d.%d" % sys.version_info[:2])')}
"$PY" build_variants.py "$("$PY" -c 'import tarfile; print(tarfile.__file__)')" "$TAG" || exit 1
"$PY" -u bench_calc_chksums.py
"$PY" -u bench_tarfile.py "$TAG" ${BENCH_ARGS:--n 25}

build_variants.py (writes mods//stock|patched/tarfile.py)

"""Build stock/ and patched/ tarfile.py for the running interpreter (from its own stdlib, or argv[1]) into mods/<ver>/."""
import os, re, sys, sysconfig
src = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else os.path.join(sysconfig.get_paths()["stdlib"], "tarfile.py")
tag = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else "%d.%d" % sys.version_info[:2]
text = open(src).read()
OLD = '''    unsigned_chksum = 256 + sum(struct.unpack_from("148B8x356B", buf))
    signed_chksum = 256 + sum(struct.unpack_from("148b8x356b", buf))
    return unsigned_chksum, signed_chksum
'''
NEW = '''    if type(buf) is bytes and len(buf) == BLOCKSIZE:
        # Fast path for the only input tarfile itself passes. The chksum
        # field (buf[148:156]) counts as eight spaces, i.e. 256. A byte with
        # the high bit set adds b to the unsigned sum and b - 256 to the
        # signed one, so signed == unsigned - 256 * (number of such bytes).
        unsigned_chksum = 256 + sum(buf) - sum(buf[148:156])
        if buf.isascii():
            return unsigned_chksum, unsigned_chksum
        head = buf[:148] + buf[156:]
        high = BLOCKSIZE - 8 - len(head.translate(None, _HIGH_BYTES))
        return unsigned_chksum, unsigned_chksum - 256 * high
    unsigned_chksum = 256 + sum(struct.unpack_from("148B8x356B", buf))
    signed_chksum = 256 + sum(struct.unpack_from("148b8x356b", buf))
    return unsigned_chksum, signed_chksum
'''
assert text.count(OLD) == 1, "calc_chksums body not found exactly once in " + src
assert text.count("def calc_chksums(buf):") == 1
patched = text.replace(OLD, NEW).replace("def calc_chksums(buf):", "_HIGH_BYTES = bytes(range(128, 256))\n\ndef calc_chksums(buf):", 1)
d = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "mods", tag)
for kind, body in (("stock", text), ("patched", patched)):
    os.makedirs(os.path.join(d, kind), exist_ok=True)
    open(os.path.join(d, kind, "tarfile.py"), "w").write(body)
print(tag, "built from", src, "BLOCKSIZE defined before calc_chksums:", text.index("BLOCKSIZE =") < text.index("def calc_chksums"))

bench_calc_chksums.py

"""Microbenchmark: original calc_chksums vs the proposed fast path, ns per call.
usage: python bench_calc_chksums.py [-n ROUNDS]
Run it under each interpreter you care about."""
import argparse, statistics as st, struct, sys, time

BLOCKSIZE = 512
_HIGH_BYTES = bytes(range(128, 256))

def orig(buf):
    unsigned_chksum = 256 + sum(struct.unpack_from("148B8x356B", buf))
    signed_chksum = 256 + sum(struct.unpack_from("148b8x356b", buf))
    return unsigned_chksum, signed_chksum

def patched(buf):
    if type(buf) is bytes and len(buf) == BLOCKSIZE:
        unsigned_chksum = 256 + sum(buf) - sum(buf[148:156])
        if buf.isascii():
            return unsigned_chksum, unsigned_chksum
        head = buf[:148] + buf[156:]
        high = BLOCKSIZE - 8 - len(head.translate(None, _HIGH_BYTES))
        return unsigned_chksum, unsigned_chksum - 256 * high
    return orig(buf)

def header(name):
    b = bytearray(BLOCKSIZE)
    b[:len(name)] = name
    b[100:107] = b"0000644"; b[124:135] = b"00000000144"; b[148:156] = b"        "
    b[257:262] = b"ustar"
    return bytes(b)

CASES = {"ascii header": header(b"config/dir001/file00001.dat"),
         "high-bit name": header("config/d\xe9r001/f\xefle\xff.dat".encode("latin-1"))}

ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(); ap.add_argument("-n", type=int, default=15); a = ap.parse_args()
LOOPS = 20000
print("python", sys.version.split()[0], "- ns per call, median of %d rounds x %d calls" % (a.n, LOOPS))
for label, buf in CASES.items():
    assert orig(buf) == patched(buf)
    res = {}
    for name, f in (("stock", orig), ("patched", patched)):
        runs = []
        for _ in range(a.n):
            t = time.perf_counter()
            for _ in range(LOOPS): f(buf)
            runs.append((time.perf_counter() - t) / LOOPS * 1e9)
        res[name] = st.median(runs)
    print("%-14s stock %6.0f  patched %6.0f  %.2fx" % (label, res["stock"], res["patched"], res["stock"] / res["patched"]))

bench_calc_chksums_pyperf.py

"""pyperf version of bench_calc_chksums.py: original calc_chksums vs the proposed fast path.
usage: python bench_calc_chksums_pyperf.py -o result.json      (then: python -m pyperf compare_to ...)
Benchmarks are named "<case>/stock" and "<case>/patched"; pyperf groups them for compare_to."""
import pyperf, struct

BLOCKSIZE = 512
_HIGH_BYTES = bytes(range(128, 256))

def orig(buf):
    unsigned_chksum = 256 + sum(struct.unpack_from("148B8x356B", buf))
    signed_chksum = 256 + sum(struct.unpack_from("148b8x356b", buf))
    return unsigned_chksum, signed_chksum

def patched(buf):
    if type(buf) is bytes and len(buf) == BLOCKSIZE:
        unsigned_chksum = 256 + sum(buf) - sum(buf[148:156])
        if buf.isascii():
            return unsigned_chksum, unsigned_chksum
        head = buf[:148] + buf[156:]
        high = BLOCKSIZE - 8 - len(head.translate(None, _HIGH_BYTES))
        return unsigned_chksum, unsigned_chksum - 256 * high
    return orig(buf)

def header(name):
    b = bytearray(BLOCKSIZE)
    b[:len(name)] = name
    b[100:107] = b"0000644"; b[124:135] = b"00000000144"; b[148:156] = b"        "
    b[257:262] = b"ustar"
    return bytes(b)

CASES = {"ascii": header(b"config/dir001/file00001.dat"),
         "highbit": header("config/d\xe9r001/f\xefle\xff.dat".encode("latin-1"))}

def time_func(loops, func, buf):
    range_it = range(loops)
    t0 = pyperf.perf_counter()
    for _ in range_it:
        func(buf)
    return pyperf.perf_counter() - t0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    runner = pyperf.Runner()
    runner.metadata["description"] = "tarfile.calc_chksums: stock vs fast path"
    for case, buf in CASES.items():
        assert orig(buf) == patched(buf)
        for variant, func in (("stock", orig), ("patched", patched)):
            runner.bench_time_func("calc_chksums/%s/%s" % (case, variant), time_func, func, buf)

bench_tarfile.py

"""Stock vs patched tarfile, many workloads, paired + interleaved (ABBA), CPU and wall time, bootstrap CI.
usage: python bench_tarfile.py MODSVER [-n ROUNDS] [--quick]
MODSVER names a directory mods/<MODSVER>/{stock,patched}/tarfile.py (see build_variants.py)."""
import argparse, bz2, gzip, importlib.util, io, lzma, os, random, statistics as st, sys, time
HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
def load(name, path):
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(name, path); m = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    sys.modules[name] = m; spec.loader.exec_module(m); return m
ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(); ap.add_argument("ver"); ap.add_argument("-n", type=int, default=25); ap.add_argument("--quick", action="store_true"); a = ap.parse_args()
S = load("tf_stock", "%s/mods/%s/stock/tarfile.py" % (HERE, a.ver)); P = load("tf_patched", "%s/mods/%s/patched/tarfile.py" % (HERE, a.ver))
rng = random.Random(1)
def synth(n, size, namefn, fmt=None, enc="utf-8"):
    bio = io.BytesIO(); body = bytes(rng.randrange(256) for _ in range(size)) if size < 5000 else os.urandom(size)
    with S.open(fileobj=bio, mode="w", format=fmt if fmt is not None else S.PAX_FORMAT, encoding=enc, errors="surrogateescape") as tf:
        for i in range(n):
            ti = S.TarInfo(namefn(i)); ti.size = size; ti.mtime = 1700000000 + i; ti.uid = ti.gid = 1000; ti.uname = ti.gname = "u"; ti.mode = 0o644
            tf.addfile(ti, io.BytesIO(body))
    return bio.getvalue()
ascii_name = lambda i: "config/dir%03d/file%05d.dat" % (i % 50, i)
hi_name = lambda i: "config/d\xe9r%03d/f\xefle\xff%05d.dat" % (i % 50, i)
W = []   # (label, data, mode)
raw = lambda b: b
many = synth(20000, 100, ascii_name); few = synth(20, 4_000_000, ascii_name, S.GNU_FORMAT); mid = synth(2000, 20000, ascii_name, S.USTAR_FORMAT)
hi = synth(5000, 100, hi_name, S.GNU_FORMAT, "latin-1"); hipax = synth(5000, 100, hi_name, S.PAX_FORMAT)
W += [("synth 20k x 100B pax", many, "r:"), ("synth 20k x 100B pax .gz", gzip.compress(many, 6), "r:gz"), ("synth 20k x 100B .bz2", bz2.compress(many), "r:bz2"), ("synth 20k x 100B .xz", lzma.compress(many, preset=1), "r:xz"),
      ("synth 2000 x 20KB ustar", mid, "r:"), ("synth 20 x 4MB gnu", few, "r:"), ("synth 5k hi-bit names gnu/latin1", hi, "r:"), ("synth 5k hi-bit names pax/utf8", hipax, "r:")]
if a.quick: W = W[:3] + W[-4:]
def op_read(mod, data, mode):    # mkreports-style: iterate + read every regular member
    with mod.open(fileobj=io.BytesIO(data), mode=mode) as tf:
        n = 0
        for m in tf:
            if m.isreg(): n += len(tf.extractfile(m).read())
    return n
def op_list(mod, data, mode):    # header parsing only
    with mod.open(fileobj=io.BytesIO(data), mode=mode) as tf: return len(tf.getmembers())
def op_stream(mod, data, mode):
    with mod.open(fileobj=io.BytesIO(data), mode="r|" + mode.split(":")[1] if mode != "r:" else "r|") as tf:
        n = 0
        for m in tf:
            if m.isreg(): n += len(tf.extractfile(m).read())
    return n
def op_write(mod, data, mode):   # write path: 3000 members
    bio = io.BytesIO(); body = b"x" * 100
    with mod.open(fileobj=bio, mode="w", format=mod.PAX_FORMAT) as tf:
        for i in range(3000):
            ti = mod.TarInfo(ascii_name(i)); ti.size = 100; ti.mtime = 1700000000; tf.addfile(ti, io.BytesIO(body))
    return len(bio.getvalue())
def boot(ratios, B=2000):
    r = random.Random(0); m = sorted(st.median([r.choice(ratios) for _ in ratios]) for _ in range(B)); return m[int(.025 * B)], m[int(.975 * B)]
def timeit(op, mod, data, mode, clock):
    t = clock(); op(mod, data, mode); return clock() - t
def row(label, opname, op, data, mode):
    assert op(S, data, mode) == op(P, data, mode)
    cs, cp, ws, wp = [], [], [], []
    for i in range(a.n):
        order = ((S, cs, ws), (P, cp, wp)) if i % 2 == 0 else ((P, cp, wp), (S, cs, ws))       # alternate who goes first (cancels drift/cache order)
        for mod, c, w in order:
            c.append(timeit(op, mod, data, mode, time.process_time)); w.append(timeit(op, mod, data, mode, time.perf_counter))
    pr = [x / y for x, y in zip(cs, cp)]; lo, hi_ = boot(pr)
    print("%-34s %-6s stock med %8.2fms (sd %5.2f)  patched med %8.2fms (sd %5.2f)  speedup med %.3fx  min/min %.3fx  95%%CI [%.3f, %.3f]  wall %.3fx  faster-in %d/%d" % (
        label[:34], opname, st.median(cs) * 1e3, st.pstdev(cs) * 1e3, st.median(cp) * 1e3, st.pstdev(cp) * 1e3, st.median(pr), min(cs) / min(cp), lo, hi_, st.median(ws) / st.median(wp), sum(r > 1 for r in pr), len(pr)))
    return st.median(pr)
print("python %s  modsver %s  rounds %d (CPU=process_time, paired ratios stock/patched, >1 = patched faster)" % (sys.version.split()[0], a.ver, a.n))
agg = {}
for label, data, mode in W:
    for opname, op in (("read", op_read), ("list", op_list)):
        agg.setdefault(opname, []).append(row(label, opname, op, data, mode))
for label, data, mode in W:
    if mode in ("r:gz", "r:bz2", "r:xz") and not a.quick: agg.setdefault("stream", []).append(row(label, "stream", op_stream, data, mode))
agg.setdefault("write", []).append(row("write 3000 members pax", "write", op_write, None, None))
print("geomean of median speedups:", {k: round(st.geometric_mean(v), 3) for k, v in agg.items()})

thread.author: picnixz
thread.html:
For the sake of keep a simple code, I don't think I'm going to actually accept this change considering that, as you observed, the overall E2E operation isn't really affected.

What I find odd is that 3.15+ has a larger speed-up for the stream mode as if we were somehow slower. The speed-ups on previous versions are less pronounced.

That being said, I find it attractive as an overall speed-up but I'm not confident in accepting (I still need to convince myself that the checksum computation is equivalent which I hadn't check yet, even if it's valid with your assertions I want to convince myself of the equal arithmetic). I also wonder how it fares on real data (say, compressed Python sources) or when it comes to images.

Also, why limiting yourself to bytes of size BLOCKSIZE only? wouldn't it work for any bytes-like object (memoryviews, etc)? the only thing you need is len(head.translate(None, _HIGH_BYTES)) to count the number of occurrences of high bytes right? this can be achieved in a more generic way for sequences (or simply converting to bytes for the method).

Alternatively, since calc_chksums() is only used with a blocks of size 512, let's have a private _calc_chksums512() which would be your optimization. The public (albeit undocumented function) could still be left as is (the fast path looks weird when you check the code).

cc @encukou @StanFromIreland

thread.author: turtle-byte-17
thread.html:
@picnixz

I don't think speed up is indicitive that 3.15 is slower, what I measured was roughly a 55ms gain, however the baseline was different

r:gz stock → patched, 20k×100B read stream
3.14 208 → 158 ms 609 → 555 ms (saves 54)
3.15 196 → 141 ms 191 → 135 ms (saves 55)

On 3.14 and earlier, stream mode is about 3x slower than read, so a fixed ~55 ms saving shows as only 1.05–1.1x. On 3.15+ the stream path is fast, so the same saving shows as 1.39-1.41x.

I agree with you that we should try to keep it simple and extract it into a private function, here's the diff I ran with initially, as you'll see it introduced a regression in the reading of non-ASCII header, signed checksum and the corrupt checksum cases, which my original proposal did not. Below this section I'm leaning towards

Revised proposal: private _calc_chksum512()

calc_chksums() is left as is. The optimisation is a private helper used by _create_header and as a quick first check in _frombuf:

--- a/Lib/tarfile.py
+++ b/Lib/tarfile.py
@@ -232,6 +232,11 @@
     signed_chksum = 256 + sum(struct.unpack_from("148b8x356b", buf))
     return unsigned_chksum, signed_chksum
 
+def _calc_chksum512(buf):
+    """Return the unsigned checksum of a 512-byte header block."""
+    # The checksum field (buf[148:156]) is summed as eight spaces (256).
+    return 256 + sum(buf) - sum(buf[148:156])
+
 def copyfileobj(src, dst, length=None, exception=OSError, bufsize=None):
     """Copy length bytes from fileobj src to fileobj dst.
        If length is None, copy the entire content.
@@ -1250,7 +1255,7 @@
         ]
 
         buf = struct.pack("%ds" % BLOCKSIZE, b"".join(parts))
-        chksum = calc_chksums(buf[-BLOCKSIZE:])[0]
+        chksum = _calc_chksum512(buf)
         buf = buf[:-364] + bytes("%06o\0" % chksum, "ascii") + buf[-357:]
         return buf
 
@@ -1358,7 +1363,7 @@
             raise EOFHeaderError("end of file header")
 
         chksum = nti(buf[148:156])
-        if chksum not in calc_chksums(buf):
+        if chksum != _calc_chksum512(buf) and chksum not in calc_chksums(buf):
             raise InvalidHeaderError("bad checksum")
 
         obj = cls()

pyperf comparison (plain build)

bench_chksum_check_pyperf.py, pyperf 2.10.0, --processes 20 --values 3, mean ± std dev. It times the checksum check _frombuf does per header (and the one _create_header does for writes) for stock vs the proposal:

case stock new speedup
read, ASCII header, normal checksum 5.76 ± 0.19 µs 1.67 ± 0.14 µs 3.45x
read, non-ASCII header, normal checksum 5.85 ± 0.29 µs 1.61 ± 0.15 µs 3.63x
write (_create_header) 5.80 ± 0.26 µs 1.60 ± 0.18 µs 3.62x
read, non-ASCII header, signed checksum (Sun/NeXT) 5.78 ± 0.25 µs 7.46 ± 0.47 µs 0.77x
read, ASCII header, corrupt checksum 5.74 ± 0.19 µs 7.43 ± 0.48 µs 0.77x
read, non-ASCII header, corrupt checksum 5.80 ± 0.26 µs 7.40 ± 0.39 µs 0.78x

Normal archives, including non-ASCII headers, get about 3.3-3.6x faster. The cost is on the rarely used path: a header whose stored checksum is not the unsigned one (signed checksums written by old Sun/NeXT tar, or a corrupt header) pays for one extra sum() before the original function runs.

Real data (bench_tarfile.py --lib-root, 25 rounds, CPU time)

Every Lib/**/*.py file of the checkout (2082 files, 44.9 MB tar, 8.3 MB .gz) and the 65 image files in it (4.5 MB tar), read iterates and reads every member, list is getmembers(). stock → new, median of 25 paired rounds, the ratio is stock/new:

workload op plain -O3 PGO+LTO
Lib/*.py tar read 50.41 → 33.66 ms (1.516x) 46.00 → 27.31 ms (1.690x)
Lib/*.py tar list 43.92 → 27.29 ms (1.614x) 39.87 → 21.79 ms (1.831x)
Lib/*.py tar.gz read 99.94 → 82.80 ms (1.215x) 93.43 → 74.02 ms (1.264x)
Lib/*.py tar.gz list 91.54 → 74.57 ms (1.235x) 85.66 → 66.42 ms (1.280x)
Lib/*.py tar.xz read 391.04 → 374.72 ms (1.044x) 384.58 → 364.85 ms (1.053x)
Lib/*.py tar.xz list 381.49 → 364.73 ms (1.046x) 375.50 → 356.92 ms (1.053x)
images tar read 1.62 → 1.09 ms (1.496x) 1.49 → 0.91 ms (1.636x)
images tar list 1.38 → 0.85 ms (1.645x) 1.20 → 0.66 ms (1.805x)
images tar.gz read 11.81 → 11.28 ms (1.047x) 11.55 → 10.97 ms (1.053x)
images tar.gz list 11.42 → 10.91 ms (1.047x) 11.23 → 10.65 ms (1.054x)

The gain shrinks when decompression dominates (.xz, gzip of already-compressed images). Worst case, an archive where every header carries only the signed checksum:

workload op plain -O3 PGO+LTO
5k non-ASCII headers, all with signed checksums read 62.74 → 71.27 ms (0.881x) 56.77 → 62.63 ms (0.908x)
5k non-ASCII headers, all with signed checksums list 48.76 → 56.96 ms (0.860x) 45.78 → 51.09 ms (0.893x)

So I think best of both worlds is to keep the private function but with the original proposal for the checksum calculation

Revised proposal: private _calc_chksums512()

calc_chksums() is left as is. The optimisation is a private helper that returns both checksums for the 512-byte header block, and _create_header / _frombuf use it instead of calc_chksums():

--- a/Lib/tarfile.py
+++ b/Lib/tarfile.py
@@ -219,6 +219,8 @@
 
     return s
 
+_HIGH_BYTES = bytes(range(128, 256))
+
 def calc_chksums(buf):
     """Calculate the checksum for a member's header by summing up all
        characters except for the chksum field which is treated as if
@@ -232,6 +234,17 @@
     signed_chksum = 256 + sum(struct.unpack_from("148b8x356b", buf))
     return unsigned_chksum, signed_chksum
 
+def _calc_chksums512(buf):
+    """Return the unsigned and signed checksums of a 512-byte header block."""
+    # The checksum field (buf[148:156]) is summed as eight spaces (256).
+    unsigned_chksum = 256 + sum(buf) - sum(buf[148:156])
+    if buf.isascii():
+        return unsigned_chksum, unsigned_chksum
+    # Each byte >= 128 adds b to the unsigned sum but b - 256 to the signed one.
+    head = buf[:148] + buf[156:]
+    high = BLOCKSIZE - 8 - len(head.translate(None, _HIGH_BYTES))
+    return unsigned_chksum, unsigned_chksum - 256 * high
+
 def copyfileobj(src, dst, length=None, exception=OSError, bufsize=None):
     """Copy length bytes from fileobj src to fileobj dst.
        If length is None, copy the entire content.
@@ -1250,7 +1263,7 @@
         ]
 
         buf = struct.pack("%ds" % BLOCKSIZE, b"".join(parts))
-        chksum = calc_chksums(buf[-BLOCKSIZE:])[0]
+        chksum = _calc_chksums512(buf)[0]
         buf = buf[:-364] + bytes("%06o\0" % chksum, "ascii") + buf[-357:]
         return buf
 
@@ -1358,7 +1371,7 @@
             raise EOFHeaderError("end of file header")
 
         chksum = nti(buf[148:156])
-        if chksum not in calc_chksums(buf):
+        if chksum not in _calc_chksums512(buf):
             raise InvalidHeaderError("bad checksum")
 
         obj = cls()

Both callers only ever pass exactly BLOCKSIZE bytes (_frombuf raises TruncatedHeaderError for any other length before it gets to the checksum, and _create_header builds its buffer with struct.pack("%ds" % BLOCKSIZE, ...)), so the helper has no type or length checks. There is no fallback path, so every header gets the fast computation: ASCII headers need one sum() and an isascii(), non-ASCII ones also count their high bytes. calc_chksums() is no longer called by tarfile itself and is left in place for compatibility.

Numbers are for CPython 3.16.0a1+dev built from main at 4a9b98115f on an Apple M5 Pro (arm64, macOS), not isolated, so compare the ratios and not the absolute times between tables. "plain" is the -O3 -DNDEBUG build, "PGO+LTO" is --enable-optimizations --with-lto (that tree also had unrelated uncommitted edits to Lib/csv.py and Lib/gettext.py, which don't touch tarfile).

pyperf comparison (plain build)

pyperf 2.10.0, --processes 20 --values 3, mean ± std dev. It times the checksum check _frombuf does per header (and the one _create_header does for writes), stock vs the proposal:

case stock new speedup
read, ASCII header, normal checksum 3.85 ± 0.15 µs 1.12 ± 0.08 µs 3.44x
read, non-ASCII header, normal checksum 3.85 ± 0.13 µs 1.44 ± 0.05 µs 2.67x
write (_create_header) 3.84 ± 0.09 µs 1.09 ± 0.06 µs 3.52x
read, non-ASCII header, signed checksum (Sun/NeXT) 3.86 ± 0.15 µs 1.45 ± 0.05 µs 2.66x
read, ASCII header, corrupt checksum 3.84 ± 0.10 µs 1.12 ± 0.06 µs 3.43x
read, non-ASCII header, corrupt checksum 3.86 ± 0.11 µs 1.45 ± 0.07 µs 2.66x

Every case is faster (2.7x-3.5x), including non-ASCII headers carrying the signed checksum that old Sun/NeXT tar wrote and headers with a corrupt checksum. No case regresses.

Real data (bench_tarfile.py --lib-root, 25 rounds, CPU time)

Every Lib/**/*.py file of the checkout (2082 files, 44.9 MB tar, 8.3 MB .gz) and the 65 image files in it (4.5 MB tar). read iterates and reads every member, list is getmembers(). Stock → new, median of 25 paired rounds, the ratio is stock/new:

workload op plain -O3 PGO+LTO
Lib/*.py tar read 35.06 → 23.19 ms (1.510x) 30.29 → 18.86 ms (1.598x)
Lib/*.py tar list 31.04 → 18.85 ms (1.647x) 26.29 → 15.09 ms (1.737x)
Lib/*.py tar.gz read 68.50 → 55.31 ms (1.239x) 61.82 → 49.81 ms (1.234x)
Lib/*.py tar.gz list 61.84 → 49.87 ms (1.241x) 56.25 → 44.73 ms (1.254x)
Lib/*.py tar.xz read 255.40 → 241.67 ms (1.053x) 254.17 → 241.61 ms (1.053x)
Lib/*.py tar.xz list 249.44 → 235.26 ms (1.054x) 247.21 → 235.39 ms (1.049x)
images tar read 1.16 → 0.78 ms (1.496x) 0.99 → 0.63 ms (1.538x)
images tar list 0.93 → 0.57 ms (1.625x) 0.84 → 0.47 ms (1.777x)
images tar.gz read 7.59 → 7.21 ms (1.052x) 7.51 → 7.16 ms (1.046x)
images tar.gz list 7.34 → 6.95 ms (1.055x) 7.14 → 6.85 ms (1.043x)

The gain shrinks when decompression dominates (.xz, gzip of already-compressed images). An archive where every header carries only the signed checksum:

workload op plain -O3 PGO+LTO
5k non-ASCII headers, all with signed checksums read 43.10 → 30.36 ms (1.420x) 38.01 → 24.95 ms (1.512x)
5k non-ASCII headers, all with signed checksums list 34.59 → 22.05 ms (1.568x) 30.82 → 18.32 ms (1.681x)

Geometric mean of the median speedups over every row of the run (synthetic, real-data and signed-checksum archives, plus streaming and write): plain {read: 1.326, list: 1.468, stream: 1.224, write: 1.382}, PGO+LTO {read: 1.381, list: 1.525, stream: 1.245, write: 1.431}.

Checking equivalence

  • _calc_chksums512(buf) returns exactly calc_chksums(buf) on 1,118,530 buffers per interpreter (every byte value at every position of 7 base blocks, plus random, clustered-high-byte and k-high-byte buffers): 0 mismatches on 3.9, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, 3.14, 3.15 and 3.16.0a1+dev.
  • The accept/reject decision chksum in _calc_chksums512(buf) equals the original chksum in calc_chksums(buf) for stored checksums in {unsigned, signed, unsigned+1, signed-1, unsigned+256, 0, random}: 1,808,590 decisions per interpreter, 0 mismatches.
  • A differential run of stock vs patched tarfile over about 667-671 thousand archive cases (ustar/gnu/pax, signed-checksum headers, bit flips, truncations, header mutations, r:*/r:/r|, gz/bz2/xz, extractall) found 0 differences on all seven interpreters, and archives written by the patched tarfile are byte-identical to stock.

issues.title: ctypes array cache can return distinct types when types are created concurrently
issues.author: ngoldbaum
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

On the free-threaded build, this fails with TypeError: expected c_int_Array_1 instance instead of c_int_Array_1:

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from ctypes import c_int
from threading import Barrier

barrier = Barrier(8)

def make_type(n):
    barrier.wait()
    return c_int * n

with ThreadPoolExecutor(8) as pool:
    for n in range(1, 1001):
        types = list(pool.map(make_type, [n] * 8))
        for t in types:
            types[0].from_param(t())

It passes on the GIL-enabled build because there isn't an opportunity for a GIL thread switch.

If I instead create a type that has a Python hook, I can deterministically trigger the same race on the GIL-enabled build as well:

import ctypes
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from threading import Barrier

barrier = Barrier(2)

class Meta(type(ctypes.c_int)):
    def __set_name__(cls, owner, name):
        barrier.wait(timeout=5)

class C(ctypes.c_int, metaclass=Meta):
    pass

with ThreadPoolExecutor(2) as pool:
    a, b = pool.map(lambda _: C * 100, range(2))

print(a is b)
a.from_param(b())

This second script prints False and then TypeError: expected C_Array_100 instance instead of C_Array_100 on both builds, because defining __set_name__ makes python code run after the cache miss on the array type cache during creation of the array class.

I think the fix is to rewrite how PyCArrayType_from_ctype uses the array_cache:

cpython/Modules/_ctypes/_ctypes.c

Lines 5363 to 5417 in 4a9b981

PyObject *
PyCArrayType_from_ctype(ctypes_state *st, PyObject *itemtype, Py_ssize_t length)
{
PyObject *key;
char name[256];
PyObject *len;
assert(st->array_cache != NULL);
len = PyLong_FromSsize_t(length);
if (len == NULL)
return NULL;
key = _PyTuple_FromPairSteal(Py_NewRef(itemtype), len);
if (!key)
return NULL;
PyObject *result;
if (_PyDict_GetItemProxy(st->array_cache, key, &result) != 0) {
// found or error
Py_DECREF(key);
return result;
}
// not found
if (!PyType_Check(itemtype)) {
PyErr_SetString(PyExc_TypeError,
"Expected a type object");
Py_DECREF(key);
return NULL;
}
#ifdef MS_WIN64
sprintf(name, "%.200s_Array_%Id",
((PyTypeObject *)itemtype)->tp_name, length);
#else
sprintf(name, "%.200s_Array_%ld",
((PyTypeObject *)itemtype)->tp_name, (long)length);
#endif
result = PyObject_CallFunction((PyObject *)st->PyCArrayType_Type,
"s(O){s:n,s:O}",
name,
st->PyCArray_Type,
"_length_",
length,
"_type_",
itemtype
);
if (result == NULL) {
Py_DECREF(key);
return NULL;
}
if (PyDict_SetItemProxy(st, st->array_cache, key, result) < 0) {
Py_DECREF(key);
Py_DECREF(result);
return NULL;
}
Py_DECREF(key);
return result;

The current implementation has a check-then-insert TOCTOU bug.

I found this looking at the root cause of numpy/numpy#29943. See also #127945.

CPython versions tested on:

3.14, 3.15, 3.16, main

Operating systems tested on:

macOS (M1)

issues.title: asyncio: SSL transport raises AttributeError after close() in connection_lost()
issues.author: asvetlov
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

If a protocol closes its SSL transport in connection_lost(), which is a common pattern, later calls on the transport fail:

import asyncio
from test.test_asyncio import utils as tu

class Proto(asyncio.Protocol):
    def connection_made(self, tr):
        self.tr = tr
    def connection_lost(self, exc):
        self.tr.close()
        self.lost.set_result(None)

async def main():
    async def handler(reader, writer):
        writer.close()
    srv = await asyncio.start_server(handler, '127.0.0.1', 0,
                                     ssl=tu.simple_server_sslcontext())
    port = srv.sockets[0].getsockname()[1]
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    proto = Proto()
    proto.lost = loop.create_future()
    tr, _ = await loop.create_connection(
        lambda: proto, '127.0.0.1', port, ssl=tu.simple_client_sslcontext())
    await proto.lost
    tr.write(b'x')  # AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute '_write_appdata'
    srv.close()

asyncio.run(main())

set_protocol(), get_write_buffer_size() and get_extra_info() fail the same way. Plain TCP transports don't have this problem.

It also breaks the loop.sendfile() fallback over SSL: if the peer disconnects mid-transfer, restore() calls set_protocol() and raises AttributeError instead of the expected connection error.

The cause is in _SSLProtocolTransport.close(). When it's called on a transport already marked closed, it sets _ssl_protocol = None. That was added in gh-98539 so the transport doesn't keep the SSL context alive, but it leaves the transport unusable.

Affects 3.11 and later.

Linked PRs

  • gh-160965

issues.title: Null dereferencing of a pointer in initconfig.c

Potentially, if "value" equals NULL and "spec->type" equals "PyConfig_MEMBER_WSTR_OPT", null will be passed into "utf8_to_wstr" function and might cause a segmentation fault in strlen

cpython/Python/initconfig.c

Lines 4369 to 4376 in d3a1e72

if (value == NULL && spec->type != PyConfig_MEMBER_WSTR_OPT) {
initconfig_set_error(config, "config option string cannot be NULL");
return -1;
}
wchar_t **member = raw_member;
wchar_t *wstr = utf8_to_wstr(config, value);

cpython/Python/initconfig.c

Lines 4324 to 4328 in d3a1e72

utf8_to_wstr(PyInitConfig *config, const char *str)
{
wchar_t *wstr;
size_t wlen;
int res = _Py_DecodeUTF8(str, strlen(str), &wstr, &wlen, _Py_ERROR_STRICT);

Documentation states that "value" is a null-terminated UTF-8 string, but isn't clearly stating that Null is allowed

Suggested fix: separate "value" and "spec->type" checks

if (value == NULL) { 
        if (spec->type != PyConfig_MEMBER_WSTR_OPT) {
               nitconfig_set_error(config, "config option string cannot be NULL");
               return -1;
               }
    wchar_t **member = raw_member;
    free(*member);
    *member = wstr;
    return 0;
}

issues.title: _pydecimal loses companion signal flags when a signal is trapped
issues.author: arpittkhandelwal
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description

The pure-Python decimal implementation (_pydecimal) does not set the
context flags of companion conditions when an operation's result is
delivered through a trapped signal. The C implementation (_decimal,
libmpdec) records the full set of conditions in the context flags before
raising the trapped exception.

Minimal example — an overflowing multiplication signals Overflow,
Inexact and Rounded; Overflow is trapped (as it is in the default
context):

import _decimal as C
import _pydecimal as P

def probe(module):
    ctx = module.Context(prec=9, Emin=-999, Emax=999)
    ctx.clear_flags()
    try:
        ctx.multiply(module.Decimal('1E+800'), module.Decimal('1E+800'))
    except module.Overflow:
        pass
    return sorted(s.__name__ for s, v in ctx.flags.items() if v)

print("C _decimal:  ", probe(C))
print("P _pydecimal:", probe(P))

Output (verified on CPython 3.12 and on a 3.16 build):

C _decimal:   ['Inexact', 'Overflow', 'Rounded']
P _pydecimal: ['Overflow']          # Inexact and Rounded are lost

The same loss occurs for every operation that signals several conditions
at once whenever any of them is trapped, e.g.:

Case (single trap) _decimal flags after the exception _pydecimal flags
divide(1, 3), trap Inexact Inexact, Rounded Inexact
divide(1E-999, 1E+10), trap Underflow Clamped, Inexact, Rounded, Subnormal, Underflow Underflow
divide(1E-999, 1E+10), trap Subnormal Clamped, Inexact, Rounded, Subnormal, Underflow Subnormal, Underflow
divmod(5, 0), trap DivisionByZero DivisionByZero, InvalidOperation DivisionByZero
quantize(1.23, 1E+995) with clamp=1, trap Inexact Clamped, Inexact, Rounded Inexact

With no traps enabled the two implementations agree exactly.

Expected vs actual

Per the documentation (Doc/library/decimal.rst, "Signals"): "For each
signal there is a flag and a trap enabler. When a signal is encountered,
its flag is set to one, then, if the trap enabler is set to one, an
exception is raised." An overflowing operation encounters Inexact
and Rounded — both implementations set those flags whenever Overflow
is not trapped — so the flags should be set regardless of whether some
other signal is trapped. The two implementations are interchangeable
backends of the same module, so code that catches the exception and then
inspects context.flags (a documented monitoring pattern) must observe
the same state with either backend.

Root cause: in Lib/_pydecimal.py, Context._raise_error() sets one
signal's flag and raises immediately when that signal is trapped.
Operations signal companion conditions through sequential _raise_error
calls (e.g. Decimal._fix signals Overflow, then Inexact, then
Rounded), so a trapped signal makes the remaining calls unreachable.

Note that which exception is raised is correct in both implementations
(the precedence order established by bpo-8567); only the flag state left
behind differs. This is also why the existing test suite does not catch
it: the decTest driver disables the traps of the expected conditions for

issues.title: logging: Logger.setLevel() and logging.disable() are O(number of loggers)
issues.author: Ar-maan05
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Every Logger.setLevel() and logging.disable() call goes through Manager._clear_cache(), which walks the whole loggerDict and clears each logger's isEnabledFor cache, even the ones that never cached anything. So setting the level on N loggers one by one is quadratic. That shows up in apps or test suites with thousands of loggers (one per module/plugin/connection) that get configured individually.

import logging, time

for n in (1000, 2000, 4000, 8000):
    logging.root.manager.loggerDict.clear()
    loggers = [logging.getLogger(f"app.mod{i}") for i in range(n)]
    for lg in loggers:
        lg.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG)
    t = time.perf_counter()
    for lg in loggers:
        lg.setLevel(logging.INFO)
    print(f"{n:5d} loggers: {time.perf_counter() - t:.3f} s")

On 3.14.7 this gives about 0.23 s at 2000 loggers, 0.89 s at 4000 and 4.4 s at 8000 (each doubling is about 4x).

A fix is to have the manager remember which loggers actually have something in their cache (a WeakSet filled on the isEnabledFor cache-miss path, which already holds the lock) and only clear those. The cache-hit path doesn't change. I have a patch ready and can open a PR.

3.14, CPython main branch

Linux

issues.title: Skip the `__bytes__` lookup in bytes() for exact bytes and int
issues.author: cmaloney
issues.bodyHTML:
Feature or enhancement

Since 3.11 added bytes.__bytes__ (gh-68422), bytes(b) for an exact bytes looks up __bytes__, creates a bound method and calls it, only to get b back. For an exact int the lookup always misses, because int has no
__bytes__.

Both types are immutable, so bytes_new_impl() can check for them first:

  • return an exact bytes argument directly, as PyObject_Bytes() and PyBytes_FromObject() already do;
  • skip the lookup for an exact int.

Subclasses, including bool, still look up __bytes__, so there's no behaviour change.

That makes bytes(b) about 2.2x faster, a bytes subclass Sub(b) about 1.4x, and bytes(16) about 1.1x. Other bytes() calls and the controls are unchanged (pyperf, PGO+LTO).

Benchmark script 
import pyperf

runner = pyperf.Runner()
for stmt in ["bytes(b)", "bytes(16)", "bytes(ba)", "bytes(mv)", "bytes(l)",
             "bytes(s, 'ascii')", "bytes(hb)", "Sub(b)", "bytes()",
             "len(l)", "l[0]", "x + 1", "str(x)"]:
    runner.timeit(stmt, stmt,
                  "b = b'abcdefghijklmnop'; ba = bytearray(b); mv = memoryview(b); "
                  "l = list(range(16)); s = 'abcdefghijklmnop'; x = 12345\n"
                  "class Sub(bytes): pass\n"
                  "class HB:\n    def __bytes__(self): return b\n"
                  "hb = HB()")

issues.title: checksharedmods fails on non-glibc cross builds (host interpreter gets target LD_LIBRARY_PATH)
issues.author: jaipaulcheernam
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Cross-compiling 3.15 for a musl target (glibc build machine) fails in make at the checksharedmods target:

nativepython3: error while loading shared libraries: libc.so: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
make: *** [Makefile:1801: checksharedmods] Error 127

The rule runs the build python under RUNSHARED:

@$(RUNSHARED) $(PYTHON_FOR_BUILD) $(srcdir)/Tools/build/check_extension_modules.py

In a cross build PYTHON_FOR_BUILD is the host interpreter (from --with-build-python) but RUNSHARED points LD_LIBRARY_PATH at the target's build dir, so the host interpreter gets the target libraries. On glibc->glibc nobody notices, but with a musl target the glibc host binary can't load the musl libc.so and dies before Python even starts.

This started with #141926 / GH-141958, which dropped the old

if test "$cross_compiling" = yes; then
  RUNSHARED=
fi

That PR was about getting PGO to work under emulation, but checksharedmods runs in the normal build_all path even without PGO, so now every non-emulated cross build to a different libc breaks here.

As far as I can tell check_extension_modules.py doesn't actually need the target libs on LD_LIBRARY_PATH when cross-compiling — it already takes the cross path (via _PYTHON_HOST_PLATFORM) and only checks that the module files exist, it doesn't import them.

Putting the cross_compiling RUNSHARED reset back makes the build work again. Would it make sense to restore it, or to only use RUNSHARED for the build-python when a HOSTRUNNER is set?

issues.title: Decide on STORE_FAST_LOAD_FAST
issues.author: eendebakpt
issues.bodyHTML:
Feature or enhancement

After #160032 (comment) the usage of STORE_FAST_LOAD_FAST as almost none. It should either be removed or replaced with STORE_FAST_LOAD_FAST_BORROW.

Opcode counts for all code objects from compiling the 2071 files of Lib/ (nested code objects included, CACHE entries excluded):

Opcode main (2e1666f) PR which adds STORE_FAST_LOAD_FAST_BORROW
STORE_FAST_LOAD_FAST 66 0
STORE_FAST_LOAD_FAST_BORROW 0 1,997
STORE_FAST 152,996 151,065
LOAD_FAST_BORROW 539,756 538,149
LOAD_FAST (strong) 20,858 20,924
LOAD_FAST_BORROW_LOAD_FAST_BORROW 46,070 45,875
STORE_FAST_STORE_FAST 12,069 12,069
all instructions 5,147,291 5,145,554

As long as superinstructions are limited to single lines, there are not many cases where we will have a STORE_FAST_LOAD_FAST. Some benchmarks:

Benchmark (5,000 elements) main this PR
[x for x in lst] 32.0 us 29.5 us: 1.08x faster
[x + 1 for x in lst] 73.1 us 68.4 us: 1.07x faster
[x.real for x in lst] 97.7 us 89.2 us: 1.10x faster
for i in range(5000): i 36.6 us 34.1 us: 1.07x faster

Callgrind on the first benchmark: 131.7 vs 122.8 instructions per iteration. From the benchmarks only the second and third make sense in real-world code. The first and the last do not. In the pystats of the pyperformance suite the pair is about 0.08% of all executed instructions (94% of them directly after a FOR_ITER).

Scripts used for the opcode counts and the benchmark 
"""Compile every .py under LIBDIR with the running interpreter and count opcodes.
Usage: python -I count_opcodes.py LIBDIR"""
import collections, dis, json, os, sys

libdir = sys.argv[1]
CACHE = dis.opmap['CACHE']
counts = collections.Counter()

def walk(co):
    for i in range(0, len(co.co_code), 2):
        op = co.co_code[i]
        if op != CACHE:
            counts[dis.opname[op]] += 1
    for c in co.co_consts:
        if isinstance(c, type(co)):
            walk(c)

for root, dirs, files in os.walk(libdir):
    for f in sorted(files):
        if f.endswith('.py'):
            p = os.path.join(root, f)
            try:
                with open(p, 'rb') as fh:
                    co = compile(fh.read(), p, 'exec')
            except (SyntaxError, ValueError):
                continue
            walk(co)

print(json.dumps({'total': sum(counts.values()), 'counts': counts}, sort_keys=True))
import sys, timeit
lst = list(range(5000))
def ident(it): return [x for x in it]
def plus(it): return [x + 1 for x in it]
def attr(it): return [x.real for x in it]
def rng(n):
    for i in range(n): i
cases = [("[x for x in lst]", lambda: ident(lst)), ("[x + 1 for x in lst]", lambda: plus(lst)),
         ("[x.real for x in lst]", lambda: attr(lst)), ("for i in range(5000): i", lambda: rng(5000))]
print(sys.version.split()[0])
for name, fn in cases:
    best = min(timeit.repeat(fn, number=500, repeat=21)) / 500 * 1e6
    print(f"  {name:28s} {best:7.1f} us")

@markshannon @methane I have no preference. If you have no preference either, i'll toss a coin.

issues.title: `fnmatch.filter` and `filterfalse` work with pathlikes only on non-Posix platforms
issues.author: JelleZijlstra
issues.bodyHTML:
fnmatch.filter contains a check:

    if os.path is posixpath:
        # normcase on posix is NOP. Optimize it away from the loop.

It calls normcase on the paths to be filtered only on non-Posix platforms.

The check dates from 2001 and the comment was probably true then. But nowadays, os.path.normcase does do something even on Posix: it normalizes path-like objects into strs or bytes.

So on MacOS I get:

>>> import fnmatch
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> fnmatch.filter([Path("hi")], "hi")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-2>", line 1, in <module>
    fnmatch.filter([Path("hi")], "hi")
    ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/Users/jelle/py/cpython/Lib/fnmatch.py", line 61, in filter
    if match(name):
       ~~~~~^^^^^^
TypeError: expected string or bytes-like object, got 'PosixPath'

But this will work on Windows.

I think this is should be fixed for two reasons:

  • It's an unnecessary difference in behavior between platforms. Python should work the same across OSes as much as possible, and there's no good reason for the behavior to differ here.
  • In general, we want path-related functions to accept path-like objects (PEP 519)

However, we've generally treated PEP 519 changes as new features, so let's change this on main only.

Discovered in python/typeshed#16647

issues.title: The text about escaping newlines in triple-qouted strings is misleading
issues.author: prodehghan

Documentation

File: https://docs.python.org/3.16/reference/lexical_analysis.html#string-escape-ignore
Section 2.5.4.1 says:

A backslash can be added at the end of a line to ignore the newline:
(code sample)
The same result can be achieved using triple-quoted strings, or parentheses and string literal concatenation.

The current wording suggests that triple-quoted strings alone can split text across source lines without preserving newlines. In fact, unescaped newlines are retained, and omitting them requires the same backslash-newline escape used in ordinary string literals.

I suggest improving the text and clarifying that escaping newlines works the same in single- or triple-qouted string.

issues.title: `test_is_python_process_non_python_subprocess` always times out when `sleep` is a multicall binary (Alpine/BusyBox, RHEL UBI9)
issues.author: thomgree
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

The fix for gh-159534 (GH-160028, backported to 3.15 in GH-160080) makes test_is_python_process_non_python_subprocess fail every time on systems where sleep is provided by a multicall binary. That includes the Alpine buildbots, where the original gh-159534 failure was found:

FAIL: test_is_python_process_non_python_subprocess (test.test_profiling.test_sampling_profiler.test_children.TestIsPythonProcess.test_is_python_process_non_python_subprocess)
Test that a non-Python subprocess is not detected as Python.
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../Lib/test/test_profiling/test_sampling_profiler/test_children.py", line 628, in test_is_python_process_non_python_subprocess
    _wait_for_process_exec(proc, "sleep", SHORT_TIMEOUT)
  File ".../Lib/test/test_profiling/test_sampling_profiler/test_children.py", line 91, in _wait_for_process_exec
    for _ in sleeping_retry(timeout, max_delay=0.1):
  File ".../Lib/test/support/__init__.py", line 2779, in sleeping_retry
    for _ in busy_retry(timeout, err_msg, error=error):
  File ".../Lib/test/support/__init__.py", line 2749, in busy_retry
    raise AssertionError(msg)
AssertionError: timeout (45.1 seconds)

Buildbots

AMD64 Alpine Linux NoGIL 3.x:

  • build 3444 (before GH-160028): the original intermittent failure, True is not false.
  • build 3445 (first build with GH-160028): timeout (45.1 seconds). Every build since fails the same way, e.g. build 3523.

AMD64 Alpine Linux 3.15:

  • build 800 (before GH-160080): only test_lazy_import fails.
  • build 815 (first build with GH-160080) and every build since, including build 851 just before v3.15.2 was tagged: this test fails too.

This failure is separate from the test_lazy_import crash on Alpine (gh-159535). The Alpine builders will stay red after that crash is fixed.

Cause

The new _wait_for_process_exec() helper waits until os.path.basename(os.readlink(f"/proc/{pid}/exe")) == "sleep". When sleep is a multicall binary, /proc/{pid}/exe points to the multicall binary instead:

System /usr/bin/sleep or /bin/sleep /proc/{pid}/exe of a running sleep
Alpine 3.24 (BusyBox) symlink to /bin/busybox /bin/busybox
RHEL UBI9 (coreutils-single, the image default) shebang script #!/usr/bin/coreutils --coreutils-prog-shebang=sleep /usr/bin/coreutils
RHEL UBI9 after dnf swap coreutils-single coreutils regular binary /usr/bin/sleep

The condition never becomes true, so the test always times out.

Reproducer, tested in python:3-alpine and registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi:

import os, subprocess, time
proc = subprocess.Popen(["sleep", "10"])
time.sleep(0.5)
print(os.readlink(f"/proc/{proc.pid}/exe"))
proc.kill()

Suggested fix

The helper only needs to know that the child has called exec(). The program name doesn't matter. Before exec(), the forked child's /proc/{pid}/exe is the parent's Python executable, so wait until it differs from the parent's:

-def _wait_for_process_exec(proc, name, timeout):
+def _wait_for_process_exec(proc, timeout):
     # Wait until a child process calls exec() to replace the forked process
-    # executable. Raise AssertionError on timeout.
+    # executable. Don't check the executable name: it can be a multicall
+    # binary such as /bin/busybox. Raise AssertionError on timeout.
+    parent_exe = os.readlink("/proc/self/exe")
     for _ in sleeping_retry(timeout, max_delay=0.1):
         exe = os.readlink(f"/proc/{proc.pid}/exe")
-        if os.path.basename(exe) == name:
+        if exe != parent_exe:
             break
-            _wait_for_process_exec(proc, "sleep", SHORT_TIMEOUT)
+            _wait_for_process_exec(proc, SHORT_TIMEOUT)

I tested this check with the reproducer on Alpine (BusyBox) and on UBI9 with both coreutils-single and coreutils. It detects the exec() in all three cases, while the current name check fails on Alpine and on UBI9 with coreutils-single.

issues.title: Emscripten: Remove obsolete `pthread_getattr_np` workaround in `ceval.c`
issues.author: lpyu001
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Description

The workaround in Python/ceval.c was introduced to address a broken pthread_getattr_np() implementation in Emscripten versions prior to 4.0.6 (GH-130396, #131088).

The existing comment explicitly describes it as temporary:

#if defined(__EMSCRIPTEN__)

// Temporary workaround to make `pthread_getattr_np` work on Emscripten.
// Emscripten 4.0.6 will contain a fix:
// https://github.com/emscripten-core/emscripten/pull/23887

However, the workaround is still enabled for all Emscripten versions because it only checks __EMSCRIPTEN__, regardless of the toolchain version.

The upstream fix was included in Emscripten 4.0.6, and CPython now uses Emscripten 6.0.13 (Platforms/emscripten/config.toml).

Therefore, this workaround appears to be obsolete and could potentially be removed, allowing CPython to use Emscripten's native pthread_getattr_np() implementation.

The removal should be verified against the current Emscripten toolchain to ensure that stack boundary detection and recursion protection continue to work correctly.

issues.title: Keep PyLong "x_divrem" inner loop carry in 64 bits
issues.author: XiaohongGong
issues.bodyHTML:
Feature or enhancement

This is a split issue from #156443, which focus on the improvement of longobject x_divrem inner loop.

The inner loop x_divrem:

/* subtract q*w0[0:size_w] from vk[0:size_w+1] */
zhi = 0;
for (i = 0; i < size_w; ++i) {
     /* invariants: -PyLong_BASE <= -q <= zhi <= 0;
       -PyLong_BASE * q <= z < PyLong_BASE */
    z = (sdigit)vk[i] + zhi - (stwodigits)q * (stwodigits)w0[i];
    vk[i] = (digit)z & PyLong_MASK;
    zhi = (sdigit)Py_ARITHMETIC_RIGHT_SHIFT(stwodigits, z, PyLong_SHIFT);
}

zhi, the loop-carried borrow in Knuth Algorithm D, was stored as an sdigit (32-bit int) and then widened to 64-bit stwodigits on the next iteration. That extra conversion sat on the critical chain which is strong latency bounded:

    ldr     w0, [x12, x2, lsl #2]
    ldr     w1, [x27, x2, lsl #2]
    add     w0, w3, w0              // critical chain
    sxtw    x0, w0                  // critical chain (32 -> 64)
    umsubl  x0, w1, w14, x0         // critical chain
    and     w1, w0, #0x3fffffff
    str     w1, [x12, x2, lsl #2]
    asr     x0, x0, #30             // critical chain
    mov     w3, w0                  // critical chain (64 -> 32)

Store zhi as stwodigits instead to save the type conversions. Invaddition, the compiler can then compute vk[i] - q*w0[i] at first and only then add the carried borrow, so this computation no longer depends on zhi:

    ldr     w4, [x3, x1, lsl #2]
    ldr     w0, [x28, x1, lsl #2]
    umsubl  x0, w0, w13, x4
    add     x2, x0, x2              // critical chain
    and     w4, w2, #0x3fffffff
    str     w4, [x3, x1, lsl #2]
    asr     x2, x2, #30             // critical chain

The loop-carried chain shrinks to two instructions. Knuth invariants are unchanged, so quotients and remainders are the same. The pidigits benchmark improves about 8% on x86-64 and about 12% on AArch64.

The detailed performance data will be pasted later.

Has this already been discussed elsewhere?

thread.html:
This instructions inside the loop on X86_64 systems are also saved. Following is the code changed before:

cb00:	add    (%rdx,%rax,4),%ecx            ; critical chain
cb03:	movslq %ecx,%rdi                     ; critical chain (32->64 bit)
cb06:	mov    0x18(%rbx,%rax,4),%ecx
cb0a:	imul   %rsi,%rcx
cb0e:	sub    %rcx,%rdi                     ; critical chain
cb11:	mov    %edi,%ecx
cb13:	sar    $0x1e,%rdi                    ; critical chain
cb17:	and    $0x3fffffff,%ecx
cb1d:	mov    %ecx,(%rdx,%rax,4)
cb20:	add    $0x1,%rax
cb24:	mov    %edi,%ecx                     ; critical chain (64 -> 32 bit zhi)
cb26:	cmp    %r12,%rax
cb29:	jne    cb00

The code is changed after:

cb00:	mov    0x18(%rbx,%rcx,4),%edx
cb04:	mov    (%rdi,%rcx,4),%eax
cb07:	imul   %r10,%rdx
cb0b:	sub    %rdx,%rax
cb0e:	add    %rsi,%rax                        ; critical chain
cb11:	mov    %eax,%edx
cb13:	sar    $0x1e,%rax                       ; critical chain
cb17:	and    $0x3fffffff,%edx
cb1d:	mov    %rax,%rsi                        ; critical chain  (zhi)
cb20:	mov    %edx,(%rdi,%rcx,4)
cb23:	add    $0x1,%rcx
cb27:	cmp    %r12,%rcx

Instructions on the critical chain are reduced from 5 to 3.

issues.title: Thread.start() retains an unstarted thread when an audit hook raises BaseException
issues.author: GriffinCanCode
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Thread.start() leaves a thread in _limbo when the native-start audit hook raises KeyboardInterrupt or SystemExit. No OS thread was created, but threading.enumerate() keeps returning the thread. Raising RuntimeError from the same hook already cleans up correctly.

import sys
import threading

def refuse(event, args):
    if event == "_thread.start_joinable_thread":
        raise KeyboardInterrupt

sys.addaudithook(refuse)
thread = threading.Thread()
try:
    thread.start()
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

print(thread._os_thread_handle.ident)       # 0: no OS thread was created
print(thread.is_alive())                   # False
print(thread in threading.enumerate())     # True

I expect the failed thread to be removed from the registry. threading.enumerate() excludes threads that have not started.

The native-start call is wrapped in except Exception, which misses these exceptions. Cleanup must also distinguish refusal from an exception arriving as the native call returns after creating an OS thread; that thread still needs its registration.

This differs from #140746 and #153776, where an OS thread is created and then fails during bootstrap. The earlier cleanup in #51730 covers ThreadError.

CPython main, f7c39d2316e59f17148d93f9ec2d6c4d2b610029, debug build of 3.16.0a1+dev.

Operating systems tested on

macOS 26.6, arm64.

AI tools helped investigate this report and prepare its reproducer.

issues.title: tarfile filter="data" behavior slightly loosened after gh-160097
issues.author: gpshead
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

gh-160097 gave tar_filter a check that data_filter already had. In moving the check, the condition changed. It was "the member's resolved path equals the destination". It is now "the member's normalised name is ."

A symlink or hard-link member can still reach the destination, and now passes filter="data", in three ways:

  • ../dest;
  • s/. after an earlier member s -> ., which needs no knowledge of the destination;
  • ../E, where E is an existing symlink outside the destination that points at it.

vs before:

  • extract() and extractall() may raise RecursionError where they raised OutsideDestinationError.
  • The extraction completes and changes the destination directory's own permissions.
  • A symlink outside the destination that points at it is deleted or replaced. That includes the symlink through which the caller named the destination.

reproducer

common code used be the scenarios below:

import io, os, tarfile, tempfile

def archive(*members):  # (name, type, linkname, mode, data)
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    with tarfile.open(fileobj=buf, mode="w") as tf:
        for name, type, linkname, mode, data in members:
            info = tarfile.TarInfo(name)
            info.type, info.linkname, info.mode, info.size = type, linkname, mode, len(data)
            tf.addfile(info, io.BytesIO(data))
    buf.seek(0)
    return tarfile.open(fileobj=buf)
  1. RecursionError vs prior OutsideDestinationError
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as box:
    os.mkdir(box + "/dest")
    with archive(("../dest", tarfile.SYMTYPE, "dest", 0o777, b"")) as tf:
        tf.extractall(box + "/dest", filter="data")
  1. link destination permissions
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as box:
    os.mkdir(box + "/dest", 0o700)
    with archive(("d", tarfile.DIRTYPE, "", 0o755, b""),
                 ("s", tarfile.SYMTYPE, ".", 0o777, b""),
                 ("s/.", tarfile.LNKTYPE, "d", 0o777, b"")) as tf:
        tf.extractall(box + "/dest", filter="data")
    print("destination mode:", oct(os.stat(box + "/dest").st_mode & 0o7777))

that was previously an OutsideDestinationError, now it changes the mode of the destination. security regression, this one lets any destination path be targeted.

  1. symlink outside destination
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as box:
    os.mkdir(box + "/real")
    os.symlink("real", box + "/current")
    with archive(("first.txt", tarfile.REGTYPE, "", 0o644, b"1"),
                 ("../current", tarfile.SYMTYPE, "real", 0o777, b""),
                 ("later.txt", tarfile.REGTYPE, "", 0o644, b"2")) as tf:
        tf.extractall(box + "/current", filter="data")
    print("current is a symlink:", os.path.islink(box + "/current"))
    print("current/:", os.listdir(box + "/current"), " real/:", os.listdir(box + "/real"))

That should've been an OutsideDestinationError, now it mucks with things outside... security regression, but requires a pre-existing symlink to target.

Fix thoughts

Minimal: put the five removed lines in tarfile from https://patch-diff.githubusercontent.com/raw/python/cpython/pull/160098.patch back while keeping the six new ones?

Broader: judge a link member by where the link is made (ie: did the tarfile extraction write it), resolving the parent directory only.

3.13, CPython main branch

Operating systems tested on:

Linux

the broader fix might look something like https://github.com/gpshead/cpython/pull/23/files

thread.html:
