issues.title: `PyType_GetModuleByDef` isn't safe to call in `tp_dealloc`
issues.author: da-woods
issues.bodyHTML:
Crash report

// example.c

#define PY_SSIZE_T_CLEAN
#include <Python.h>
#include <stddef.h>

static PyModuleDef examplemodule = {
    PyModuleDef_HEAD_INIT,
    "example",
    "Example module with a heap type.",
    -1,
    NULL,
    NULL,
    NULL,
    NULL,
    NULL
};

typedef struct {
    PyObject_HEAD
    PyObject *first;
    PyObject *second;
} HeapPairObject;

static void
HeapPair_dealloc(HeapPairObject *self)
{
    PyTypeObject *tp = Py_TYPE(self);

    PyType_GetModuleByDef(tp, &examplemodule);

    PyObject_GC_UnTrack(self);
    Py_XDECREF(self->first);
    Py_XDECREF(self->second);

    tp->tp_free((PyObject *)self);

    Py_CLEAR(tp);
}

static void
HeapPair_clear(HeapPairObject *self) {
    Py_CLEAR(self->first);
    Py_CLEAR(self->second);
}

static int
HeapPair_traverse(HeapPairObject *self, visitproc visit, void *arg) {
    Py_VISIT(self->first);
    Py_VISIT(self->second);
    Py_VISIT(Py_TYPE(self));

    return 0;
}

static PyObject *
HeapPair_new(PyTypeObject *subtype, PyObject *args, PyObject *kwds) {
    HeapPairObject *out = (HeapPairObject*)subtype->tp_alloc(subtype, 0);
    if (out) {
        // Create some exciting circular references
        out->first = Py_NewRef(subtype);
        out->second = Py_NewRef(out);
    }
    return (PyObject*)out;
}



static PyMemberDef HeapPair_members[] = {
    {"first", Py_T_OBJECT_EX, offsetof(HeapPairObject, first), 0, "first attribute"},
    {"second", Py_T_OBJECT_EX, offsetof(HeapPairObject, second), 0, "second attribute"},
    {NULL, 0, 0, 0, NULL}
};

static PyType_Slot HeapPair_slots[] = {
    {Py_tp_dealloc, HeapPair_dealloc},
    {Py_tp_members, HeapPair_members},
    {Py_tp_new, HeapPair_new},
    {Py_tp_clear, HeapPair_clear},
    {Py_tp_traverse, HeapPair_traverse},
    {0, NULL},
};

static PyType_Spec HeapPair_spec = {
    .name = "example.HeapPair",
    .basicsize = sizeof(HeapPairObject),
    .flags = Py_TPFLAGS_DEFAULT | Py_TPFLAGS_HEAPTYPE | Py_TPFLAGS_BASETYPE | Py_TPFLAGS_HAVE_GC,
    .slots = HeapPair_slots,
};

PyMODINIT_FUNC
PyInit_example(void)
{
    PyObject *m;
    PyObject *type;

    m = PyModule_Create(&examplemodule);
    if (m == NULL) {
        return NULL;
    }

    type = PyType_FromSpec(&HeapPair_spec);
    if (type == NULL) {
        Py_DECREF(m);
        return NULL;
    }

    if (PyModule_AddObject(m, "HeapPair", type) < 0) {
        Py_DECREF(type);
        Py_DECREF(m);
        return NULL;
    }

    return m;
}
# setup.py - For convenience - you can build it how you like

from setuptools import Extension, setup

setup(
    name="example",
    version="0.1.0",
    ext_modules=[
        Extension(
            "example",
            ["example.c"],
        )
    ],
)
# test_example.py
import example

def testfun():
    class C(example.HeapPair):
        pass

    C.inst = C()

for n in range(100):
    testfun()

I build the module and then run python3 test_example.py. It crashes with:

python3: Objects/typeobject.c:5537: PyObject *PyType_GetModuleByDef(PyTypeObject *, PyModuleDef *): Assertion `mro != ((void*)0)' failed.
Aborted                    (core dumped) python3 test_example.py

What I believe is happening:

I've created a bunch of circular references so my Python type C (which inherits from my C type) and the instance of C will both need the GC to free them. I think it's pretty arbitrary which one gets cleared first. If C gets cleared first then tp_mro is cleared:

cpython/Objects/typeobject.c

Line 7175 in 19270d3

Py_CLEAR(type->tp_mro);

However the mro is needed to find the module:

cpython/Objects/typeobject.c

Lines 5919 to 5921 in 19270d3

PyObject *mro = lookup_tp_mro(type);
// The type must be ready
assert(mro != NULL);

I don't believe using the _DuringGC variant fixes the problem. I've tested on 3.14, but the relevant bits of the current main CPython source looks the same. I think the same argument also applies to tp_clear too.

Note that one good reason to get the module is if I need the module state for PyObject_GetTypeData (i.e. I need to clear up an opaque type in abi3t).

Obviously there's a bit of a general nightmare here that once the GC is involved then you could also be clearing up the module state too so it's very hard to get a good order of destruction that suits everyone (and I can't see a great solution for that). But obviously this is an assert that I'm hitting so I can't even attempt some best effort error handling.

@encukou - tagging you because I think this is something you might be interested in.

CPython versions tested on:

3.14

Operating systems tested on:

Linux

Output from running 'python -VV' on the command line:

Python 3.14.6 (main, Jun 23 2026, 15:17:22) [Clang 22.1.3 ]

thread.author: da-woods
thread.html: I think for a lot of proposed uses, PyType_GetBaseByToken would work since it doesn't seem to have the same restriction about MRO currently being non-NULL.

issues.title: No way to disable bytecode compilation when installing cpython
issues.author: rossburton
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

When building and installing cpython it can be preferable to have more control over when compileall is executed. It would be useful if there was a way to disable the compilation in the libinstall target for people who want to control the compilation without doing it twice.

(Happy to send a patch if this isn't rejected out of hand)

CPython versions tested on:

3.14

Operating systems tested on:

Linux

thread.author: picnixz
thread.html: What is the use case explicitly? is it a theoretical feature or is there a real need from redistributors?

thread.author: rossburton
thread.html: The specific use case is that we're packaging the standard library in more than one package so the easy way to handle this is to split the packaging up and then compile the py, because then the pyc goes into the right package without needing more work.

thread.author: picnixz
thread.html: I have no strong opinion here but not compiling bytecode may be relevant. cc @encukou

thread.author: encukou
thread.html:
Maybe we can turn this into a compileall.py improvement?
IMO, the invocation should be make install COMPILEALL_OPTS='--no-recursion --skip=.*', which would be possible with two patches:

  • allow multiple -x options, so Makefile's -x badsyntax doesn't overwrite COMPILEALL_OPTS
  • add long option aliases for readibility: --skip for -x, --[no-]recursion to -l; perhaps more.

thread.author: rossburton
thread.html:
I have a patch to add long options for clarity.

The public API such as compileall.compile_dir exposes a single rx regex, so this can't be just changed to a list.

However, the argument parser could allow multiple skips and construct a new regex. So something like python3 -mcompileall -x foo -x bar ... would result in rx = r"foo|bar". If this is acceptable I can post it.

issues.title: HAVE_PROTOTYPES macro should be restored
issues.author: smontanaro
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

The HAVE_PROTOTYPES macro disappeared recently (commit e4f7327c). While it's not used in Python proper, it seems to be used by some third-party packages. Removing it seems short-sighted. Without it, the pillow package fails to build, because it requires ANSI prototypes and no longer thinks Python provides them.

3.16

Operating systems tested on:

macOS

thread.author: smontanaro
thread.html: @methane @emmatyping

thread.author: hugovk
thread.html:
Don't worry about Pillow, we've (this week!) already removed HAVE_PROTOTYPES and STDC_HEADERS, they were added 30 years ago and are no longer needed.

  • python-pillow/Pillow#10324
  • python-pillow/Pillow#10323

If it shows up in other libraries, let's see if they can also remove them. The alpha period is the right time for this, and we can always restore later on if it's really necessary.

thread.author: smontanaro
thread.html: Thanks @hugovk. So I should be able to just reference the Pillow repo for the time being?

thread.author: Keith-S-Thompson
thread.html: I don't see a commit e4f7327c. The relevant commit seems to be b26fc41.

thread.author: hugovk
thread.html:
5. Thanks @hugovk. So I should be able to just reference the Pillow repo for the time being?

Yes, I think so. Prototypes are C89, long required: https://peps.python.org/pep-0007/#c-standards

From what I can tell, the oldest Python that no longer needs this macro is 2.0: if a compiler can't handle prototypes, it can't compile Python.h from 2.0 onwards. So if your library (somehow!) supports Python 2.0 up to 3.16, it's fine with these removals.

Python 1.6 is the last release that needs this macro. So if your library (somehow!!!) supports Python 1.6 up to 3.16, then the macro is needed. I doubt there are any, and we don't need to support them :)

issues.title: _sre: out-of-bounds read in the SRE code validator for IN opcode with skip < 2
issues.author: DmitryTD
issues.bodyHTML:
Crash report

_sre.compile() validates the raw code list it gets. For the IN opcode, the validator reads out of bounds when the skip operand is 0 or 1.

Found with a fuzzer.

import _sre
_sre.compile("x", 0, [13, 0, 1], 0, {}, ())

The code list is [SRE_OP_IN, skip=0, SRE_OP_SUCCESS] (13 is SRE_OP_IN, 1 is SRE_OP_SUCCESS).

==19==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x50d400012c80 (pc 0x555b6ecddef2 bp 0x7fff9102de70 sp 0x7fff9102de10 T0)
==19==The signal is caused by a READ memory access.
    #0 in _validate_inner Modules/_sre/sre.c:2218:30
    #1 in _validate_outer Modules/_sre/sre.c:2461:12
    #2 in _validate Modules/_sre/sre.c:2467:9
    #3 in _sre_compile_impl Modules/_sre/sre.c:1849:10
    #4 in _sre_compile Modules/_sre/clinic/sre.c.h:1147:20
    ...

SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: SEGV Modules/_sre/sre.c:2218:30 in _validate_inner
==19==ABORTING

The crash is the code[skip-2] read in the SRE_OP_IN branch of _validate_inner(). The code is:

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/e35424611f8/Modules/_sre/sre.c#L2214-L2220

GET_SKIP;
/* Stop 1 before the end; we check the FAILURE below */
if (_validate_charset(code, code+skip-2))
    FAIL;
if (code[skip-2] != SRE_OP_FAILURE)
    FAIL;
code += skip-1;

GET_SKIP checks only that skip is not too big (not past the end of the code). It does not check that skip is too small. When skip is 0 or 1, skip - 2 is a wrong index, so code[skip-2] reads out of bounds.

I did not find a way to reproduce this with the public re module. It looks like its compiler always emits skip >= 2 for IN.

A possible fix is to reject skip < 2 right after GET_SKIP:

GET_SKIP;
if (skip < 2)
    FAIL;

issues.title: io.TextIOWrapper.tell() can read past its snapshot buffer after seek() past a carriage return
issues.author: tonghuaroot
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

io.TextIOWrapper.tell() can compute a skip larger than its snapshot buffer after seek() to a position that follows a carriage return. with universal newlines the decoder keeps a pending \r, so the seek cookie has chars_to_skip > 0; seek() replays the input chunk into a new snapshot but leaves the bytes-per-char ratio from the previous read(). tell() then multiplies that stale ratio by chars_to_skip. on a debug build the assertion in _io_TextIOWrapper_tell_impl fires:

import io

f = io.TextIOWrapper(io.BytesIO(b"one\rtwo\rthree\r"), encoding="utf-8")
f.read(4)
pos = f.tell()
f.read(1)
f.seek(pos)
f.read(1)
print(f.tell())
Assertion failed: (skip_bytes <= PyBytes_GET_SIZE(next_input)), function _io_TextIOWrapper_tell_impl, file textio.c, line 2987.

release builds do not assert. the oversized length is handed to the decoder, which reads past the bytes object, so tell() can fail on valid input. on 3.13.13 and 3.14.7:

import io

data = ('ab\r' + '\u20ac' * 15).encode()
f = io.TextIOWrapper(io.BytesIO(data), encoding='utf-8')
f.read(3)
pos = f.tell()
f.read(1)
f.seek(pos)
f.read(1)
f.tell()

issues.title: symtable: repr() of a Symbol raises TypeError under -X lazy_imports=all
issues.author: anistark
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

With -X lazy_imports=all, repr() of a symtable.Symbol raises TypeError:

import symtable
top = symtable.symtable('x = 1', '<string>', 'exec')
print(top.get_symbols())
$ ./python -X lazy_imports=all repro.py
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "repro.py", line 3, in <module>
    print(top.get_symbols())
    ~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "Lib/symtable.py", line 264, in __repr__
    flags_str = '|'.join(self._flags_str())
  File "Lib/symtable.py", line 272, in _flags_str
    if self.__flags & flagvalue == flagvalue:
       ~~~~~~~~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for &: 'int' and 'lazy_import'

Without the option it prints [<symbol 'x': LOCAL, DEF_LOCAL>].

Lib/symtable.py builds its _flags and _scopes_value_to_name tables from globals():

cpython/Lib/symtable.py

Lines 388 to 391 in c79146a

_flags = [('USE', USE)]
_flags.extend(kv for kv in globals().items() if kv[0].startswith('DEF_'))
_scopes_names = ('FREE', 'LOCAL', 'GLOBAL_IMPLICIT', 'GLOBAL_EXPLICIT', 'CELL')
_scopes_value_to_name = frozendict({globals()[n]: n for n in _scopes_names})

With lazy_imports=all, the from _symtable import ... at the top of the module is lazy, so globals() holds lazy_import objects instead of the integer constants. _flags breaks repr() as above, and once that is fixed, _scopes_value_to_name still makes the scope print as 1 instead of LOCAL.

This is the test_symtable failure mentioned in gh-149640, and why test_symtable is in Lib/test/lazy_imports_all_exclude.txt. The 3.15 branch has the same code.

Possible fix: take the values from the _symtable module (for example getattr(_symtable, name)) instead of from globals(). With that, test_symtable passes with and without -X lazy_imports=all and can come off the exclusion list. I can open a PR if this sounds right.

CPython main branch

Linux

The _symtable fix looks right to me.

PEP 810 explicitly leaves lazy objects in globals() so introspection does not trigger imports. Resolution during iteration needs changes to dict semantics, and the imports can themselves change the dict.

As for whether we need to do something broader, I think the design of making globals() return the lazy import objects was discussed in some depth during the PEP discussions. issues.title: compile: double free of pc->fail_pop in codegen_pattern_or on allocation failure with nested or-pattern
issues.author: waroad
issues.bodyHTML:
When an allocation fails while compiling a match statement whose or-pattern contains another or-pattern, codegen_pattern_or frees pc->fail_pop and codegen_match then frees it again, so compile() crashes instead of raising MemoryError.

The failure is injected with the test-only _testcapi.call_with_nomemory:

import ast, _testcapi
tree = ast.parse('def f(x):\n match x:\n  case [1|2] | 3: pass\n')
for off in range(1500):
    held = None
    held = [[] for _ in range(128)]   # refill/empty the list freelist so PyList_New in codegen really allocates
    try:
        _testcapi.call_with_nomemory(off, off + 1, compile, tree, 'a.py', 'exec')
    except (MemoryError, SyntaxError):
        pass
print('survived')

Saved as input.py and run on an ASan build that includes _testcapi:

python input.py

Output:

ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x503000002988
READ of size 1 at 0x503000002988 thread T0
    #0 in _PyMem_DebugCheckAddress Objects/obmalloc.c:3351
    #4 in PyMem_Free Objects/obmalloc.c:1292
    #5 in codegen_match Python/codegen.c:6775
...
freed by thread T0 here:
    #5 in PyMem_Free Objects/obmalloc.c:1292
    #6 in codegen_pattern_or Python/codegen.c:6573

Every injected failure should surface as MemoryError from compile(), with the pointer freed once, and the script should print survived.

Found at commit 3646ea5. It still reproduces at 3acc941 (latest upstream checked): ASan heap-use-after-free in the checking build, and the release build segfaults (exit code 139). case (1|2) | 3, where the inner or-pattern is not inside a sequence pattern, survives.

Looks like in the inner codegen_pattern_or, old_pc = *pc copies the outer fail_pop array, and if the first PyList_New(0) in the loop fails, goto error runs before pc->fail_pop = NULL. The error block then frees old_pc.fail_pop while pc->fail_pop still points to it, and codegen_match frees it again.

Found with an LLM-based testing tool; I used Claude to reduce it and look for the cause.

issues.title: codeobject: == on code objects takes exponential time in scope nesting depth (30 nested classes still running after 120 s)
issues.author: waroad
issues.bodyHTML:
Comparing two equal code objects with == takes time that doubles with each level of nested class or def scope, so a 30-deep nest is still running after 2 minutes.

import ast
depth = 30
source = ''.join(' ' * d + 'class C%d:\n' % d for d in range(depth)) + ' ' * depth + 'pass\n'
tree = ast.parse(source)
a = compile(tree, 'f.py', 'exec'); b = compile(tree, 'f.py', 'exec')
print(a == b)

Saved as input.py and run with python input.py, it printed nothing within 120 s and was killed by timeout (exit 124). With smaller depth, a == b on a release build took about 0.3 s at depth 16, 3.6 s at 20 and 14 s at 22 (the host was heavily loaded, so only the factor of about 2 per level matters).

It should print True promptly, since the two code objects come from the same tree and are equal, with time roughly linear in the nesting depth.

Found at commit 3646ea5; it still reproduces at 3acc941 (latest upstream, release build: killed at the timeout). Both the checking build (ASan/UBSan) and the release build hang the same way, with no assertion or sanitizer report. Nested defs and annotated class bodies show the same growth.

Looks like code_richcompare in Objects/codeobject.c compares _PyCode_ConstantKey(co_consts). For a tuple the key is the pair (tuple_of_item_keys, original_tuple), so comparing two keys recurses into each nested code object twice (once through the item keys, once through the original tuple), which doubles the work per level.

Related: #101346 ("The hash and equals methods of code objects are large, complex and unnecessary").

The deep nesting comes from a generated test, not from a real program.

Found with an LLM-based testing tool; I used Claude to reduce it and look for the cause.

issues.title: `subprocess.run()` can warn that a child is still running after killing it on Ctrl-C
issues.author: jelle-openai
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Run this on Linux or MacOS and press Ctrl-C while sleep is running. start_new_session=True keeps the child from receiving the terminal's SIGINT.

python3 -Wd -c 'import subprocess; subprocess.run(["sleep", "60"], start_new_session=True)'

After the expected KeyboardInterrupt traceback, Python prints an additional warning.

ResourceWarning: subprocess 9 is still running

I would expect run() to take care of reaping the child it killed. The caller never gets a Popen object to wait on. In a separate run I used os.waitid() with WNOWAIT inside the KeyboardInterrupt handler and confirmed that the child had already died from SIGKILL before the warning was emitted.

It looks like Popen.wait() uses its 250 ms grace period after SIGINT. When that expires, run() calls kill() and reraises, relying on Popen.__exit__() to wait. But the KeyboardInterrupt branch in __exit__() skips the wait once the grace period has been used. Then __del__() sees returncode is None and warns before polling. run() exception handler · Popen cleanup · Original rationale for the grace period

Reproduced on Linux with CPython 3.14.8, 3.15.0, and a 3.16 development build, and on MacOS with 3.12 and a 3.16 dev build.

3.12, 3.13, 3.14, 3.15, 3.16

issues.author: hroncok
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

In Fedora, we have recently triaged some CVE that were publicly displosed for pypa/virtualenv. I decided to check if anything is also reproducible via plain venv and it is.

CVE-2026-113723, CVE-2026-113725, CVE-2026-113726, CVE-2026-113732, CVE-2026-113715, CVE-2026-113716, CVE-2026-113721

Neither is considered a security vulnerability in CPython:

Vulnerabilities must not depend on malicious control of Python’s launch conditions, including (but not limited to) command line arguments, environment variables, or modifications to files on the target system. We assume that, at the time Python is executed, the environment is as intended by the legitimate user, and any malicious variation from this cannot be mitigated by Python itself.

However, those issues are still nice to fix.

To reproduce:

#!/bin/bash
set -u
for PY in python3.14 python3.15 python3.16; do
  echo "################## $PY ##################"
  WORK=$(mktemp -d)
  cd "$WORK"

  echo "=== 1. bash/zsh PS1 redraw injection ==="
  echo "    cf. virtualenv CVE-2026-113723, CVE-2026-113725, CVE-2026-113726"
  "$PY" -m venv --without-pip --prompt "x\$(touch $WORK/PWNED_BASH)y" "$WORK/venv1" >/dev/null 2>&1
  bash -c "source $WORK/venv1/bin/activate; echo \"\${PS1@P}\"" >/dev/null 2>&1
  test -e "$WORK/PWNED_BASH" && echo "BASH: VULNERABLE" || echo "BASH: not reproduced"

  "$PY" -m venv --without-pip --prompt "x\$(touch $WORK/PWNED_ZSH)y" "$WORK/venv1z" >/dev/null 2>&1
  zsh -c "setopt PROMPT_SUBST; source $WORK/venv1z/bin/activate; print -P \"\$PS1\"" >/dev/null 2>&1
  test -e "$WORK/PWNED_ZSH" && echo "ZSH: VULNERABLE" || echo "ZSH: not reproduced"

  echo "=== 2. fish quote-escaping gap ==="
  echo "    cf. virtualenv CVE-2026-113732"
  mkdir -p "$WORK/workdir2"
  "$PY" -m venv --without-pip --prompt "x\\'\$(touch PWNED)'\\'" "$WORK/venv2" >/dev/null 2>&1
  (cd "$WORK/workdir2" && fish --no-config -c "source $WORK/venv2/bin/activate.fish" >/dev/null 2>&1)
  test -e "$WORK/workdir2/PWNED" && echo "FISH: VULNERABLE" || echo "FISH: not reproduced"

  echo "=== 3. pyvenv.cfg injection via command= ==="
  echo "    cf. virtualenv CVE-2026-113715"
  "$PY" -m venv --without-pip --prompt $'legit\ninclude-system-site-packages = true\n#' "$WORK/venv3" >/dev/null 2>&1
  RESULT=$("$WORK/venv3/bin/$PY" -c "import site; print(site.ENABLE_USER_SITE)" 2>&1)
  echo "ENABLE_USER_SITE=$RESULT"

  echo "=== 4. site-packages redirected via symlinked intermediate dir ==="
  echo "    cf. virtualenv CVE-2026-113716"
  mkdir -p "$WORK/envdir4" "$WORK/outside4"
  ln -s "$WORK/outside4" "$WORK/envdir4/lib"
  "$PY" -m venv --without-pip "$WORK/envdir4" >/dev/null 2>&1
  test -d "$WORK/outside4/$PY/site-packages" && echo "SYMLINK-DIR: VULNERABLE" || echo "SYMLINK-DIR: not reproduced"

  echo "=== 5. file overwrite through pre-existing symlink ==="
  echo "    cf. virtualenv CVE-2026-113721"
  mkdir -p "$WORK/envdir5/bin"
  echo SENSITIVE > "$WORK/outside5"
  ln -s "$WORK/outside5" "$WORK/envdir5/bin/activate"
  "$PY" -m venv --without-pip "$WORK/envdir5" >/dev/null 2>&1
  grep -q "virtualenv\|venv" "$WORK/outside5" 2>/dev/null && echo "SYMLINK-FILE: VULNERABLE" || echo "SYMLINK-FILE: not reproduced"

  rm -rf "$WORK"
  echo
done

issues.title: tarfile: extractfile(member).read() of a sparse member is slow due to repeated bytes concatenation
issues.author: devdavidejesus
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

_FileInFile.read() in Lib/tarfile.py builds its result with buf += b for each data segment and buf += NUL * length for each hole of a sparse member. Each bytes concatenation copies the whole accumulated buffer, so reading a sparse member with TarFile.extractfile(member).read() takes time proportional to the member size times the number of sparse segments.

Holes take no space in the archive, so a small archive is enough to make this noticeable. extract(), extractall() and reading the member in small chunks (for example with shutil.copyfileobj()) are not affected.

Reproducer

import io, tarfile, time

def build(n, blk=4096):
    # GNU sparse 0.1 (pax) member: n data blocks separated by holes.
    t = tarfile.TarInfo("GNUSparseFile.0/a.img")
    t.size = n * blk
    t.pax_headers = {
        "GNU.sparse.map": ",".join(f"{2 * i * blk},{blk}" for i in range(n)),
        "GNU.sparse.name": "a.img",
        "GNU.sparse.realsize": str(2 * n * blk),
    }
    bio = io.BytesIO()
    with tarfile.open(fileobj=bio, mode="w", format=tarfile.PAX_FORMAT) as tf:
        tf.addfile(t, io.BytesIO(b"D" * t.size))
    return bio.getvalue()

def read_time(n):
    with tarfile.open(fileobj=io.BytesIO(build(n))) as tf:
        f = tf.extractfile(tf.next())
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        f.read()
        return time.perf_counter() - t0

for n in (1000, 2000, 4000):
    print(f"{n} segments: {read_time(n):.2f}s")

On a release build (macOS, Apple M3) the read of a sparse member with 4000 segments takes several seconds; the time roughly quadruples when the segment count doubles. With the change below each read is a fraction of a second.

Suggested fix

Accumulate the pieces in a list and join once, instead of repeated concatenation:

-        buf = b""
+        chunks = []
         while size > 0:
             ...
-                buf += b
+                chunks.append(b)
             else:
-                buf += NUL * length
+                chunks.append(NUL * length)
             size -= length
             self.position += length
-        return buf
+        return b"".join(chunks)

I have a branch with this change and a regression test that reads a multi-segment sparse member through extractfile().read() and in chunks, and compares both to the expected content. I can open a PR if this looks right.

issues.title: TypeError when pickling directly instantiated urllib.parse result objects
issues.author: austinaviv
issues.bodyHTML:
Python Version

Python 3.15 / main

Operating System

All platforms

Description

When directly instantiating result objects from urllib.parse (SplitResult, ParseResult, DefragResult, or their bytes counterparts), pickling or calling __getstate__() raises a TypeError:

import urllib.parse, pickle
res = urllib.parse.SplitResult('http', 'example.com', '/', '', '')
pickle.dumps(res)

Output:

TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable

This occurs because _ResultBase.__getstate__() assumes super().__getstate__() returns a 2-tuple:

def __getstate__(self):
    state = super().__getstate__()
    try:
        if state[1]['_keep_empty'] == _MISSING_AS_NONE_DEFAULT:
            del state[1]['_keep_empty']
            if state == (None, {}):
                state = None
    except LookupError:
        pass
    return state

When _keep_empty has not been set (for instance, when constructing the result class directly rather than via urlsplit() or urlparse()), object.__getstate__() returns None. state[1] then fails with TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable, which is not handled by except LookupError:.

Checking if state is not None: before subscripting resolves the error.

issues.title: asyncio: run newly scheduled callbacks eagerly before polling for I/O
issues.author: asvetlov
issues.bodyHTML:
Feature or enhancement

Currently, BaseEventLoop._run_once() runs only the callbacks that were ready when the iteration started. Callbacks scheduled by those callbacks wait for the next iteration, which first polls the selector (select()/epoll_wait()) with a zero timeout. Code that resolves futures, wakes tasks or chains call_soon() therefore pays for one I/O poll per hop, even when there is no I/O to process.

The good example is using asyncio.Queue: await q.put(item) pushes an item into the queue and wakes up the getter on the next event loop iteration only.
The same is true with network protocols: StreamReaderProtocol.data.received() feeds data to StreamReader and wakes await reader.read() after selector.select() call. Custom code that works with asyncio protocols (or loop.sock_recv()) explicitly suffers from the same problem.
If the code uses more moving parts, e.g. protocol->message-parser->user-code, each indirection level adds its own delayed call that increases latency.

I propose letting the loop keep running newly scheduled callbacks for a short, bounded time before it polls for I/O again (“eager processing”).

If after running scheduled callbacks (asyncio.Handler instances) there are new callbacks registered for the next loop iteration, they are executed immediately.

The implementation adds time- and count-based limits for eager callback execution for preventing possible infinite callbacks chain.

Has this already been discussed elsewhere?

I have already discussed this feature proposal on Discourse

Links to previous discussion of this feature:

https://discuss.python.org/t/an-eager-way-to-set-result-on-asyncio-future/106161/27

issues.title: documentation of `tp_alloc` and `tp_free` inheritance for heap types is incorrect
issues.author: davidhewitt
issues.bodyHTML:
Documentation

The documentation for tp_alloc currently reads:

Inheritance:

Static subtypes inherit this slot, which will be PyType_GenericAlloc() if inherited from object.

Heap subtypes do not inherit this slot.

Default:

For heap subtypes, this field is always set to PyType_GenericAlloc().

For static subtypes, this slot is inherited (see above).

The information for heap subtypes is not correct. If not set, the slot is inherited in inherit_slots unconditionally.

It appears that "heap subtypes" in this statement might incorrectly refer to those allocated by type() or class Python operations rather than via C-API constructors.

tp_free seems to have a similar issue. The documentation for "static types" seems to again apply to all types constructed through the C API, whether a static or heap type. The documentation for "heap types" seems to instead apply to Python-created types.

Should the behaviour be adjusted to match documentation, or the documentation corrected? cc @encukou @vstinner

issues.title: Tachyon: GeckoCollector closes open markers too early when replay batches arrive out of order
issues.author: ivonastojanovic
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

GeckoCollector.collect() sets last_sample_time to the last timestamp of the most recent call, not the latest one seen. During binary replay, batches from different threads can arrive out of time order, so markers get closed too early and can even end before they start.

from _remote_debugging import FrameInfo, InterpreterInfo, LocationInfo, ThreadInfo
from profiling.sampling.gecko_collector import GeckoCollector

collector = GeckoCollector(1000)
frames = [FrameInfo(("t.py", LocationInfo((1, 1, 0, 0)), "f", None))]
# Thread 2's last batch arrives after thread 1's, as binary replay can deliver them
for tid, timestamps in [(1, [1000]), (2, [1500]), (1, [3000, 4000]), (2, [2500])]:
    collector.collect([InterpreterInfo((0, [ThreadInfo((tid, 0, frames))]))],
                      timestamps_us=timestamps)
print(collector.last_sample_time)  # 1.5, should be 3.0

issues.title: venv: --prompt / env-dir value is not escaped for the shell's prompt-display pass in generated activate (bash/zsh)
issues.author: apocalypse-agent
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Context

This was first reported privately to PSRT and triaged as outside Python's security threat model (it depends on launch conditions — --prompt or the environment directory name). I'm opening it here as a robustness / least-surprise improvement, as suggested on the advisory — not as a security report, and not to re-litigate that decision.

What happens

python -m venv writes the environment prompt (from --prompt, or by default the env directory's basename) into the generated bin/activate:

PS1="("__VENV_PROMPT__") ${PS1:-}"

replace_variables() quotes __VENV_PROMPT__ with shlex.quote, which is correct for the assignment. But bash (and zsh with PROMPT_SUBST) re-expand PS1 on every prompt draw (promptvars, on by default), and shlex.quote does not neutralize that second pass. So a prompt containing $(...) or backticks executes when the prompt is rendered:

$ python3 -m venv --prompt '$(id)' venv
$ grep 'PS1=' venv/bin/activate
    PS1="("'$(id)'") ${PS1:-}"
$ bash -c 'source venv/bin/activate; : "${PS1@P}"'   # ${PS1@P} = bash's prompt render
uid=1000(...) gid=1000(...) ...                       # runs

In an interactive shell this runs on the first prompt after source. The same activate template + shlex.quote-only handling are present on main, so it's unfixed there too.

Why it's worth hardening (not a security claim)

  • Surprising: a documented, seemingly-cosmetic option (--prompt) and the default prompt (the directory name) can execute shell code on activation.
  • Consistency: virtualenv treats this as in-scope and already escapes the prompt for the display pass (CVE-2026-113725 / -113726 / -113732); venv diverges.
  • It's the display-pass complement to the assignment-pass quoting that gh-124651 (CVE-2024-9287) added.

Suggested change

Escape the prompt for the shell's prompt-display expansion in addition to the assignment: for bash/zsh, neutralize `, $, and backslash before substitution — since bash expands PS1 in two passes, the escaping must survive both (double-escaping), mirroring virtualenv's fix. Apply the equivalent to activate.csh (history !) and verify Activate.ps1.

issues.title: Speed up `print()` by looking up `file.write` once per call
issues.author: cmaloney
issues.bodyHTML:
Feature or enhancement

print() currently looks up file.write, creating a new bound method, for every argument, separator, and line ending. Currently print('a', 1, 2.5) does six lookups. The default sep and end also go through PyFile_WriteString(), which converts " " and "\n" from C strings with strlen() and the UTF-8 decoder each time, only to return CPython's cached one-character strings. Looking write up once per call and passing the cached strings directly makes print() 1.20x faster (geometric mean), and write() is still called exactly as before.

Measurements

Benchmark main patched Time Instructions
print('hello world'), /dev/null 291 ns 234 ns 1.25x faster −18%
print('hello world'), StringIO 253 ns 193 ns 1.31x faster −14%
print('a', 1, 2.5), /dev/null 996 ns 687 ns 1.45x faster −31%
print(*range(10)), /dev/null 2.86 µs 1.73 µs 1.66x faster −39%
print(), /dev/null n.s. −3%
print('x' * 2**20), /dev/null n.s.
print(list(range(1000))), /dev/null n.s. −0.1%
print('hello world', flush=True), disk file 1.55 µs 1.38 µs 1.12x faster

Time: pyperf, -p 10, release build without PGO, Linux x86_64. n.s. = not significant. Instructions: per print() call, measured with valgrind (cachegrind) and PYTHONHASHSEED=0, with a noise floor of about ±1%.

Behavior change

write is looked up once per call. If an argument's __str__ rebinds file.write, the new method is used from the next print() call on. A file without a write method still raises AttributeError before any argument is converted.

Benchmark

Benchmark script 
import pyperf

SETUP = """
import io, os, tempfile
devnull = open(os.devnull, 'w')
sio = io.StringIO()
disk = tempfile.TemporaryFile('w')
ten_ints = tuple(range(10))
big = 'x' * 2**20
big_list = list(range(1000))
"""

CASES = {
    "one_str[devnull]": "print('hello world', file=devnull)",
    "one_str[sio]": "print('hello world', file=sio)",
    "three_args[devnull]": "print('a', 1, 2.5, file=devnull)",
    "ten_ints[devnull]": "print(*ten_ints, file=devnull)",
    "empty[devnull]": "print(file=devnull)",
    "str_1mib[devnull]": "print(big, file=devnull)",
    "list_1000[devnull]": "print(big_list, file=devnull)",
    "flush[disk]": "print('hello world', file=disk, flush=True)",
}

runner = pyperf.Runner()
for name, stmt in CASES.items():
    runner.timeit(name, stmt, SETUP)
./python-main bench_print.py -p 10 -o main.json
./python-patched bench_print.py -p 10 -o patched.json
python -m pyperf compare_to main.json patched.json --table

Has this already been discussed elsewhere?

This is a minor feature, which does not need previous discussion elsewhere

No response

issues.title: Add `list.discard()` and `deque.discard()`
issues.author: StanFromIreland
issues.bodyHTML:
I suggest adding a list.discard(x) method, which removes the first occurrence of x if present and does nothing otherwise, mirroring set.discard(). This was previously discussed on Discourse.

Removing a value that may not be in a list is a reasonably common pattern, and is generally written today as either:

if x in lst:
    lst.remove(x)

or

try:
    lst.remove(x)
except ValueError:
    pass

The in version scans the list twice on a hit, and the try/except has to deal with the exception. A quick pyperf run on a 1000-element list, removing the last element:

discard:          20.0 us
in + remove:      38.0 us
try/except:       21.0 us

Importantly, the implementation is cheap. The search-and-remove loop in list_remove_impl can be moved into a shared helper so remove() and discard() become thin wrappers around it. There is little extra maintenance cost since the two methods share the same logic.

For now I am just proposing adding the method to list, deque can be done as a follow-up.

Linked PRs

  • gh-160726

thread.author: JelleZijlstra
thread.html:
I believe adding methods to a builtin generally requires a PEP, like for str.removeprefix.

The timings you give aren't very convincing as an argument for adding a new method; it's hardly any faster than the try-except route.

thread.author: StanFromIreland
thread.html:
I believe adding methods to a builtin generally requires a PEP, like for str.removeprefix.

int.is_integer(), bytearray.take_bytes(), bytearray.resize() and float.from_number() / complex.from_number() were all added recently without a PEP. Given that this is a similarly small addition, I thought it would be fine to go through an issue, provided there is general consensus here.

The timings you give aren't very convincing as an argument for adding a new method; it's hardly any faster than the try-except route.

Indeed, and I don't think performance is the main argument. The gain over try/except is small, and it is only the in + remove() idiom that pays for a second scan. However, there are additional reasons:

  • It is a reasonably common operation that currently takes three or four lines (or a double scan) to express. lst.discard(x) states the intent directly, so it is admittedly a bit of syntactic sugar, but sugar that removes a try/except block from the reader's path.
  • It is cheap to implement and maintain (the removal logic already exists).
  • It is consistent with set.discard(), which already has these semantics, and learners are familiar with. Similar reasoning was used for adding int.is_integer().

thread.author: zware
thread.html:
Agreed that a PEP seems appropriate here; there are a few questions to settle.

Off the top of my head:

  • why only list? deque was also mentioned in the inciting discussion, and there could even be an argument for a tuple.discard that returns a new tuple (though tuple.remove does not currently exist).
  • what happens in [1, 1, 2, 3, 5].discard(1)? Should you get [2, 3, 5] or [1, 2, 3, 5]? What about [1, 2, 3, 5, 1].discard(1)?

thread.author: gvanrossum
thread.html:
Can it please return True iff an item was removed? I'd like to write

while l.discard(a):
    pass

to remove all occurrences.

I agree with adding this for convenience.

thread.author: StanFromIreland
thread.html:
why only list?

deque is a possible follow-up, I left it out here to keep the scope small (but it seems this needed more discussion anyway ;-).

tuple.discard() doesn't fit, like set.discard(), this is an in-place mutation, and tuples have no remove() to mirror. A method returning a new tuple would be a different kind of operation.

what happens in [1, 1, 2, 3, 5].discard(1)?

Exactly the same as list.remove(), the first occurrence is removed, so [1, 1, 2, 3, 5].discard(1) gives [1, 2, 3, 5] and [1, 2, 3, 5, 1].discard(1) gives [2, 3, 5, 1]. The only difference from remove() is that a missing value is a no-op instead of a ValueError. The implementation shares the search-and-remove loop with remove(), so the semantics can't drift.

thread.author: StanFromIreland
thread.html:
Can it please return True iff an item was removed?

I like it, and the implementation is simple. It is a minor departure from set.discard, but I don't think that will be much of an issue in practice. Added to the PR in 687d42d.

thread.author: zware
thread.html:
Exactly the same as list.remove(), the first occurrence is removed, so [1, 1, 2, 3, 5].discard(1) gives [1, 2, 3, 5] and [1, 2, 3, 5, 1].discard(1) gives [2, 3, 5, 1]. The only difference from remove() is that a missing value is a no-op instead of a ValueError. The implementation shares the search-and-remove loop with remove(), so the semantics can't drift.

That makes perfect sense from an implementation point of view and is a perfectly reasonable choice to make. I just worry that the name "discard" may imply the other interpretation: after all, set.discard does ensure that the value will no longer be in the set after return. Documentation may be enough to overcome that, or maybe I'm over-worrying :)

FTR, I do like the idea overall and am in favor, particularly with Guido's suggestion to return whether anything changed.

thread.author: gvanrossum
thread.html:
I've been asked to review this. I don't think we need a PEP (Stan answered the objections sensibly, IMO) but I want to wait a little until we're reasonably sure there are no objections here.

I'm not sure if I can ensure all the technical details are correct, but I suppose I can approve it trusting that Stan knows the implementation better than I do at this point. (@StanFromIreland, did you make sure your new code avoids free-threading race conditions?)

Regarding deque, can we change the Issue title to include deque.discard()? It should be a separate PR, since the implementation is entirely different.

thread.author: StanFromIreland
thread.html:
I want to wait a little until we're reasonably sure there are no objections here.

Sounds good, I'm happy to wait a few weeks :-) And no pressure to review. (Zach, could you however please take a look at the docs? Do you think they should be more explicit about the removal behaviour, or do they address your concerns?)

did you make sure your new code avoids free-threading race conditions?

discard() shares its implementation with list.remove(), so it runs under the same critical section and has the same thread-safety guarantees. That is, it cannot corrupt the list, but it is not atomic, since __eq__ can run arbitrary code and release the lock. I documented this (alongside remove()) on the thread safety page.

Regarding deque, can we change the Issue title to include deque.discard()?

Edited, I will open a separate PR for deque.discard() once this one has settled.

thread.author: ZeroIntensity
thread.html:
I personally would like a PEP. The other cited cases for modifying builtins involved providing genuinely new functionality, so if there was a compelling use case, there was little to argue against. In contrast, this is a convenience function, meaning that there's a lot more to discuss about what users actually want. I have several comments, which should be addressed in a PEP:

  1. It'd be nice to see some concrete numbers on how many things are using the in or try workaround (via a code search).
  2. Is discard really the best name? We're already deviating from what set.discard does by returning True, so there's a false symmetry here.
  3. Why not just add a noexcept=True parameter or something like that to remove()?
  4. There are a bunch of other things that have remove methods where this could apply, beyond just deque (such as array.array and bytearray). Should those get discard() methods too? Should we just add discard() to the whole collections.abc.MutableSequence interface?

thread.author: StanFromIreland
thread.html:
If this many people would like a PEP, I can write one, though personally I don't see what it would add over the discussion already happening here. (The questions are the same, we would just be answering them in a different thread.)

It'd be nice to see some concrete numbers

There are a few examples from the stdlib earlier in the Discourse thread. I can try run a search later.

this is a convenience function

Many of the methods on builtins are convenience functions, e.g. bytearray.take_bytes or int.is_integer() (was added purely for consistency with float, which seems a weaker justification than a pattern people already write regularly today).

Is discard really the best name?

Personally, I find it clear. "Discard" carries the implication that you don't care whether the item was there, which is exactly the semantics, and it has precedent in set.discard(), so learners can connect the two. The return value is extra information, but not a change in what the method does.

Why not just add a noexcept=True parameter

Also possible, but nothing else in the list API works that way. There are several ways to spell this, and I don't think any of the alternatives are drastically better than the others, but this one has existing precedent.

Should those get discard() methods too?

deque is a planned follow-up. array.array and bytearray could follow if there is demand, but I don't think the MutableSequence ABC should change, that forces a new method onto every third-party subclass, which is a much bigger compatibility question than adding a method to the concrete types (and... based on recent comments, it seems there's little support for just a list method).

thread.author: zware
thread.html:
Zach, could you however please take a look at the docs? Do you think they should be more explicit about the removal behaviour, or do they address your concerns?

The docs in the PR are fine; they document the behavior explicitly and accurately. My concern is more philosophical: is any documentation (assuming it to be perfect) enough to outweigh the likelihood that users would confidently guess the behavior incorrectly from just the name? There's no objective measure for this that I can see.

"Discard" carries the implication that you don't care whether the item was there, which is exactly the semantics

It also carries the implication that you just want it gone, which is the root of my concern.

thread.author: ZeroIntensity
thread.html:
My point is more that there are clearly some questions here, which is why I think this needs a wider discussion. It's not fair to users to make these kinds of decisions without giving them a chance to voice their opinions.

Many of the methods on builtins are convenience functions, e.g. bytearray.take_bytes or int.is_integer() (was added purely for consistency with float, which seems a weaker justification than a pattern people already write regularly today).

bytearray.take_bytes is precisely not a convenience function. It was added for creating bytes objects from a bytearray without a copy. is_integer was also not entirely for convenience -- it was added for duck typing purposes, so you don't have to do an instance check when looking at something that is potentially an int object. My point is that I don't think they are comparable examples here.

I don't think the MutableSequence ABC should change, that forces a new method onto every third-party subclass, which is a much bigger compatibility question than adding a method to the concrete types

Keep in mind that we are also forcing the method onto every third-party list subclass! If there are legitimate backward compatibility reasons to avoid adding discard to the MutableSequence interface, I'd expect those to also apply to list subclasses.

thread.author: Gerardwx
thread.html: I am willing to write a draft of the PEP.

thread.author: StanFromIreland
thread.html:
Sorry @Gerardwx I had already started on a PEP since I saw quite a few people requested one.

PEP 851 is now live, please discuss at https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-851-add-list-discard/109701. :-)

issues.title: `subprocess.run(timeout=...)` swallows a signal handler's `InterruptedError` on macOS in Python 3.15
issues.author: nick-inkeep
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

On macOS, a timed subprocess.run() does not propagate an exception raised by a Python signal handler while the child is still running. In Python 3.15.2 the handler below raises InterruptedError, but run() returns the child's exit status after the child finishes. Python 3.14.10 raises the exception immediately.

import os
import signal
import subprocess
import sys
import time


def handler(signum, frame):
    signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, signal.SIG_IGN)
    raise InterruptedError(f"interrupted by signal {signum}")


signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, handler)
started = time.monotonic()
child = "import os, time; os.kill(os.getppid(), 15); time.sleep(5)"
try:
    result = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", child], timeout=60)
    print("returned", result.returncode, "after", round(time.monotonic() - started, 2), "seconds")
except BaseException as error:
    print("raised", type(error).__name__, "after", round(time.monotonic() - started, 2), "seconds")

On macOS 26.7 arm64 (Darwin 25.6.0 arm), repeated five times:

  • Python 3.15.2 (v3.15.2, commit 5e58eaad7c58df58dfa8ea549c87996e01dd1077): returned 0 after 5.07–5.08 seconds (5/5).
  • Python 3.14.10 (commit b703b2c5e704341d61e367b9b940b77ed11dded0): raised InterruptedError after 0.01–0.03 seconds (5/5).
  • CPython main at c436e8d83597c6f8c1bc7e37812c98d46670c29a (Python 3.16.0a1+dev): returned 0 after 5.04–5.08 seconds (5/5).

The expected result is for the InterruptedError raised by the handler to escape the timed wait, as it does in 3.14.10. PEP 475 specifies that when a Python signal handler raises, the interrupted system-call wrapper must fail with that exception: https://peps.python.org/pep-0475/#proposal.

CPython versions tested on:

3.15.2, 3.14.10, and CPython main (built at c436e8d83597c6f8c1bc7e37812c98d46670c29a; Python 3.16.0a1+dev).

Operating systems tested on:

macOS 26.7 arm64.

Additional information

At v3.15.2, Lib/subprocess.py:2279-2282 catches OSError around kq.control() and returns False; Python documents InterruptedError as an OSError subclass, so this catch covers the handler exception and _wait() falls back to polling instead of propagating it. The same catch is present on CPython main at Lib/subprocess.py:2303-2306:

cpython/Lib/subprocess.py

Lines 2303 to 2306 in c436e8d

try:
events = kq.control(changelist, 1, max(delay, 0))
except OSError:
return False
.

The release code is at

cpython/Lib/subprocess.py

Lines 2279 to 2282 in 5e58eaa

try:
events = kq.control(changelist, 1, max(delay, 0))
except OSError:
return False
. The 3.15 maintenance branch has the same source at Lib/subprocess.py:2279-2282. The existing test_kqueue_control_error only exercises generic OSError fallback with EPERM at Lib/test/test_subprocess.py:4217-4231; it does not distinguish InterruptedError. The select.kqueue.control() documentation specifies that a signal-handler-raised exception is not retried at Doc/library/select.rst:535-538. Popen._internal_poll() has a separate broad OSError catch around waitpid(WNOHANG) at Lib/subprocess.py:2190; it should be audited for the same signal-handler exception issue.

issues.title: sqlite3: concurrent execute() on a shared Connection crashes the process with a native access violation (threadsafety == 3)
issues.author: BlueDestination
issues.bodyHTML:
Summary

Sharing a single sqlite3.Connection between multiple threads (check_same_thread=False) and calling execute() concurrently on it kills the process with a native access violation (0xC0000005) on 64-bit Windows. sqlite3.threadsafety on this build is 3 (SQLITE_THREADSAFE=1, serialized mode), and the docs for check_same_thread state that the connection may be shared between threads as long as writes are serialized by the user — here nothing is being written at all, only SELECTs of BLOBs.

No Python-level exception is raised; the interpreter dies silently. faulthandler reports the fault on the CONN.execute(...) line (or on the very next byte-consuming line), i.e. the heap has already been corrupted.

The same pattern with no third-party packages at all reproduces, so this is not a C-extension interaction problem.

Reproduction

import faulthandler
import hashlib
import os
import sqlite3
import threading
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

faulthandler.enable(all_threads=True)

CONN = sqlite3.connect(':memory:', check_same_thread=False)
CONN.execute('create table entries (key blob primary key, value blob)')
for i in range(8):
    CONN.execute(
        'insert into entries values (?, ?)',
        (f'k{i}'.encode(), os.urandom(1_400_000)),
    )
CONN.commit()
KEYS = [f'k{i}'.encode() for i in range(8)]


def load(key):
    row = CONN.execute('select value from entries where key = ?', (key,)).fetchone()
    blob = row[0][:]
    return hashlib.blake2b(blob).digest()[0]


def burst():
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:
        sum(executor.map(load, KEYS))


threads = []
start = time.time()
while time.time() - start < 70:
    if sum(t.is_alive() for t in threads) < 4:
        thread = threading.Thread(target=burst, daemon=True)
        thread.start()
        threads.append(thread)
    time.sleep(0.05)
print('no crash', len(threads))

Run it a few times; it usually dies within 10-70 seconds.

Observed output:

Windows fatal exception: access violation

Current thread 0x000079d0 [ThreadPoolExecutor-11_3] (most recent call first):
  File "repro.py", line 29 in load
    row = CONN.execute('select value from entries where key = ?', (key,)).fetchone()
  File ".../concurrent/futures/thread.py", line 73 in run
  File ".../concurrent/futures/thread.py", line 86 in run
  File ".../concurrent/futures/thread.py", line 119 in _worker
  File ".../threading.py", line 1160 in run

In other runs the fault is reported one line later (hashlib.blake2b(blob)), the process exits with code 3221225477 (0xC0000005).

Expected behavior

Either it works (as threadsafety == 3 implies), or a Python-level exception is raised. It should never be possible for concurrent execute() on a shared connection to corrupt the process heap.

Your environment

  • CPython 3.15.1 (tags/v3.15.1:c37e74c, Oct 21 2026), 64-bit, MSC v.1951
  • Windows 11 (10.0.26200)
  • sqlite3.sqlite_version 3.53.4, sqlite3.threadsafety 3
  • No third-party packages involved in the reproduction

Additional context

  • Adding heavy native work in other threads (e.g. polars.read_ipc() on the returned blob) makes the crash appear inside that unrelated library instead, because the corruption has already happened. This is how the problem was originally found: a Streamlit app was dying with 0xC0000005 inside polars, and the crash site moved around randomly.
  • Serializing all execute()/fetchone() calls with a single threading.Lock did not help in the original application; my guess is that cursor teardown (pysqlite_cursor_dealloc -> sqlite3_finalize) happens after the lock is released, and therefore races with another thread reusing the same cached prepared statement.
  • Suspected cause: the per-connection prepared-statement cache and cursor state are shared between threads, while sqlite3_step releases the GIL. Another thread can reset/reuse the same cached sqlite3_stmt while it is still being stepped, or finalize it concurrently.
  • Workaround that works here: one connection per thread (thread-local), which stops the crash.

Happy to add tracing, test a patch, or try a build with Py_DEBUG if that helps.

Feature or enhancement

unquote() runs every string containing % through a regex that splits it into ASCII and non-ASCII chunks. For pure ASCII input, the a common case for URLs and form data, we can skip the regex and generator and decode directly:

if string.isascii():

issues.title: Windows: remote pdb loses its interrupt connection after about 120 seconds
issues.author: philipplc
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Windows: remote pdb loses its interrupt connection after about 120 seconds

Tested on Windows 11 x64 (build 26100), CPython 3.16.0a1+dev,
main commit 7b12a415c85d88eeb22a806b2bc9472d471b8e60, Release/MSVC build.

Remote debugging initially works, but its Windows interrupt channel fails after
about two minutes.

Use this target script:

import os
import time

print(os.getpid(), flush=True)
while True:
    time.sleep(0.1)
  1. Run the target with the newly built interpreter
  2. Attach from another terminal using the same build typing python -m pdb -p <PID>
  3. Enter c, wait 135 seconds, then interrupt from the debugger client (Ctrl+C)

The expected result should be the target stopping and another debugger prompt appearing.

But in this case the target's listener thread fails in sock.recv(1024) with
ConnectionResetError: [WinError 10054]. Forwarding the subsequent client
interrupt fails in self.interrupt_sock.sendall(...) with
ConnectionAbortedError: [WinError 10053]. The target application keeps running.

Confirmed in two automated real pdb.attach() / sys.remote_exec() sessions,
raising SIGINT in the client after 135 seconds. Removing only
sock.shutdown(socket.SHUT_WR) from _PdbServer._start_signal_listener() in
memory made both control runs succeed, including variable evaluation and
detach after the interrupt.

The regular test_remote_pdb still passes (47 passed, 2 skipped), since
its interrupt test does not wait for this tested 120 second idle interval.

CPython main branch

Operating systems tested on:

Windows

thread.author: summeriver13
thread.html:
Root cause is likely the half-close at Lib/pdb.py:3009: the client only writes to that socket (Lib/pdb.py:3517), so shutdown(SHUT_WR) buys nothing and parks the connection in FIN_WAIT_2, which Windows reaps after TcpFinWait2Delay (120 s).
Plain sockets reproduce it without CPython: FIN_WAIT_2 at t=0, then at exactly 120.0 s recv → 10054 and the peer's sendall → 10053, the same pair you saw.
Dropping that one call fixes it locally: test_remote_pdb and test_pdb pass (289 run), and a new test that asserts the interrupt socket never sees EOF fails on main and passes with the change.
Want me to send the PR?

thread.author: cfbolz
thread.html: this was added in 9434709, @godlygeek, do you remember why the half-close is there?

thread.author: summeriver13
thread.html:
I went looking for the rationale, since it decides whether the call can be dropped.

git log -S "SHUT_WR" -- Lib/pdb.py finds two commits. It first appears in 5993e06 ("Use a thread to manage interrupts on Windows") and only moves in dd7c9b1. 5993e06 is the first version of the listener, its commit message does not mention the shutdown, and #133223 has no review or conversation comment about it.

In 5993e06 the client already did nothing but sendall() on this socket, the same as today (Lib/pdb.py:3517). So no code ever read the EOF that the half-close produces. Either it was meant to document that the channel is one-way, or it is vestigial.

If there is a reason I cannot see from the history, it settles the question. Otherwise I suggest dropping the call and keeping the test that asserts this socket never sees EOF.

thread.author: godlygeek
thread.html:
Either it was meant to document that the channel is one-way

That was definitely the intention. If the half closed socket is getting timed out by the OS, we should definitely just stop half closing it.

issues.title: Lazy imports break dataclass InitVars in extremely rare scenarios
issues.author: lor1113
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

3 files are required to get this bug to happen:

testing.py

from testing_2 import A
from testing_3 import B

a = A()

b = B(a)

testing_2.py

from dataclasses import dataclass

from testing_3 import B


@dataclass
class A:
    pass

testing_3.py

from dataclasses import InitVar, dataclass

lazy from testing_2 import A


@dataclass
class B:
    a: InitVar[A]

    def __post_init__(self, a: A) -> None:
        print(a)

If you run testing.py with python 3.15 you will get TypeError: B.__post_init__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'a'
The key thing that causes the error seems to be the presence of the import cycle combined with the lazy import. It's worth noting that if you use a TYPE_CHECKING guard instead as described below, it does also work on 3.15.

I found this issue while migrating a bunch of my TYPE_CHECKING guards to lazy imports - infact as PEP 810 says "Lazy imports eliminate the common need for TYPE_CHECKING guards". The version of python that breaks is cpython-3.15.0a7-linux-x86_64-gnu. The code instead works on cpython-3.14.3-linux-x86_64-gnu, if of course you replace the lazy import in testing_3.py with a if TYPE_CHECKING: block

3.15

Operating systems tested on:

Linux

thread.author: DavidCEllis
thread.html:
I think this is more of a direct annotations issue than a dataclasses one.

Dataclasses is failing to pick up the InitVar because the failing lazy import causes the whole annotation to fail to evaluate, while if only the name doesn't exist, then __missing__ is triggered in the stringifier dict and the name eventually gets replaced with a ForwardRef.

Demonstrating the same idea with list[...] on the current main:

from annotationlib import get_annotations, Format
from pprint import pp
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

lazy from failing_import import LazyFail

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from fake_import import FakeSucceed

class Example:
    a: list[LazyFail]
    b: list[FakeSucceed]

pp(get_annotations(Example, format=Format.FORWARDREF))
{'a': ForwardRef('list[LazyFail]', is_class=True, owner=<class '__main__.Example'>),
 'b': list[ForwardRef('FakeSucceed', is_class=True, owner=<class '__main__.Example'>)]}

Here we get ForwardRef('list[...]') where a lazy import fails, but list[ForwardRef('...')] for a standard unresolvable name.

I think the fix is making annotationlib handle unresolvable lazy imports better, rather than making dataclasses handle strings again like in the current PR.

thread.author: DavidCEllis
thread.html:
This also fails even under 3.14 without any lazy imports if you use a module import for testing_2:

testing3.py

from dataclasses import InitVar, dataclass

import testing_2  # or lazy import testing_2 in 3.15


@dataclass
class B:
    a: InitVar[testing_2.A]

    def __post_init__(self, a: testing_2.A) -> None:
        print(a)

The solution for this is a little more complicated as it requires handling AttributeErrors better in general than we currently do as the import resolves but the attribute doesn't exist yet.

issues.title: test_subprocess: test_getoutput fails on non-English Windows, as text mode decodes cmd.exe's OEM output as UTF-8
issues.author: summeriver13
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

test_subprocess.test_getoutput fails on any Windows whose console code page is not UTF-8, because the child's output is decoded as UTF-8. The dependency on the system language can be removed — a child that simply writes non-UTF-8 bytes shows the same thing:

import subprocess, sys
subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c",
                "import sys; sys.stdout.buffer.write('版本'.encode('cp936'))"],
               stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True).stdout
interpreter sys.flags.utf8_mode result
3.14.7 0 '\u7248\u672c'
3.16.0a1 (main) 1 UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xb0 in position 0
3.12.10 with -X utf8=1 1 same UnicodeDecodeError

Lib/subprocess.py:1063 resolves text mode through _text_encoding(), which returns utf-8 whenever UTF-8 mode is on — the default since 3.15 (PEP 686). The child is not under Python's control: cmd.exe built-ins still write the console's OEM code page (936 here; GetACP() = GetOEMCP() = GetConsoleOutputCP() = 936, while locale.getencoding() stays cp936).

That is what breaks the test: it runs getstatusoutput("type <missing file>") and only asserts a non-zero status, but dies while decoding the localized error message:

File "Lib/subprocess.py", line 1382, in communicate
    stdout = self.stdout.read()
UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xd5 in position 4: invalid continuation byte

On the same machine, chcp 437 turns the message into ASCII (Access is denied.) and the test passes, and -X utf8=0 makes it pass too — the failure tracks the child's code page, not the build. CPython's Windows CI runs English images, so it stays green.

Suggested fix (test-side): stop depending on the child's localized text, e.g. subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", "sys.exit(1)"], stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True) and assert the status only.

Two neighbours, both distinct: gh-158006 (with two pipes the decode error stays in the reader thread and stdout becomes None), gh-158633 (the docs don't say the default encoding is a guess about the child).

environment and full traceback 
$ ./PCbuild/amd64/python_d.exe -c "import ctypes,locale,sys;k=ctypes.windll.kernel32;print(k.GetACP(),k.GetOEMCP(),k.GetConsoleOutputCP(),locale.getencoding(),locale.getpreferredencoding(False),sys.flags.utf8_mode)"
936 936 936 cp936 utf-8 1

$ ./PCbuild/amd64/python_d.exe -m test -v test_subprocess -m test_getoutput
ERROR: test_getoutput (test.test_subprocess.MiscTests.test_getoutput)
  File "Lib/test/test_subprocess.py", line 4135, in test_getoutput
    status, output = subprocess.getstatusoutput(
  File "Lib/subprocess.py", line 792, in getstatusoutput
    data = check_output(cmd, shell=True, text=True, stderr=STDOUT,
  File "Lib/subprocess.py", line 1382, in communicate
    stdout = self.stdout.read()
  File "Lib/codecs.py", line 327, in decode
    (result, consumed) = self._buffer_decode(data, self.errors, final)
UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xd5 in position 4: invalid continuation byte

Machine: Windows 11 (10.0.26100), zh-CN, CPython built from heads/main:11598362a3e with MSVC 14.44, Debug x64.

issues.title: textwrap truncation discards a broken long word (and, for shorten(), the whole text) instead of breaking it further
issues.author: qiyuhuating
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug description

With max_lines set (or with shorten(), which uses max_lines=1), when the last line consists of a single full-width chunk produced by _handle_long_word() — i.e. a piece of a long word that break_long_words=True (the default) broke across lines — the truncation loop in _wrap_chunks() drops the whole chunk instead of breaking it further to make room for the placeholder. All remaining text can be silently replaced by the placeholder alone:

>>> import textwrap
>>> textwrap.shorten('x' * 30, width=10)
'[...]'
>>> textwrap.wrap('x' * 30, width=10, max_lines=2)
['xxxxxxxxxx', '[...]']
>>> textwrap.fill('x' * 30, width=10, max_lines=2)
'xxxxxxxxxx\n[...]'

Expected output — the piece of the word is broken further, keeping width - len(placeholder) characters before the placeholder:

>>> textwrap.shorten('x' * 30, width=10)
'xxxx [...]'
>>> textwrap.wrap('x' * 30, width=10, max_lines=2)
['xxxxxxxxxx', 'xxxx [...]']

The docs for shorten() promise that "enough words are dropped from the end so that the remaining words plus the placeholder fit within width", and the docstring says "as many words as possible are joined". When the text is a single long word, the current implementation cannot keep any part of it at all — the output carries no information about the text. Since break_long_words=True is the default, the wrapper already breaks this word on earlier lines; refusing to break it on the final truncation line discards content that would fit.

This only affects lines consisting of a single full-width chunk. All other documented truncation behavior (dropping whole words from the end, backtracking the placeholder onto the previous line, and the eager "placeholder too large for max width" check) stays exactly the same.

Analysis

In TextWrapper._wrap_chunks() (Lib/textwrap.py), the else branch that places the placeholder drops chunks one at a time until the placeholder fits:

while cur_line:
    if (cur_line[-1].strip() and
        cur_len + len(self.placeholder) <= width):
        cur_line.append(self.placeholder)
        lines.append(indent + ''.join(cur_line))
        break
    cur_len -= len(cur_line[-1])
    del cur_line[-1]

For a line whose only chunk is a full-width piece of a broken long word, no chunk ever fits with the placeholder, so the loop empties cur_line and the bare placeholder is emitted. Breaking the chunk instead (to width - len(self.placeholder) characters) preserves part of the word and is consistent with break_long_words=True and with how _handle_long_word() already broke the word on previous lines.

The affected expectations were frozen when the feature was implemented in gh-62925 (bpo-18585, 2015) and were never discussed separately.

Linked PRs

Will submit a fix shortly.

issues.title: Windows: python.exe fails to start from a long path because of DLL manifests
issues.author: mkanat
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Problem

python.exe fails to start with STATUS_NAME_TOO_LONG once its path is 247 characters or longer, even with LongPathsEnabled=1. It turns out this is actually from loading the DLL, not from python.exe itself.

Extension modules like _ctypes and _ssl also fail to import when the install is at a long path.

Cause

The build is creating DLLs with a manifest, and as noted in #126929, Windows can't load a DLL with an embedded manifest from a path near MAX_PATH.

Since about 2010, the manifest doesn't do anything in a DLL. Windows takes the supported OS versions and the Common Controls dependency from the EXE's manifest, not a DLL's.

History

DLLs used to need a manifest. With Visual C++ 2008, which Python 2.6 through 3.2 were built with, a DLL had to declare its dependency on the C runtime in an embedded manifest to find it. However, Visual C++ 2010 stopped using manifests to find the C runtime, so DLLs haven't needed one since.

#67207 (bpo-23018) added the manifest to python_nt.rc in 2015, at the same time as the one for python[w].exe, to declare supportedOS so that GetVersion would stop reporting Windows 8 on newer versions.

In 2016, #71496 (bpo-27309) added the Common Controls dependency so that tkinter's native dialogs would get the right styles. From that change: "Windows needs to load a different version of a particular DLL for the entire process." However, that's only information that the process needs, not the DLLs.

#71918 (bpo-27731) added longPathAware later that year.

Where the manifest comes from now

PC/python_nt.rc embeds PC/python.manifest as resource ID 2, and pythoncore, python3dll, and every extension module project in PCbuild use that resource script. PC/sqlite3.rc does the same for sqlite3.dll.

Possible Solution

Remove the 2 RT_MANIFEST "python.manifest" line, and the RT_MANIFEST fallback define above it, from PC/python_nt.rc and PC/sqlite3.rc. python_exe.rc and pythonw_exe.rc keep embedding the manifest as ID 1.

Note: #156759 doesn't help here, because Windows loads python3XY.dll as a static import of python.exe, before any Python code runs.

3.14

issues.title: socket.recv() and recvfrom() with MSG_TRUNC raise ValueError and lose the datagram since 3.15.1
issues.author: kolyshkin
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

Since 3.15.1, socket.recv(bufsize, MSG_TRUNC) and socket.recvfrom(bufsize, MSG_TRUNC) raise ValueError: size larger than allocated size when the datagram is longer than bufsize. Without MSG_PEEK, the datagram is already consumed by the time the exception is raised, so the data is lost:

import socket
a, b = socket.socketpair(socket.AF_UNIX, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
a.send(b"abcdefgh")
a.send(b"second")
try:
    print(b.recv(2, socket.MSG_TRUNC))
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)
try:
    print(b.recvfrom(2, socket.MSG_TRUNC))
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)
b.setblocking(False)
b.recv(100)  # BlockingIOError: both datagrams are gone

3.15.1:

size larger than allocated size
size larger than allocated size

3.15.0 and 3.14 (the long-standing behavior, see gh-69121):

b'ab\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00'
(b'se\x00\x00\x00\x00', None)

With MSG_TRUNC, Linux recv(2) returns the real length of the datagram even if it was longer than the buffer. sock_recv() and sock_recvfrom() pass that length to PyBytesWriter_FinishWithSize(), which, after c38a347 (backport of gh-157226 to 3.15), rejects a size larger than the allocated one. The same code is in main.

The old behavior was a bug too (gh-69121): the returned object was grown to the real datagram length, with only the first bufsize bytes being valid. Still, it is a behavior change in a bugfix release that breaks working code. For example, CRIU's pycriu used len(s.recv(1, socket.MSG_TRUNC | socket.MSG_PEEK)) to find out the message size (fixed in checkpoint-restore/criu#3268 by using recv_into(), which returns the value from recv(2) as is).

Raising after the data is consumed seems to be the worst option. Returning the min(outlen, bufsize) bytes actually received (as suggested in gh-69121, and similar to what recvmsg() does) would avoid both the data loss and the garbage bytes.

thread.author: patrick-5546
thread.html:
A minimal way to trigger the same error, in case it helps. On Linux, Python decodes a file name that isn't valid UTF-8 with surrogateescape, so a script in such a directory has a co_filename containing a lone surrogate:

cd "$(mktemp -d)"
dir=$(printf 'caf\351')   # Latin-1 "café": not valid UTF-8
mkdir "$dir"
cat > "$dir/busy.py" <<'PY'
import time

def busy():
    deadline = time.monotonic() + 2
    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
        pass

busy()
PY
python3.15 -m profiling.sampling run --binary -o out.bin "$dir/busy.py"

This fails with the same traceback, ending in UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't encode character '\udce9' in position 23: surrogates not allowed, and leaves a 64-byte out.bin that replay rejects. --pstats profiles the same script without error. A function whose co_name contains a lone surrogate fails the same way. Reproduced with 3.15.1 and 3.16.0a1 on Linux.

The cause appears to be (links at main, 94942ba):

  • The binary writer encodes file and function names with PyUnicode_AsUTF8AndSize, which rejects lone surrogates.
  • BinaryCollector.collect catches only OverflowError, and the sampling loop treats a UnicodeDecodeError, but not a UnicodeEncodeError, as a failed sample, so the error ends the profile before the file is finalized.

The '\uddd0' in your traceback is outside U+DC80–U+DCFF, the only range surrogateescape produces, so in your run the surrogate came from somewhere other than a file name decoded that way. Either way, the writer would need to accept any str, for example by encoding with surrogatepass or backslashreplace; the reader already decodes with "replace".

I used an AI assistant (GitHub Copilot CLI) to narrow this down and write the reproducer, and I've reviewed the above.

issues.title: mailbox.Babyl returns labels as bytes after reading a mailbox file
issues.author: devdavidejesus
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

When a Babyl mailbox is read back from its file, the message labels are bytes instead of str:

import mailbox

box = mailbox.Babyl('box.babyl')
msg = mailbox.BabylMessage('Subject: one\n\nbody\n')
msg.set_labels(['unseen', 'work'])
box.add(msg)
box.add(mailbox.BabylMessage('Subject: two\n\nbody\n'))
box.close()

box = mailbox.Babyl('box.babyl')
msg = box[0]
print(sorted(msg.get_labels()))  # [b'unseen', b'work']
print(sorted(box.get_labels()))  # [b'unseen', b'work']
print(mailbox.MaildirMessage(msg).get_flags(), mailbox.mboxMessage(msg).get_flags())  # S RO
box.remove(1)
box.flush()  # AttributeError: 'bytes' object has no attribute 'encode'

As a result:

  • 'unseen' in msg.get_labels() is false, so converting the message to MaildirMessage or mboxMessage marks an unseen message as read (S, R).
  • Babyl.get_labels() does not leave out the special labels such as unseen.
  • If any message has labels, a change that makes flush() rewrite the file, such as remove(), fails with AttributeError, and so does adding such a message to another Babyl mailbox.

Babyl._generate_toc() reads the labels line in binary mode and keeps the labels as bytes, while _install_message() and _pre_mailbox_hook() write them with label.encode(). Decoding them in _generate_toc() fixes all of the above. Using errors='surrogateescape' for both the decoding and the encoding keeps files with labels that are not valid UTF-8 readable (today they can be read, only rewriting them fails). The existing test_labels never reopens the mailbox, so it doesn't catch this.

In the releases I tried (3.13.17, 3.14.9, 3.15.0) the example fails even earlier, with an AssertionError in get_message(), because of gh-157880, which is fixed on main, 3.15 and 3.14 after those releases. With the gh-157880 fix applied, 3.13 shows the same label problem.
