issues.title: free-threaded: setiter_iternext releases the set once per racing thread
issues.author: scrieve
issues.bodyHTML:
setiter_iternext reads the set before taking the critical section and then clears it outside the critical section, so every thread that reaches the exhausted branch decrements the same set.

  • Objects/setobject.c:1098 reads PySetObject *so = si->si_set; unlocked.
  • 1100 if (so == NULL) return NULL; lets every racing thread through, because si_set is still set at that point.
  • 1113-1124 the critical section covers only the table scan.
  • 1126-1129 clears si->si_set and calls Py_DECREF(so) after Py_END_CRITICAL_SECTION().

Eight threads that arrive together each hold a non-NULL so and each run one decrement, so the set loses seven references it should not.

Reproduction on an unmodified Py_DEBUG free-threading build (3.16.0a1+dev free-threading build, main at 53b0004):

import sys, threading
N = 300000
s = set(range(N))
for i in range(1, N):
    s.discard(i)          # one element, 299,999 dummy entries
keep = [s] * 1000         # extra decrefs must not free the set
base = sys.getrefcount(s)
it = iter(s); next(it)
barrier = threading.Barrier(8)
def worker():
    barrier.wait()
    try: next(it)
    except StopIteration: pass
for r in range(3):
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(8)]
    [t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
    print(r, base, sys.getrefcount(s))

Output:

0 1002 996
1 1002 996
2 1002 996
Python/gc_free_threading.c:1118: validate_gc_objects: Assertion "gc_get_refs(op) >= 0" failed: refcount is too small
object address  : 0x20002375e10
object refcount : 995
object type name: set
object repr     : {0}

Fatal Python error: _PyObject_AssertFailed: _PyObject_AssertFailed
Python runtime state: finalizing (tstate=0x00005f29df1515f0)

exit status 134.

This is a sample from one run. The final count lands at 995 or 996 depending on how many of the eight threads lose a reference (six or seven); the abort itself is stable across runs. Rounds 1 and 2 are flat because si_set is already NULL by then. The process aborts while finalizing, and the object it complains about is the set itself.

The large table is what makes the window wide enough to hit. The scan after the unlocked read takes long enough for all eight threads to pass the so == NULL check. With a one-element set the same eight-thread barrier loop ran 31,020 rounds on the same build with no hit.

This has the same shape as the dict iterator in gh-154130. #144356 covers the setiter_len length hint only, and I did not find a report for the iternext path.

Clearing si->si_set inside the critical section at 1113-1124 and decref'ing after Py_END_CRITICAL_SECTION() would make the release happen once. Treating si_set like di_dict, with _Py_XGetRef and an atomic exchange, is the other route.

I have the harness that produced this (repros/set_iter_double_release.py, with an instrumented build that counts second releases) if it is useful.

Linked PRs

  • gh-160619

thread.author: scrieve
thread.html:
ThreadSanitizer reports the race directly, so this no longer rests on refcount arithmetic.

Build the way the CI sanitizer job does (gcc 15.2 works as well as clang):

./configure --without-ensurepip OPT="-O2 -g" --with-thread-sanitizer --with-pydebug --disable-gil
make -j4
TSAN_OPTIONS="suppressions=Tools/tsan/suppressions_free_threading.txt handle_segv=0" ./python repro.py

repro.py is two threads calling next() on one iter(set) behind a threading.Barrier. Three races come back, all in setiter_iternext:

WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race
  Read of size 8 by thread T1 at Objects/setobject.c:1114     <- i = si->si_pos
  Previous write of size 8 by thread T8 at Objects/setobject.c:1125  <- si->si_pos = i+1
SUMMARY: ThreadSanitizer: data race Objects/setobject.c:1114 in setiter_iternext

SUMMARY: ThreadSanitizer: data race Objects/setobject.c:1127 in setiter_iternext
                                                             <- si->si_set = NULL

si_pos is read at 1114 and written at 1125 with no lock held on either side, and si_set is cleared at 1127 while the other thread is still inside the function. That also explains the refcount loss in the original report: the thread that sees key == NULL clears si_set and drops the set while the other is mid-setiter_iternext.

Taking the lock for the si_pos read and the si_set clear, and releasing before returning, removes two of the three reports. The third survives because the clear is a plain store while the entry check at 1104 is a relaxed atomic load, so the two disagree about being atomic:

Write of size 8 by thread T8 at Objects/setobject.c:1137   <- si->si_set = NULL
Read of size 8 by thread T1 at Objects/setobject.c:1104    <- FT_ATOMIC_LOAD_PTR_RELAXED(si->si_set)

Writing the clear through FT_ATOMIC_STORE_PTR_RELAXED as well makes the repro exit 0 with no reports, refs steady at 1002 across 200 rounds and double_release=0. Both parts are in one diff if that is the direction you want to take.

The four other unlocked si_set uses on main at dc28c3a stay open even with setiter_iternext fixed, so the full fix has to reach them too:

  • setiter_dealloc (1042) runs Py_XDECREF(si->si_set) with no lock.
  • setiter_traverse (1050) runs Py_VISIT(si->si_set) while the clearing thread may already have released it, so the collector can be handed a pointer that is being freed.
  • setiter_len (1059) reads si->si_set, then dereferences si->si_set->used; already tracked in gh-144356.
  • setiter_reduce (1073-1077) does setiterobject tmp = *si; and then Py_XINCREF(tmp.si_set). The struct copy is not atomic, so the increment can land on a pointer the clearing thread has released, which is an increment on freed memory rather than a net refcount error.

The complete shape is the one gh-154130 proposes for di_dict: atomic load, atomic exchange to NULL, and exactly one Py_DECREF performed by whichever thread saw the non-NULL exchange.

issues.title: csv.Sniffer.sniff() takes quadratic time on long runs of spaces
issues.author: devdavidejesus
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

On main, csv.Sniffer().sniff() takes quadratic time when the sample contains a quote character and a long run of spaces that is not followed by one:

import csv, time

for n in (8000, 16000, 32000, 64000):
    sample = 'a' + ' ' * n + 'x"\n'
    t = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        csv.Sniffer().sniff(sample)
    except csv.Error:
        pass
    print(n, round(time.perf_counter() - t, 4))

Seconds, on macOS 27.0.1 (Apple M3):

n main (debug build) main + fix (debug build) 3.15.0 (release, for comparison)
8000 0.050 0.011 0.010
16000 0.153 0.002 0.004
32000 0.598 0.004 0.007
64000 2.373 0.008 0.015

The sample ('a,b' + ' ' * 100_000 + 'c"\n') * 4 takes 23.2 s on main and 0.06 s with the fix.

The cause is the regex in Sniffer._split_dormant() (Lib/csv.py):

m = re.compile(fr'(?:^|([\r\n{cls}]))'
               fr' *{quotechar}').search(part, pos)

The space is a delimiter candidate whenever the sample contains one, so it is in cls. The search then tries a match at every space of the run: [...] matches that space, * consumes the rest of the run, and the match fails on the next character. A run of n spaces costs O(n**2).

A match that starts at a space preceded by a space is never the leftmost one: a match with the same group and the same end also starts at the beginning of the run. Adding the lookbehind (?<! ) after the group skips those positions without changing any result.

This was introduced in gh-83273 (25fea6d) and is in 3.16.0a1. 3.15 and older are not affected.

issues.title: regrtest --parallel-threads shares TestCase._cleanups between threads
issues.author: mpage
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

regrtest's --parallel-threads runs the same test concurrently in multiple threads. To do so it creates independent copies of the tests using copy.copy():

cpython/Lib/test/libregrtest/parallel_case.py

Line 38 in 5ca490b

cases = [copy.copy(self.test_case) for _ in range(self.num_threads)]

copy.copy() does a shallow copy, so the test's _cleanups list is shared between threads. Each thread runs the test's doCleanup method, popping and running methods from _cleanups until it's empty:

cpython/Lib/unittest/case.py

Lines 721 to 732 in eacae21

def doCleanups(self):
"""Execute all cleanup functions. Normally called for you after
tearDown."""
outcome = self._outcome or _Outcome()
while self._cleanups:
function, args, kwargs = self._cleanups.pop()
with outcome.testPartExecutor(self):
self._callCleanup(function, *args, **kwargs)
# return this for backwards compatibility
# even though we no longer use it internally
return outcome.success

Some cleanup functions may run more than once in a thread or may not run at all, because _cleanups is shared across all threads.

issues.title: `xml.dom.minidom.parseString()` takes quadratic time on text delivered in many pieces
issues.author: gpshead
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

xml.dom.minidom.parse() and parseString() take time quadratic in the number of pieces in which Expat delivers a run of character data. xml.dom.expatbuilder extends the current Text node with node.data = node.data + data on every CharacterDataHandler call, and pyexpat flushes its text buffer before every other handler, so markup that adds no node (an empty CDATA section, a reference to an external entity) splits one text node into many callbacks. With the pieces placed in an internal entity that is referenced repeatedly, a few kilobytes of input are enough.

Whoever supplies the document controls this; a program that parses XML from an untrusted source with minidom's default arguments can be made to spend about a minute of CPU on a 7 kB document.

import time
from xml.dom import minidom

def make(k):
    return ('<!DOCTYPE r [<!ENTITY x "%s">]><r>%s</r>'
            % ('ab<![CDATA[]]>' * k, '&x;' * k))

for k in 100, 200, 400:
    doc = make(k)
    t = time.process_time()
    dom = minidom.parseString(doc)
    t = time.process_time() - t
    print(f'{len(doc)} bytes -> {len(dom.documentElement.firstChild.data)} chars of text, {t:.2f} s')

Output on a debug build of main:

1736 bytes -> 20000 chars of text, 0.44 s
3436 bytes -> 80000 chars of text, 3.25 s
6836 bytes -> 320000 chars of text, 68.81 s

The time should grow with the amount of text (4x per step here), not with its square. The code is unchanged since Python 2.3. gh-158860 is the same pattern in Node.normalize(); gh-142145 was a similar issue elsewhere in minidom.

issues.title: test_urllib: two urlopen_HttpTests tests fail when an HTTPS proxy is configured
issues.author: devdavidejesus
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

Two tests in test_urllib.urlopen_HttpTests fail when https_proxy (or HTTPS_PROXY) is set in the environment, as it often is behind a corporate proxy. http_proxy alone does not trigger it.

$ https_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:9 ./python.exe -m test test_urllib -v
...
ERROR: test_url_host_with_control_char_rejected (test.test_urllib.urlopen_HttpTests.test_url_host_with_control_char_rejected)
...
urllib.error.URLError: <urlopen error [Errno 61] Connection refused>
...
ERROR: test_url_host_with_newline_header_injection_rejected (test.test_urllib.urlopen_HttpTests.test_url_host_with_newline_header_injection_rejected)
...
ValueError: Invalid header value b'localhost\r\nX-injected: header\r\n:8080'
...
FAILED (errors=2, skipped=2)

Both errors come from the https: half of each test, which expects http.client.InvalidURL from the host check in HTTPConnection.__init__(). With an HTTPS proxy, the connection is created for the proxy and the bad host is passed to set_tunnel(), so it is rejected later with a different error:

  • test_url_host_with_control_char_rejected: _tunnel() raises ValueError after connecting to the proxy. Here nothing listens on the proxy address, so the test gets URLError first.
  • test_url_host_with_newline_header_injection_rejected: putheader() raises ValueError for the Host header, before connecting.

The tests call urllib.request.urlopen(), whose default opener includes ProxyHandler(), so they depend on what getproxies() returns: the environment, or on macOS also the system proxy settings. The opener is also cached at module level: when the whole file runs, urlopen_FileTests has already built it with the proxies of that moment. ProxyTests in the same file already removes the proxy variables in setUp().

The tests pass when no proxy is set. The same tests and code are in 3.14 and 3.15.

issues.title: test_str: the UCS4 adaptive search path is never exercised
issues.author: scrieve
issues.bodyHTML:
Summary

Objects/stringlib/fastsearch.h compiles adaptive_find once per character
width. The UCS4 copy never ran under the entire test suite, because the only test
that reaches the adaptive path, string_tests.BaseTest.test_adaptive_find, uses
ASCII strings.

Evidence

Coverage from a --coverage build of main running the full suite
(./python -m test -j4, 552 files, 52,070 tests):

Function 'ucs4lib_adaptive_find'   Lines executed:0.00% of 39
Function 'ucs2lib_adaptive_find'   Lines executed:66.67% of 39
Function 'ucs1lib_adaptive_find'   Lines executed:71.79% of 39
Function 'asciilib_adaptive_find'  Lines executed:79.49% of 39

Why the existing test misses it

The adaptive branch is taken only when, in Objects/stringlib/fastsearch.h:800:

  • the haystack is at least 2500 characters,
  • the needle is at least 100 characters (or the haystack at least 30000),
  • the needle is at least a third of the haystack.

test_adaptive_find meets all three, but with 'a' and 'b', so the code that
runs is the ASCII or UCS1 instantiation. Nothing in the suite builds a haystack
that wide-and-long out of non-BMP characters, so the UCS4 instantiation stays
cold.

Proposal

Add a test next to test_find in Lib/test/test_str.py that repeats the same
shape with '\U0001d11e' and '\U0001d11f'. With that test present,
ucs4lib_adaptive_find goes from 0.00% to 89.74% of 39 lines, and the remaining
branches are the count and reverse-search modes, which are separate entry points.

This is a test-only change, so it does not alter behaviour. I have it ready and
will open a PR against this issue.

issues.title: tarfile and zipfile write through an existing symlink or hard link when extracting a file
issues.author: haampie
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug description:

When extracting a regular file, tarfile and zipfile open the destination with open(path, "wb"). If something already exists at that path, it is truncated in place:

  • a symlink is followed and its target is overwritten (a dangling symlink creates its target),
  • a hard link is modified, meaning that python technically modifies data outside the prefix it extracts into

The existing entry can come from an earlier member of the same archive or already be on disk. The extraction filters don't prevent this: they reject links that point outside the destination, but a link inside it is accepted, and links already on disk aren't filtered. zipfile does not have extraction filters.

import io, os, tarfile, tempfile

def add(tar, name, data=b"", symlink=None):
    info = tarfile.TarInfo(name)
    if symlink is not None:
        info.type, info.linkname = tarfile.SYMTYPE, symlink
    info.size = len(data)
    tar.addfile(info, io.BytesIO(data))

buf = io.BytesIO()
with tarfile.open(fileobj=buf, mode="w") as tar:
    add(tar, "target", b"original")
    add(tar, "link", symlink="target")
    add(tar, "link", b"replaced")

dest = tempfile.mkdtemp()
buf.seek(0)
with tarfile.open(fileobj=buf) as tar:
    tar.extractall(dest, filter="data")

with open(os.path.join(dest, "target"), "rb") as f:
    print(f.read())                                   # b'replaced'
print(os.path.islink(os.path.join(dest, "link")))     # True

The same happens with zipfile.ZipFile.extractall() when the destination already contains a symlink or hard link at a member's path.

Expected: link becomes a regular file and target keeps its content. This is what GNU tar does, and follows from a reasonable interpretation of the POSIX requirement of pax: "In read mode, the extracted output files shall be of the archived file type." The Python docs also say later members "are expected to overwrite any earlier ones", and TarFile.makelink() already removes an existing entry before creating a link.

Related:

  • gh-88189 reported this for tarfile. It was closed after PEP 706, but the filters only cover links that lead outside the destination. The concern raised there was that unlinking first wouldn't help against races; see below.
  • gh-79664 is the same report, closed as a duplicate.
  • gh-114959 added tests in Lib/test/archiver_tests.py that pin the current behaviour for both modules, marked "XXX: It is potential security vulnerability", and noted that both modules "should be more cautious when extract on top of symlinks".

Proposed fix

Open the file with "xb", and on FileExistsError remove the existing entry and retry once. This is efficient cause it's a single open() call. On POSIX, O_EXCL never follows a symlink, so a link created concurrently makes open() fail instead of being followed. Windows and Emscripten do follow a dangling symlink even with O_EXCL, so there the path is unlinked before opening at the cost of an extra syscall. The helper would live in a private module shared by both modules.

Observable changes:

  • An existing regular file is replaced by a new one instead of being truncated, so the old file's owner, mode and extended attributes are not kept, and its other hard links keep the old content.
  • A file member at the path of an existing directory still fails and the directory is left alone, but on macOS the error becomes PermissionError instead of IsADirectoryError. Linux and Windows are unchanged.

Not covered: directory members over an existing symlink (gh-64173), and symlinks in parent directories of a member.

issues.title: Concurrent mutation of cached slot names can crash default object state collection
issues.author: SonicField
issues.bodyHTML:
The default state collector reads the user-accessible cached __slotnames__
list using Py_NewRef(PyList_GET_ITEM(slotnames, i)). In a free-threaded
build, concurrent resizing can invalidate the index, and same-size replacement
can release a name before its reference is acquired. This affects direct
object.__getstate__() and the default object.__reduce_ex__() path used by
pickle protocols 2 and above.

Expected behaviour is valid collected state or the existing size-change
RuntimeError, without a native crash or invalid reference access. Attribute
lookup should retain its existing callback order.

Standalone reproducer

Save the code in Reproducer code below as reproduce_slotnames.py.
It uses only the standard library and rejects runs with the GIL enabled.
From the directory containing that file, run a free-threaded CPython interpreter:

python3.14t -X gil=0 reproduce_slotnames.py --mode resize --operation reduce --protocol 5 --calls 100000

For an ASan-enabled free-threaded CPython build, use that build's executable:

ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0 ./python -X gil=0 reproduce_slotnames.py --mode resize --operation reduce --protocol 5 --calls 100000

Use --mode replace for same-size replacement of non-interned names, or
--operation state for direct __getstate__(). Normal completion prints
valid-result, expected-size-change-error and concurrent-mutation counts.
The race is scheduling-dependent: a clean run does not establish its absence.

Observed reproductions

The author supplied crash logs for the default resize/reduce/protocol-5
workload, with 100,000 requested calls and the GIL disabled:

  • Native ARM64, CPython 3.16.0a1+dev, upstream base d3ada45, GCC 11.5.0,
    free-threaded ASan build: segmentation fault. The stack includes
    object_getstate_default, PyObject_GetOptionalAttr and PyObject_Hash.
  • Native ARM64, downstream CPython 3.14.8 free-threaded build,
    revision cb5a736, Clang 21.1.0: segmentation fault in the reproducer's
    __reduce_ex__() call. This establishes a reproduction on that downstream
    build; an unmodified upstream 3.14 build has not been tested.
  • An earlier x86-64 Python 3.14t run under QEMU on ARM64 also crashed.
    Two earlier native ARM runs completed without a crash; their exact build
    details and commands were not retained in the supplied report.

Native 3.16 ASan excerpt

Paths have been reduced to repository-relative paths or filenames. Process
IDs, raw addresses and unrelated frames are omitted. ASan reports SEGV;
this excerpt is not a classified heap-use-after-free diagnostic.

Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault
Stack (most recent call first):
  File "reproduce_slotnames.py", line 79 in main
  File "reproduce_slotnames.py", line 120 in <module>
AddressSanitizer:DEADLYSIGNAL
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address [address omitted]
The signal is caused by a READ memory access.
Selected frames from the supplied ASan trace:
  PyObject_Hash                           Objects/object.c:1162
  _PyObject_HashDictKey                   Include/internal/pycore_object.h:846
  PyDict_GetItemRef                       Objects/dictobject.c:2624
  _PyObject_GenericGetAttrWithDict        Objects/object.c:1980
  PyObject_GetOptionalAttr                Objects/object.c:1406
  object_getstate_default                 Objects/typeobject.c:7893
  object_getstate                         Objects/typeobject.c:7963
  reduce_newobj                           Objects/typeobject.c:8198
  _common_reduce                          Objects/typeobject.c:8241
  object___reduce_ex___impl                Objects/typeobject.c:8306
AddressSanitizer can not provide additional info.
ABORTING

Native downstream 3.14.8 excerpt

Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault
Stack (most recent call first):
  File "reproduce_slotnames.py", line 79 in main
  File "reproduce_slotnames.py", line 120 in <module>
Selected symbolised C frames:
  python3.14t: _Py_DumpStack+0x34
  [unsymbolised frames omitted]
  python3.14t: PyEval_EvalCode+0xc8
  [unsymbolised frames omitted]
  python3.14t: Py_RunMain+0xb4c
  [remaining frames omitted]
Segmentation fault (core dumped)

The proposed fix uses PyList_GetItemRef() and preserves the existing
size-change error and ordered attribute lookup. The exact three-file patch
passed the relevant suites on free-threaded ASan and PGO/LTO builds, with
1,271 tests and 58 skips per build. Retained direct ASan stress passed
1.2 million calls on the fixed build. Those earlier checks used the original
stress program; the newly packaged standalone script has not yet been rerun
by the worker on the fixed interpreter.

Alternative considered

We considered making the slot-name cache immutable. We chose to preserve its
current representation for this fix: enforcing immutability would change
existing behaviour and could expose compatibility edge cases in real-world
code. We have not measured a benefit that would justify that additional
stability risk. The proposed change therefore addresses unsafe reference
acquisition while retaining the existing cache and lookup behaviour.

This is a scope decision for this fix, not a conclusion that an immutable
cache would never be worthwhile.

Fork CI

CPython GitHub Actions run 39960172407 tested
commit fede7f7d6d26ec8e261b8fc570c3c5f877cadef9 on pr/slotnames-state-access.
All 44 executed jobs succeeded. The two skipped jobs were
CIFuzz and the removed-HTML-ID documentation check.

Successful jobs cover Linux x86-64/ARM64, Windows x64/Win32/ARM64,
macOS Intel/Apple Silicon, Android ARM64/x86-64, iOS, Emscripten and WASI.
Free-threaded jobs passed where configured, including Linux, Windows,
macOS and iOS. ASan, UBSan, MSan and both TSan configurations succeeded.
These are job-level results; individual test skips have not been inventoried.

AI tools assisted with investigation and preparation.

Reproducer code

reproduce_slotnames.py (standard library only) 
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Exercise concurrent mutation of CPython's cached default-state slot names.

Run with a free-threaded CPython interpreter and the GIL disabled. A clean
run is finite stress evidence; it does not prove that the race is absent.
"""

import argparse
import faulthandler
import json
import sys
import threading
import time


class Name(str):
    """A fresh, non-interned name whose lifetime depends on owned references."""


class Sample:
    pass


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--mode", choices=("resize", "replace"), default="resize")
    parser.add_argument("--operation", choices=("state", "reduce"), default="reduce")
    parser.add_argument("--protocol", choices=range(2, 6), type=int, default=5)
    parser.add_argument("--calls", type=int, default=100_000)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    if args.calls <= 0:
        parser.error("--calls must be positive")
    gil_enabled = getattr(sys, "_is_gil_enabled", lambda: True)()
    if gil_enabled:
        parser.error("requires a free-threaded CPython interpreter with the GIL disabled")

    faulthandler.enable()
    obj = Sample()
    obj.value = 42
    obj.other = 99
    Sample.__slotnames__ = [Name("value")]
    names = Sample.__slotnames__
    stopped = threading.Event()
    started = threading.Event()
    mutations = 0
    writer_errors = []

    def writer():
        nonlocal mutations
        try:
            while not stopped.is_set():
                names[:] = [Name("value")]
                if args.mode == "resize":
                    names.clear()
                else:
                    names[:] = [Name("other")]
                mutations += 1
                started.set()
        except BaseException as exc:
            writer_errors.append(exc)
            started.set()

    print(json.dumps({"event": "start", "python_version": list(sys.version_info[:3]),
                      "implementation": sys.implementation.name, "gil_enabled": gil_enabled,
                      "arguments": vars(args)}), flush=True)
    thread = threading.Thread(target=writer, daemon=True)
    thread.start()
    successes = size_change_errors = 0
    begin = time.monotonic()
    try:
        if not started.wait(10):
            raise RuntimeError("writer did not start within 10 seconds")
        initial_mutations = mutations
        for _ in range(args.calls):
            try:
                if args.operation == "state":
                    state = obj.__getstate__()
                else:
                    reduced = obj.__reduce_ex__(args.protocol)
                    if reduced[1] != (Sample,) or reduced[3:] != (None, None):
                        raise AssertionError(f"unexpected reduction: {reduced!r}")
                    state = reduced[2]
            except RuntimeError as exc:
                if (args.mode != "resize" or
                    str(exc) != "__slotnames__ changed size during iteration"):
                    raise
                size_change_errors += 1
                continue

            if type(state) is tuple:
                if len(state) != 2:
                    raise AssertionError(f"unexpected state tuple: {state!r}")
                dictionary, slots = state
                if slots not in ({"value": 42}, {"other": 99}):
                    raise AssertionError(f"unexpected slot state: {slots!r}")
            else:
                if args.mode == "replace":
                    raise AssertionError(f"missing slot state: {state!r}")
                dictionary = state
            if dictionary is not obj.__dict__ or dictionary != {"value": 42, "other": 99}:
                raise AssertionError(f"unexpected dictionary state: {dictionary!r}")
            successes += 1
        concurrent_mutations = mutations - initial_mutations
    finally:
        stopped.set()
        thread.join(10)
    if thread.is_alive():
        raise RuntimeError("writer did not stop within 10 seconds")
    if writer_errors:
        raise writer_errors[0]
    if concurrent_mutations <= 0:
        raise RuntimeError("inconclusive: no writer progress observed during reader calls")
    print(json.dumps({"event": "complete", "successes": successes,
                      "size_change_errors": size_change_errors,
                      "concurrent_mutations": concurrent_mutations,
                      "elapsed_seconds": time.monotonic() - begin}), flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

issues.title: C API: copying a PyStatus emits -Wdeprecated-declarations in C++ with clang since gh-158080
issues.author: davidnich
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug description:

Since gh-158080 (GH-158085), PyStatus.exitcode is declared with Py_DEPRECATED(3.16) in Include/cpython/initconfig.h. Because the C API passes and returns PyStatus by value (PyStatus_Exception(), PyStatus_IsError(), Py_InitializeFromConfig(), ...), C++ code that uses the API in the documented way makes clang generate the implicit copy constructor / move assignment operator of PyStatus. These use the deprecated member, so clang emits -Wdeprecated-declarations even though the code never touches exitcode. With -Werror, the build fails.

The usage pattern of the Doc/c-api/init_config.rst examples (ex: init_python()), compiled as C++, is enough to reproduce:

#include <Python.h>

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    PyStatus status;
    PyConfig config;
    PyConfig_InitPythonConfig(&config);
    status = PyConfig_SetBytesString(&config, &config.program_name, argv[0]);
    if (PyStatus_Exception(status)) {
        goto exception;
    }
    status = Py_InitializeFromConfig(&config);
    if (PyStatus_Exception(status)) {
        goto exception;
    }
    PyConfig_Clear(&config);
    return Py_RunMain();
exception:
    PyConfig_Clear(&config);
    Py_ExitStatusException(status);
}
$ clang++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Werror -I<cpython>/Include -I<build> -c embed.cpp
Include/cpython/initconfig.h:10:9: error: 'exitcode' is deprecated [-Werror,-Wdeprecated-declarations]
embed.cpp:7:12: note: in implicit move assignment operator for 'PyStatus' first required here
Include/cpython/initconfig.h:10:9: error: 'exitcode' is deprecated [-Werror,-Wdeprecated-declarations]
Include/cpython/initconfig.h:10:9: error: 'exitcode' is deprecated [-Werror,-Wdeprecated-declarations]
embed.cpp:8:28: note: in implicit copy constructor for 'PyStatus' first required here
  • Reproduced with 3.16.0a1, with Ubuntu clang 21.1.8 (Linux aarch64) and Apple clang 21.0.0 (macOS arm64); the PyStatus definition is unchanged on current main.
  • g++ 15, and clang compiling the same file as C, emit no warning.
  • The diagnostic is reported at the definition of the structure in initconfig.h, so users cannot silence it locally with a pragma around their own calls; they have to wrap the #include <Python.h> itself.

Possible fix

Suppress the warning around the definition of the structure, with the existing _Py_COMP_DIAG_* macros of pyport.h:

 /* --- PyStatus ----------------------------------------------- */

+_Py_COMP_DIAG_PUSH
+_Py_COMP_DIAG_IGNORE_DEPR_DECLS
 typedef struct {
     enum {
         _PyStatus_TYPE_OK=0,
         _PyStatus_TYPE_ERROR=1,
         _PyStatus_TYPE_EXIT=2  // deprecated
     } _type;
     const char *func;
     const char *err_msg;
     Py_DEPRECATED(3.16) int exitcode;
 } PyStatus;
+_Py_COMP_DIAG_POP

With this change the example above compiles cleanly with clang++ -Werror, while real uses (status.exitcode, PyStatus_Exit(), PyStatus_IsExit()) still emit the deprecation warning. (Alternatively, only the functions could be marked deprecated and the member documented as deprecated.)

A C++ test in Lib/test/test_cppext that copies a PyStatus would catch regressions of this kind.

Linux, macOS

return _Py_atomic_load_ssize_relaxed(&self->ob_shash);

thread.author: vstinner
thread.html:
I cannot reproduce the C++ warning on Fedora 44 with g++ 16.2.1 or clang++ 22.1.8 using your example.

Building this C++ code with g++ -std=c++17 x.cpp -o -x -Wall -Wextra or clang++ -std=c++17 x.cpp -o -x -Wall -Wextra doesn't emit compiler warnings neither:

struct PyStatus {
    int status;
    __attribute__((__deprecated__)) int exitcode;
};

PyStatus func(void)
{
#if defined(__clang__)
_Pragma("clang diagnostic push")
_Pragma("clang diagnostic ignored \"-Wdeprecated-declarations\"")
#else
_Pragma("GCC diagnostic push")
_Pragma("GCC diagnostic ignored \"-Wdeprecated-declarations\"")
#endif
    PyStatus status = {1, 0};
#if defined(__clang__)
_Pragma("clang diagnostic pop")
#else
_Pragma("GCC diagnostic pop")
#endif
    return status;
}

int main(void)
{
    PyStatus copy = func();
    return copy.status == 0;
}

thread.author: vstinner
thread.html:
Can you please try this patch?

diff --git a/Include/cpython/initconfig.h b/Include/cpython/initconfig.h
index 846e05fb26a..1dcb7807761 100644
--- a/Include/cpython/initconfig.h
+++ b/Include/cpython/initconfig.h
@@ -15,7 +15,13 @@ typedef struct {
     } _type;
     const char *func;
     const char *err_msg;
+#ifndef __cplusplus
     Py_DEPRECATED(3.16) int exitcode;
+#else
+    // Avoid Py_DEPRECATED() on C++ to avoid a compile warning on an (implicit)
+    // PyStatus move assignment operator.
+    int exitcode;
+#endif
 } PyStatus;
 
 PyAPI_FUNC(PyStatus) PyStatus_Ok(void);

thread.author: vstinner
thread.html: @NekoAsakura: _Py_COMP_DIAG_IGNORE_DEPR_DECLS is designed to ignore a deprecation warning when using a deprecated function/API. I don't think that it should be used when marking an API as deprecated.

thread.author: NekoAsakura
thread.html:
I cannot reproduce the C++ warning on Fedora 44 with g++ 16.2.1 or clang++ 22.1.8 using your example.

@vstinner That's because it was fixed in clang >= 22 (#147400). I can confirm your example also warns on older versions.

I also tried your patch. It fixes the issue, but it causes a regression where using status.exitcode in C++ no longer warns.

_Py_COMP_DIAG_IGNORE_DEPR_DECLS is designed to ignore a deprecation warning when using a deprecated function/API. I don't think that it should be used when marking an API as deprecated.

It is usually used around code that uses a deprecated API, but here the warning is reported inside Python.h, so users can't silence it in their own code.

thread.author: davidnich
thread.html:
Tested with Apple clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.3.34.2, current Xcode, arm64), using a copy of the 3.14 headers with PyStatus.exitcode declared as in 3.16, with -std=c++17 -Wall:

initconfig.h example from the report s.exitcode in C++ s.exitcode in C
current (3.16) 3 warnings warning warning
#ifndef __cplusplus patch no warning no warning warning
_Py_COMP_DIAG_PUSH / _Py_COMP_DIAG_IGNORE_DEPR_DECLS around the struct definition no warning warning warning

So, as @NekoAsakura says, the #ifndef __cplusplus patch fixes the false positive but drops the deprecation for real C++ uses. Suppressing the warning only around the definition keeps it. Clang reports the warning for a use in the user's own code, outside the push/pop region, so only the implicit copy/move members generated from the definition are affected. Apple's current clang 21 still has the behavior fixed in clang 22 (llvm/llvm-project#147400), so macOS embedders building with Xcode will hit this until Xcode ships clang 22+.

issues.title: selectors: modify() of poll-based selectors accepts an invalid event mask
issues.author: tonghuaroot
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug description:

BaseSelector.modify() is documented to raise ValueError "in case of invalid event mask". SelectSelector and KqueueSelector do, but PollSelector, EpollSelector and DevpollSelector accept the mask and store it in the key:

import os, selectors
r, w = os.pipe()
sel = selectors.PollSelector()
sel.register(r, selectors.EVENT_READ)
print(sel.modify(r, 0).events)  # 0, expected ValueError

modify(r, -1) and modify(r, 999999) are accepted too, while register(r, 0) raises ValueError: Invalid events: 0. _PollLikeSelector.modify() has skipped the check since its fast path was added in 3.7 (bpo-30014). EpollSelector is the DefaultSelector on Linux.

issues.title: asyncio: Windows socket reset during Proactor cleanup skips socket closure and transport detachment
issues.author: h3har
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug description

On Windows, _ProactorBasePipeTransport._call_connection_lost() can raise ConnectionResetError: [WinError 10054] from self._sock.shutdown(socket.SHUT_RDWR) while cleaning up a connection. The exception escapes into the event loop's exception handler before the subsequent socket closure, server detachment, and _called_connection_lost = True execute.

This was observed in an active application on CPython 3.14.5 (Windows), producing Exception in callback _ProactorBasePipeTransport._call_connection_lost() errors. The application continued running. The defect is the interrupted cleanup, beyond the unexpected error log: a socket can remain open until later finalization, and transport bookkeeping remains incomplete.

Deterministic reproducer

This standard-library-only example injects the observed socket-shutdown error and calls the unmodified CPython cleanup method. It demonstrates the skipped cleanup without depending on network timing; it does not reproduce the original TCP reset timing. Run it on Windows in a fresh interpreter without an application-installed asyncio patch.

from asyncio.proactor_events import _ProactorBasePipeTransport
from types import SimpleNamespace
from unittest.mock import Mock

reset = ConnectionResetError("connection reset during shutdown")
reset.winerror = 10054
sock = Mock()
sock.shutdown.side_effect = reset
server = Mock()
transport = SimpleNamespace(
    _called_connection_lost=False,
    _protocol=Mock(),
    _sock=sock,
    _server=server,
)

try:
    _ProactorBasePipeTransport._call_connection_lost(transport, None)
except ConnectionResetError:
    print("ConnectionResetError escaped cleanup")

print("socket.close calls:", sock.close.call_count)
print("server detach calls:", server._detach.call_count)
print("cleanup complete:", transport._called_connection_lost)

Observed output on CPython 3.14.5:

ConnectionResetError escaped cleanup
socket.close calls: 0
server detach calls: 0
cleanup complete: False

Expected behavior

An already-reset socket should still be closed and the transport detached and marked complete. Handle the expected reset around the socket shutdown operation, while ensuring remaining cleanup runs. Exceptions from protocol.connection_lost() and unexpected shutdown failures should remain observable; broadly suppressing exceptions around the whole callback would hide unrelated failures.

A potential improvement would prevent noisy error log messages by catching 'reasonable' shutdown failures and logging them via asyncio's debug logger (if debug mode is enabled for that proactor transport's event loop). Either way, shutdown errors should not cause cleanup to be skipped.

CPython versions tested on

CPython 3.14.5, Windows x86-64. Both the application traceback and the deterministic reproducer were observed on this version.

Source inspection, rather than execution on those interpreters, found the same method implementation in releases 3.14.6–3.14.9 and 3.15.0–3.15.1. See the 3.14.5 source and 3.15.1 source.

Related reports

  • The same shutdown traceback appears in a comment on #125981, a closed issue about SSL: APPLICATION_DATA_AFTER_CLOSE_NOTIFY. I could not find a dedicated issue tracking the interrupted Proactor socket cleanup.
  • #149388 concerned WinError 6 from PipeHandle.close() in this callback. That issue was fixed in PipeHandle; this report concerns WinError 10054 from the preceding socket shutdown() call.

issues.title: `hasattr(stream, "buffer")` fails with ValueError if buffer is detached
issues.author: pekkaklarck
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

>>> stream  =  open("example.txt", "w")
>>> hasattr(stream, "buffer")
True
>>> stream.detach()
<_io.BufferedWriter name='example.txt'>
>>> hasattr(stream, "buffer")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-2>", line 1, in <module>
    hasattr(stream, "buffer")
    ~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
ValueError: underlying buffer has been detached

This occurs with Python 3.14.9 and 3.15.1, but not with earlier versions such as 3.14.8 and 3.15.0. Tested both on Linux and on Windows. I consider hasattr failing with an exception pretty bad, especially when using it with standard library objects, and the behavior changing in a bug fix release makes it even worse.

I noticed this when a unit test for our custom isatty utility started to fail (robotframework/robotframework#5825). We have that utility so that we can safely check is a stream connected to console or not. It used to look like this:

def isatty(stream):
    # first check if buffer was detached
    if hasattr(stream, "buffer") and stream.buffer is None:
        return False
    if not hasattr(stream, "isatty"):
        return False
    try:
        return stream.isatty()
    except ValueError:  # Occurs if file is closed.
        return False

I already fixed this in our end by simply removing the separate detached buffer check. stream.isatty() raised a ValueError if its buffer is detached, similarly when the stream is closed, and we already handle that. Apparently the separate check was added before handling closed streams and nobody noticed earlier that the check is redundant.

3.14, 3.15

Operating systems tested on:

Linux, Windows

thread.author: scrieve
thread.html:
I would like to settle the intended behaviour here before asking anyone to review a patch.

The case for None:

  • In 3.14.8 buffer was a member descriptor (_Py_T_OBJECT), so a detached wrapper read as None and hasattr() did not raise.
  • _pyio.TextIOWrapper.buffer still returns None after detach, so the two implementations disagree today.
  • Nothing in the io docs says the attribute raises. The nearest statement is that the TextIOBase is unusable after detach, which reads as being about operations.

The case for the current ValueError is that gh-157364 deliberately routed the attribute through buffer_access_safe() while closing a use-after-free. That guard is still needed for reads and writes; the open question is only whether the attribute getter is the right place to raise it.

Proposal: the getter returns None when the wrapper is detached but initialised, and keeps raising ValueError for the uninitialised case. Every other caller keeps the existing guard, so nothing that gh-157364 protected changes.

If a triager or developer would rather keep the ValueError, that is a fine answer and I will drop the patch. A patch against this proposal is at #160467, held as a draft until there is agreement here.

issues.title: Possible lost notification in threading.Condition when a waiter times out
issues.author: 0x-bala
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Hi,

I noticed some unexpected behavior while testing threading.Condition on Python 3.14.4.

I created two threads waiting on the same condition. The first thread has a short timeout, while the second has a longer timeout. I then held the condition lock until the first waiter's timeout expired and called notify(1).

In my test, both wait() calls returned False, even though I called notify(1) while two waiters were still present in the internal wait queue. I observed the same result in 100 consecutive runs.

I'm not sure whether this is expected behavior or a race condition in how timed-out waiters are handled. Could someone clarify whether this behavior is expected? If not, it may be possible for a notification to be consumed by a waiter whose timeout has already expired, leaving another waiter waiting until its own timeout.

I can provide the minimal reproduction script and terminal output to help investigate.

CPython versions tested on:

3.14

Operating systems tested on:

Linux

thread.author: 0x-bala
thread.html:
import sys
import threading
import time

def poc_condition_notify_lost():
cond = threading.Condition()
res = {}

t1_in = threading.Event()
t2_in = threading.Event()

def w1():
    with cond:
        t1_in.set()
        res["t1"] = cond.wait(timeout=0.02)

def w2():
    t1_in.wait()
    with cond:
        t2_in.set()
        res["t2"] = cond.wait(timeout=0.2)

a = threading.Thread(target=w1)
b = threading.Thread(target=w2)

a.start()
b.start()
t2_in.wait()

with cond:
    time.sleep(0.05)
    cond.notify(1)

a.join()
b.join()

print("Python:", sys.version)
print("Results:", res)

if res == {"t1": False, "t2": False}:
    print("Observed: both wait calls returned False")
else:
    print("Observed:", res)

if name == "main":
poc_condition_notify_lost()

issues.title: Sync with importlib_metadata for Python 3.16
issues.author: jaraco
issues.bodyHTML:
Tracking issue for applying importlib_metadata changes to importlib.metadata in 3.16, continuing the pattern of #132947 (3.15) and #117089 (3.13).

This covers importlib_metadata 10.0.0, a change in functionality rather than a fix:

  • Shared protocols for consumers. IDistribution and IPackagePath join
    the existing PackageMetadata in _meta.py, and the functions returning
    distributions and files are annotated with them. A consumer can target one
    interface across importlib.metadata and the backport instead of either
    library's concrete classes, which is what a custom provider's objects
    require: the provider serves consumers of both libraries and cannot subclass
    its way into satisfying both (python/importlib_metadata#486,
    python/importlib_metadata#505). All three protocols are
    @runtime_checkable, so isinstance answers the question without
    evaluating a distribution's properties on 3.12 and later.

    What does not come downstream is the other half of that release. The backport
    substitutes its own classes for the importlib.metadata objects a provider
    supplies, and warns where a provider's class omits a member IDistribution
    requires; both live in its _compat package, which is excluded from the
    port. Only the protocols those mechanisms are defined against are synced, so
    the guidance for providers is documented here as the backport's behavior
    (gh-123976).

issues.title: `io.StringIO` crashes or returns garbage when used after a `MemoryError`
issues.author: gpshead
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

When io.StringIO fails with MemoryError while converting its accumulated writes to the internal buffer (first readline(), iteration, partial read(), truncate() or a write that is not at the end), the text is dropped but the object keeps its old length. Later calls then index outside a 2-character buffer: they crash or return unrelated memory as text. getvalue() and a full read() can leave the object in the same state.

import io, resource
resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_DATA, (128 << 20, 128 << 20))
f = io.StringIO()
f.write("x" * (32 << 20))
f.seek(0)
try:
    f.readline()
except MemoryError:
    print("MemoryError")
print(f.seek(0, 2))
f.seek(0)
f.readline()

On a debug build of main this prints MemoryError, then 33554432, then dies with a segmentation fault in the second readline(). Expected: the object still holds its text or is empty, and the second call raises MemoryError or returns normally.

email.feedparser can reach this: FeedParser.close() after a feed() that raised MemoryError on a very long first line. gh-157242 was a similar state-after-MemoryError bug in bytearray.

issues.title: `codecs.StreamReader.read()` silently drops an incomplete character at the end of the stream
issues.author: pganssle
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug description

StreamReader.read() decodes with the stateless codec function and keeps any undecoded trailing bytes for the next call. When the stream is exhausted there is no next call, so an incomplete final character is neither reported nor replaced; it just disappears:

>>> import codecs, io
>>> reader = codecs.getreader('utf-8')(io.BytesIO(b'ab\xe2'))
>>> reader.read()
'ab'
>>> reader.read()
''

Every other way of decoding the same bytes either raises or applies the error handler:

>>> b'ab\xe2'.decode('utf-8')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-3>", line 1, in <module>
    b'ab\xe2'.decode('utf-8')
UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xe2 in position 2: unexpected end of data
>>> io.TextIOWrapper(io.BytesIO(b'ab\xe2'), encoding='utf-8').read()
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xe2 in position 2: unexpected end of data
>>> codecs.getreader('utf-8')(io.BytesIO(b'ab\xe2'), 'replace').read()
'ab'
>>> b'ab\xe2'.decode('utf-8', 'replace')
'ab�'

So with errors='strict' a truncated file reads as if it were well-formed, and with 'replace' the replacement character that would mark the damage is missing. The same happens with utf-16, utf-32 and the escape codecs (unicode_escape with a trailing backslash); the CJK codecs are not affected, because their stateless decoders raise on an incomplete sequence themselves.

The cause is in read(): self.decode is the codec's stateless function with its default final=False (Lib/codecs.py line 512), and the loop exits on empty newdata without ever telling the decoder that the input is complete; self.bytebuffer keeps the fragment forever. Fixing it would mean a final decode pass once the underlying stream returns nothing, and raising (or applying the handler) if bytes remain, which is what IncrementalDecoder.decode(b'', final=True) does. The incremental decoders did not exist when StreamReader was written, which I assume is how this came about.

I realise codecs.open() is deprecated since 3.14 and StreamReader is on its way out with it, so feel free to say this is not worth touching; but it is silent data loss in the strict mode, which seemed worth having on record.

This is the same mechanism as #56717 (bpo-12508, 2011), which describes it for UTF-8 with errors='replace' and has had no activity since; I am filing it anyway because it applies to every codec with multi-byte characters and the strict-mode data loss is the part that matters, but feel free to fold this into that one.

Found by the Hypothesis tests in #160155, where it is pinned as StreamReaderTruncationBug.test_read_reports_truncated_input under expectedFailure.

issues.title: `euc_jp` and `gb18030` incremental decoders drop input after an incomplete trailing sequence under `surrogateescape`
issues.author: pganssle
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug description

With errors='surrogateescape', the incremental decoders of the CJK codecs that have sequences longer than two bytes (euc_jp, euc_jis_2004, euc_jisx0213, gb18030) lose data when the input ends in an incomplete sequence: the first byte is escaped, and whatever followed it is gone. The stateless decoder escapes the byte and keeps going:

>>> import codecs
>>> b'\x8f\x00'.decode('euc_jp', 'surrogateescape')
'\udc8f\x00'
>>> codecs.getincrementaldecoder('euc_jp')('surrogateescape').decode(b'\x8f\x00', final=True)
'\udc8f'
>>> b'\x806'.decode('gb18030', 'surrogateescape')
'\udc806'
>>> codecs.getincrementaldecoder('gb18030')('surrogateescape').decode(b'\x806', final=True)
'\udc80'

The 6 and the \x00 are plain ASCII; they are simply never looked at again. TextIOWrapper uses the incremental decoder, so this is reachable through ordinary file reading:

>>> import io
>>> io.TextIOWrapper(io.BytesIO(b'\xa8\x8fl'), encoding='euc_jp', errors='surrogateescape').read()
'\udca8\udc8f'

The other handlers do not lose anything because they consume the whole trailing range in one go (replace gives one � for it, backslashreplace escapes every byte). surrogateescape escapes a single byte and returns a resume position before the end of the input, and the final-flush path in _multibytecodec does not go back to the decoder from there: after the one multibytecodec_decerror(..., MBERR_TOOFEW) call it finishes up with whatever has been written so far, Modules/cjkcodecs/multibytecodec.c lines 1211-1218. The stateless entry point in the same file loops until the input is consumed, which is why it gets this right. That is from reading the code rather than tracing it, so treat the mechanism as a best guess. It also explains why the two-byte codecs (big5, euc_kr, gbk, shift_jis, ...) are not affected: with one pending byte there is nothing left to drop after escaping it.

Found by the Hypothesis tests in #160155, where it is pinned as MultibyteSurrogateescapeBug.test_trailing_bytes_after_escape under expectedFailure; the chunked-decoding tests there leave surrogateescape out for these four codecs until it is fixed.

issues.title: `iso2022_jp_3` encodes U+9B1D but decodes the result as U+9B1C
issues.author: pganssle
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug description

>>> '鬝'.encode('iso2022_jp_3')
b'\x1b$(P};\x1b(B'
>>> _.decode('iso2022_jp_3')
'鬜'
>>> hex(ord(_))
'0x9b1c'

JIS X 0213:2004 changed plane 2 row 93 cell 27 (0x7D3B) from U+9B1D to U+9B1C, and CPython emulates the 2000 mapping in the codecs named after that edition. euc_jisx0213 and shift_jisx0213 do so in both directions:

>>> '鬝'.encode('euc_jisx0213').decode('euc_jisx0213')
'鬝'
>>> '鬜'.encode('euc_jisx0213')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-5>", line 1, in <module>
    '鬜'.encode('euc_jisx0213')
    ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
UnicodeEncodeError: 'euc_jisx0213' codec can't encode character '鬜' in position 0: illegal multibyte sequence

iso2022_jp_3 only does it when encoding: it accepts U+9B1D and rejects U+9B1C like the other 2000 codecs, but decodes 0x7D3B as U+9B1C, as iso2022_jp_2004 does.

The cause is in jisx0213_2000_2_decoder, Modules/cjkcodecs/_codecs_iso2022.c lines 728-739. The EMULATE_JISX0213_2000_DECODE_PLANE2_CHAR macro expands to an if that sets u = 0x9B1D for this cell, but the table lookup that follows it is a plain if (TRYMAP_DEC_ST(jisx0213_2_bmp, ...)) rather than else if, so it runs regardless and overwrites u with the 2004 value. The plane 1 decoder just above uses else if after its emulation macro and is fine, as are the EUC and Shift_JIS codecs, which use the OUTCHAR form of the macro in _codecs_jp.c. So the fix is the missing else.

A scan of every code point through iso2022_jp_3 found no other character that comes back different, so it should be just this one cell.

Found by the Hypothesis tests in #160155, where it is pinned as RoundTripBugs.test_iso2022_jp_3_mapping under expectedFailure and kept out of the generated text otherwise.

issues.title: `bytearray` reads and writes outside its buffer after `del b[:n]` fails with `MemoryError`
issues.author: gpshead
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

If the allocation that shrinks the storage fails during del b[:n] (or b[:n] = shorter) on a bytearray, MemoryError is raised and the bytearray keeps its old length but starts n bytes before its buffer. Later reads return memory in front of the buffer and later writes modify it. bytearray_setslice_linear() undoes its ob_start advance on failure, but since gh-157242 (GH-157340) bytearray_resize_storage() has already moved the data and reset ob_start before the allocation is attempted.

import _testcapi

b = bytearray(b"A" * 100 + b"B" * 20)
_testcapi.set_nomemory(0, 1)
try:
    del b[:100]
except MemoryError:
    print("MemoryError")
finally:
    _testcapi.remove_mem_hooks()
print(len(b), b == b"A" * 100 + b"B" * 20)
print(bytes(b)[60:])

Expected 120 True and the original contents. On a debug build of main this prints

MemoryError
120 False
b'o\xfd\xfd\xfd\xfd\xfd\xfd\xfd\x01\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\xa0\xdd\x86\xc8(^\x00\x00x\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\xff\xff\xff\xff\xff\xff\xff\xffBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBB'

The bytes before the Bs are allocator padding and the header of the internal bytes object. The 3.15 branch has the same bytearray_resize_storage() code; 3.14 is not affected.

import os
from pathlib import Path

from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

with TemporaryDirectory() as name:

        ("clear-regular-directory", ["-I"], ["--clear"], False),
    ]
    if len(sys.argv) > 1:
        cases.append(("vscode", ["-I"], [], True))
    for case, interpreter_options, venv_options, expected in cases:
        project = root / case
        target = project / ".venv"
        target.mkdir(parents=True)
        marker = home / case
        (target / "ensurepip.py").write_text(
            "import os, runpy, sys\n"
            "from pathlib import Path\n"
            f"Path({str(marker)!r}).write_text('bootstrap executed')\n"
            "sys.path[:] = [s for s in sys.path if os.path.realpath(s) != os.getcwd()]\n"
            "runpy.run_module('ensurepip', run_name='__main__')\n"
        )
        if case == "vscode":
            arguments = [str(Path(sys.argv[1]).resolve())]
        else:
            arguments = ["-m", "venv", *venv_options, ".venv"]
        command = [sys.executable, *interpreter_options, *arguments]
        subprocess.run(command, env=env, cwd=project, check=True, timeout=90)
        print(case, "marker", marker.exists(), flush=True)

thread.author: rogdham
thread.html:
Hello,

The lzma module does not works well with XZ stream padding. Depending on the case, it may work; or it may stops the stream prematurely without error; or an error may be raised; or no error may be raised when it must.

In the XZ file format, stream padding is a number of null bytes (multiple of 4) that can be between and after streams.

From the specification (section 2.2):

Only the decoders that support decoding of concatenated Streams MUST support Stream Padding.

Since the lzma module supports decoding of concatenated streams, it must support stream padding as well.

#### Examples to reproduce the issue:

  1. example1.xz:
    • made of one stream followed by 4 null bytes:
      $ (echo 'Hi!' | xz; head -c 4 /dev/zero) > example1.xz
    • will raise an exception in both modes (FORMAT_AUTO and FORMAT_XZ)
>>> with lzma.open('/example1.xz', format=lzma.FORMAT_AUTO) as f:
...     f.read()
...
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 2, in <module>
  File "/usr/lib/python3.9/lzma.py", line 200, in read
    return self._buffer.read(size)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.9/_compression.py", line 99, in read
    raise EOFError("Compressed file ended before the "
EOFError: Compressed file ended before the end-of-stream marker was reached
>>> with lzma.open('/example1.xz', format=lzma.FORMAT_XZ) as f:
...     f.read()
...
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 2, in <module>
  File "/usr/lib/python3.9/lzma.py", line 200, in read
    return self._buffer.read(size)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.9/_compression.py", line 99, in read
    raise EOFError("Compressed file ended before the "
EOFError: Compressed file ended before the end-of-stream marker was reached
  1. example2.xz:
    • made of two streams with 18 null bytes of stream padding between them
      $ (echo 'Hi!' | xz; head -c 18 /dev/zero; echo 'Second stream' | xz) > example2.xz
    • second stream will be ignored with FORMAT_XZ
    • the two streams will be decoded with FORMAT_AUTO, where it should raise an error (18 null bytes is not multiple of 4, so the stream padding is invalid according to the XZ specification and the decoder “MUST indicate an error”)
>>> with lzma.open('/tmp/example2.xz', format=lzma.FORMAT_AUTO) as f:
...     f.read()
...
b'Hi!\nSecond stream\n'
>>> with lzma.open('/tmp/example2.xz', format=lzma.FORMAT_XZ) as f:
...     f.read()
...
b'Hi!\n'

#### Analysis

This issue comes from the relation between _lzma and _compression. In _lzma, the C library is called without the LZMA_CONCATENATED flag, which means that multiple streams and stream padding must be supported in Python.

In _compression, when a LZMADecompressor is done (.eof is True), an other one is created to decompress from that point. If the new one fails to decompress the remaining data, the LZMAError is ignored and we assume we reached the end.

So the behavior seen above can be explained as follows:

  • In FORMAT_AUTO, it seems that .eof is False while we haven't read 18 bytes
  • In FORMAT_AUTO, 18 null bytes will be decompressed as b'' with .eof being True afterwards
  • In FORMAT_XZ, it seems that .eof is False while we haven't read 12 bytes
  • In FORMAT_XZ, no stream padding is valid, so as soon as we have more than 12 bytes an LZMAError is raised

#### Possible solution

A possible solution would be to add a finish method on the decompressor interface, and support it appropriately in _compression when we reached EOF on the input. Then, in LZMADecompressor implementation, use the LZMA_CONCATENATED flag, and implement the finish method to call lzma_code with LZMA_FINISH as action.

I think this would be preferred than trying to solve the issue in Python, because if the format is FORMAT_AUTO we don't know if the format is XZ (and we should support stream padding) or not.

thread.author: rogdham
thread.html:
It must be decided what to do in the following cases, which are not valid per the XZ file specification, but supported by the lzma module (and tested):

  1. different format concatenated together (e.g. a .xz and a .lzma); this somehow includes tailing null bytes (12 null bytes is a valid .lzma)
  2. trailing junk (i.e. non-null bytes after the stream)

The answer may be different depending on the format arg (e.g. FORMAT_AUTO vs FORMAT_XZ).

thread.author: gpshead
thread.html:
the draft PR I've attached should address the spec compliant example1 from the original report. I don't think example2 is compliant, the \0 bytes are not a multiple of 4 padding in that one.

is there a practical use for this? what produces padded xz files? or what did so that has left some lying around that people need to parse?

The linked PR #161057 skips stream padding (null bytes in multiples of four) after every .xz stream in lzma.decompress() and LZMAFile, in Python rather than with LZMA_CONCATENATED, so no new decompressor API is needed. On the open questions: FORMAT_AUTO still decodes a .xz stream followed by a .lzma stream, trailing data that does not start with the .xz magic is still ignored, and padding whose size is not a multiple of four is left as it was rather than starting to raise, since some such files decode today.

thread.author: Rogdham
thread.html:
Hello, the example 2 is indeed non-compliant, I reported it initially because CPython was not raising any exceptions on it although data is no valid with respect to the xz format.

To answer your question, I don't have a practical use for this myself. I reported it when working on python-xz because I noticed that CPython implementation was not compliant with the xz specification on that point.

However I know that there padding is used by some, because I recently had a bug report on python-xz from a user that involved padding.

thread.author: gpshead
thread.html:
For reference on the expected behaviour: RFC 9110 section 15.4 lists the changes a user agent should make when it follows a redirect automatically, and they include removing "Header fields specific to the client's proxy configuration, including (but not limited to) Proxy-Authorization". Section 11.7.2 says Proxy-Authorization "applies only to the next inbound proxy that demanded authentication", so it should never reach an origin server, which is what happens today when the redirect target is opened without the proxy.

With the change, ProxyHandler adds the header again whenever the redirected request goes through a proxy configured with credentials. If you relied on the header being carried over a redirect some other way, please say so here.

issues.title: sum() deallocates float subclass instances as exact floats in the complex fast path
issues.author: opale-c
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

Bug report

Description

In builtin_sum_impl() (Python/bltinmodule.c), the complex-number fast
path tests items with PyFloat_Check() but releases them with
_Py_DECREF_SPECIALIZED(item, _PyFloat_ExactDealloc).

PyFloat_Check() also matches subclasses of float, whereas
_PyFloat_ExactDealloc is only valid for exact float objects. When a
float subclass instance reaches refcount 0 through this path, it is
deallocated as an exact float, bypassing its real tp_dealloc
(instance __dict__, weakref list, and GC bookkeeping). This can leak
memory and leave the cyclic GC in an inconsistent state.

The adjacent float fast path in the same function already guards the
identical specialized dealloc with PyFloat_CheckExact(); only the
complex branch uses the broader PyFloat_Check().

Reproducer

class F(float):
    pass

# complex start value selects the complex fast path
sum([F(1.0), F(2.0)], 0j)

Proposed fix

In the complex branch, use PyFloat_CheckExact(item) instead of
PyFloat_Check(item), so subclass instances fall through to the generic
PyNumber_Add path with a normal Py_DECREF. Numeric behavior is
unchanged.

Environment

  • CPython: main branch (please confirm the line is still present)

CPython versions tested on:

CPython main branch

Operating systems tested on:

Linux

Linked PRs

  • gh-150869
  • gh-151063
  • gh-161048
  • gh-161049

thread.author: skirpichev
thread.html:
Thanks for the fix, that's my fault. That was noticed before, but not fixed, unfortunately.

Though, note that in some branches - subclasses are handled. I think we should apply also

diff --git a/Python/bltinmodule.c b/Python/bltinmodule.c
index fbdd637a3fc..6af21fbef6f 100644
--- a/Python/bltinmodule.c
+++ b/Python/bltinmodule.c
@@ -2981,15 +2981,15 @@ builtin_sum_impl(PyObject *module, PyObject *iterable, PyObject *start)
                 _Py_DECREF_SPECIALIZED(item, _PyFloat_ExactDealloc);
                 continue;
             }
-            if (PyLong_Check(item)) {
+            if (PyLong_CheckExact(item)) {
                 double value = PyLong_AsDouble(item);
                 if (value != -1.0 || !PyErr_Occurred()) {
                     re_sum = cs_add(re_sum, value);
-                    Py_DECREF(item);
+                    _Py_DECREF_SPECIALIZED(item, _PyLong_ExactDealloc);
                     continue;
                 }
                 else {
-                    Py_DECREF(item);
+                    _Py_DECREF_SPECIALIZED(item, _PyLong_ExactDealloc);
                     Py_DECREF(iter);
                     return NULL;
                 }
@@ -3033,15 +3033,15 @@ builtin_sum_impl(PyObject *module, PyObject *iterable, PyObject *start)
                 Py_DECREF(item);
                 continue;
             }
-            if (PyLong_Check(item)) {
+            if (PyLong_CheckExact(item)) {
                 double value = PyLong_AsDouble(item);
                 if (value != -1.0 || !PyErr_Occurred()) {
                     re_sum = cs_add(re_sum, value);
-                    Py_DECREF(item);
+                    _Py_DECREF_SPECIALIZED(item, _PyLong_ExactDealloc);
                     continue;
                 }
                 else {
-                    Py_DECREF(item);
+                    _Py_DECREF_SPECIALIZED(item, _PyLong_ExactDealloc);
                     Py_DECREF(iter);
                     return NULL;
                 }

CC @rhettinger

issues.title: multiprocessing.Pool terminate shuts down workers too early
issues.author: mtrofin
issues.bodyHTML:
Environment:
Debian 5.10.113-1, python 3.7 (can repro on python 3.10, too)

Repro:
This was found in a LLVM test, easiest way to repro (not the most minimal, though):

git clone git@github.com:llvm/llvm-project.git

while true ; do llvm/utils/lit/lit.py -j1 --order=lexical --max-failures=1 llvm/utils/lit/tests/Inputs/max-failures ; done

This sets up a 1-worker pool (-j1). The debug output looks like this:

-- Testing: 3 tests, 1 workers --
created semlock with handle 140702642597888
created semlock with handle 140702642593792
created semlock with handle 140702628683776
created semlock with handle 140702628679680
created semlock with handle 140702628675584
created semlock with handle 140702628671488
added worker
closing pool
FAIL: max-failures :: fail1.txt (1 of 3)
terminating pool
finalizing pool
helping task handler/workers to finish
removing tasks from inqueue until task handler finished
result handler found thread._state=TERMINATE
ensuring that outqueue is not full
joining worker handler
worker handler exiting
result handler exiting: len(cache)=%s, thread._state=%s 2 TERMINATE
terminating workers
task handler got sentinel
joining task handler
task handler sending sentinel to result handler

...and now it hangs

After attaching with gdb:

(gdb) py-bt
Traceback (most recent call first):
  File "/usr/lib/python3.10/multiprocessing/synchronize.py", line 95, in __enter__
    return self._semlock.__enter__()
  File "/usr/lib/python3.10/multiprocessing/queues.py", line 376, in put
    with self._wlock:
  File "/usr/lib/python3.10/multiprocessing/pool.py", line 562, in _handle_tasks
    outqueue.put(None)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.10/threading.py", line 953, in run
    self._target(*self._args, **self._kwargs)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.10/threading.py", line 1016, in _bootstrap_inner
    self.run()
  File "/usr/lib/python3.10/threading.py", line 973, in _bootstrap
    self._bootstrap_inner()

Upon looking further: looks like multiprocessing.Pool's terminate attempts to terminate (as in Popen.terminate) the worker processes too early. If worker was in outqueue's critical section (that _wlock was taken) when it's shut down, that may explain the issue.

I tried calling terminate on the pool processes only after joining the task_handler and result_handler, i.e. :

711,716d710
<         # Terminate workers which haven't already finished.
<         if pool and hasattr(pool[0], 'terminate'):
<             util.debug('terminating workers')
<             for p in pool:
<                 if p.exitcode is None:
<                     p.terminate()
724a719,725
>
>         # Terminate workers which haven't already finished.
>         if pool and hasattr(pool[0], 'terminate'):
>             util.debug('terminating workers')
>             for p in pool:
>                 if p.exitcode is None:
>                     p.terminate()

That appears to address the issue - the script runs now indefinitely.

The code in Pool.terminate seems to have been around for a while, so maybe I am missing something? If not, happy to submit a patch!

thread.author: lorenzph
thread.html:
I have experienced the same issue and the following snippet triggers this deadlock quite reliably on my machine (Python 3.12.7 on Linux):

import multiprocessing
import os
import faulthandler

def func(value):
    if value >= 32:
        raise Exception
    return None

def run():
    print("Start")
    faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(10)
    try:
        with multiprocessing.Pool(processes=16) as pool:
            result = list(pool.imap(func, range(0, 100)))
    except Exception as e:
        pass
    print("Done")

while True:
    print("Next run")
    run()

Switching imap to map mitigates the issue as in this particular case map doesn't seem to raise the exception until the workers are finished (hence avoiding the issue that the lock is held by one when the pool is torn down).

thread.author: ondrejch
thread.html:
We hit what looks like a second mechanism behind this hang, in a batch job on Linux x86-64 workers (Python 3.12.15, also reproduced on 3.12.3). The reordering proposed here is not sufficient alone.

Mechanism. Connection._send_bytes sends a message larger than 16384 bytes as two writes, a 4-byte header and then the payload (connection.py, 3.12: lines 417-421). SimpleQueue.put holds outqueue._wlock across both. If terminate() SIGTERMs a worker between the two writes, the worker dies holding _wlock and leaves a truncated message in the result pipe. The parent keeps the write end open, so there is no EOF:

  • the result handler waits in its exit drain for the rest of the payload: pool.py:626 get() -> connection.py:250 recv -> 437 _recv_bytes -> 395 _recv (in the field case, read(fd, 19770) with 0 bytes unread);
  • the task handler, if it has not yet sent its sentinel, blocks at pool.py:562 outqueue.put(None) -> queues.py:398 with self._wlock;
  • the caller of terminate() waits in _terminate_pool at pool.py:720 (task_handler.join()), or at 724 (result_handler.join()) if the task handler had already exited.

The frames are identical on 3.12.3 and 3.12.15. The split send and SimpleQueue.put are unchanged in 3.13, 3.14, 3.15 and main; if n > 16384 is at connection.py line 417 on 3.12, 422 on 3.13 and 439 on 3.14, 3.15 and main. Those pool.py lines stay at 562, 626, 703, 720 and 724 through 3.15, and _terminate_pool is unchanged through 3.15. On main the sentinel put is at 728 and the joins at 745 and 749, and _terminate_pool also releases the task-queue buffer semaphores after task_handler._state = TERMINATE; that does not release _wlock. The same truncation is the subject of the open gh-159689 and the open, unmerged PR #159697 (checked 2026-10-31). That PR teaches the ProcessPoolExecutor result read to watch worker sentinels. Pool is unchanged there, and a recv() without sentinels still blocks.

Reordering alone. Separately, a hang with no kill at all has the caller of terminate() at pool.py:703 (outqueue.put(None) -> queues.py:398, with self._wlock). One trial of a longer, instrumented version of the script below (8 workers, 64 tasks, and a 300 ms pause after the last input item) was snapshotted on unpatched 3.12.3 in that state: the task handler at pool.py:562 -> queues.py:398, the workers alive, 3687 of the 4096 bytes of the result pipe unread, and the _wlock semaphore value 0. The diff in this issue does not move line 703. It lies above the worker terminate() loop (lines 712-716) and the joins (720, 724), so a live holder of _wlock stops _terminate_pool there whether or not the loop is moved. I did not apply the diff and rerun; this follows from the unpatched snapshot and the line order.

Reproducer (stdlib only, Linux). It widens the window with two tricks: the result pipe is shrunk to 4 KiB with F_SETPIPE_SZ, and unpickling a result in the parent sleeps 20 ms. Neither patches multiprocessing.

import faulthandler, fcntl, multiprocessing as mp, os, sys, threading, time

def rebuild(payload, delay):
    time.sleep(delay)
    return payload

class Slow:
    def __init__(self, payload): self.payload = payload
    def __reduce__(self): return (rebuild, (self.payload, 0.02))

def work(_):
    time.sleep(0.03)
    return Slow(b"x" * 20000)       # pickled size > 16384

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ctx = mp.get_context("spawn")
    for trial in range(1, 31):
        pool = ctx.Pool(4)
        fcntl.fcntl(pool._outqueue._reader.fileno(), fcntl.F_SETPIPE_SZ, 4096)
        it = pool.imap_unordered(work, range(32))
        for _ in range(4):
            next(it)
        t = threading.Thread(target=pool.terminate, daemon=True)
        t.start(); t.join(5)
        if t.is_alive():
            print("HANG in trial", trial, file=sys.stderr)
            faulthandler.dump_traceback()
            os._exit(3)
        pool.join()
    print("no hang in 30 trials")

On one host (3.12.3) this exits 3 with the stacks above in the first 30 trials in 3 of 3 invocations (trials 6, 5 and 8). A longer, instrumented version of the same script hung 3 times in 22 trials across four invocations (the last invocation stopped after 2 trials without a hang); the task and result handlers were stuck as above in one, the result handler only in two. These numbers are from one machine.

This looks like the same root cause as gh-79448 (the _wlock held by a killed worker) and gh-78178 (the result handler stuck in the drain). A fix probably has to stop the workers cooperatively, or make the two-part send safe against a kill, rather than only reorder the joins.

issues.title: time/datetime.fromisoformat: C accelerator accepts a fractional seconds component with no decimal mark
issues.author: SEPURI-SAI-KRISHNA
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

In the basic ISO 8601 time format, the C implementation of
time.fromisoformat() / datetime.fromisoformat() accepts digits following
HHMMSS and silently interprets them as a fractional seconds component, even
though no decimal mark (. or ,) is present. ISO 8601 requires a decimal
sign to introduce a fraction, and the pure-Python implementation correctly
rejects these strings.

>>> from datetime import time, datetime
>>> time.fromisoformat('12345678')
datetime.time(12, 34, 56, 780000)          # expected ValueError
>>> time.fromisoformat('123456789')
datetime.time(12, 34, 56, 789000)          # expected ValueError
>>> datetime.fromisoformat('2020-01-01T12345678')
datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 1, 12, 34, 56, 780000)   # expected ValueError

The pure-Python implementation rejects all of the above:

>>> import _pydatetime
>>> _pydatetime.time.fromisoformat('12345678')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: Invalid isoformat string: '12345678'

The same parser is used for the UTC offset, so a malformed offset is accepted
too, with the extra digits silently discarded:

>>> time.fromisoformat('12:34:56+00000000')
datetime.time(12, 34, 56, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc)   # expected ValueError

Two further details show the leniency is unintended rather than deliberate:

  • The equivalent extended-format string is correctly rejected —
    time.fromisoformat('12:34:5678') raises ValueError.
  • The behaviour is not even self-consistent across lengths. '1234567'
    (7 digits) raises ValueError, while '12345678' (8 digits) is accepted.

This matters because the failure is silent and produces a wrong value rather
than an error: a truncated or corrupted timestamp string parses successfully
into a time/datetime that differs from the input.

Cause

In parse_hh_mm_ss_ff() (Modules/_datetimemodule.c), the HH/MM/SS loop
breaks when it sees a decimal mark, but in the basic format it can also fall
out of the loop normally after SS with characters still unconsumed (the
!has_separator branch does --p). The code following the loop then parses
whatever remains as a fraction, without ever checking that a decimal mark
introduced it.

The pure-Python _parse_hh_mm_ss_ff() in Lib/_pydatetime.py performs that
check explicitly:

if pos < len_str:
    if tstr[pos] not in '.,':
        raise ValueError("Invalid microsecond separator")

Documentation

fromisoformat() is documented to accept "any valid ISO 8601 format" subject to
an explicit list of exceptions; a fraction without a decimal sign is not among
them.

This is the same class of C/pure-Python divergence as gh-152157 (empty fraction
before a timezone designator) and gh-152079.

Affected versions

Reproduced directly on 3.12.3 and on main (3.16.0a0). I did not have 3.13,
3.14 or 3.15 interpreters to hand, but comparing parse_hh_mm_ss_ff() across
the branches shows the cause is present in all of them: the
else if (!has_separator) { --p; } branch and the unguarded "Parse fractional
components" block that follows the loop are unchanged on every active branch.
The 3.14, 3.15 and main copies of the function are identical; the 3.12 and
3.13 copies differ only in other validation paths (decimal mark on
hour/minute, empty fraction, microsecond separator).

CPython versions tested on:

3.12, 3.16, CPython main branch

Operating systems tested on:

Linux

Linked PRs

  • gh-161018
