thread.author: aisk
thread.html:
This was discussed before in gh-83594. Using SetEnvironmentVariableW would solve this, but it bypasses the CRT, so C code in the same process that calls getenv() won't see the variable. That's why _wputenv is used, which leads to the current inconsistency.

I think it might be reasonable to just treat this as platform-specific behavior and document it? It's easy to work around at the application level.

Another option is to combine the two APIs for empty values, but that's a bit messy.

So I'd like to hear what @eryksun and @zooba think.

thread.author: asottile
thread.html: seems wrong to me to care that the CRT environ is in sync over os.environ itself

thread.author: zooba
thread.html:
seems wrong to me to care that the CRT environ is in sync over os.environ itself

Perhaps, but it's a long-standing deliberate behaviour, and to change it will require a deprecation period.

We care about the CRT state because embedders will share that state with the runtime they've loaded. That's been very intentional for a long time.

Adding an additional SetEnvironmentVariable call to set an empty variable after wputenv has deleted it would be possible, I guess. I have no idea whether that will achieve what is desired here (as far as I can tell, the original "problem" is that there is code that expects an empty environment variable to exist, which just means it's made an assumption that isn't necessarily true and doesn't necessarily mean that it's useful or important to work that way - but I'm totally missing context on this, since I've only got this issue and the linked one to look at).

thread.author: aisk
thread.html:
Hi, I tried to add an additional SetEnvironmentVariableW call to set an empty variable after _wputenv, as @zooba mentioned. But after os.reload_environ(), the key is still missing (though it can be read with GetEnvironmentVariableW). So I think the variable is written to Windows but not to the CRT.

I think this is already an existing behavior, and there seems to be no simple way to resolve it completely. Since platform differences are hard to avoid, I suggest we just document this behavior.

thread.author: UriOkrent
thread.html:
Attempting to unpickle an xmlrpc.client.Fault will raise a TypeError:

>>> import xmlrpc.client as xmlrpclib
>>> f = xmlrpclib.Fault(42, 'Test Fault')
>>> import pickle
>>> s = pickle.dumps(f)
>>> pickle.loads(s)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
TypeError: __init__() missing 2 required positional arguments: 'faultCode' and 'faultString'

Apparently unpickle relies on BaseException's args attribute when reconstructing an Exception class that inherits from BaseException (Fault inherits from Exception). Unfortunately, Fault implements __init__() and does call the base class constructor, but does not pass its arguments, so Fault.args is always an empty tuple.

Simply passing Fault's arguments to the base class constructor allows it to be unpickled.

I've included a patch for 3.x but the issue is present in 2.x as well (the code and fix are exactly the same except in xmlrpclib.py).

thread.author: berkerpeksag
thread.html: Looks good to me, thanks.

thread.author: serhiy-storchaka
thread.html: Why you need to pickle Fault?

thread.author: UriOkrent
thread.html:
I'm not pickling/unpickling it directly, I'm using multiprocessing to handle queries to my server in worker processes which is using pickle to propagate exceptions raised in the worker to the parent.

I could instead raise a different exception and wrap it in a Fault later (which is what I ended up doing to avoid the issue), but it seems like a case of "to-may-to" vs. "to-mah-to". Either way an Exception should be able to be propagated up to the parent in multiprocessing, whether it's my own or Fault.

thread.author: serhiy-storchaka
thread.html:
This looks reasonable.

But since Fault never was unpickleable, this issue is in gray zone between bug fixing and adding new feature. The latter can be done only in new Python version. I hesitate with classification of this issue.

There are a lot of other exceptions that can't be unpickled (including xmlrpc.client.ProtocolError). This may be a part of larger issue.

As for the patch itself, it solves the issue. But faultCode and faultString are saved twice (this is not a large problem for multiprocessing). Test should test pickling with all possible protocols (see how other pickle tests are written).

thread.author: UriOkrent
thread.html:
My reading of the docs leads me to lean towards bug since this seems to break the contract of BaseException API in a standard lib module:

https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#BaseException says BaseExceptions have args and with_traceback so those probably should be preserved in all standard lib inheritors.

This excerpt from the tutorial also seems to imply the same:
https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/errors.html#user-defined-exceptions

"In this example, the default __init__() of Exception has been overridden. The new behavior simply creates the value attribute. This replaces the default behavior of creating the args attribute."

The tutorial goes out of its way to note that the default behavior of creating args has been replaced in this simple example -- i.e., one would expect args to be present.

As for your other comments, should I make a similar change to other inheritors of xmlrpc.client that inherit from xmlrpc.client.Error? Should I instead completely remove Fault's constructor and just make faultCode and faultString properties so the attributes aren't duplicated (that seems like it may be dangerous)?

I will update the test for pickling with the other protocols.

thread.author: UriOkrent
thread.html:
I updated the patch to improve the tests and made the same change to xmlrpc.client.ProtocolError (which was the only other place in xmlrpc.client). I'll let you decide if this patch is better despite the fact that it suffers from the same data duplication as Fault.

If not, we can go back to just fixing Fault, or come up with a fancier solution entirely that doesn't duplicate data. Though, I hesitate to start getting too fancy for two reasons: 1) this module is old and stable, and 2) these are exception objects, so while the data duplication is ugly, the instances themselves should be short-lived.

I have worked up a monkey patch for urllib2/httplib for the issue of setting the authentication using a Proxy(Basic|Digest)AuthHandler.

The basic approach was to create a new httplib exception (ProxyTunnelError) and raise that with the http response attached so that the HTTPSHandler can determine when 407 Proxy authentication required is present, and then reroute the urllib2.OpenerDirector to error handling mode.

Unfortunately, there is a backwards compatibility issue - cases where a socket.error was previously being raised now get an ProxyTunnelError. Not that you could do much useful with the socket.error in the first place, but I suppose you could look for '407' in the text. Ugh.

thread.author: vadmium
thread.html:
I believe this also affects Python 3; see bpo-24333.

I think making the CONNECT response object available to the caller is the right general approach. But I really dislike raising an exception that holds a socket connection to be closed. (I know this is already done with urllib.error.HTTPError; let’s not repeat this in the “http.client” module!)

Ideally, at the “http.client” level I would prefer to avoid all the special set_tunnel() calls, and use the usual request() and getresponse() API to make the CONNECT request. This way the response status and header fields would be available just like any other response. For this approach to work, we would probably need to add a new HTTPConnection.detach() method that released the original socket reader and writer, and add a way to create a new HTTPConnection instance using these socket objects. This enhancement probably wouldn’t be appropriate for Python 2 or a bug fix release. But it seems the cleanest approach to me, and may also allow using HTTPConnection with the Upgrade header (e.g. for opportunistic encryption, HTTP 2, Web etc), and proxying non-HTTP connections, as bonuses.

A less revolutionary approach might be to add a HTTPSConnection.tunnel() method, that always returns the proxy’s response, but only does the SSL wrapping for a successful response.

thread.author: vadmium
thread.html:
For the record, a while ago I think I made a patch implementing my HTTPConnection.detach() proposal. I can probably dig it up if anyone is interested.

However I gave up on fixing this bug in “urllib.request”. As far as I understand it, the framework does not distinguish the 407 Proxy Authentication Required error of the initial proxy CONNECT request from any potential 407 response from a tunnelled connection. Perhaps a special case could be made; I think there are already lots of special cases. But the maze of urlopen() handlers is already too complicated and I decided this was too hard to bother working on. Sorry :)

thread.author: OneMoreZanuda
thread.html:
It has been 5 years, now the urllib3 is actively used, but it also inherited this problem: if no authentication data has been received, then the method _tunnel raises an exception OSError that does not contain response headers. Accordingly, this exception cannot be handled. And perhaps this is an obstacle to building a convenient system of authentication on a proxy server in a widely used library requests (it would be nice to be able to just provide an argument proxy_auth, similar to how it is done for server authorization). Now, if a user wants to send a https request through a proxy that requires complex authentication (Kerberos, NTLM, Digest, other) using the urllib3, he must first send a separate request to the proxy, receive a response, extract the necessary data to form the header Proxy-Authorization, then generate this header and pass it to the ProxyManager. And if we are talking about Requests, then the situation there is worse, because you cannot pass proxy headers directly (psf/requests#2708).
If we were to aim to simplify the authentication procedure on the proxy server for the user, then where would we start, do we need to change the http.client so that the error returned by the method _tunnel contains headers? Or maybe it's not worth changing anything at all and the path with preliminary preparation by user of the header Proxy-Authorization is the only correct one? Martin Panter, could you also give your opinion? Thank you in advance.

issues.title: Out-of-bounds read in integrated mimalloc (fixed upstream)
issues.author: fuhsnn
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

The integrated mimalloc has out-of-bounds bug in the generic implementation of ctz/clz:

cpython/Include/internal/mimalloc/mimalloc/internal.h

Lines 847 to 870 in 6a22963

static inline size_t mi_ctz32(uint32_t x) {
// de Bruijn multiplication, see <http://supertech.csail.mit.edu/papers/debruijn.pdf>
static const unsigned char debruijn[32] = {
0, 1, 28, 2, 29, 14, 24, 3, 30, 22, 20, 15, 25, 17, 4, 8,
31, 27, 13, 23, 21, 19, 16, 7, 26, 12, 18, 6, 11, 5, 10, 9
};
if (x==0) return 32;
return debruijn[((x & -(int32_t)x) * 0x077CB531UL) >> 27];
}
static inline size_t mi_clz32(uint32_t x) {
// de Bruijn multiplication, see <http://supertech.csail.mit.edu/papers/debruijn.pdf>
static const uint8_t debruijn[32] = {
31, 22, 30, 21, 18, 10, 29, 2, 20, 17, 15, 13, 9, 6, 28, 1,
23, 19, 11, 3, 16, 14, 7, 24, 12, 4, 8, 25, 5, 26, 27, 0
};
if (x==0) return 32;
x |= x >> 1;
x |= x >> 2;
x |= x >> 4;
x |= x >> 8;
x |= x >> 16;
return debruijn[(uint32_t)(x * 0x07C4ACDDUL) >> 27];
}

On platforms with 64-bit UL, the multiplication in index calculation can grow much larger than array debruijn[].

It has been fixed in this upstream commit:
microsoft/mimalloc@ed31847

3.14, CPython main branch, 3.13, 3.15

issues.title: Ctypes: Unclear Error Message for WinFunctionType Mismatch in Windows API Calls
issues.author: songyuc
issues.bodyHTML:
Description:

When working with Windows API functions (such as SetWindowsHookExW) using ctypes, providing a HOOKPROC callback function of an incorrect type results in an unclear error message. This can be confusing, especially for beginners or when debugging complex scenarios.

Current error message:
TypeError: expected WinFunctionType instance instead of WinFunctionType

Suggested improved error message:
TypeError: expected WinFunctionType with signature (restype=wintypes.LPARAM, argtypes=[ctypes.c_int32, wintypes.WPARAM, wintypes.LPARAM]) but received WinFunctionType with signature (restype=ctypes.c_int, argtypes=[ctypes.c_int, wintypes.WPARAM, wintypes.LPARAM])

Steps to Reproduce:

  1. Create a Python script with the following content:
import ctypes
import ctypes.wintypes

HOOKPROC = ctypes.WINFUNCTYPE(ctypes.c_int, ctypes.c_int, ctypes.wintypes.WPARAM, ctypes.wintypes.LPARAM)

user32 = ctypes.windll.user32
user32.SetWindowsHookExW.argtypes = [ctypes.c_int, HOOKPROC, ctypes.wintypes.HINSTANCE, ctypes.wintypes.DWORD]
user32.SetWindowsHookExW.restype = ctypes.wintypes.HHOOK

def callback(nCode, wParam, lParam):
    return user32.CallNextHookEx(None, nCode, wParam, lParam)

pointer = HOOKPROC(callback)
hook_id = user32.SetWindowsHookExW(13, pointer, None, 0)  # 13 corresponds to WH_KEYBOARD_LL

# At this point, import pynput, which modifies the SetWindowsHookExW function
from pynput import keyboard, mouse

# Attempt to set the hook again, which now fails due to type mismatch
hook_id = user32.SetWindowsHookExW(13, pointer, None, 0)
  1. Run the script

Expected Result:
A clear error message indicating the mismatch between the expected and provided WinFunctionType, including details about their signatures.

Actual Result:
An unclear error message: "TypeError: expected WinFunctionType instance instead of WinFunctionType"

Python Version: 3.12.7
Operating System: Windows

Suggested Improvement:
Modify the logic in ctypes that generates these error messages to include more detailed information about the expected and actual WinFunctionType instances, such as their return types and argument types. This would greatly improve the readability and usefulness of the error message, especially for beginners and when debugging complex scenarios.

Additional Notes:
This issue becomes apparent when using libraries like pynput that modify Windows API function signatures. A more descriptive error message would help users identify and resolve such conflicts more easily.

CPython versions tested on:

3.12

Operating systems tested on:

Windows

Linked PRs

  • gh-160995

thread.author: zooba
thread.html:
Improving an error message is a feature, not a bug, but there shouldn't be any reason why it can't be done here (it just won't be backported to maintenance releases).

(The bugfix in pynput (or the user's own code) is to use ctypes.WinDLL("user32") rather than ctypes.windll.user32 so that they aren't modifying shared objects. This should already be documented, I'm pretty sure.)

libc.qsort(None, 0, ctypes.sizeof(ctypes.c_int), CMPFUNC_LONG(cmp))
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/peter/develop/cpython/a.py", line 14, in <module>
    libc.qsort(None, 0, ctypes.sizeof(ctypes.c_int), CMPFUNC_LONG(cmp))
    ~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
ctypes.ArgumentError: argument 4: TypeError: expected CFunctionType instance instead of CFunctionType

thread.author: assilrguez
thread.html:
I worked through a local proposal for this. The mismatch is handled by CDataType_from_param_impl() in Modules/_ctypes/_ctypes.c; callback function types currently reach its generic type error, where both types have the same tp_name.

For mismatched ctypes callback types, the proposed special case uses each callback type's StgInfo to show the expected and actual return and argument types, while leaving the existing generic error unchanged for other mismatches:

if (PyCFuncPtrTypeObject_Check(st, type) &&
    PyCFuncPtrObject_Check(st, value)) {
    StgInfo *expected_info, *actual_info;
    if (PyStgInfo_FromType(st, type, &expected_info) < 0 ||
        PyStgInfo_FromType(st, (PyObject *)Py_TYPE(value),
                           &actual_info) < 0) {
        return NULL;
    }
    if (expected_info != NULL && actual_info != NULL) {
        PyErr_Format(PyExc_TypeError,
                     "expected %s with signature (restype=%R, argtypes=%R), "
                     "got %s with signature (restype=%R, argtypes=%R)",
                     ((PyTypeObject *)type)->tp_name,
                     expected_info->restype ? expected_info->restype : Py_None,
                     expected_info->argtypes ? expected_info->argtypes : Py_None,
                     Py_TYPE(value)->tp_name,
                     actual_info->restype ? actual_info->restype : Py_None,
                     actual_info->argtypes ? actual_info->argtypes : Py_None);
        return NULL;
    }
}

The resulting message is in the familiar “expected …, got …” form, for example:

expected CFunctionType with signature (restype=<class 'ctypes.c_float'>, argtypes=(<class 'ctypes.c_void_p'>,)), got CFunctionType with signature (restype=<class 'ctypes.c_double'>, argtypes=(<class 'ctypes.c_short'>,))

I added a regression test in Lib/test/test_ctypes/test_parameters.py that passes a callback with a different restype and argtype and checks that both signatures appear in the TypeError. I also added a Misc/NEWS.d/next/Library entry.

On my local Windows Release build, the focused test passed and the complete test_ctypes suite passed (701 tests run, 43 skipped). This proposal is for the in-development branch; I have not tested the reporter's exact pynput scenario.

issues.title: PyGILStateEnsure() (Probably) Crashes If Called After Finalization
issues.author: ericsnowcurrently
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

I'm pretty sure PyGILState_Ensure() will crash if called after finalization, particularly in the case where the thread doesn't already have a thread state active. I noticed this while looking at the function for something else.

CC @gpshead

CPython versions tested on:

CPython main branch

Operating systems tested on:

No response

thread.author: Sccucci84
thread.html:
Hitting what looks like this same crash in real-world (non-synthetic) code, via PyGObject + GDBus, on Python 3.14.7 — so this is still unfixed on stable 3.14, not just the 3.14.0a7 build from #132948.

Reproducer: powerprofilesctl get (a short-lived Python script shipped with power-profiles-daemon, using PyGObject to talk to power-profiles-daemon over D-Bus). It queries the current profile, prints it, and exits. Invoked frequently (once per status-bar poll interval) it segfaults intermittently with SIGSEGV / SEGV_MAPERR.

coredumpctl info backtrace of the crashing thread (a GDBus worker thread, not the main thread):

Stack trace of thread 284370 (gdbus):
#0  0x00007fa616eaa612 n/a (libpython3.14.so.1.0 + 0x2aa612)
#1  0x00007fa616e393ad PyEval_RestoreThread (libpython3.14.so.1.0 + 0x2393ad)
#2  0x00007fa616f2a66a PyGILState_Ensure (libpython3.14.so.1.0 + 0x32a66a)
#3  0x00007fa616a6156e n/a (_gi.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so + 0x1156e)
#4  0x00007fa615fd2cd9 n/a (libglib-2.0.so.0 + 0x35cd9)
#5  0x00007fa615f5ca90 g_object_unref (libgobject-2.0.so.0 + 0x22a90)
#6  0x00007fa614920720 n/a (libgio-2.0.so.0 + 0x10c720)
...
#11 0x00007fa616001217 g_main_loop_run (libglib-2.0.so.0 + 0x64217)

Frame #0 is unresolved (no debug symbols on this build), but given PyEval_RestoreThread → PyGILState_Ensure directly above it, it's almost certainly the same _PyThreadState_Attach/bind_gilstate_tstate path as the original report.

At the same instant, the main thread is already inside exit():

Stack trace of thread 284367 (main):
#2  n/a (libc.so.6 + 0x40fbf)
#3  exit (libc.so.6 + 0x4109e)
#4  n/a (libc.so.6 + 0x27788)
#5  __libc_start_main (libc.so.6 + 0x278b9)

Mechanism appears to be: the main thread finishes and calls exit(), kicking off interpreter finalization, while a GDBus-owned worker thread is mid-g_object_unref on a proxy/connection object and its GObject finalizer calls back into Python (PyGObject's _gi), which calls PyGILState_Ensure() on a thread state that finalization has already begun tearing down.

Reproduced twice on this machine so far (identical stack both times), a few days apart, under ordinary desktop use — no synthetic thread-spam required, just a program that talks to D-Bus from a background thread and exits promptly afterward. Given power-profiles-daemon, NetworkManager's Python bindings, and plenty of other GLib/GDBus-using Python tools follow this same "spin up async D-Bus, do one thing, exit" pattern, this is likely to affect more than just this one tool as more distros ship 3.14.

thread.author: russfellows
thread.html:
We hit this in a Rust/PyO3 extension (russfellows/s3dlio#302) and narrowed it to a pure C reproducer with no Rust or PyO3 involved. The results add something to this issue: 3.13.8+ survives this pattern and 3.14 does not, so it is a regression in 3.14, not only a long-standing API hazard.

Reproducer

N native (non-Python) threads loop on PyGILState_Ensure() / small Python work / PyGILState_Release(), with a short random sleep between attaches, while the main thread returns and the interpreter finalizes. Many objects with __del__ keep bytecode running during finalization.

attacher.c (build with gcc -O2 -shared -fPIC -I$(python3 -c 'import sysconfig;print(sysconfig.get_path("include"))') attacher.c -o attacher.so):

// Pure-CPython repro for s3dlio #302 (no s3dlio, no Rust): N native (non-Python) threads
// repeatedly do PyGILState_Ensure / light Python work / PyGILState_Release, like tokio workers that
// Python::attach after an await.  Every Ensure on a thread that has no thread state creates a NEW one.
#include <Python.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdatomic.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#if PY_VERSION_HEX < 0x030D0000
#define FIN() _Py_IsFinalizing()
#else
#define FIN() Py_IsFinalizing()
#endif
static atomic_long attached_while_finalizing = 0;
static int check_first = 0; static unsigned max_sleep = 3000;
void set_sleep(unsigned v) { max_sleep = v; }
void set_check(int v) { check_first = v; }
static atomic_long attaches = 0;
static atomic_long began_final = 0, began_final_returned = 0;
static void *run(void *arg) {
    unsigned seed = (unsigned)(size_t)&seed ^ (unsigned)pthread_self();
    for (;;) {
        if (check_first && FIN()) { usleep(1000); continue; }   // what pyo3 Python::attach does (best-effort, racy)
        int bf = FIN();
        if (bf) atomic_fetch_add(&began_final, 1);
        PyGILState_STATE g = PyGILState_Ensure();
        if (bf) atomic_fetch_add(&began_final_returned, 1);
        if (FIN()) atomic_fetch_add(&attached_while_finalizing, 1);
        PyObject *b = PyBytes_FromStringAndSize("x", 1);   // light Python work, like Py::new(BytesView)
        Py_XDECREF(b);
        atomic_fetch_add(&attaches, 1);
        PyGILState_Release(g);
        usleep(max_sleep ? 1 + (unsigned)rand_r(&seed) % max_sleep : 0);  // I/O-like gap: threads are often NOT inside Ensure when finalization starts
    }
    return NULL;
}
static void report(void){ fprintf(stderr,"C-REPORT attaches=%ld attached_while_finalizing=%ld ensure_called_while_finalizing=%ld ensure_RETURNED_for_those=%ld\n", atomic_load(&attaches), atomic_load(&attached_while_finalizing), atomic_load(&began_final), atomic_load(&began_final_returned)); }
int start(int n) {
    atexit(report);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { pthread_t t; pthread_create(&t, NULL, run, NULL); pthread_detach(t); }
    return n;
}
long finalizing_attaches(void) { return atomic_load(&attached_while_finalizing); }
long total_attaches(void) { return atomic_load(&attaches); }

drv.py (run: python3 drv.py ./attacher.so 64, where 64 is the number of native threads):

import ctypes, sys, time, os
lib = ctypes.CDLL(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), sys.argv[1]))
class D:
    def __del__(self):          # bytecode runs during finalization -> the eval breaker honours GIL-drop requests
        x = [1, 2, 3]; x.append(4)
KEEP = [D() for _ in range(int(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 50000)]
lib.set_sleep(int(os.environ.get("SLEEP","3000")))
lib.set_check(int(os.environ.get("CHECK","0")))
lib.start(int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 8)
time.sleep(0.5)
print("READY", lib.total_attaches(), flush=True)

Results (Linux x86_64 glibc, default GIL build, 64 native threads, 30 runs each)

CPython abnormal exits
3.14.10 23/30 and 25/30 in two batches: double free or corruption (out), SIGSEGV, Fatal Python error: PyInterpreterState_Delete: remaining threads
3.13.18 0/30
3.13.7, 3.12.16 0/30 (from our investigation's runs)

Analysis (3.14.10 vs 3.13.18 sources)

  1. _Py_Finalize marks only the thread states that already exist. _PyThreadState_RemoveExcept() takes the list of thread states, and only those get _PyThreadState_SetShuttingDown() (pylifecycle.c ~2092). The comment at ~2118 notes the gap: "XXX Make sure we are preventing the creating of any new thread states".
  2. New thread states are still created. A native thread calling PyGILState_Ensure() during finalization has no thread state, so new_threadstate() creates a fresh one with no finalization check. On a default (GIL) build _PyEval_StopTheWorldAll is a no-op.
  3. In 3.14, take_gil parks only flagged thread states. It decides via _PyThreadState_MustExit(tstate), which checks the thread state's own shutting-down flag. The fresh thread state is not flagged, so the thread proceeds and later races PyInterpreterState_Delete / zapthreads. That race produces the three failure modes above:
    • a SIGSEGV in _PyThreadState_Attach while zapthreads frees the thread state;
    • a double free when the thread's own PyGILState_Release frees it too;
    • "remaining threads" when the thread state is created after zapthreads ran.
  4. 3.13.8+ asks the runtime instead. Its _PyThreadState_MustExit checks globally whether the runtime is finalizing, so the late thread state is parked too (gh-87135 backport), and there is no crash.

The thread-state-based check in 3.14 appears to have lost the "late native thread" case that 3.13.8+ handles. Refusing (or parking) thread-state creation in PyGILState_Ensure once finalization has started would close it.

Workaround on our side: no native thread attaches during shutdown; Python objects are built only on Python threads. Happy to test a patch.

issues.title: Free-threading: stop-the-world from a callback under TYPE_LOCK can deadlock
issues.author: scasella
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug description:

On free-threaded builds, the interpreter can deadlock when Python code running under an unpinned TYPE_LOCK stops the world, directly or through an automatic GC, while another thread holds TYPE_LOCK pinned and waits to stop the world. The callbacks are a metaclass mro() (from type_ready()) and a str-subclass class-dict key's __eq__ (from type_setattro()).

Observed on fresh free-threaded builds of main a000129 (which includes PR #152826), main 8c056c3 and 3.15 13b1659 (macOS arm64, Clang, 2026-09-25), and earlier on main 6757482, 3.15 2dafe2a and 3.14 1d8c9f8. The default build is not affected.

This is the same lock-order family as gh-158194 (PyType_Freeze()), gh-156910 and gh-155400, but a distinct bug. Those were fixed by pinning at C call sites, which cannot cover arbitrary Python code or the GC. The broader approach below might also cover gh-158194; gh-158194's pin does not fix this.

Reproducer (main, 3.15 and 3.14.4+)

Trimmed from the attached repro.py (mro bug):

import faulthandler, sys, threading, time
print("sys._is_gil_enabled() =", sys._is_gil_enabled())
if sys._is_gil_enabled() is not False:
    sys.exit("needs a free-threaded build with the GIL disabled")
faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(20, exit=True)   # dump stacks and exit if hung

def f(): pass

class Meta(type):
    def mro(cls):             # called by type_ready() with TYPE_LOCK held, not pinned
        f.__qualname__ = "f"  # stops the world (func_set_qualname)
        return type.mro(cls)

stop, errors = threading.Event(), []

def guarded(fn):
    def run():
        try: fn()
        except BaseException as e: errors.append(e); raise
    return run

def setter():
    while not stop.is_set():
        Meta("K", (), {})

def pinner():                 # type_set_bases(): pinned TYPE_LOCK, then stop-the-world
    class A: pass
    class B: pass
    class X(A): pass
    while not stop.is_set():
        X.__bases__ = (B,); X.__bases__ = (A,)

def contender():              # plain stop-the-world; keeps stw->mutex contended
    def g(): pass
    while not stop.is_set():
        g.__qualname__ = "g"

ts = [threading.Thread(target=guarded(fn)) for fn in (setter, pinner, contender) for _ in range(2)]
for t in ts: t.start()
time.sleep(5); stop.set()
for t in ts: t.join()
if errors: sys.exit(f"FAIL: {errors[0]!r}")
print("done")
  • Actual: the process hangs. faulthandler dumps the stacks after 20 s and exits with status 1.
  • Expected: done after about 5 s.

repro_realistic.py (ABC subclasses + functools.wraps + GC) and repro_dunder_pinner.py hang on main and 3.15 only: 3.14 (from 3.14.4, which backported type_lock_prevent_release()) pins only the __bases__/MRO path.

Native stacks of a hang

Stock main 8c056c3 (free-threaded debug, no patch), repro.py mro bug, captured with macOS sample (trimmed):

setter   type_ready_publish typeobject.c:9513 -> mro_internal typeobject.c:3641 -> [Python mro()]
         -> func_set_qualname funcobject.c:755 -> stop_the_world pystate.c:2475 -> _PyMutex_LockTimed
         -> _PyThreadState_Attach pystate.c:2305 -> _PyCriticalSection_Resume critical_section.c:152
         -> _PyMutex_LockTimed
pinner   type_set_bases typeobject.c:2002 -> stop_the_world pystate.c:2475 -> _PyMutex_LockTimed

These stacks are consistent with the lock-cycle diagnosis below; lock ownership is inferred from the code paths, not read from the samples.

Mechanism

  1. T1's callback under unpinned TYPE_LOCK stops the world and parks on a busy stw->mutex. Parking detaches T1, which releases TYPE_LOCK.
  2. T2 takes TYPE_LOCK pinned (e.g. __bases__ assignment) and parks on stw->mutex.
  3. stw->mutex is handed to T1, whose re-attach (_PyCriticalSection_Resume()) waits for TYPE_LOCK: ABBA.

A proposed approach, for specialist review

fix-{main,3.15,3.14}.diff change Python/pystate.c so that stop_the_world() never waits for a critical-section mutex while owning the stop-the-world locks: if the critical section cannot be resumed without blocking, it drops stw->mutex and the rwmutex, waits, and retries. Regression-tested candidate fix. Broader attachment, finalization, progress, and interaction concerns remain for specialist review:

  • Re-attaching with tstate->critical_section temporarily set to 0 around _PyThreadState_Attach(): every attachment outcome, including shutdown/finalization and free-threaded builds running with the GIL enabled.
  • Nested and two-mutex critical sections; pinned sections. Only the topmost critical section is restored, which matches what _PyCriticalSection_Resume() already does.
  • Global vs per-interpreter stop-the-world; progress under contention.
  • PR #152826 (gh-151518), merged on 2026-09-25, changes attach and the stop-the-world state machine. The bug still reproduces on main a000129, which includes it: repro.py mro bug hung 5/5 there with the same stack shape (stop_the_world now at pystate.c:2523). fix-main.diff applies cleanly to a000129 and completed 5/5, but the two changes still need review together; applying cleanly does not establish that they are compatible.
  • Maintainability: the try-resume could move into the critical-section implementation instead of duplicating its private representation in pystate.c.

Performance impact has not been measured. No failure was observed on the patched build tested (main 8c056c3 debug, exactly fix-main.diff): each configuration that hung on stock main debug ran 0/5 or 0/3 hung, and both regression tests passed 3/3.

Validation on fresh builds and environment

Fresh out-of-tree free-threaded builds of main 8c056c3 (stock, and with exactly the attached fix-main.diff, sha256 844eee86…) and 3.15 13b1659 (stock), run one at a time on 2026-09-25. A run counts as hung only when the process stopped using CPU and a native sample showed stacks consistent with the lock cycle above.

main debug stock patched
repro.py mro bug / strkey bug 5/5 / 5/5 hung 0/5 / 0/5 hung
repro.py mro gc, repro_realistic.py gc, repro_dunder_pinner.py mro bug 3/3 hung each 0/3 hung each
ctl modes 0/4 0/4
regression tests 3/3 hung (standalone) 3/3 pass (in-tree)

mro bug also hung on stock main release (5/5) and stock 3.15 debug (3/3). On main a000129 (after PR #152826, debug), repro.py mro bug hung 5/5 stock and completed 5/5 with fix-main.diff; a native sample of one stock hang had the same shape as above. test_free_threading, test_types and test_descr pass when patched. Not built: patched main release, patched 3.15 and 3.14 (fix-3.15.diff, fix-3.14.diff).

python -VV of the fresh stock builds:

Python 3.16.0a0 free-threading build (heads/val/main-base-dirty:8c056c3, Sep 25 2026, 08:58:37) [Clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.3.34.2)]
Python 3.15.0rc2+dev free-threading build (heads/val/315-base-dirty:13b1659, Sep 25 2026, 09:07:27) [Clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.3.34.2)]

Earlier stock builds (used for the older results below):

The -dirty suffix comes from CPython's Makefile running git describe --dirty from the out-of-tree build directory, where git sees every tracked file as missing. All of these builds were made out-of-tree, and their source trees show no tracked changes; the fresh trees were verified clean after each build.

Older results, code locations, patch details and open questions

Attached files. Each reproducer prints sys._is_gil_enabled() and exits with status 2 unless it is False. A worker exception exits with status 3.

  • repro.py [mro|strkey] [bug|gc|ctl] [secs]: bug stops the world directly inside the callback, gc only allocates cycles (the automatic GC stops the world), and ctl is the control (no stop-the-world, GC disabled).
  • repro_dunder_pinner.py: the same, with X.__repr__ assignment as the pinned partner (main and 3.15).
  • repro_realistic.py [gc|bug]: ABC subclass creation plus functools.wraps plus GC (main and 3.15).
  • test_type_stw_deadlock.py: a standalone copy of the two regression tests in the diffs.

Older stock-build results. These are stock builds (no patch) of main @ 6757482, 3.15 @ 2dafe2a and 3.14 @ 1d8c9f8, run on 2026-09-25 with the reproducers as they were before the GIL check and the exception propagation were added (the stress logic is the same). CPU-time inactivity was used only to screen for a hang. A native sample was taken of the first hang in each cell; those samples had the same shape as the stacks above (with stop_the_world at pystate.c:2454 on 6757482).

Build repro.py mro bug repro.py strkey bug repro_realistic.py gc
main FT debug 2/2 hung 2/2 hung 1/1 hung
main FT release 2/2 hung 2/2 hung 2/2 hung
3.15 FT debug 2/2 hung 2/2 hung 2/2 hung
3.14 FT debug 2/2 hung 2/2 hung 0/2 (expected: not pinned on 3.14)

Control: repro.py mro ctl completed on main release. The standalone regression tests hung on stock main release. In the earlier investigation (2026-09-23, same stock commits), the gc modes of repro.py hung on all three branches, and repro_dunder_pinner.py hung on main and 3.15.

Earlier investigation (2026-09-23; stock main 6757482 / 3.15 2dafe2a / 3.14 1d8c9f8; earlier revision of the patch). Most of these patched builds were made before the attached diffs were finalized, so the exact source they were built from may differ.

  • All reproducer configurations that hang on stock builds completed on patched main debug and release, 3.15 debug and 3.14 debug.
  • The two new tests passed in 2.4–5.6 s.
  • test_free_threading, test_threading, test_gc, test_descr, test_capi and related suites passed on the patched debug builds.
  • After the diffs were finalized, patched main release was re-run: 2/2 repro.py mro bug and 3/3 regression-test runs completed.

Code locations.

Step main @ 6757482 3.15 @ 2dafe2a 3.14 @ 1d8c9f8
mro_invoke() calls Python mro() under unpinned TYPE_LOCK typeobject.c:3578 :3643 :3502
type_setattro() calls a str-subclass __eq__ under TYPE_LOCK :6715 :6872 :6317
stop_the_world() blocks on stw->mutex pystate.c:2454 :2423 :2387
Attach resumes the critical section pystate.c:2305 → critical_section.c:152 :2274 :2242
Pinned TYPE_LOCK then stop-the-world typeobject.c 672, 1712, 1908, 1974, 3903, 6401 686, 1782, 1978, 2044, 3968, 6558 set_tp_mro 647 only

The unpinned sites are unchanged at the current tips (checked 2026-09-25). stop_the_world() was reworked by PR #152826, but the hang remains on main after it. On 3.14, v3.14.3 has no type_lock_prevent_release() and v3.14.4 does (the backport of gh-145685). This is the same hand-off-after-detach hazard described in gh-144513.

How the patch works. A new stw_lock() replaces the direct PyMutex_Lock(&stw->mutex). If the thread has a resumable critical section and the fast path fails, it:

  1. detaches, which suspends its critical sections;
  2. takes stw->mutex without detaching;
  3. re-attaches without resuming;
  4. tries to resume the critical section with PyMutex_LockFast;
  5. on failure, releases stw->mutex and the rwmutex, blocks in _PyCriticalSection_Resume() while owning nothing, and retries.

A mutex pinned by type_lock_prevent_release() is not stored in the critical section, so pinned holders take the unchanged path. The rwmutex is released too, because holding it while waiting for TYPE_LOCK could still deadlock against a pending global stop-the-world such as os.fork().

Alternatives considered:

  • Call mro() outside TYPE_LOCK. This is incomplete: the str-key path and GC inside such code remain.
  • Never run Python code under TYPE_LOCK. This would be a large restructuring.
  • Disable hand-off for stw->mutex. This is not enough, because a consumed wake-up can still hang.
  • Pin at the callback sites. This is not possible across arbitrary Python code.

As noted above, the try-resume helpers could instead live in critical_section.c, for example as _PyCriticalSection_TryResume(), so that pystate.c does not depend on the critical section's private representation.

Open questions and gaps.

  • Starvation on the retry path is not ruled out.
  • Linux, Windows, subinterpreters and a real os.fork() racing this path were not tested.
  • How often real programs combine a Python-level mro() or a str-subclass class-dict key with a concurrent pinned type update is unknown.
  • 3.15.0 final is expected on 2026-10-01 (PEP 790). gh-155400, from the same family, was marked release blocker. I leave any priority decision to the release manager.

How it was found

An audit of stop_the_world() callers for locks that are held across the wait.

CPython versions tested on:

3.14, 3.15, CPython main branch

Operating systems tested on:

macOS

thread.author: scasella
thread.html:
Thanks, both fair points. I've followed up on each. All runs below are on free-threaded builds of main @ 8c056c3, 3.15 @ 13b1659 and 3.14 @ 1d8c9f8, on macOS arm64.

Realism. I agree the str-subclass key path is contrived: setattr normalizes the name to an exact str, so it's only reachable through the class namespace. Two other routes need less:

  1. No metaclass at all, through the class's dict mutex. repr(K.__dict__) holds the dict's critical section while calling the values' __repr__. If one of those triggers an automatic GC while another thread uses unittest.mock.patch.object(K, "__lt__", ...), the setter's apply_type_slot_updates() pins TYPE_LOCK and the dict mutex and waits for the stop-the-world, which closes the same cycle.

    • repro_dict_repr.py, run with no arguments, hangs 3/3 on main debug, 2/2 on main release and 2/2 on 3.15 debug.
    • 3.14 isn't affected (2/2 pass), since it doesn't pin on dunder assignment.
    • The attached patch fixes it (3/3 pass).
    • The native stacks show dict_repr → … → gc_collect_main → stop_the_world → _PyCriticalSection_Resume in one thread and type_setattro → update_slot_after_setattr → stop_the_world in another.

    The unpinned side here is dict_repr, not code in typeobject.c. Pinning more call sites can't close this: any critical section on a type's __dict__ that ends up running Python can play that role. That's why the patch handles it in stop_the_world().

  2. A Python mro() that does nothing unusual. Python-level mro() overrides do ship: PyGObject's GObjectMeta defines one (gi/types.py), so it runs for every GObject class, and pydantic's ModelMetaclass had one in 2.10.0–2.10.4.

    • repro_c3_mro.py uses a metaclass whose mro() only computes the C3 linearization in Python, with no stop-the-world of its own. Alongside it run one thread creating ordinary cyclic garbage and one defining ABC subclasses.
    • In its default 30 s run it hung 3/4 on main debug and 2/4 on main release, with an automatic GC inside mro_internal() in the stack.
    • It passed 3/3 with the patch, though at that base rate three passes don't show much.
    • I haven't tested PyGObject itself.

Both are still stress tests, and I don't have evidence of this hitting a real application.

Performance. I ran pyperf microbenchmarks of the stop-the-world paths the patch touches: gc.collect(), __qualname__ and __bases__ assignment, ABC subclass creation, and a stop-the-world inside mro(). They ran on release builds of main @ 8c056c3 with and without the patch, same flags, on an untuned M4 Pro.

  • Uncontended, two interleaved runs: the patched build's geometric mean was 1.02–1.04x slower. The same binary measured against itself varied by up to 1.03x (up to 9% per benchmark), so I can't detect a difference above noise.
    • Single-threaded, stop_the_world() still takes the rwmutex and stw->mutex before it finds no other threads. The __qualname__ row (29 ns stock vs 30 ns patched) therefore times exactly the lock path the patch changes.
    • The only extra work there is reading tstate->critical_section, plus a PyMutex_LockFast inside a critical section in place of the lock PyMutex_Lock would have taken.
  • With 2 or 6 contending threads, lock scheduling dominates. The sign flips between runs (1.21x slower, then 1.28x faster, at 2 threads), so I can't claim anything either way.

pyperformance is running on both builds. I'll post the comparison, and note any benchmarks that don't run on 3.16t, when it finishes. The raw pyperf JSON is available if useful.

repro_dict_repr.py.txt
repro_c3_mro.py.txt

Looking at fix-main.diff.txt, the proposed fix seems very invasive. We should fix the lock ordering issues in typeobject.c, not try to retrofit the critical section API to work with it.

I think @colesbury or @nascheme should take a look at this.

thread.author: scasella
thread.html:
One observation that may help: in every hang I've captured, the pinned side is in typeobject.c (type_set_bases, type_set_abstractmethods, apply_type_slot_updates), waiting for the stop-the-world while holding TYPE_LOCK pinned (plus the type's dict mutex for slot updates). The unpinned side can be outside it (dict_repr in repro_dict_repr.py). So a fix on the pinned side, not waiting for the stop-the-world while holding pinned mutexes, should cover both repros, whereas pinning more of the unpinned sites wouldn't.

Happy to run the repros against any candidate patch on main and 3.15.

For completeness, pyperformance for the current diff (92 of 97 benchmarks; dask, genshi, fastapi and both sqlalchemy benchmarks don't run on 3.16t): geometric mean 1.03x faster with the patch. I read that as run-to-run drift rather than an effect of the diff, since the speedups cluster early in the run order and the slowdowns late. There's no sign of a regression; the largest slowdown is tornado_http at 1.06x (±3 ms).

thread.author: nascheme
thread.html:
I came up with an alternative fix, less invasive and it seems safe to me.

We should fix the lock ordering issues in typeobject.c, not try to retrofit the critical section API to work with it.

I considered options along those lines but did not find a feasible one. Type structures are read very often and modified rarely, so reads need to be cheap, and the cost of synchronization should fall on writers. A mutex on the read side is not an option; it scales too badly.

Atomics could work in principle. Relaxed loads are essentially free on x86-64 and ARM64, so the issue is not load cost but the extent of the changes. Every place that reads type members with a plain load (e.g. Py_TYPE(op)->tp_flags or a slot pointer) would need to use an atomic load instead. That affects the C API: inline header functions like PyType_HasFeature() and direct tp_* access in extensions and generated code (Cython). Already-compiled extensions would keep their plain loads, which would then formally race with the writers. Atomics also give no consistency across fields: a slot update currently changes several slots across a type and its subclasses as one step, and readers could then see a partial update.

I have looked at this closely and it appears Python 3.6.5 has a search path for libraries and frameworks that is missing in the newer versions (3.7 onwards).

thread.author: ned-deily
thread.html:
Thanks for the report! I've spent some time investigating it and the story behind it turns out to be a bit complicated, so bear with me. It's all tied in to Apple's attempts to improve the security of macOS.

As of macOS 10.15 Catalina, Apple introduced new requirements for downloadable installer packages, like those we provide for macOS on python.org; in order for such packages to be installed with the macOS installer, they would now have to be "notarized" by Apple. The notarization process is somewhat similar in concept to the process that an app has to go through to be submitted to the Mac App Store but with less stringent requirements. In particular, the installer package is automatically inspected to ensure that all executables are codesigned, are linked with the more-secure "hardened runtime", and do not request certain less-secure entitlements. Although originally announced for enforcement starting with the release of Catalina in the fall of 2019, Apple delayed the enforcement until February 2020 to give application developers more time to modify their packages to meet the new requirements. (See, for example, https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=12232019a).

The first python.org macOS installers that conformed to the new requirements and were notarized were for the 3.8.2 and 3.7.7 releases, staring in 2020-02. In those first releases, we used two entitlements:

com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation
com.apple.security.cs.disable-executable-page-protection

Some issues were reported (like bpo-40198) when using those first releases, so we added two additional entitlements for subsequent releases:

com.apple.security.automation.apple-events
com.apple.security.cs.allow-dyld-environment-variables

While we didn't realize it until your issue, that did have an effect on ctype's behavior when trying to find shared libraries and frameworks. Using the hardened runtime, as now required for notarization, causes the system dlopen() interface, which ctypes uses, to no longer search relative paths. The dlopen man page (for macOS 11, at least) includes this warning:

Note: If the main executable is a set[ug]id binary or codesigned with
entitlements, then all environment variables are ignored, and only a
full path can be used.

After some experimentation, it looks like that statement isn't exactly correct at least on macOS 11 Big Sur: unprefixed paths can still be used to find libraries and frameworks in system locations, i.e. /usr/lib and /System/Library/Frameworks. But it is true that, when using the hardened runtime, dlopen() no longer searches the user-controlled paths /usr/local/lib or /Library/Frameworks by default. And there apparently is no way for a notarized executable to revert to the previous behavior by adding other entitlements (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/666066).

With the allow-dyld-environment-variables entitlement included after the initial releases, it *is* now possible to change this behavior externally, if necessary, by explicitly setting the DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH and/or DYLD_FRAMEWORK_PATH environment variables (see man 1 dyld).

To demonstrate using a third-party library in /usr/local/lib (similar results with third-party frameworks in /Library/Frameworks):

$ /usr/local/bin/python3.7

$ /usr/local/bin/python3.7

[Clang 6.0 (clang-600.0.57)] on darwin
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> import ctypes
>>> ctypes.cdll.LoadLibrary('libsodium.dylib')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.7/lib/python3.7/ctypes/__init__.py", line 442, in LoadLibrary
    return self._dlltype(name)
  File "/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.7/lib/python3.7/ctypes/__init__.py", line 364, in __init__
    self._handle = _dlopen(self._name, mode)

>>> ctypes.cdll.LoadLibrary('libsodium.dylib')
<CDLL 'libsodium.dylib', handle 7f9a9fc58ae0 at 0x7f9a90321310>

It is rather unfortunate that, when including the allow-dyld-environment-variables entitlement, you now receive a less helpful error message "image not found" rather than "file system relative paths not allowed in hardened programs".

So, what to do?

  1. Remove the use of the hardened runtime?

That would mean that python.org installer packages could not be notarized and thus would no longer be installable without going through various onerous steps to override Gatekeeper protections (and would presumably also reduce somewhat system security). Since the primary target of python.org installers is for inexpert users, this option seems unacceptable.

  1. Add code to ctypes to try to mimic the previous behavior?

So something like: if the path passed to ctypes is not absolute and the initial call to dlopen() fails with an "image not found" error, try again by making an absolute path by prepending '/usr/local/lib' and/or '/Library/Frameworks' and retrying. I assume we could make that work somehow but the question is should we? That seems very kludgey and would be re-opening a potential security hole that Apple clearly thinks is significant and is trying to discourage.

  1. Update the ctypes documentation?

In particular, document this change in behavior for codesigned installations using the hardened runtime (like python.org installers) and suggest avoid using relative paths on macOS or, if necessary, have the DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH or DYLD_FRAMEWORK_PATH environment variables set appropriately when launching the interpreter. (I did a quick experiment and it seemed that it was not possible to change dlopen()'s behavior by setting those variables from inside the running interpreter process by using OS.ENVIRON, an unsurprising result.)

It seems to me that changing the ctypes documentation (and adding a changelog blurb), option 3, is the least bad of the available options. One would hope that this does not affect *too* many third-party packages and user applications. Obviously it does some :(

@ronald, what do you think?

thread.author: vlazzarini
thread.html:
Hi Ned,

thanks for your detailed response. I have to say that the LD_LIBRARY_PATH partially worked in some cases, the library got loaded. However in cases where there were dependencies, further issues appeared particularly when the link (as revealed by otool -L) was prefixed by '@rpath'. I was able to fix these by editing these paths (which is possible in my use case), but we just need to note that it may cause difficulties for others.

We also found a solution to avoid needing to set the environment var. We use the following code

ct.CDLL(ctypes.util.find_library('mylib'))

instead of just passing the library. That works well, and perhaps you may recommend it in the docs.

thread.author: ccabrera
thread.html:
Re option 3: relying on DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH or DYLD_FRAMEWORK_PATH isn't a great solution either because of SIP. It's can get impractical to use in many standard Makefile-based build systems, for example. (cf. qmk/qmk_cli#60, Homebrew/discussions#1737) I imagine it can get quite vexing to set these variables but find them to not have the effect you expected them to.

One workaround for the example above would be to compile your own make program (or use one from a package manager) so that SIP doesn't sanitise your environment, but I imagine that's not an ideal solution either.

issues.title: Audit all built-in modules for thread safety
issues.author: swtaarrs
issues.bodyHTML:
Feature or enhancement

Proposal:

We should audit every built-in module for thread safety and make any necessary fixes. This can be done separately from tagging the modules as safe using Py_mod_gil; any data races in built-in modules are considered bugs in the free-threaded build and not incompatibilities.

Below is a list of all source files that contain at least one module definition, as defined by files that contain a call to PyModule_Create(), an array of PyModuleDef_Slots, or a PyModExport_* function definition. If you'd like to help out with this task, take a look at one of the incomplete files. If the conversion is trivial, check it off and attach the PR to this issue. Otherwise, convert the line into an issue and assign it to yourself.

For modules split across multiple files, the audit should include their implementation helpers, not just the file defining the module.

Every module is different, but here are a few high-level points to guide the work:

  1. Use PyMutex as the basic unit of locking.
  2. If you need to hold a lock for a longer period of time, especially across calls that may reenter Python code or acquire other locks, use critical sections.
  3. If the module you're looking at is a thin wrapper around related code elsewhere in CPython (e.g., Modules/_codecsmodule.c and Python/codecs.c), you can also audit/convert the related non-module code. Otherwise, try to contain your work to just the module code, and create separate issues for any dependencies that aren't thread-safe.
  4. Remember that C API functions are generally expected to handle thread-safety internally. C code that operates on Python objects using only C API calls is usually thread-safe by default (but look out for code that reads or modifies PyObject*s in C structs, since that needs synchronization).
  5. Watch out for functions/macros that return borrowed references, like PyList_GetItem() or PyDict_GetItem(). If other threads could have references to the object, prefer functions like PyList_GetItemRef() or PyDict_GetItemRef() that return owned references (and will safely raise an error if the index/key doesn't exist).

thread.author: rhdxmr
thread.html:
The items that haven't finished the put aren't actually "in" the queue yet, so I don't see how non-FIFO order of insertion violates any FIFO guarantees for the contents of the queue; until the items are actually "in", they're not sequenced for the purposes of when they come "out". Mandating such a guarantee effectively means orchestrating a queue with a real maxsize equal to the configured maxsize plus the total number of coroutines competing to put items into it.

Your explanation is correct technically. But without enough explanation, this
behavior can confuse many users.

For instance it happens to put data into asyncio.Queue at asyncio protocol
callbacks by creating new task. This logic will work nicely for a long time but
in the corner case the queue gets full and at the point of view of a consumer
the data come out from the queue are out of order.

IMHO, it would be better to add some note into the document, describing what
FIFO means in regard to asyncio.Queue.

thread.author: asvetlov
thread.html:
I still don't understand the problem.
If the queue is full new items still are added in the order of await q.put() calls.
If there are multiple producers the order of adding items into the queue is still the order of q.put().

Do you have a code example that demonstrates the opposite behavior?

thread.author: rhdxmr
thread.html:
Thanks for having an interest in this issue.

I thought asyncio.Queue guarantees the order of items as .put called after I
read the code. But it does not.

I attach poc code here.
In my machine, this program prints this message and exits.

This shows you that the 33rd item is put before the 2nd item.

thread.author: MojoVampire
thread.html:
Yes, five outstanding blocked puts can be bypassed by a put that comes in immediately after a get creates space. But this isn't really a problem; there are no guarantees on what order puts are executed in, only a guarantee that once a put succeeds, it's FIFO ordered with respect to all other puts.

Nothing in the docs even implies the behavior you're expecting, so I'm not seeing how even a documentation fix is warranted here. The docs on put clearly say:

"Put an item into the queue. If the queue is full, wait until a free slot is available before adding the item."

If we forcibly hand off on put even when a slot is available (to allow older puts to finish first), then we violate the expectation that waiting is only performed when the queue is full (if I test myqueue.full() and it returns False, I can reasonably expect that put won't block). This would be especially impossible to fix if people write code like if not myqueue.full(): myqueue.put_nowait(). put_nowait isn't even a coroutine, so it can't hand off control to the event loop to allow waiting puts to complete, even if it wanted to, and it can't fail to put (e.g. by determining the empty slots will be filled by outstanding puts in some relatively expensive way), because you literally just verified the queue wasn't full and had no awaits between the test and the put_nowait, so it must succeed.

In short: Yes, it's somewhat unpleasant that a queue slot can become free and someone else can swoop in and steal it before older waiting puts can finish. But any change that "fixed" that would make all code slower (forcing unnecessary coroutine switches), and violate existing documentation guarantees.

thread.author: nmuise-barclay
thread.html:
But any change that "fixed" that would make all code slower (forcing unnecessary coroutine switches), and violate existing documentation guarantees.

This issue should be closed then, right?

thread.author: YvesDup
thread.html:
But any change that "fixed" that would make all code slower (forcing unnecessary coroutine switches), and violate existing documentation guarantees

I don't really agree with the first statement above because the main problem is how to handle waiting and moving tasks with the Queue._putters deque.

Here is an a very simple example to point out this use case:

async def simplier_put_case():
    q = asyncio.Queue(1)
    for n in range(3):
        asyncio.create_task(q.put(n:=n+1))
        print(f"PUT: {n}")
    await asyncio.sleep(0.0)

    # queue full: 1 item in queue, 2 items waiting into the _putters
    print(f'{str(q) = }/{q.full() = }')
    print(f'GET: {await q.get()}')
    # queue not full: 1 item out of queue, 1 item waiting in the _putters, the last 1 out of _putters moving into the queue
    print(f'{str(q) = }/{q.full() = }')

    # steal the free solt
    print(f"PUT_NOWAIT: {q.put_nowait(n:=n+1) or n}")
    print(f'{str(q) = }/{q.full() = }')

    # get all items
    while (n:=n-1):
        print(f'GET: {await q.get()}')
    print(f'END {(str(q)) = }/{q.full() = }')

asyncio.run(simplier_put_case())

Ouput is:

PUT: 1
PUT: 2
PUT: 3
str(q) = '<Queue maxsize=1 _queue=[1] _putters[2] tasks=1>'/q.full() = True
GET: 1
str(q) = '<Queue maxsize=1 _putters[1] tasks=1>'/q.full() = False
PUT_NOWAIT: 4
str(q) = '<Queue maxsize=1 _queue=[4] _putters[1] tasks=2>'/q.full() = True
GET: 4
GET: 2
GET: 3
END (str(q)) = '<Queue maxsize=1 tasks=4>'/q.full() = False

To avoid stealing a free slot, when entering in Queue.put or Queue.put_nowait, moreover to check that queue is not full, we have also to check that Queue._putters is not empty. This could indicate that there are pending task(s) or at least one item moving to a free slot.
To make that possible, we have to modify the Queue._wakeup_next method. I suggest to leave the first 'not done' future in the Queue._putters deque, and remove it only in the Queue.put method, just after the await putter.

Having said that, the fix seems simple.

  • preserve a 'Queue._putters' containing all pending or moving items (via their attached future). We have to move the removing of a future from _wakeup_next to Queue.put method.
  • prevent stealing a empty slot
    • in the Queue.put_nowait method, raising a new exception as QFullWithPendingOrMovingItems when Queue._putters is not empty,
    • in the Queue.put method, adding a new item in the queue only when the queue is not full and Queue._putters is empty. otherwise append it into Queue._putters deque.

Finally, I am wondering if it should simplier to handle pending items with a Semaphore than a deque.

thread.author: vadmium
thread.html:
This is split off a large patch I posted at bpo-20132. My new patch here fixes the following two flaws.

1. There is special code in the bz2 decoder that returns an empty text str object at EOF, even though bz2-codec is a bytes-to-bytes codec:
>>> import codecs
>>> decoder = codecs.getincrementaldecoder("bz2")()
>>> decoder.decode(codecs.encode(b"data", "bz2"))
b'data'
>>> decoder.decode(b"", final=True)  # Should return bytes object
''

2. The base64 decoder does not handle partial sets of four codes, because it treats each input chunk as a stand-alone base64 encoding:
>>> tuple(codecs.iterdecode((b"AA", b"AA\r\n"), "base64"))
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/usr/lib/python3.5/codecs.py", line 1039, in iterdecode
    output = decoder.decode(input)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.5/encodings/base64_codec.py", line 35, in decode
    return base64.decodebytes(input)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.5/base64.py", line 554, in decodebytes
    return binascii.a2b_base64(s)

issues.title: Support redefinition of named capture groups in regular expressions
issues.author: serhiy-storchaka
issues.bodyHTML:
Feature or enhancement

Currently the re module rejects any reuse of a group name with "redefinition of group name 'x' as group N; was group M". This prevents the natural idiom of giving the same name to corresponding groups in alternative spellings of a pattern.

For example, parsing a date written in either order currently cannot reuse names:

re.compile(r'(?P<m>\d+)/(?P<d>\d+)/(?P<y>\d+)|(?P<y>\d+)-(?P<m>\d+)-(?P<d>\d+)')
# error: redefinition of group name 'y' as group 4; was group 3

Proposal

Allow a group name to be used for more than one group. All such groups share a single group number; the name (and that number) refer to whichever of the groups matched, or to the last one if more than one matched. The group's width spans the union of the definitions.

This matches the behavior of the third-party regex module and of PCRE's duplicate-names feature ((?J)), whose own canonical example — matching a weekday written as an abbreviation or in full and extracting it under one name — is exactly this alternative-spellings case.

Implementation note

This also needs a small fix in the SRE matching engine. Outside of repeats the matcher restores capture-group marks lazily (it only rewinds the lastmark high-water index), which assumes each group number is written at a single place in the bytecode. A reused group number could otherwise leak a mark from a branch that matched and was then backtracked away, or raise SystemError: The span of capturing group is wrong. Reused group numbers can be detected during code validation, and such patterns save and restore the full mark array on backtracking, exactly as is already done inside repeats; other patterns are unaffected.

The same mark save/restore flag also subsumes the existing workaround for the possessive-quantifier SystemError of gh-101955 (which currently installs a placeholder repeat context for the same purpose).

I have a working implementation and will open a PR.

Linked PRs

  • gh-152027
  • gh-153160

thread.author: wjssz
thread.html:
Personal opinion -1

This may lead careless people to write incorrect regular expressions, and it makes the code for sre a bit more complicated.

Moreover, this requirement is quite niche, it's not difficult for those who really need it to write their own code to achieve this goal.

thread.author: serhiy-storchaka
thread.html: Other engines already support this. Actually, it is so natural extension, that it needs minimal changes in sre -- two lines in C code excluding validator.

thread.author: wjssz
thread.html:
My primary reason for opposition is, some novice regex users may copy, paste, piece together regex when they don't fully understand them, this feature may makes them more confused. Even for experienced users, it also increases the possibility of making mistakes.

IMHO, if no one has submitted a feature request for many years, maybe most people don't really need this. It's not hard to write code to achieve the same functionality.

Of course, these are just my personal opinions. I would suggest asking more core developers, maybe many of them will support this feature.

thread.author: 5j9
thread.html:
I think this is a long-desired feature that would be a welcome addition to Python's re module.

There has been interest in this functionality for years. For example, this Stack Overflow question from 2017 asks specifically about reusing named groups across alternatives:

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/44460642/python-regex-duplicate-names-in-named-groups

The question illustrates the limitation and the need for workarounds, including using the third-party regex module.

Being able to use the same named group in mutually exclusive alternatives is a natural and useful pattern. It avoids having to define separate group names and then manually reconcile them after matching (e.g. m[1] or m[2]).

I think this proposal addresses a genuine usability gap in the standard library. Of-course, there are workarounds, but none is as clean as reusing the same named group in mutually exclusive alternatives, IMHO.

enumerate_vectorcall(PyObject *type, PyObject *const *args,

PyTypeObject *tp = _PyType_CAST(type);

thread.author: cmaloney
thread.html:
Continuing to iterate on this. For str, list, and int the generated vectorcall is slower than the hand-written vectorcall because the hand written inlines special cases which Argument Clinic has no way, currently, of knowing about. The slowdown is ~20% on microbenchmarks. I built a prototype I call "pyspec" which would make these inlnining critical special cases visible to AC as well as available to pieces like the JIT. The core is to use plain python to write the if tree to get to C functions then lower that to C. That makes it so AC no longer reuqires the custom language/parser. Nothing revolutionary in the python ecosystems but I think has some nice side-effects.

This currently only supports static types. GH-157968 makes it support non-static types. That is necessary to support Decimal. That makes both heap and static types supported and tested. It would be nice to get reviewed as it changes the asserts in generated code a little.

As a demonstration of speedup and applying to new types I put together GH-158891 for bytes and bytearray. That turns on one of the core things I hope to enable with this work: minimal copy bytes(bytearray(bytes(bytearray(b'123'))). Before Vectorcall there were references in arguments so every constructor had to copy. Now there is a uniquely referenced temporaty where we can "pass along" the storage avoiding copies.

thread.author: vstinner
thread.html:
Continuing to iterate on this. For str, list, and int the generated vectorcall is slower than the hand-written vectorcall because the hand written inlines special cases which Argument Clinic has no way, currently, of knowing about.

What is missing from AC generated code to get the same speed?

thread.author: cmaloney
thread.html:
AC needs to be able to direct dispatch / inline the "special" cases of 0, 1, and 2:

cpython/Objects/longobject.c

Lines 6529 to 6549 in 64bad23

long_vectorcall(PyObject *type, PyObject * const*args,
size_t nargsf, PyObject *kwnames)
{
Py_ssize_t nargs = PyVectorcall_NARGS(nargsf);
if (kwnames != NULL) {
PyThreadState *tstate = PyThreadState_GET();
return _PyObject_MakeTpCall(tstate, type, args, nargs, kwnames);
}
switch (nargs) {
case 0:
return _PyLong_GetZero();
case 1:
return PyNumber_Long(args[0]);
case 2:
return long_new_impl(_PyType_CAST(type), args[0], args[1]);
default:
return PyErr_Format(PyExc_TypeError,
"int expected at most 2 arguments, got %zd",
nargs);
}
}

In the first iteration I called this zero_arg, one_arg etc. To solve that I'm hoping to make the information available both to Argument Clinic and projects like the JIT. That was too specialized of infra in a lot of ways.

Currently functions like bytes_new_impl are fully opaque. I'm hoping to make them be less opaque by giving the base decision tree in some Python syntax. Need some help from core devs what is preferred (an if tree like existing code, match statements, overloads, ...). That keeps to very basic operations and can lower directly from AST -> C as well as building an "overload" table that the JIT can potentially consume.

My prototype of a simple stub: https://github.com/cmaloney/cpython/blob/7abb5c4b7d1d9925e837d14205c6658ef97ae051/Objects/pyspec/bytesobject.py#L139-L155

And the full bytes __new__: https://github.com/cmaloney/cpython/blob/7abb5c4b7d1d9925e837d14205c6658ef97ae051/Objects/pyspec/bytesobject.py#L69-L122

The hope is we can have one core definition which we can efficiently codegen to the set of functions we need + metadata that says "single unique bytearray arg -> use this C function directly". That should reduce the number of instructions needed while keeping things maintainable. Argument for pushing towards Python syntax is to make it look just like everything else the JIT must optimize / less special cases and less custom parsers.

thread.author: encukou
thread.html:
The replace method of code allows setting e.g.

  • co_filename to a subclass of str
  • co_consts to an arbitrary tuple
    and possibly more weird cases.

This makes code objects unmarshallable.

One way to create such a code object is to call compileall.compile_file with a str subclass as path. See the attached reproducers.

This hit pip, see: pypa/pip#10358 (comment)

thread.author: encukou
thread.html:
How to fix this? I guess:

  • co_filename should be converted to an actual str, or reject subclasses with an exception
  • for co_consts, the marshal docs could be updated to add code objects to "containers". The code docs already say co_consts "is a tuple containing the literals"; if someone's putting in non-literals they're voiding the warranty.

And so on for all other fields of code objects.

thread.author: encukou
thread.html: See also gh-87005

thread.author: vasiliyk
thread.html:
I want to propose to keep code objects unrestricted at creation and just improve the error at save time.

Marshal already raises on dump, but the message does not say where the problem is. A code object can contain many values, and with nested code objects it is hard to tell what MyStr refers to.

>>> import marshal
>>> class MyStr(str): pass
... marshal.dumps(compile("", MyStr("foo.py"), "exec"))
...
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-1>", line 2, in <module>
    marshal.dumps(compile("", MyStr("foo.py"), "exec"))
    ~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
ValueError: cannot marshal MyStr objects

The error could carry context to make it more helpful:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-1>", line 2, in <module>
    marshal.dumps(compile("", MyStr("foo.py"), "exec"))
    ~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
ValueError: cannot marshal MyStr objects: 'foo.py' (subclasses of str are not supported)
when marshalling code object field co_filename
when marshalling code object '<module>' (foo.py, line 1)

This covers every path that creates a code object.

Why not reject such objects at creation?

  • Most code objects are never written to a .pyc (exec, bytecode tools, replace() in tests); restricting creation would break code that works today.
  • Nothing changes for code that is not saved, so there is no compatibility concern.
  • It seems Java/.Net use a similar model (allow runtime-only code to reference arbitrary objects and restrict what can be saved). Not sure how much weight 'others do it too' can carry :]

thread.author: picnixz
thread.html: @serhiy-storchaka

thread.author: picnixz
thread.html: FTR, if someone messes up with code.replace, it is at their own discretion and we do not want to validate their modifications. This is why we closes previous similar issues

thread.author: serhiy-storchaka
thread.html:
I agree with @vasiliyk. We should not restrict the use which does not involve marshalling.

Adding notes to locate error like in pickle and json is also a good idea. It was impossibly to implement it before the changes which were made few days ago -- we did not have a raised exception, only an error code.

thread.author: vasiliyk
thread.html:
I have implemented the notes support for marshalling, but I am at the open PR limit that was set on Oct 20 for the repo.

  • diff: main...vasiliyk:cpython:gh-89290-marshal-notes
  • branch: https://github.com/vasiliyk/cpython/tree/gh-89290-marshal-notes

The notes follow pickle's convention: one note per enclosing level, innermost first, with the same wording for container items, dict values and set elements.

3 differences with pickle:

  • a failing dict key gets a note, pickle leaves it unannotated;
  • a failing slice field is named directly (start, stop, step), pickle reports a tuple index inside the reconstructor arguments;
  • code object fields are identified by name, qualified name, file and line, pickle rejects code objects.

>>> class MyStr(str): pass

When calling subnet_of() or supernet_of() on an IPv4Network or IPv6Network and passing an address object (e.g., IPv6Address) instead of a network object, the module attempts to access the network_address attribute on the address object. issues.title: IPv6Address ordering is scope-id-blind, breaking trichotomy and making sorted()/min()/max() non-deterministic for scoped addresses
issues.author: Builder106
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

COMPONENT: Library (Lib/ipaddress.py)

AFFECTED VERSIONS: main (3.16.0a0) and 3.14 (reproduced on 3.14.6). The defect dates to when scope_id was added to IPv6Address.__eq__/__hash__/__str__ but not to ordering.

SUMMARY

IPv6Address.__eq__ and __hash__ fold in the interface scope_id (so fe80::1 and fe80::1%eth0 are unequal and hash differently), but IPv6Address does not override ordering — it inherits _BaseAddress.__lt__, which compares only the integer address and ignores _scope_id. _BaseAddress is decorated with @functools.total_ordering, which synthesizes __gt__/__le__/__ge__ from __lt__ and __eq__. The synthesized __gt__ is effectively not (a < b) and a != b. For two addresses with the same integer but different scope, a < b is False (scope-blind __lt__) while a != b is True (scope-aware __eq__), so a > b is True — and symmetrically b > a is also True. The relation is not a strict order: trichotomy and antisymmetry both fail, and sorting is non-deterministic.

MINIMAL REPRODUCTION

ROOT CAUSE

scope_id was added to IPv6Address.__eq__/__hash__/__str__ but not to ordering, and IPv6Address defines no __lt__. The @functools.total_ordering operators on _BaseAddress dispatch through type(self).__lt__, which (absent an override) resolves to the scope-blind _BaseAddress.__lt__ while total_ordering also consults the scope-aware __eq__ — so they disagree. The functools docs note total_ordering "makes no attempt to override methods declared in the class or its superclasses," which is exactly why the subclass inherits a __lt__ inconsistent with its own __eq__.

The minimal fix is a scope-aware IPv6Address.__lt__ (tie-break on scope_id only when the integer address is equal; unscoped sorts before scoped; scope ids compare lexicographically). Because the derived operators dispatch through type(self).__lt__, overriding only __lt__ on the subclass routes all four comparisons through the scope-aware path. This also transitively repairs scoped IPv6Interface and IPv6Network ordering, which delegate to address comparison. _BaseAddress.__lt__ is untouched, so IPv4Address is unaffected.

RELATION TO CONCURRENT WORK (#141647 / PR #141842) — please don't close as a dup

There is concurrent activity in gh-141647 / PR gh-141842 touching the comparison dunders, but it is orthogonal: that PR's rewritten _BaseAddress.__lt__ stays scope-blind (return self._ip < other._ip) and adds no IPv6Address override, and its test_mixed_type_ordering skips same-type pairs, so this same-type scoped trichotomy failure survives that PR untested. This fix adds a scope-aware override on the IPv6Address subclass only and does not modify _BaseAddress.__lt__, so it composes cleanly regardless of merge order (or could be folded into #141842).
