thread.author: picnixz
thread.html:
I'm not sure but could os.scandir also have the same weirdness as os.close?

os.close, close() methods and os.dup2() are a special case: they will ignore EINTR instead of retrying. The reason is complex but involves behaviour under Linux and the fact that the file descriptor may really be closed even if EINTR is returned.

Anyway, I think we should treat it as a feature request.

thread.author: larryhastings
thread.html:
I'd like to propose broadening this issue. I hit the same class of failure in a real program, and after reading the kernel side I think the problem affects a bunch of functions.

Disclosure: this whole message was written for me by Claude Fable 5.1, after having read this existing issue, and examining both Python source and Linux kernel source. I read it over and confirmed it's basically accurate, but I'm not a signal expert by any stretch.

What happened

I have a custom-written podcast downloader. The main process installs a SIGCHLD handler with signal.signal() (which uses a a loopback pipe to wake up a selectors loop), then runs download/transcode jobs as subprocess children, and maintains / updates a large tree of files--the cached RSS feeds, the downloaded MP3 files--using conventional filesystem APIS, e.g. os.stat(), os.rename(), os.utime(), os.unlink() and so on. During development, I mounted the downloader's data via NFS (version 4).

Every time a child exited, Linux sent my downloader's main process a SIGCHLD signal, and eventually one of those path operations in the main thread died with OSError: [Errno 4] Interrupted system call. (I didn't keep the traceback, so I can't say which call it was that time; the analysis below suggests many candidates.)

Why this happened

  • signal.signal() installs handlers through PyOS_setsig(), which uses sigaction() with sa_flags = SA_ONSTACK only (Python/pylifecycle.c). No SA_RESTART. So the moment a program installs any Python-level handler, every syscall that the kernel would otherwise restart transparently starts failing with EINTR instead.
  • PEP 475 added automatic retries for a number of POSIX functions (open, read, write, fstat, fsync, ftruncate, fchmod, fchown, the wait* family, select, sockets, ...). These detect the EINTR error and automatically retry. But this was does not done for path-based os functions: stat, lstat, rename, replace, utime, unlink, mkdir, rmdir, listdir, scandir, access, chmod, chown, link, symlink, readlink, truncate, statvfs, chdir. I checked Modules/posixmodule.c on main: none of these have the while (res != 0 && errno == EINTR && !(async_err = PyErr_CheckSignals())) loop that fchmod/fchown/mkfifo have. So os.fchmod() retries but os.chmod() doesn't.

The PEP's implicit assumption was that these calls don't block long enough to be interrupted. But for network and userspace filesystems that assumption doesn't hold.

Behavior on Linux 7.2.11

NFSv4 (fs/nfs/nfs4proc.c). When the server answers NFS4ERR_DELAY, NFS4ERR_GRACE, NFS4ERR_FILE_OPEN, or a few layout/recall errors, the client backs off with nfs4_delay(), sleeping between 0.1s and 15s per round. Operations that set .interruptible = true do that sleep in TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE, and nfs4_delay_interruptible() returns -ERESTARTSYS when any signal is pending. Those operations include lookup, getattr, access, readdir, remove, rmdir, mkdir, link, symlink, readlink, open, statfs. Since every path walk goes through lookup, permission (access) and attribute revalidation (getattr), any path-based syscall can come back -ERESTARTSYS when a signal lands mid-backoff: stat, rename, utime, unlink, listdir, all of them. (The RENAME and SETATTR operations themselves are not interruptible; they're hit through the path walk.) Everything else in the NFS client and sunrpc (rpc_wait_bit_killable, nfs_wait_bit_killable, the v3 jukebox retry) is TASK_KILLABLE, so only fatal signals break it.

For NFS the error is always -ERESTARTSYS, so a handler installed with SA_RESTART makes the kernel restart the call and nothing ever reaches userspace. signal.siginterrupt(sig, False) is therefore a working workaround for NFS, and it's what I did.

FUSE (fs/fuse/dev.c, request_wait_answer()). This is why I think the workaround isn't the answer. The kernel waits for the daemon with wait_event_interruptible(), so any signal interrupts. If the request hasn't been read by the daemon yet, the kernel pulls it off the queue and sets the error to a hard -EINTR (fuse_remove_pending_req()). If it has been read, the kernel sends FUSE_INTERRUPT and the daemon decides whether to fail the operation with EINTR. A hard -EINTR is not restartable: SA_RESTART does nothing for it. So on sshfs, rclone, or any FUSE filesystem, a Python program with a signal handler can get EINTR from os.stat() and friends, and the only fix is to retry in userspace, which is exactly what PEP 475 was created to do.

I don't know how other POSIX OSes behave here, but I'd be surprised if adding an automatic retry after EINTR was a bad move on those other OSes.

Proposal

Extend PEP 475 retry-on-EINTR to the remaining os functions that take a path or an fd and currently don't retry. The idiom already exists in posixmodule.c; this is mostly mechanical. The PEP's own rationale applies unchanged: the alternative is for every caller of os.stat() to wrap it in a retry loop, which nobody does, so programs fail intermittently on network filesystems whenever they also handle a signal.

I'm happy to work on a PR if there's agreement on the direction. (I'm at the core dev sprint right now! Lookin' for something to do!)

thread.author: vstinner
thread.html:
SA_RESTART flag is not used on signal handlers, since Python has to call PyErr_CheckSignals() which can set an exception.

These detect the EINTR error and automatically retry. But this was does not done for path-based os functions: stat, lstat, rename, replace, utime, unlink, mkdir, rmdir, listdir, scandir, access, chmod, chown, link, symlink, readlink, truncate, statvfs, chdir.

Well, it's a bug :-) The should implement PEP 475. For example, use a loop such as:

    do {
        ...
    } while (res != 0 && errno == EINTR && !(async_err = PyErr_CheckSignals()));

It does appear that os.scandir doesn't always retry

Same here: it should implement PEP 475, so retry on EINTR and call PyErr_CheckSignals() in the meanwhile.

issues.title: Speed up integer searching in memoryview and array.array
issues.author: cmaloney
issues.bodyHTML:
Feature or enhancement

Currently for memoryview and array.array operations like .index() and .count() convert elements from native byte format to a PyObject then call PyObject_RichCompareBool to compare them. This is significantly slower than the equivalent bytes as reported on discord.

data = memoryview(bytearray(64 * 1024))
data[-1] = 10
data.index(10, 100)   # ~860x slower than bytes(data).index(10, 100)

For one dimensional memoryview and array.array when the items are native integer formats (struct formats bBhHiIlLqQnN) we can do the comparison as event bytes using optimized methods for 1-, 2-, 4- and 8-byte comparison.

Note this does not apply for objects like float where exact-byte comparison does not work (0.0 == -0.0).

Detect the cases we can make faster and generalize existing helpers for "packing" into native bytes and comparing buffer protocol objects with 1-, 2-, 4-, and 8-byte types which are exact-byte comparable.

Has this already been discussed elsewhere?

I have already discussed this feature proposal on Discourse

Links to previous discussion of this feature:

  • https://discuss.python.org/t/memoryview-index-860x-slower-than-bytes-index/104973
  • gh-125420: addition of memoryview.index() and count()

Linked PRs

  • gh-160541

thread.author: picnixz
thread.html: FTR: this was a deliberate choice of being slow because I still didn't have a real use case for that one. How likely do you need to look for integers in memorviews in general? or counting them?

thread.author: cmaloney
thread.html:
My goal here is to make memoryview() usable as a default in more cases to avoid issues with slicing bytes() and bytearray() which when sliced must allocate and copy data. Having the same methods available and them be equivalently fast means when people experiment after learning "memoryview might be faster in a parser" don't hit as many speedbumps. memoryview serves as a "fast" slice which doesn't own the data it points at. It just keeps a reference to the object and some offset + length information.

I plan in this to have the bytes, array.array, and memoryview share the same implementation for these as much as possible to minimize maintenance cost. bytes is a special case of what array.array and memoryview need. Could only optimize the bytes case but doing 1-byte, 2-byte, 4-byte, and 8-byte integer-like objects isn't a lot of added code and are fairly common in codebases.

issues.title: `ZstdDecompressor` and `LZMADecompressor` raise on repeated `decompress(b'', max_length=0)` calls with output pending
issues.author: pganssle
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug description

When a compression.zstd.ZstdDecompressor has decompressed output waiting (because an earlier max_length cut it short), calling decompress with max_length=0 works 15 times and fails on the 16th:

>>> from compression import zstd
>>> d = zstd.ZstdDecompressor()
>>> d.decompress(zstd.compress(b"\x00"), max_length=0)
b''
>>> for _ in range(15):
...     d.decompress(b"", max_length=0)
...
>>> d.decompress(b"", max_length=0)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-4>", line 1, in <module>
    d.decompress(b"", max_length=0)
_zstd.ZstdError: Unable to decompress Zstandard data: Operation made no progress over multiple calls, due to output buffer being full

Every one of those calls is a legitimate "buffer this, give me nothing yet" request, and needs_input is False throughout, so I would expect b'' each time with no error. The decompressor is not actually broken afterwards: a following decompress(b"", -1) still returns b"\x00" with eof set, so this is an error raised on a valid call rather than lost data.

LZMADecompressor fails the same sequence, on the fourth call rather than the sixteenth:

>>> import lzma
>>> d = lzma.LZMADecompressor()
>>> d.decompress(lzma.compress(b"\x00"), max_length=0)
b''
>>> for _ in range(3):
...     d.decompress(b"", max_length=0)
...
>>> d.decompress(b"", max_length=0)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-4>", line 1, in <module>
    d.decompress(b"", max_length=0)
_lzma.LZMAError: Insufficient buffer space

That is the mechanism described in #160000 (liblzma's LZMA_BUF_ERROR leaking through when the output buffer is empty) showing up with input buffered rather than on a fresh decompressor; I expect the fix for that issue covers it, but it seemed worth recording the second shape since the fresh-decompressor test alone would not catch a regression here. BZ2Decompressor and zlib._ZlibDecompressor return b'' for any number of such calls.

The zstd mechanism: decompress_lock_held calls ZSTD_decompressStream even when max_length is 0, so with a zero-size output buffer: Modules/_zstd/decompressor.c lines 229-233. libzstd counts consecutive ZSTD_decompressStream calls that consume no input and produce no output (ZSTD_NO_FORWARD_PROGRESS_MAX, which is 16) and returns ZSTD_error_noForwardProgress_destFull once the limit is hit, as protection against callers looping forever. The simplest fix is probably to return b'' without calling into libzstd at all when max_length == 0, since there is nothing such a call can do except (with new input) append to the internal input buffer, which happens outside this loop anyway.

Found by running the Hypothesis tests from #159960 under Atheris, with the _zstd module compiled with -fsanitize=fuzzer-no-link. libFuzzer hit it within about twenty seconds, whereas plain Hypothesis had not found it in many runs, because it needs sixteen consecutive max_length=0 values; the zstd reproducer above is the shrunk result. Both backends are now pinned in that PR as test_max_length_zero_with_pending_output under expectedFailure.

issues.title: Free-threaded CPython 3.14: concurrent functools.partial.__setstate__ crashes with repr(), calls, or another __setstate__
issues.author: espressolee
issues.bodyHTML:
Prior report

gh-157099 (2026-09-07) reported the same missing synchronization in partial_setstate, reaching it through partial_new (a crash in tuple_concat under ASan, 3.14.7 @ 823f032). It was closed by its reporter after a request to consolidate a batch of reports (gh-157124), and the consolidated issues gh-157196 / gh-157197 / gh-157198 were then withdrawn by the reporter on 2026-09-11 to be resubmitted under the security policy. As far as I can see nothing tracks it now, and main @ 89c67a9 still crashes. This report was found independently (static analysis of partial_repr on 3.14.0rc1, then runtime confirmation) and adds a sanitizer-free 25-line reproducer covering repr(), calls and writer/writer, with a GIL control on the same binary. If you would rather reopen gh-157099, please close this one as a duplicate. Filed on the public tracker because triggering it requires running Python code in the process (the assessment given on gh-157196).

What happened?

On the free-threaded build, calling partial.__setstate__ on a functools.partial object while another thread uses the same object (repr(p) or p()), or while a second thread also calls __setstate__, crashes the interpreter within seconds. The read-only control completed all five four-second runs without a crash. The same binary with PYTHON_GIL=1 completed every run without a crash.

Standalone reproducer (repro_partial.py <mode>):

import functools, itertools, os, sys, threading
if os.environ.get("ALLOW_GIL") != "1":
    assert not sys._is_gil_enabled()
mode = sys.argv[1]
counter = itertools.count(10**12)          # fresh heap ints, never cached
def fresh(): return next(counter)
def f(*a, **k): return None
p = functools.partial(f, fresh(), fresh())
stop = threading.Event()
def reader_repr(): repr(p)
def reader_call(): p()
def writer(): p.__setstate__((f, (fresh(), fresh()), {}, None))
reader, nr, nw = {"ro": (reader_repr, 4, 0), "rw": (reader_repr, 4, 1),
                  "ww": (None, 0, 2), "cw": (reader_call, 4, 1)}[mode]
def loop(fn):
    while not stop.is_set():
        fn()
ts = [threading.Thread(target=loop, args=(reader,)) for _ in range(nr)] + \
     [threading.Thread(target=loop, args=(writer,)) for _ in range(nw)]
for t in ts: t.start()
stop.wait(4); stop.set()
for t in ts: t.join()
print("ok")

Results, 5 runs × 4 s per mode, run with -X faulthandler ("hang" = the process had not exited 30 s after start and was killed):

mode threads 3.14.6t 3.14.6t, PYTHONMALLOC=debug same binary, PYTHON_GIL=1 main @ 89c67a9 (--disable-gil) main, PYTHONMALLOC=debug
ro 4 × repr(p) 5/5 ok 5/5 ok — 5/5 ok 5/5 ok
rw 4 × repr(p) + 1 × __setstate__ 0/5 (SIGILL, SIGABRT, 3 hangs) 0/5 (SIGSEGV ×5) 3/3 ok 0/5 (SIGABRT ×2, SIGILL, 2 hangs) 0/5 (SIGSEGV ×5)
ww 2 × __setstate__ 4/5 (SIGSEGV ×1) 1/5 (SIGSEGV ×4) 3/3 ok 2/5 (SIGSEGV ×3) 4/5 (SIGSEGV ×1)
cw 4 × p() + 1 × __setstate__ 0/5 (SIGILL ×2, SIGTRAP ×2, SIGSEGV) 0/5 (SIGSEGV ×5) 3/3 ok 0/5 (SIGSEGV ×3, SIGILL, 1 hang) 0/5 (SIGSEGV ×5)

ww is intermittent: over several runs of this script today it crashed in 1 to 4 of 5 runs per configuration. rw and cw failed in every run of every free-threaded configuration. The SIGABRT cases are

Fatal Python error: PyMutex_Unlock: unlocking mutex that is not locked

raised from the repr thread (faulthandler shows reader_repr). The repr/__setstate__ shape also crashes on 3.14.0rc1 free-threaded (5/5, PYTHONMALLOC=debug). Note that main already carries the partial_vectorcall snapshot from gh-154189, and cw still crashes there.

Analysis

partial_setstate replaces pto->fn, pto->args and pto->kw with Py_SETREF and holds no critical section on the partial object (3.13 branch Modules/_functoolsmodule.c:514; 3.14 branch :762; main :857). The readers take strong references from the fields — partial_repr since gh-144475 (3.14 branch :630), partial_vectorcall since gh-154189 (main only; not in 3.14). The source suggests an unsynchronized reference-acquisition gap: Py_NewRef(pto->args) does not protect the interval between loading the field and acquiring a strong reference while another thread replaces it. The observed crashes have not yet been attributed to a particular native access. Two concurrent __setstate__ writers also crash without a reader thread; the failing access in that case has not yet been identified. gh-144475 and gh-154189 addressed the re-entrant, same-thread shape of this; gh-157099 and this report are the cross-thread shape.

Expected behaviour

I expect concurrent use to avoid interpreter crashes; no particular ordering or consistent result is required by this reproducer. The free-threading HOWTO says the build "aims to provide similar thread-safety behavior at the Python level to the default GIL-enabled build" while noting that this "should be treated as a description of the current implementation, not a guarantee"; the same binary with the GIL enabled runs the reproducer without a crash.

Possible approach

A possible approach is to synchronize state publication and acquisition of coherent reader snapshots on the partial object, including associated placeholder and vectorcall state; the complete access and reentrancy audit remains to be done. Happy to test a patch.

CPython versions tested on

3.14.6 (free-threaded, python-build-standalone via uv), 3.14.0rc1 (free-threaded), CPython main branch @ 89c67a9 (2026-09-20, local --disable-gil build; Modules/_functoolsmodule.c identical to upstream at that commit)

Operating systems tested on

macOS (arm64, Darwin 25.6)

Output from running 'python -VV' on the command line

Python 3.14.6 free-threading build (main, Jul 18 2026, 17:07:52) [Clang 22.1.3 ]
Python 3.16.0a0 free-threading build (remotes/origin/HEAD-dirty:89c67a9, Sep 20 2026, 14:12:46) [Clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.3.34.2)]

Related

gh-157099 (same root cause, closed not_planned), gh-144475, gh-154189, gh-140590

thread.author: Adarsh-Me
thread.html:
I'd like to work on this, subject to one question.

The analysis looks right: partial_setstate mutates p->args / p->keywords / p->func without holding the per-object mutex that guards the readers in partial_repr and partial_call, so the fix is to take partial->lock in partial_setstate (Modules/_functoolsmodule.c) with the same ordering the readers already use, and to make the swap atomic under free-threading rather than reassigning the fields in place.

Two things before I write it: (1) the report notes gh-157196 was withdrawn to be resubmitted under the security policy — is this issue intended to be fixed in the open, or does it belong on the security tracker? (2) partial_new may need the same treatment if __setstate__ can race with a fresh construction. Happy to take whichever path you prefer, with a free-threaded regression test and a Misc/NEWS.d entry.

thread.author: espressolee
thread.html:
Thanks for picking this up — and yes, please do.

(1) Tracker. I filed this publicly on the assessment quoted in the report: triggering it requires already running Python code in the process, which was the assessment given on gh-157196. gh-157099, gh-157124 and gh-157196 are all closed as not planned by their author, and as far as I can see from the public trackers nothing follows them — but I can't see any non-public tracker, so whether this should move to the security process is for the maintainers to say, not me.

(2) One correction to the premise, and it widens the patch. You wrote that partial_setstate mutates the fields "without holding the per-object mutex that guards the readers in partial_repr and partial_call". In the code I audited at 89c67a9, those readers do not take a critical section on the partial either — so there is no existing reader-side ordering for the writer to join:

at 89c67a9
partial_setstate :801 no critical section; assigns fn, args, kw, phcount, dict at :856-860, then partial_setvectorcall at :861
partial_repr :705 Py_NewRef(pto->fn/args/kw) at :724-726. The Py_BEGIN_CRITICAL_SECTION at :745 is on kw, entered after that reference is acquired, and protects the dict iteration
partial_vectorcall :369 reads pto->phcount at :377, then Py_NewRef(pto->fn/args/kw) at :386-388
partial_call :592 reads pto->phcount at :600 and PyDict_GET_SIZE(pto->kw) at :610 without taking a reference first

I read your proposal as two parts, and I think the second is the load-bearing one. Making the swap atomic in the writer is necessary, but on its own it does not give a reader a coherent, live state: with no shared protocol, a reader still loads each field independently. So whatever the writer does, partial_repr / partial_vectorcall / partial_call need a matching acquisition path. Worth stating explicitly in the PR how readers get their snapshot.

Two invariants that I think the fix has to establish, since they are separate:

  • Lifetime. Py_NewRef(pto->args) loads the field and then increments. A concurrent replacement can drop the last reference in between, so the acquisition itself needs to be safe, not just the use afterwards.
  • Coherence. partial_vectorcall samples phcount at :377 and args at :387 and combines them at :419 (tot_nargs = pto_nargs + nargs - pto_phcount). Nothing currently makes those two come from the same state. The nargs < pto_phcount guard at :378 does keep tot_nargs >= pto_nargs, so a stale count does not shrink that total below the sampled tuple — but it does not make the pair consistent either, and protecting object lifetimes alone would not fix it.

I have not attributed the observed crashes to a particular native access, so please treat the second point as an invariant that needs to hold rather than as my diagnosis of the signal you'll see.

Two directions I can see, without a view on which suits this object — that's a call for the core devs:

  • take a critical section on self in the writer and in each reader, acquiring the strong references and copying phcount out of one coherent state, then doing the formatting or the call after leaving it; or
  • keep the readers lock-free with a safe acquisition protocol, publishing the whole state as one unit so phcount cannot be sampled apart from args.

Either way, two things are easy to miss: the displaced values' decrefs can run arbitrary code, so the new state should be fully installed before they run; and the vectorcall function pointer is part of the state too, not just the four fields.

On partial_new: gh-157099 reached the same crash through it, so it belongs in the audit. My reproducer doesn't exercise that shape, so I'd rather see it covered by the access audit than guessed at.

What I can offer. Both reader/writer modes — repr + __setstate__, and call + __setstate__ — crashed in all five runs of every free-threaded configuration I tried, while the writer/writer mode was intermittent (one to four crashes in five) and the read-only control never crashed. I haven't tested a writer-only patch, so I can't tell you from measurement what it would leave behind. Point me at a branch and I'll run all four modes, 5 runs × 4 s each, with and without PYTHONMALLOC=debug, on 3.14.6t and on a local --disable-gil build of main, plus the PYTHON_GIL=1 control on the same binary.

thread.author: Adarsh-Me
thread.html:
Opened as #157979.

@espressolee your correction of my premise was right and it changed the shape of the patch, so thank you for it. I had written "without holding the per-object mutex that guards the readers in partial_repr and partial_call", and as you pointed out there is no reader-side ordering there to join — so a writer-only atomic swap would have been the wrong fix. The PR takes the first of the two directions you sketched (a critical section on self in the writer and in each reader) because it is the one that reuses the protocol the object already has:

  • lifetime — the strong references are acquired inside the section, so nothing can drop the last reference between the load and the incref;
  • coherence — phcount and args are copied out of one state and the formatting or the call happens after leaving the section, so tot_nargs cannot mix two states;
  • the displaced values' decrefs run only after the new state is fully installed, and the vectorcall slot is published as part of the state rather than after it;
  • partial_new()'s flatten path is treated as a reader too, which is the gh-157099 shape you asked to be covered rather than guessed at.

On measurement: your offer is exactly what this needs, because everything I have is one platform. The build I have is a Windows amd64t Release (MSC v.1929, 3.16.0a0). Against main's _functoolsmodule.c with the new tests present, test_concurrent_setstate_and_reads dies with Fatal Python error: PyMutex_Unlock: unlocking mutex that is not locked; against the PR branch all 7 tests in that file pass. The tests do not only watch for a crash — every state they install carries the same value twice, once positionally and once as a keyword, so a torn read fails an assertion. If you run your four modes against #157979's head, that would tell us whether the reader-side behaviour you measured (both reader/writer modes crashing in 5/5 runs) actually goes away, which is the claim I cannot make from a Windows box.

On the tracker question, agreed that it is a call for the core devs rather than either of us — raising it explicitly in #157979 so whoever picks it up sees it: this is triggerable from already-running Python code, which is the assessment gh-157196 was closed under, but the earlier closures were by the author and there may be a non-public tracker nobody here can see.

thread.author: espressolee
thread.html:
#157979 was closed because the CLA was not signed, not on technical grounds, so this issue currently has no open fix. On main at 036d309 (checked today by reading the source; I have not re-run the reproducer on that revision), partial_setstate still replaces fn, args and kw without synchronization.

Would a new PR along those lines be welcome, and is there a preferred direction — a critical section on the partial in the writer and every reader, as #157979 did, or the free-threading-only immutable-adapter approach from that comment?

issues.title: Unclosed interpreter causes segfault after fork() in child process.
issues.author: aurelwildfellner
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

Bug description:

With concurrent.interpreters now available in 3.14 it's possible to trigger a probably already known issue with cleaning up interpreters after a fork.

This minimal example creates an interpreter (on the same thread), doesn't close it and then forks. The child process segfaults.

#!/usr/bin/python3.14

import os
from concurrent import interpreters

GLOBAL_INTERP = None

def create_subinter(do_close: bool) -> None:
    global GLOBAL_INTERP
    interp = interpreters.create()
    GLOBAL_INTERP = interp
    interp.exec("""
x = 42 * 23
""")
    if do_close:
        interp.close()


def main():
    global GLOBAL_INTERP

    create_subinter(do_close=False)
    print("Before fork")
    child_pid = os.fork()

    if child_pid == 0:
        print("in child")
    else:
        print("in parent")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

There seems to be a more general issue with the implementation of PyOS_AfterFork_Child() or PyInterpreterState_Clear() specifically:

cpython/Python/pystate.c

Lines 992 to 994 in a15aeec

// XXX Won't this fail since PyInterpreterState_Clear() requires
// the "current" tstate to be set?
PyInterpreterState_Clear(interp); // XXX must activate?

As the comment points out, the PyInterpreterState_Clear() won't be able to clear any interpreters, as the tstate is set to NULL before calling the function. Which finally results in a Py_DECREF on NULL.

I guess the expected behavior is that manually closing interpreters before a fork is not required and a working clear in the fork. While the combination of subinterpreters and fork() seems a bit obscure, we already ran into this issue in a CI setup.

It also seems that there is a lack of test coverage with the mentioned implementation in pystate.c. If appreciated, I could also follow up with a pull request adding more tests.

thread.author: davidnich
thread.html:
I can reproduce this without any third-party code: os.fork() in the main interpreter while a single subinterpreter exists. The child either crashes or hangs in PyOS_AfterFork_Child(), depending on the version.

import os, sys
try:
    import _interpreters as interpreters
except ImportError:
    import _xxsubinterpreters as interpreters
if hasattr(interpreters, "new_config"):
    iid = interpreters.create(interpreters.new_config("legacy"))
else:
    iid = interpreters.create(isolated=False) if "isolated" in interpreters.create.__doc__ else interpreters.create()
interpreters.run_string(iid, "x = 1") if hasattr(interpreters, "run_string") else interpreters.exec(iid, "x = 1")
pid = os.fork()
if pid == 0:
    os._exit(0)
_, status = os.waitpid(pid, 0)
print(sys.version.split()[0], "child status:", status)
Python Platform Child
3.14.6 (python.org framework) macOS 26.6, arm64 SIGSEGV
3.14.4 Ubuntu 26.04, x86_64 SIGSEGV
3.13.15 (MacPorts) macOS 26.6, arm64 SIGABRT
3.12.13 (MacPorts) macOS 26.6, arm64 SIGSEGV
3.12.14 Alpine 3.23 (musl), x86_64 hangs
3.11.15 (MacPorts) macOS 26.6, arm64 hangs
3.10.20 (MacPorts) macOS 26.6, arm64 hangs

  • 3.14: the result is the same with new_config("isolated"), and when no code was run in the subinterpreter. The crash with faulthandler on (3.14.6, macOS) is:

    _Py_Dealloc
_PyImport_ClearCore
PyInterpreterState_Clear
_PyInterpreterState_DeleteExceptMain
PyOS_AfterFork_Child
os_fork_impl

  • 3.11: the child waits forever in PyOS_AfterFork_Child() -> PyThread_acquire_lock_timed().

We hit this in an embedding application. Its subinterpreters are created with allow_fork = 0, and it forks from the main interpreter of a Python process. For now it skips PyOS_BeforeFork() / PyOS_AfterFork_*() for its own fork() calls while subinterpreters exist.

issues.title: modulo for huge integers has the wrong complexity
issues.author: cfbolz
issues.bodyHTML:
Bug report

in PR #96673 the complexity of integer division and divmod was improved. however, plain modulo still uses the previous code path. specifically, long_div and long_divmod call l_divmod, which dispatches to pylong_int_divmod when the sizes get large enough. otoh, long_mod calls l_mod, which calls long_rem, never going to the asymptotically faster pure python version.

this has the paradoxical effect that calling divmod and discarding the division result can become arbitrarily much faster than just using %.

trivial benchmark script:

import random
import timeit

rng = random.Random(1729)
bits = 1000

# import the python implementation early
divmod((1 << 32768) - 1, (1 << 16384) + 1)

print("divisor bits       // (s)        % (s)   divmod (s)   mod vs div slowdown")
while True:
    a = rng.getrandbits(2 * bits) | (1 << (2 * bits - 1))
    b = rng.getrandbits(bits) | (1 << (bits - 1))
    print(f"{bits:12,d}", end="", flush=True)
    results = []
    for expression in ("a // b", "a % b", "divmod(a, b)"):
        elapsed = timeit.timeit(expression, number=1, globals={"a": a, "b": b})
        results.append(elapsed)
        print(f" {elapsed:12.6f}", end="", flush=True)
    print(f" {results[1]/results[0]:12.3}x")
    bits *= 2

issues.title: Upstream downstream patches for allowing to make a relocatable (standalone) Python installation
issues.author: FFY00
issues.bodyHTML:
Feature or enhancement

Proposal:

I am currently looking at https://github.com/indygreg/python-build-standalone/tree/main/cpython-unix

This would be the first step towards python.org possibly providing a binary build for Linux.

cc @jezdez @indygreg

Has this already been discussed elsewhere?

No response given

Links to previous discussion of this feature:

No response

Linked PRs

  • gh-160377

thread.author: zanieb
thread.html: That's good to know, thanks for sharing that additional context. It makes sense that it's mostly historical and aligned with the distribution mechanisms of the time. I think it's fair to say that lately there is an increasing focus on portable distribution mechanisms for applications and it'd be great to see Python move towards supporting those use-cases. I'm curious if there are reasons this wouldn't be desirable? (Other than the obvious large amount of work necessary to get there)

thread.author: zooba
thread.html:
The main reason that I find it undesirable is that portable (particularly "many-Linux" portable) distributions will put the build, maintenance, and release burden back on the volunteer team. Right now, it's either handled by paid or volunteer employees of the companies that produce their own distributions.

If we were to maintain our current policy (no binaries for security-fix only releases) but get users onto our own portable releases, many users would find themselves stuck when they need to switch to a different release mechanism to get trustworthy security fixes. It's possible that new companies would start distributing portable builds with fixes integrated (it's worth noting that Anaconda already does this), but I expect most Linux distros would stick with the builds that integrate into the rest of their OS.

Now, don't get me wrong, I think most Python users should avoid their distro's own build of Python (it's usually the system Python, meant for system apps, and the user's app shouldn't blindly adopt the system's one). But I don't think that most are ready to do it, and at best will end up relying on repackaged builds from upstream. So there's a pretty significant community dynamic here that is not obviously going to work out in users' favour.

All that said, having the capability to build a relocatable install would be great. I have my own set of build hacks to make it possible for my $WORK scenarios, so I'd love to drop those. Making relocatable releases is actually a totally separate question, but as it's the motivation for having the changes upstream, until somebody says they're going to make those releases, it looks like pretty pointless churn unfortunately.

thread.author: vstinner
thread.html: The cpython-unix/ directory of https://github.com/indygreg/python-build-standalone contains 37 patches. Which patches are the most important? I don't see which patch magically makes Python relocatable. Is it another script which makes it relocatable?

thread.author: zanieb
thread.html: That's a good question — I can try to answer it but I'll need to dig around quite a bit since I didn't write the project. Let me loop in @indygreg, if he has time.

thread.author: zooba
thread.html:
This is the most critical (native) part:

https://github.com/indygreg/python-build-standalone/blob/ef71d13ba98706995ef056801fea1e88e172d7c6/cpython-unix/build-cpython.sh#L516-L566

Changes in the build script would presumably pass different linker options rather than patching the built binaries.

I believe most of the other changes are to clean up assumptions within the stdlib (primarily sysconfig I'd imagine) about the layout.

thread.author: tanzim
thread.html:
Did I get the TL;DR; right on this?

  • CPython maintainers are happy to accept patches and work with contributors to make CPython relocatable on Linux (and hopefully macOS too)
  • The stated goal of distributing standalone relocatable distributions via python.org is out of scope as put extra burden on the maintainers

If that's the case makes a lot of sense to me. I too for $WORK create embeddable and relocatable Python distributions for macOS and Windows and would love it if I didn't have to maintain my own patches/hacks etc. Having the support in CPython would be invaluable.

thread.author: vstinner
thread.html:
CPython maintainers are happy to accept patches and work with contributors to make CPython relocatable on Linux (and hopefully macOS too)

So far, no pull request was proposed.

thread.author: FFY00
thread.html:
Maybe this should be a PEP?

Perhaps, I think there are two parts of this work:

  1. Make sure the Python runtime works on relocatable builds
  2. Add support for relocatable builds in the build system

Since I don't think we currently rely on the build prefix for path calculation, 1) should already be supported, and shouldn't require any major changes. Runtime issues relocatable builds hit are likely bugs anyway. Considering this, I think 1) shouldn't need a PEP, as long as we don't run into any major issues or design constrains while working on it.

Regarding 2), I think that might need PEP. Though, if there are any build system improvements we can make to help minimize the patching required for projects like python-build-standalone, I think it should be okay to do so, but that can be evaluated on a case-by-case basis.

CPython maintainers are happy to accept patches and work with contributors to make CPython relocatable on Linux (and hopefully macOS too)

Yes. You can ping me to review such contributions.

The stated goal of distributing standalone relocatable distributions via python.org is out of scope as put extra burden on the maintainers

I don't think that's out of the picture, but it's out of scope for this issue, and it would require a PEP. It's something to maybe consider if the work covered in this issue is successful, but for now we should focus on bridging the gap between the upstream and dowstreams, given how critical to the Python ecosystem this use-case is.

thread.author: zooba
thread.html:
Regarding 2), I think that might need PEP. Though, if there are any build system improvements we can make to help minimize the patching required for projects like python-build-standalone, I think it should be okay to do so, but that can be evaluated on a case-by-case basis.

Nah, provided it doesn't change the default or break any existing options, we can add support to the build system like any other feature. I would like to be able to argue for certain changes to be treated as bugfixes, since they're important to users who build from source and so are very impactful beyond our maintenance period, but we certainly shouldn't need a PEP to introduce improvements.

thread.author: emmatyping
thread.html:
I'm interested in helping to make a relocatable Linux build of CPython a supported build option. I went through the build script and patches and here are the patches I think should be applied or adopted in some way to enable that. Note this list does not include a number of patches which should probably be upstreamed related to macOS and Linux cross compiling. It also only includes patches targeting the latest CPython.

  • patch-make-testembed-nolink-tcltk.patch - This patch handles the situation where testembed and libpython link against Tcl/Tk when built statically. In a static build, this causes duplicate symbols, so testembed should not link against Tcl/Tk when libpython links to modules statically.

  • patch-python-link-modules-3.11.patch - This patch is targeted towards macOS, but I think it motivates changes more generally:

    # Also on macOS, the `python` executable is linked against libraries defined by statically
# linked modules. But those libraries should only get linked into libpython, not the
# executable. This behavior is kinda suspect on all platforms, as it could be adding
# library dependencies that shouldn't need to be there.

    I think I would agree it would be better to link libraries against libpython rather than the python executable. This is a pretty significant change however, so I don't know if it is worth the risk, especially if we're just focusing on Linux for now.

  • patch-tkinter-3.13.patch - This patch updates how unix builds find Tcl/Tk libraries to search in a few more places, which seems useful for a portable build.

  • patch-ctypes-static-binary.patch - This patches resolves #81241 by simply not making the ctypes.pythonapi object available. I'm not totally sure what the best path forward here is, but perhaps just noting it is unavailable on static CPython builds in documentation is sufficient?

  • patch-configure-disable-stdlib-mod-3.12 and patch-pwd-remove-conditional.patch - These patches hack around not using the configure script's module enable/disable logic. The patch comments say:

    # Python 3.11 has configure support for configuring extension modules. We really,
# really, really want to use this feature because it looks promising. But at the
# time we added this code the functionality didn't support all extension modules
# nor did it easily support static linking, including static linking of extra
# libraries (which appears to be a limitation of `makesetup`). So for now we
# disable the functionality and require our auto-generated Setup.local to provide
# everything.

    So to me this seems like the work left to do is make sure that the module enable/disable logic and makesetup script support static linking. This also affects patch-checksharedmods-disable.patch, which disables the shared module check because of the above patches.

  • patch-test-embed-prevent-segfault.patch - This may be an issue with the BOLT optimization when CPython is compiled statically? This needs more investigation to figure out why there is a crash.

I'll take a look at the more obvious ones (e.g. addressing #81241) as a start.

thread.author: geofft
thread.html:
I think there's a couple of different definitions of "relocatable". For instance, patch-ctypes-static-binary seems to be specifically needed where the Python interpreter is fully statically linked (does not use the ELF interpreter, ld.so), but our current releases are dynamically linked (uses the systemwide ld.so) and so I think this patch is not needed. There are probably a couple of other patches in python-build-standalone/cpython-unix/ that aren't relevant for what python-build-standalone is doing these days.

Another distinction is whether third-party libraries that are used by Python (zlib, Expat, Tcl/Tk, etc.) are statically linked into libpython or the Python binary (which is orthogonal to whether the Python binary itself uses ld.so or not), and if not, whether they're picked up from the system or from something shipped along with the relocatable Python installation. I think python-build-standalone could ship all of these third-party libraries as separate shared libraries, but it's just that because of its history as targeting a static single-file interpreter, it doesn't.

Out of curiosity, @emmatyping, do you have some specific use case in mind for a relocatable Python?

thread.author: emmatyping
thread.html:
I think there's a couple of different definitions of "relocatable".

Very true! In my mind it is merely "if I take this install, and scp it to another machine, it should continue to work". Which implies a lot about runtime dependency and module loading (e.g. all dependent libraries are consistently loaded).

For instance, patch-ctypes-static-binary seems to be specifically needed where the Python interpreter is fully statically linked (does not use the ELF interpreter, ld.so), but our current releases are dynamically linked (uses the systemwide ld.so) and so I think this patch is not needed.

I'll check if this is the case, it would make sense it isn't needed.

I think python-build-standalone could ship all of these third-party libraries as separate shared libraries, but it's just that because of its history as targeting a static single-file interpreter, it doesn't.

I'm a little concerned ld.so.cache may cause problems here. In a scenario where libpython.so is embedded in a program, if the program loads any library of the same SONAME, the bundled dependent library wouldn't be used, which could cause errors about missing symbols if the system library is older than the one used for the relocatable Python.

Out of curiosity, @emmatyping, do you have some specific use case in mind for a relocatable Python?

I would love to see an official relocatable build of CPython for Linux for many reasons (not needing to build CPython myself to get a version my OS doesn't package, a more official/signed equivalent to python-build-standalone, etc.) . I realize working on this won't mean that happens, and that'd probably require a PEP, but I think it is generally useful if a relocatable Linux (and probably macOS as well) build is a supported build configuration.

thread.author: brettcannon
thread.html:
Since https://github.com/python/prebuilt-cpython/ is now a thing and we are working towards relocatable, prebuilt binaries for releases, I think we should start working towards upstreaming relevant patches.

I think for simple stuff it can be tied to this issue, but anything that might require discussions we should have separate issues.

thread.author: daanx
thread.html:
Just an update: recently started working on integrating mimalloc v3 in CPython (sorry, I hope this does not interfere with your work @corona10 -- I wasn't aware this effort was started).

I am hoping mimalloc v3 can become a "drop-in" without needing any patches from the CPython side -- so we can easily upgrade mimalloc in the future if there are security fixes or new features (like the recent profiler hooks) etc.

The main item that I added is a good interface for the quiescent-state-based-reclamation (QSBR), and I think I found a good
abstraction for this where all lifetime management is now done on the mimalloc side (and part of the regular release).
Hope this design can work as the interface is now more general and abstract (so maybe it can work for other runtimes as well).

With the new first-class heaps in mimalloc v3, we can make heaps that are QSBR enabled and for those the pages are
tracked so we never free the memory if there might still be outstanding readers. The CPython side only needs to define
helpers for the actual QSBR goals etc. This is quite minimal now (https://github.com/microsoft/mimalloc/blob/dev3/include/mimalloc/qsbr.h):

typedef struct mi_page_qsbr_s mi_page_qsbr_t;
typedef struct mi_heap_qsbr_s mi_heap_qsbr_t;
void mi_heap_qsbr_init(mi_heap_qsbr_t* heap);
void mi_page_qsbr_clear(mi_page_qsbr_t* page);
bool mi_page_qsbr_is_clear(const mi_page_qsbr_t* page);
bool mi_page_qsbr_should_delay(mi_page_qsbr_t* page, mi_heap_qsbr_t* heap, size_t page_bytes);

I implemented all this on the mimalloc side where this gets enabled by defining MI_QSBR=1.
Now, I don't know CPython very well, so I used an agent to interface CPython with the new v3 API and
created a fork here: https://github.com/daanx/cpython/tree/mimalloc-v3 (this is temporary and more
a proof of concept and to help others/Sam to integrate this; I can make it into a PR if that is better?)

The actual changes to CPython are in commit e253ecc2, while the other commits are just including the new vendored mimalloc v3 sources.

It all seems to work already :-) -- but again, I am not an expert here so someone needs
to review the changes and see if it indeed is all ok; @colesbury: hope you can take a look?

Here are some other more minor parts that were addressed as summarized by an agent:

CPython-side changes in my fork

The following are in commit e253ecc2 in the cpython fork.

  • Heaps per interpreter instead of tags. Create 4 mi_heap_t*  per interpreter (mem, object, gc, gc_pre). Each thread state gets its per-thread heaps once with mi_heap_theap()  and allocates through  mi_theap_* . Pages never leave their heap and reclaim only happens within a heap. So tag, the per-interpreter abandoned pools and  _mi_heap_init_ex / _mi_tld_init  all go away. Subprocs aren't needed, and wouldn't fit: one OS thread can run thread states from several interpreters, but can only belong to one subproc.

  • Simpler GC walk. It becomes  mi_heap_visit_blocks(gc_heap, ...)  per interpreter, covering all threads and abandoned pages. No loop over thread states, no lock, no separate abandoned visit.

  • Smaller installed headers.  pycore_mimalloc.h then only needs opaque pointers, so only mimalloc.h has to be installed.

  • Cache the per-thread theaps in the thread state.  mi_heap_malloc has a single cache slot, so switching between 4 heaps would keep hitting the slow lookup. Get a mi_theap_t with mi_heap_theap(heap) in each thread state and use mi_theap_malloc.
    (or mi_theap_malloc_csize if the size is statically known).

  • Already upstream in v3: the MI_PRIM_THREAD_ID macro, the configurable debug fill bytes, MI_TSAN, the UWP fix and the microsoft/mimalloc#1321 CodeQL fixes. The gh-123022 patch no longer applies.

Mimalloc v3 changes

These are already committed in the latest dev3 in mimalloc.

  • Per-heap debug-fill offset. v3 fills whole blocks on alloc and free. Py_DEBUG free-threaded builds need the object header
    bytes left intact. Fixed in commit fc238b62.

  • Public "page owner thread id" call. gc_restore_tid needs it. Abandoned pages in v3 report 0 or 4, so it should return 0 for both. CPython would replace the segment lookup with: op->ob_tid = mi_thread_id_of(op);.
    Added size_t mi_thread_id_of(const void* p) in commit 9dac1fec.

  • Explicit "abandon this thread's per-heap state" call. The internal version, _mi_theap_delete, is commented out. CPython needs one on the owning thread (thread state cleared while the OS thread lives on), and one usable from another thread when the owner is dead (PyThreadState_Clear of other threads, fork child).
    Add mi_theap_delete and mi_theap_quiescent_abandon (commit 318f6817). Not sure in-how-far this is still needed
    with first-class heaps and heap-destroy/delete. Hope we can avoid calling this.

  • Fork safety. v2 was nearly lock-free. v3 uses some pthread mutexes and has no fork handlers, so a fork can deadlock the child. In the child, dead threads' pages also stay "owned", and a new thread can reuse the same thread id. Suggest mi_fork_prepare/parent/child()  or  pthread_atfork. Fixed in commit 1b7e73f3, 7ea8bfc0, and c084f15a.

  • Heap-walk bug (reproduced). Live blocks in OS-allocated pages that a live thread still owns are not visited. With  mi_option_disallow_arena_alloc, only 1 of 2 blocks was visited. The CPython GC would miss objects whenever mimalloc falls back to OS pages. Also, area->used over-counts blocks freed by other threads but not yet collected (fixed in 85f49529ca). fixed in commit b85f2d06, a9d447d3, f9262ecb.

  • Nice to have:

    • Public size-class thresholds or stats for _debugmallocstats. (not sure what to do?)
    • Fix the one -Wstatic-in-inline  warning (mi_forall_arenas). Otherwise static.c compiles cleanly with CPython-like flags. Fixed in commit cee18e1c.

Running

This is how I tested CPython on macOS from my fork:

git clone --depth 1 --single-branch --branch mimalloc-v3 \
  https://github.com/daanx/cpython.git cpython-mimalloc-v3

cd cpython-mimalloc-v3
mkdir -p build/nogil
cd build/nogil

../../configure --disable-gil
make -j8
./python.exe -VV

The version output should contain free-threading build. (On Linux, use ./python instead of ./python.exe

Simple no-GIL test

Run this from the same build directory. It checks that the GIL is actually disabled and runs four CPU-bound workers—not merely sleeping threads.

./python.exe -I - <<'PY'
import sys
import sysconfig
import threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

assert sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED") == 1, "Not a free-threaded build"
assert not sys._is_gil_enabled(), "GIL is enabled"

n = 1_000_000
barrier = threading.Barrier(4)

def work(_):
    barrier.wait(timeout=30)
    return sum(i * i for i in range(n))

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(work, range(4)))

expected = n * (n - 1) * (2 * n - 1) // 6
assert results == [expected] * 4
assert not sys._is_gil_enabled()
print("GIL enabled:", sys._is_gil_enabled())
print("PASS: four CPU-bound worker threads completed correctly")
PY

Repeat the regression tests:

./python.exe -m test -j4 --timeout 180 \
  test_gc test_threading test_capi.test_mem test_free_threading

issues.title: C implementation for strptime
issues.author: pganssle
issues.bodyHTML:
Feature or enhancement

Proposal:

I have long known that dt.strptime is very slow, despite being an extremely commonly used function. This is basically because it is written in Python. If you for example compare datetime.fromisoformat (C) to datetime.strptime (Python) for parsing "2024-02-29T12:34:56.123456+05:30", strptime takes about 39× as long to produce the same result:

Method Time per call
datetime.strptime 3.43 µs
datetime.fromisoformat 88.5 ns
Reproducer 
python -m timeit -s 'import datetime; import _strptime' \
  'datetime.datetime.strptime("2024-02-29T12:34:56.123456+05:30", "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%f%z")'
python -m timeit -s 'import datetime' \
  'datetime.datetime.fromisoformat("2024-02-29T12:34:56.123456+05:30")'

Ages ago, I suggested this to @StanFromIreland as something to do with a Claude subscription that he had gotten and he produced this experiment, which had some real improvements, (~2x faster), but was clearly bottlenecking on some sort of round trip through Python. (Expand below for benchmarks)

Benchmarks

%Y-%m-%d (date only)                     491ns     8419ns     4352ns     1.9x
%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S (datetime)             549ns    11903ns     4430ns     2.7x
%F (compound date)                       477ns     8993ns     4129ns     2.2x

year+julian day                          512ns     9173ns     4309ns     2.1x
year+week+weekday                        535ns    11619ns     4191ns     2.8x
year+week(Mon)+weekday                   548ns    11475ns     4257ns     2.7x

2-digit year only                        487ns     7396ns     4118ns     1.8x

FALLBACK PATH
Format                                  Python   w/ C try   Overhead
%b (abbrev month)                       9299ns     9466ns      1.8%

default ctime format                   13074ns    13131ns      0.4%

I recently had ChatGPT 6.0 take another crack at it (I'm sure Claude also would be able to do the same I just happened to be using ChatGPT 6.0), specifically telling it to make sure to avoid doubling back into Python and it produced something more consistent with fromisoformat. fromisoformat() gives 88.5ns but and the fully-C fast path gives 121ns for the same format as above. I will send a PR with more extensive benchmarks, but I figured I would create this bug to track an effort to speed up strptime in case that one withers.

Overall it's adding complexity, but this is a pretty significant speed-up for a very common function, I think it's going to be worth doing.

issues.title: [Meta] Research: what can we test with Hypothesis?
issues.author: sobolevn
issues.bodyHTML:
We now have both the code and CI job to run hypothesis tests.

In this issue I invite everyone to propose ideas: what can we test with it?
Criteria:

  1. Tests should be suitable for property-based nature of hypothesis
  2. The action under test should be fast and reliable (since hypothesis will produce a lot of cases to tests, we cannot do any slow / network related things)
  3. Strategies for data generation should be rather simple (I think that later we can get to more complex strategies, but for now for the sake of simplicity and maintability I propose not to get too crazy with them)

What else?

Known applications

Property-based tests are great when there are certain patterns:

  • decode and encode
  • dumps and loads

There are also some hidden patterns as (example):

  • If 'a' in s then
  • s.index('a') must return an integer

Existing work

Good examples of exising stuff:

  • Existing hypothesis tests in test_zoneinfo by @pganssle
  • Existing tests in https://github.com/Zac-HD/stdlib-property-tests by @Zac-HD and others

thread.author: Zac-HD
thread.html:
I'd suggest looking at PyPy's property-based tests, since they're known to be useful for developers of a Python implementation.

I'd also reconsider (3). While complicated strategies are obviously more work to develop and use, in my experience they're also disproportionately likely to find bugs - precisely because code working with complicated data structures are even more difficult to test without Hypothesis, and so there are usually weird edge cases.

Examples of this effect include #84838, #86384, #89901, and #83134. The hypothesmith source-code strategies are at a pre-alpha / proof-of-concept stage and have more third-party dependencies so I'm not sure they'd be a good fit for CPython at this time, but you get the idea. I don't have capacity to implement it myself, but could supervise a volunteer or contractor to build a production-ready strategy if there's interest.

thread.author: rhettinger
thread.html:
Personally, I don't think we should go down this path. Hypothesis has a certain amount of randomness to it. In general, our tests should be specifically designed to cover every path of interest.

When someone is designing new code, it is perfectly reasonable to use Hypothesis. However, for existing code, we "let's use Hypothesis" isn't a goal directed as a specific problem. One issue that we've had with people pursuing a "let's use Hypothesis" goal is that they are rarely working on modules that they fully understand, that the invariants they mentally invent aren't the actual invariants and reflect bugs in their own understanding rather than actual bugs in the code. For example, we got reports on colorsys conversions not being exactly invertible; however, due to color gamut limitations they can't always be inverted (information is lost) and the conversion tables were dictated by published standards that were invertible. We also got false report on the random module methods by people who just let Hypothesis plug in extreme values without any thought of what the method was actually supposed to do in real use cases. There may have been one actual (but very minor) bug in the standard library found by Hypothesis, but everything else was just noise.

It would be perfectly reasonable to use Hypothesis outside of our test suite and then report an actual bug if found. Otherwise, I think actually checking in the h-tests would just garbage-up our test suite, make it run less deterministically, and no explicitly write-out all the cases being covered.

test_hypothesis:
name: "Hypothesis tests on Ubuntu"
runs-on: ubuntu-20.04
timeout-minutes: 60
needs: check_source
if: needs.check_source.outputs.run_tests == 'true' && needs.check_source.outputs.run_hypothesis == 'true'
env:
OPENSSL_VER: 1.1.1v
PYTHONSTRICTEXTENSIONBUILD: 1
steps:
- uses: actions/checkout@v3
- name: Register gcc problem matcher
run: echo "::add-matcher::.github/problem-matchers/gcc.json"
- name: Install Dependencies
run: sudo ./.github/workflows/posix-deps-apt.sh
- name: Configure OpenSSL env vars
run: |
echo "MULTISSL_DIR=${GITHUB_WORKSPACE}/multissl" >> $GITHUB_ENV
echo "OPENSSL_DIR=${GITHUB_WORKSPACE}/multissl/openssl/${OPENSSL_VER}" >> $GITHUB_ENV
echo "LD_LIBRARY_PATH=${GITHUB_WORKSPACE}/multissl/openssl/${OPENSSL_VER}/lib" >> $GITHUB_ENV
- name: 'Restore OpenSSL build'
id: cache-openssl
uses: actions/cache@v3
with:
path: ./multissl/openssl/${{ env.OPENSSL_VER }}
key: ${{ runner.os }}-multissl-openssl-${{ env.OPENSSL_VER }}
- name: Install OpenSSL
if: steps.cache-openssl.outputs.cache-hit != 'true'
run: python3 Tools/ssl/multissltests.py --steps=library --base-directory $MULTISSL_DIR --openssl $OPENSSL_VER --system Linux
- name: Add ccache to PATH
run: |
echo "PATH=/usr/lib/ccache:$PATH" >> $GITHUB_ENV
- name: Configure ccache action
uses: hendrikmuhs/ccache-action@v1.2
- name: Setup directory envs for out-of-tree builds
run: |
echo "CPYTHON_RO_SRCDIR=$(realpath -m ${GITHUB_WORKSPACE}/../cpython-ro-srcdir)" >> $GITHUB_ENV
echo "CPYTHON_BUILDDIR=$(realpath -m ${GITHUB_WORKSPACE}/../cpython-builddir)" >> $GITHUB_ENV
- name: Create directories for read-only out-of-tree builds
run: mkdir -p $CPYTHON_RO_SRCDIR $CPYTHON_BUILDDIR
- name: Bind mount sources read-only
run: sudo mount --bind -o ro $GITHUB_WORKSPACE $CPYTHON_RO_SRCDIR
- name: Restore config.cache
uses: actions/cache@v3
with:
path: ${{ env.CPYTHON_BUILDDIR }}/config.cache
key: ${{ github.job }}-${{ runner.os }}-${{ needs.check_source.outputs.config_hash }}
- name: Configure CPython out-of-tree
working-directory: ${{ env.CPYTHON_BUILDDIR }}
run: |
../cpython-ro-srcdir/configure \
--config-cache \
--with-pydebug \
--with-openssl=$OPENSSL_DIR
- name: Build CPython out-of-tree
working-directory: ${{ env.CPYTHON_BUILDDIR }}
run: make -j4
- name: Display build info
working-directory: ${{ env.CPYTHON_BUILDDIR }}

I propose adding more cases, where it makes sense.

In general, our tests should be specifically designed to cover every path of interest.

I agree that our regular tests should cover all paths, but there are more to it. Path coverage is only as good as 100%. But, we are obviously limited by the number of data we can provide. We cannot come up with lots of data, our current test suites proove my point.

But, Hypothesis can. This is exactly what it is good at: proving lots of correctly structured data.

Hypothesis has a certain amount of randomness to it

There are different way on how we control the randomness. First, we use a database with examples:

cpython/Lib/test/support/hypothesis_helper.py

Lines 22 to 35 in 5d936b6

Plus, Hypothesis itself controls how data is generated to be repeatable.

One issue that we've had with people pursuing a "let's use Hypothesis" goal is that they are rarely working on modules that they fully understand, that the invariants they mentally invent aren't the actual invariants and reflect bugs in their own understanding rather than actual bugs in the code

This is a valid concern, I hope that collaboration among developers can solve this.
And this is exactly why I created this issue: to figure out what is worth testing and what not.

There may have been one actual (but very minor) bug in the standard library found by Hypothesis, but everything else was just noise.

I don't think that this is actually correct. First, we cannot know what bugs were found by Hypothesis, because people might just post the simplest repro without naming the tool.

issues.title: Tachyon: use bounded columnar blocks for binary profiles
issues.author: pablogsal
issues.bodyHTML:
Tachyon currently stores samples in one compressed stream. The reader decompresses the whole sample section before replay, so long captures need a large allocation.

I propose small blocks with separate columns for thread and interpreter IDs, timestamps, flags, stack changes, and frame indices. Each block stores each thread/interpreter pair once. Samples refer to that pair with a small index. Timestamps store the difference from the expected sample time, without loss of precision. Stacks reuse common frames or refer to a previous stack in the same block.

Each column can use zstd, a single repeated value, or raw bytes, whichever is smaller. Similar values sit together, which can help compression. The reader processes one block at a time, so its sample buffer no longer grows with capture length. Shared string and frame tables still need memory.

The aim is smaller files and cheaper replay. We need to preserve the current format’s efficiency for repeated stacks. This needs a new format version, with the same public collector and replay APIs. Live output remains separate work in #145464.

Linked PRs

  • gh-160313

thread.author: pablogsal
thread.html: I tried a C prototype against current main. The captured JSON/zlib workload gives a 63% smaller file and uses 16% less replay CPU time. For an eight-million-sample synthetic capture, peak replay RSS drops from 268 MiB to 22 MiB.

thread.author: pablogsal
thread.html: I plan for @ivonastojanovic to implement this :)

thread.author: maurycy
thread.html: I'm very excited about this one! More than happy to help / review!

thread.author: pablogsal
thread.html:
OK, some pieces we could consider for this design:

  • We could try independent blocks of about 1 MiB, with one block decoded at a time. We would also need limits on samples, bytes, stack storage, and caches.

  • One possible split is six columns: stream dictionary, stream indices, timestamp residuals, status flags, stack edits, and new frame indices.

  • We could give each block a dictionary of thread/interpreter pairs. Each sample would then need only a small index.

    dictionary: 0 = (thread 41, interpreter 0)
            1 = (thread 82, interpreter 1)
samples:    [0, 1, 0, 0]

  • Perhaps timestamps could store the difference from the expected sample time, separately for each stream. The first prediction would be the block’s base timestamp. This would preserve exact values.

    base:       10000 us
interval:    1000 us
timestamps: 10000, 11003, 12001
residuals:      0,    +3,    -2

  • An unchanged stack could have a single repeat command, with no frame payload. For [A, B, C] -> [A, B, C], that would be just repeat.

  • We could store stacks from root to leaf and retain common root frames when the stack changes.

    previous: [A, B, C, D]
next:     [A, B, E]
stored:   keep 2, append [E]

  • A small cache of complete stacks may help within each block. For stack 1, stack 2, stack 1, the third sample could refer to the first stack’s frame range. We could cap the search work and confirm matches with a full comparison.

  • We could store frame indices in byte planes, with the smallest width that fits. Similar bytes would then sit together for compression.

    indices: [0x0123, 0x0456]
encoded: [width=2] [0x23, 0x56] [0x01, 0x04]
                   low bytes    high bytes

  • Perhaps constant status bits could appear once, with each variable bit in its own bit plane. Tachyon’s flag meanings would stay the same.

    sample flags:  [0x03, 0x01, 0x03]
constant bits:  0x01
variable flag: 0x02 -> [1, 0, 1] -> packed byte 0b00000101

    Here, the first sample occupies the lowest bit in the packed byte.

  • Compact varint headers could reduce overhead for small captures. Small counts, lengths, and codec tags would need only one byte.

  • We could compress each column separately and choose the smallest representation: raw bytes, one repeated byte, or zstd. For [7, 7, 7, 7], that could be one byte with value 7 and a decoded length of 4.

  • We could start with zstd level 3. For large frame columns, a small probe could select level 1 when level 3 gives little extra compression.

  • The shared string and frame tables may benefit from compression too. We could retain raw storage when compression does not help and decode the tables incrementally. These tables would still grow with the capture.

  • We could decode frame indices and status flags in batches. One byte from each status bit plane gives that flag for eight samples.

  • Replay could retain batches for repeated stacks. For 100 consecutive samples from one stream with the same stack, we could reconstruct it once and retain all timestamps and status values.

  • We could reuse buffers and compression contexts across blocks, but reset stream history and stack caches. Each completed block could go through one output call.

  • This would need a new format version. The aim would be to preserve Tachyon’s APIs, output stack order, 64-bit sample count, capture settings, and profile statistics.
