Thanks! This is actually very close to what I’ve been prototyping, so here’s where I am at the moment.

The sample section is split into independent blocks, while the string and frame tables are still stored once for the whole file. I’m keeping this scoped to file exports for now, streaming would probably need block-local metadata, so I think that’s better handled separately.

The decoded size of each block is currently capped at a hardcoded value. I’ll lower that to around 1 MiB as you suggested, and then we can experiment to find a good default.

Each block currently has six columns:

  • the (thread ID, interpreter ID) pairs used in the block
  • one stream index per sample
  • timestamp residuals
  • status flags, with constant bits stored once in the block header and one bit plane for each bit that varies
  • stack instructions
  • frame indices

Compression follows the existing compression option. Each column is compressed independently and stored as raw bytes, a single repeated byte, or zstd, whichever is smallest.

For stacks, the reader keeps the previous stack for each stream and supports three instructions:

  • REPEAT count: same stack for the stream's next count samples, even if other threads' samples come in between.
  • REPLACE_SUFFIX keep_count new_count: keep the outer frames and append new ones.
  • REUSE offset count: point at a stack stored earlier in the block.

I'll try the rest of your list next (varint headers, zstd level 3, limits, shared table compression, batched replay).

One question: should we keep the repeat count per stream? It saves a byte per repeated sample and gives replay batches for free, but the reader then needs a counter per stream. With zstd, a plain REPEAT per sample is almost free too.

thread.author: pablogsal
thread.html:
Some extra info on the status stuff...

Today Tachyon stores one status byte per sample. We could split that into bits that stay fixed for the block and bits that change.

E.g. take 03 01 03 (all values here are hex). Bit 0, HAS_GIL, stays set. Bit 1, ON_CPU, goes 1, 0, 1.

We could store var=02 to say that bit 1 changes, and const=01 for the bits that are always set. Then we pack the CPU flag across samples into 05, binary 00000101. The first sample goes in the lowest bit, the second in the next bit, etc.

old: 03 01 03
new: 02 01 05   # var, const, packed CPU bits

To decode, we start each status with const, then put that sample’s CPU bit back in bit 1. So sample 0 gets 01 | 02 = 03, sample 1 gets 01, and sample 2 gets 03.

If another flag changes, it gets another packed sequence. We could store these in flag-bit order, so var tells the reader which sequence belongs to which flag. Each sequence needs ceil(n / 8) bytes for n samples. Unused bits in the last byte would be zero.

Still 3 bytes in this example. With 1,000 samples and one variable flag, it becomes 2 mask bytes + 125 packed bytes = 127 bytes. Two variable flags would take 252 bytes. The current layout takes 1,000 bytes.

If every status is identical, we could store just that one byte. The block already gives us the sample count.

These are sizes before zstd. We would need to compare compressed size and decode cost, especially for small blocks or blocks where many flags change.

thread.author: pablogsal
thread.html:
A few extra things we could consider:

  • We could make REUSE lookup cheaper with a small key from the stack depth and a few frame IDs. Different keys mean different stacks. If the keys match, we still compare all frames before emitting REUSE. That avoids full comparisons for most misses.

  • On the reader side, we could cache decoded frame ranges. E.g. if REUSE points to the same 20 frames several times, we decode those IDs once. Later references can copy the decoded IDs. Perhaps we cap both the entry count and total cached frames, since a few deep stacks could take lots of memory.

  • For status bits, we could expand eight samples at once with a small lookup table. E.g. packed byte 05 becomes [1,0,1,0,0,0,0,0]. We shift those values to the original flag position and combine them with the other flags. This could reduce the work per sample.

  • For frame IDs, we could check the byte width once per range. E.g. with width 2, the whole loop reads one low byte and one high byte per ID. We then avoid checking “is this 1, 2, 3 or 4 bytes?” for every frame.

  • Perhaps large frame columns could get a quick compression probe. We compress a small part at two zstd levels. If the slower level barely saves any bytes, we could pick the faster one for that column. We would still compare the final result with raw storage. The probe adds work, so this probably only makes sense for larger columns.

  • We could keep column headers small by storing only sizes we need. A raw column needs one length. A constant column needs its decoded length and one value. Only a compressed column needs both decoded and stored lengths. The codec could fit in the low 2 bits of the length field, with the length in the remaining bits.

issues.title: Sharing a dict iterator across threads double-DECREFs di_dict under free-threading
issues.author: devdanzin
issues.bodyHTML:
Crash report

What happened?

On a free-threaded build, advancing a single, shared dict iterator (iter({...})) from multiple threads double-frees the underlying dict and crashes.

All three dict iterators (dict_keyiterator / dict_valueiterator / dict_itemiterator) route next() through dictiter_iternext_threadsafe (Objects/dictobject.c). Its exhaustion path drops the iterator's owning reference to the dict:

fail:
    di->di_dict = NULL;   /* non-atomic clear */
    Py_DECREF(d);         /* drop the iterator's ONE owning ref to the dict */
    return -1;

and the caller reads that reference with no lock:

static PyObject*
dictiter_iternextkey(PyObject *self)
{
    dictiterobject *di = (dictiterobject *)self;
    PyDictObject *d = di->di_dict;      /* plain read */
    if (d == NULL)
        return NULL;
    PyObject *value;
    if (dictiter_iternext_threadsafe(d, self, &value, NULL) < 0) {
        value = NULL;
    }
    return value;
}

The iterator holds exactly one reference to the dict (di_dict). Two threads calling next() on the same near-exhausted iterator interleave as: both read d = di->di_dict (non-NULL), both reach fail:, and both run Py_DECREF(d). The second Py_DECREF has no matching reference — the dict's refcount underflows / it is freed one owner too early, and a sibling thread still walking d (and the dict freelist / keys object) then touches freed memory.

This fail: di->di_dict = NULL; Py_DECREF(d) pattern predates free-threading (it is correct under the GIL, where only one thread runs the iterator); the lock-free dictiter_iternext_threadsafe wrapper carried it over unguarded.

Reproducer

import threading

NT = 8
ITERS = 200_000

def newit():
    return iter({k: k for k in range(32)})

cell = [newit()]

def worker():
    for _ in range(ITERS):
        it = cell[0]
        try:
            next(it)                 # dictiter_iternextkey -> dictiter_iternext_threadsafe
        except StopIteration:
            cell[0] = newit()        # refill so the fail: (exhaustion) path is hit repeatedly
        except Exception:
            pass

threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(NT)]
for t in threads: t.start()
for t in threads: t.join()
print("done, no crash")

PYTHON_GIL=0 ./python repro.py on a free-threaded build:

  • Debug build → SIGABRT within seconds, ~8/8 runs, with _Py_NegativeRefcount on the dict (Objects/dictobject.c:6159), plus downstream corruption faces as the freed dict/keys object is reused (dictkeys_incref immortal-refcount assert :484; new_dict type assert :978; clear_freelist Objects/object.c:909; validate_refcounts in gc_free_threading.c).
  • Release build (-O0, no sanitizer) → SIGSEGV (use-after-free), or occasionally Fatal Python error: PyMutex_Unlock: unlocking mutex that is not locked from the corrupted dict mutex.

So it is neither debug-only nor sanitizer-only. Debug backtrace (the negative-refcount object is the dict d):

#8  _PyObject_AssertFailed (obj=0x...dict...) at Objects/object.c:3278
#9  _Py_NegativeRefcount               at Objects/object.c:275
#12 Py_DECREF                          at ./Include/refcount.h:363
#13 dictiter_iternext_threadsafe (d=0x...dict...) at Objects/dictobject.c:6159    <-- fail: Py_DECREF(d)
#14 dictiter_iternextkey                at Objects/dictobject.c:5791
#15 builtin_next                        at Python/bltinmodule.c:1776

Suggested fix

Consume the reference atomically so exactly one thread performs the DECREF:

fail:
    PyDictObject *old = _Py_atomic_exchange_ptr(&di->di_dict, NULL);
    if (old != NULL) {
        Py_DECREF(old);
    }
    return -1;

and keep the dict alive for the duration of the lock-free walk (the caller uses d and its keys/values across the whole dictiter_iternext_threadsafe body) so a sibling that wins the exchange cannot free it mid-iteration — take a strong reference or the dict's critical section for the walk. One fix covers keys/values/items, since all three route through dictiter_iternext_threadsafe.

Why this is not the documented value-benign iterator race

This function was written to be shared across threads, and a crash is explicitly out of contract:

  • The lock-free dict iterator dictiter_iternext_threadsafe was added by gh-112075 / PR #115108 ("Iterating a dict shouldn't require locks"), under the umbrella gh-112075 ("Make dict objects thread-safe in --disable-gil builds"). PR #115108 states it "[handles] races against the dict as well as allowing the iterator to be used from multiple threads simultaneously." It made the value read safe (_Py_TryIncrefCompare / acquire_key_value) but carried the old fail: di->di_dict = NULL; Py_DECREF(d) exhaustion path in unchanged — hence this double-free.
  • gh-120496 ("Sequence iterator thread-safety") decided not to fix the fact that concurrent iteration can return duplicate/skipped values, and documented it instead (only the Doc/glossary.rst note, PR #120685, merged; the code-fix PRs were closed). But the contract agreed on that issue is explicit — @colesbury and @eendebakpt: iterating from multiple threads "will not crash the interpreter" (that's the acceptable line; wrong values are OK, crashes are not), and @eendebakpt flagged "the risks of overflows inside the C code."
  • gh-148873 reported this iterator's data-race face and was closed as a duplicate of gh-120496 — folding a double-free into the value-benign class. That is the gap this issue closes: the same unsynchronized clear-and-DECREF is not benign — it double-frees the dict and crashes (negative refcount / UAF / SIGSEGV) on plain free-threaded builds, which gh-120496 / gh-124397 put squarely on the not-acceptable side.

(Found by fusil --tsan, a ThreadSanitizer fuzzer; crash confirmed by re-running the reproducer without a sanitizer on a plain free-threaded build. Draft and reproducer by Claude Code, minimized and reviewed by hand.)

CPython versions tested on:

CPython main branch

Operating systems tested on:

Linux

Output from running 'python -VV' on the command line:

Python 3.16.0a0 free-threading build (heads/main:a1d580430c8, Jul 18 2026, 20:23:36) [Clang 21.1.8 (6ubuntu1)]

Linked PRs

  • gh-160312

thread.author: BHUVANSH855
thread.html:
Hi! I've been investigating this issue and wanted to ask for some guidance on the intended fix.

I first tried implementing the suggested atomic exchange on the exhaustion path:

fail:
    PyDictObject *old = _Py_atomic_exchange_ptr(&di->di_dict, NULL);
    if (old != NULL) {
        Py_DECREF(old);
    }
    return -1;

This compiles successfully, but rebuilding CPython causes _bootstrap_python to abort during the freezing step with assertions in interpreter_clear() (cold->vm_data.valid / cold_dynamic->vm_data.valid), so it doesn't appear to be sufficient on its own.

While reading through dictiter_iternext_threadsafe(), I also noticed that the callers pass a borrowed PyDictObject *d = di->di_dict, and the helper dereferences d throughout the lock-free walk. The issue description mentions "keep the dict alive for the duration of the lock-free walk", but doesn't specify the intended mechanism.

Could you clarify what the preferred approach is here?

  • Should the iterator acquire a temporary strong reference to the dict for the duration of dictiter_iternext_threadsafe()?
  • Should the dict's critical section be used instead?
  • Or is there another intended approach?

I'd appreciate any guidance before continuing with the implementation.

thread.author: devdanzin
thread.html:
Thanks for taking a look at this! Are you building with the JIT? That error message seems to be the same in #154014. I reproduced this issue on a free-threaded non-JIT debug build (--disable-gil --with-assertions, no --enable-experimental-jit) and don't hit the freezing abort. If you're not using the JIT, could you share your exact configure options?

You're right that the atomic exchange alone isn't enough. The exchange fixes the double-DECREF (so the iterator's owning reference is dropped exactly once), but as you noticed, the caller reads d = di->di_dict as a borrowed pointer and the helper dereferences it throughout the lock-free walk, so a sibling thread that wins the exchange and drops the last reference can still free the dict out from under an in-flight walk (a use-after-free).

I think the cleanest fix keeps the lock-free forward-iteration design (the point of gh-112075 / #115108) by having the caller take a temporary strong reference for the duration of the walk:

  • in dictiter_iternextkey / ...value / ...item, atomically load-and-incref di->di_dict (e.g. _Py_TryXGetRef) so it can't be freed mid-walk, pass that kept-alive d to dictiter_iternext_threadsafe, and Py_DECREF it after the call;
  • keep the atomic-exchange in the fail: path so the iterator's owning reference is cleared and dropped exactly once.

That way the walk always operates on a dict kept alive by the temporary reference, and only one thread performs the owning-ref DECREF on exhaustion.

What do you think?

Drafted with help from Claude Code

thread.author: devdanzin
thread.html:
Follow-up on the reproducer: the same dictiter_iternext_threadsafe double-DECREF is not limited to throwaway iter({...}). It hits any long-lived shared dict — and, because iter(frozendict) returns a dict_keyiterator, any shared frozendict (e.g. a module-level constant) too. On a long-lived object (refcount > 1) the double-DECREF doesn't go immediately negative — the corruption is silent until the next gc.collect() catches it:

import threading, gc

fd = frozendict({4:'FREE',1:'LOCAL',3:'GLOBAL_IMPLICIT',2:'GLOBAL_EXPLICIT',5:'CELL'})
NT = 8
cell = [iter(fd)]
def worker(role):
    for i in range(100_000):
        it = cell[0]
        try:
            next(it)
        except StopIteration:
            cell[0] = iter(fd)
        except Exception:
            pass
        if role == 2 and i % 32 == 0:
            gc.collect()
ts = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(i % 3,)) for i in range(NT)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()

PYTHON_GIL=0 ./python repro.py → Python/gc_free_threading.c:1116: validate_gc_objects: Assertion "gc_get_refs(op) >= 0" failed: refcount is too small, object type frozendict, ~8/8 on a debug free-threaded build (SIGSEGV on release).

This is the more concerning form of the bug: a real program that keeps a shared module-level dict/frozendict and iterates it from several threads silently corrupts its refcount, surfacing as an unrelated GC crash. A ThreadSanitizer fuzzer (fusil --tsan) hit it across ~9 unrelated stdlib modules that each expose a module-level frozendict (symtable, functools, gettext, json, …) — the module is incidental; the shared frozendict iterator is the cause.

(Reproducer + note draft by Claude Code, reviewed by hand.)

thread.author: BHUVANSH855
thread.html:
Thanks! That direction makes sense, and I agree that taking a temporary strong reference in the caller seems like the right approach.

I have one implementation question before I start coding it. _Py_TryXGetRef() returns NULL both when the pointer is actually NULL and when _Py_TryIncrefCompare() loses a race.

For the iterator callers (dictiter_iternextkey, dictiter_iternextvalue, and dictiter_iternextitem), what would be the preferred behavior if _Py_TryXGetRef((PyObject **)&di->di_dict) returns NULL due to that optimistic race?

Should the caller:

  • retry,
  • fall back to a locked path,
  • or simply return NULL and let the next next() call retry?

I just want to make sure I follow the intended pattern rather than introducing a new one.

thread.author: devdanzin
thread.html:
I think the ambiguity you spotted is exactly why the one-shot _Py_TryXGetRef is the wrong tool for the caller here.

Use _Py_XGetRef, not _Py_TryXGetRef. In Include/internal/pycore_object.h, _Py_TryXGetRef is the one-shot variant that returns NULL on either a NULL pointer or a lost _Py_TryIncrefCompare race. _Py_XGetRef is the for(;;) version that re-loads the pointer and retries the incref, returning NULL only when it actually observes di_dict == NULL. So it collapses your three options into the correct one automatically:

static PyObject*
dictiter_iternextkey(PyObject *self)
{
    dictiterobject *di = (dictiterobject *)self;
#ifdef Py_GIL_DISABLED
    // Loops past a lost optimistic incref; returns NULL only if di_dict is really NULL.
    PyDictObject *d = (PyDictObject *)_Py_XGetRef((PyObject **)&di->di_dict);
    if (d == NULL)
        return NULL;                 // genuine exhaustion -> StopIteration
    PyObject *value;
    if (dictiter_iternext_threadsafe(d, self, &value, NULL) < 0) {
        value = NULL;
    }
    Py_DECREF(d);                    // drop the temporary walk ref
    return value;
#else
    PyDictObject *d = di->di_dict;
    if (d == NULL)
        return NULL;
    return dictiter_iternextkey_lock_held(d, self);
#endif
}

A couple of reasons this is the right shape:

  • Don't surface the race as a return-NULL. Returning NULL without an exception is StopIteration, so a NULL on a merely-lost optimistic race would end iteration early: a spurious StopIteration. gh-120496 explicitly tolerates imprecise results (duplicated/skipped values) but this would be a premature end of a non-exhausted iterator, which is a step worse than the imprecision that issue signed off on. _Py_XGetRef avoids it by only returning NULL for a real NULL.
  • It matches the function's own precedent. When the value incref races today, dictiter_iternext_threadsafe doesn't spin ad-hoc or bail — acquire_key_value returns -1 and it does goto try_locked, finishing under Py_BEGIN_CRITICAL_SECTION(d) (dictobject.c ~6162). _Py_XGetRef is the equivalent "resolve the race rather than expose it" choice for the dict pointer. (For the di_dict read specifically, the internal retry is cleaner than a locked fallback, since we can't take d's critical section before we hold a live ref to it.)
  • No livelock risk. di_dict is monotonic — set once when the iterator is created and only ever transitioned to NULL on exhaustion, never re-pointed — so _Py_XGetRef's loop terminates in a couple of iterations at most (either the incref wins, or the atomic exchange in the fail: path publishes NULL).

Ref accounting stays balanced: the iterator's single owning ref is consumed exactly once via the atomic exchange in fail:, and each caller's temporary _Py_XGetRef ref is dropped by the matching Py_DECREF(d) after the walk, which is also what keeps d alive for the duration.

One thing I'd want a core dev to confirm before you build on this (@colesbury, as the author of the lock-free iterator in gh-112075/#115108): _Py_XGetRef/_Py_TryXGetRef carry the precondition "the writer must set maybe-weakref on the stored object," so this isn't purely a read-site change — the site that stores di_dict (dictiter_new) and the atomic clear in fail: need to cooperate so the try-incref on di_dict is valid. I'm not certain whether the dict stored in di_dict already satisfies that or needs explicit setup, and getting it wrong reintroduces exactly the kind of race we're closing. I'd confirm that detail (and that a temporary strong-ref-per-next() is the preferred trade-off vs. a short critical section on the iterator itself) before finalizing.

Drafted with help from Claude Code

thread.author: devdanzin
thread.html: For the record, this double-free also surfaces as the freelist-corruption assertion in #152125: on a debug free-threaded build the exhausted-iterator double-DECREF desyncs the dict freelist's size, so clear_freelist (Objects/object.c:909) aborts with freelist->size == 0 || freelist->size == -1 (~90% of runs of the shared-iterator repro) — the allocation-failure-free counterpart of that issue's set_nomemory path.

As mentioned on the other issue, my inclination would be to have a way to output debug info without the GIL drop.  Likely we can't be using sys.stderr and have to write directly to the stderr file descriptor.   It would be nicer if we could output to whatever sys.stderr is bound to, more user friendly, but I'm afraid that could make the GC implementation a fair bit more complex.
OTOH, if we look what's done for resource warnings, they do get written to sys.stderr.  PyErr_ResourceWarning takes extra trouble to try to write to it.
Another possible solution: write the debugging output to a buffer while GC is in the middle of its work.  Then, write that buffer to sys.stderr at a safe place.  Buffering the output should be fine.

posts.text: Based on a suggestion from Sam, I changed it to instead estimate mimalloc memory use by counting full mimalloc pages.  This requires a couple of changes to mimalloc itself but avoids the STW blocks and so should perform better.  The accounting happens when a page transitions from non-full->full and so should have minimal performance overhead.

This PR has some serious issues:

Moving all the JIT state to the thread does not make things thread safe. It might do the opposite by introducing race conditions.
There is a possible use after free bug, when an executor created by one thread is run in another
It leaks an unbounded amount of memory, as it doesn't collect executors.

Executors are not "effectively immortal"; cold executors do get freed.
There are some useful improvements here, such as locking when inserting/removing executors from the linked list, but those should be in separate small PRs.

import _thread

So, please, check first which instructions have empty argrepr and let's decide afterwards which ones should be rendered.

posts.author: picnixz
posts.text:
Actually, after reading the code (now that I'm on my laptop), I see that _opcode.has_const(_opcode_metadata.opmap["LOAD_SMALL_INT"]) returns False, hence the "bug" and only LOAD_SMALL_INT has some special handling.
However, _get_const_info calls _get_const_value which itself checks whether the op has constants or if it's LOAD_SMALL_INT. So, I think we should indeed set it because argrepr is not necessarily set on the (raw) instruction itself (the instruction doesn't have a constant as its argument but it can be deduced).
We have other places where we do op in hasconst or op == LOAD_SMALL_INT (e.g., in find_imports or in the assert of _get_const_value. So I would suggest the following:

Keep what you did. Even if we duplicate the output for now.
Add a helper (private) function that checks if it has constants, e.g., _hasconst_like() which checks whether op is in hasconst or op == LOAD_SMALL_INT and replace the checks with that method. If we decide to change the meaning of "having a constant" later this would help a lot.
I'll decide then whether we can modify print_instruction_line to remove the duplicated output. An alternative would be to have some field on instr that says "hide duplicated fields" and then we can use this in the formatter.

For instance:
class Instruction(_Instruction):
   
   ...
   

   @property
   def _simplify_repr(self):
       return self.baseopcode == LOAD_SMALL_INT
and then in the formatter, we would only print the argrepr if _simplify_repr is False.

posts.author: markshannon
posts.text: Unlinking a thread before clearing seems strange. Why do we do that during interpreter shutdown?

posts.author: colesbury
posts.text:
It looks like we've been doing it this way since 3.9:

Looping over the interpreter's linked list of thread states requires HEAD_LOCK()
It's not safe to call PyThreadState_Clear() inside of HEAD_LOCK()

Prior to 3.9 we called PyThreadState_Clear() inside of HEAD_LOCK(), which has it's own problems.

prs.title: gh-83055: Prevent `get/put` item in `asyncio.Queue` when there are pending task or woken tasks
prs.author: YvesDup

recentCommits.headline: Initial commit
Merge branch 'main' into queue-asyncio-keep-insertion-order-fix

posts.author: YvesDup
posts.text:
@asvetlov : A draft PR with an another proposal.
This PR also fixes this issue for the following example:
async def simplier_get_case():
    async def get_and_print(q):
        item = await q.get()
        print(f"\tGET: {item}, {str(q) = }")
 
    q = asyncio.Queue(1)
    g = 3
    for n in range(g):
        asyncio.create_task(get_and_print(q))
    await asyncio.sleep(0.0)

    # queue full: 1 item in queue, 2 items waiting into the _putters
    n = 1
    print(f'PUT: {await q.put(n) or n}')
    n += 1
    # queue not empty: 1 item in queue, 2 tasks the _putters
 
    # steal the free solt
    try:
        print(f"\tGET_NOWAIT steal a free slot: {q.get_nowait()}")
    except asyncio.QueueWithPendingTasks:
        g -= 1
        print("Failed to GET_NOWAIT item".center(60, '-'))
  
    # get all items
    for _ in range(g):
        print(f'PUT: {await q.put(n) or n}')
        n += 1
    await asyncio.sleep(0.0)

asyncio.run(simplier_get_case())

posts.author: picnixz

posts.author: arpittkhandelwal
posts.text:
Thanks @DavidCEllis for the demonstration, and @picnixz for the review. You are both right: the cell holds a nonlocal binding, and David's generic example shows that the multi-name path already places the nonlocals between the locals and the globals. The globals expectation in my issue report was wrong, so I have narrowed this PR to the locals handling only:

The resolution order for a single-cell reference is now: explicit locals, then the cell, then globals, then builtins — matching the dict-of-cells path, where the cells are merged into the locals with setdefault.
The regression tests are updated accordingly: evaluate(globals={"x": 43}) keeps returning the cell value (99), while evaluate(locals={"x": 42}) now returns 42. test_annotationlib and test_typing pass, and both tests still fail on the unmodified code. I have also updated the PR description and the NEWS entry, and added a correction to the issue.

On the question about past issues: I searched the tracker for prior reports of this behaviour (annotationlib / ForwardRef / evaluate combined with cell, closure, globals and locals) and could not find one. The closest matches are gh-141174 (ForwardRef test coverage) and the separate issue about evaluate()'s type_params handling; neither covers the single-cell namespace precedence. If you remember where you saw it, I am happy to link it or close this as a duplicate.

I have made the requested changes; please review again.

_raise_error() in the _defer_traps docstring, as suggested.
On keeping _deferred_error when an exception propagates: you are right to question it. The C implementation never stores an exception on the context at all — operations only accumulate condition flags in the context status (dec_addstatus ORs them into ctx->status), and the exception is created from those flags once the operation completes; if the operation itself fails, no decimal error is left behind. _defer_traps now clears _deferred_error unconditionally when an exception propagates, at every nesting level: the operation is aborted, so the propagating exception wins, and the context never retains an exception object (the clean-exit path already detached it before raising). The signal flags themselves are still set, as in C. The new test_deferred_traps_exception_discards_error covers the nested case.

prs.title: gh-160936: Make logging setLevel() and disable() cost O(cached loggers)
prs.author: Ar-maan05

recentCommits.headline: gh-160936: Make logging setLevel() and disable() cost O(cached loggers)

posts.author: eendebakpt
posts.text:
As mentioned on the issue, is this a real-world problem? There are some issues with the current approach:

Loggers that fail the loggerDict.get(logger.name) is logger check (e.g. created directly with logging.Logger(name)) are never discarded, so every setLevel() keeps visiting them. With 4000 such loggers alive, setLevel() goes from ~1 µs on main to ~1 ms.
Per-item discard() leaves dummy slots in the set, and re-adding the same logger reuses them, so the table never shrinks after one bulk invalidation. After 4000 cached loggers are cleared once, every later setLevel() stays 5-10x slower than on main.

Both go away by clearing all loggers in the set unconditionally and then emptying the set:
        with _lock:
            for logger in self._cached_loggers:
                logger._cache.clear()
            self._cached_loggers.clear()
            self.root._cache.clear()
Some more details
Clearing a superset of what `main` clears is safe, and as a bonus it fixes a stale cache for loggers not in `loggerDict` (`Logger("x").setLevel(ERROR)` currently leaves `isEnabledFor(DEBUG)` True). Please add a test for that and for `_cached_loggers` being empty after `setLevel()`.
Reproducer for both:
import logging, time

lg = logging.getLogger("one")

def us_per_setlevel():
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(2000):
        lg.setLevel(logging.INFO)
        lg.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG)
    return (time.perf_counter() - t0) / 2000 * 1e6

print(f"baseline:              {us_per_setlevel():7.1f} us")

registered = [logging.getLogger(f"app.mod{i}") for i in range(4000)]
for l in registered:
    l.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG)
lg.setLevel(logging.INFO)
print(f"after bulk invalidate: {us_per_setlevel():7.1f} us")   # (2)

logging.root.manager.loggerDict.clear()
standalone = [logging.Logger(f"s{i}") for i in range(4000)]
for l in standalone:
    l.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG)
print(f"4000 standalone alive: {us_per_setlevel():7.1f} us")   # (1)

posts.author: cmaloney
posts.text: (force pushed to fixup author line and make cla bot happy)

posts.author: methane
posts.text: How about concatenating everything and making a single write() call instead of calling file.write() repeatedly? This would likely improve performance significantly. It would also prevent standard output from getting garbled when multiple threads call print(a, b), since another thread could otherwise call print() between the file.write(a) and file.write(b) calls.

posts.author: cmaloney
posts.text:
I started with that but then found it didn't produce uniform speedup: Copying strings of various sizes into a PyUnicodeWriter instead of doing the "pending" list that TextIOWrapper does would slowdown for some string sizes. It also very significantly changes behavior if a __str__ implementation causes a fault / SIGSEGV. I then profiled and found the repeated method binding was actually most of the runtime so built this PR.
In the longer term I'm hoping to add what I call a "Coherent" print; everything in one print statement gets write() to the underlying device not interleaved with any other print statement. That is a couple versions away though: need to support list of buffers through a lot more of the stack.

posts.author: methane
cmaloney
posts.text:
I tried the PyObject_CallMethodOneArg approach in PyFile_WriteObject (your patch, plus the cached ' '/'\n' for the default sep/end) and compared it with this PR and main. print() with no args is faster in your code but all other cases are equal or slightly slower patching PyFile_WriteObject.

Benchmark script
import pyperf

SETUP = """
import io, os, tempfile
devnull = open(os.devnull, 'w')
sio = io.StringIO()
disk = tempfile.TemporaryFile('w')
ten_ints = tuple(range(10))
big = 'x' * 2**20
big_list = list(range(1000))
"""

CASES = {
    "one_str[devnull]": "print('hello world', file=devnull)",
    "one_str[sio]": "print('hello world', file=sio)",
    "three_args[devnull]": "print('a', 1, 2.5, file=devnull)",
    "ten_ints[devnull]": "print(*ten_ints, file=devnull)",
    "empty[devnull]": "print(file=devnull)",
    "str_1mib[devnull]": "print(big, file=devnull)",
    "list_1000[devnull]": "print(big_list, file=devnull)",
    "flush[disk]": "print('hello world', file=disk, flush=True)",
}

runner = pyperf.Runner()
for name, stmt in CASES.items():
    runner.timeit(name, stmt, SETUP)

posts.author: methane
posts.text:
Part of what I like for this particular refactoring is that it simplifies the amount of conditional code inside print. It eliminates branching around NULL vs. provided sep and end in the main implementation

Wouldn't combining that improvement with an optimization of PyFile_WriteString() achieve the same performance as this PR?

as well as needing to tracing through the Py_File internal branches for Py_PRINT_RAW.

I don't think the benefits are significant enough to justify the additional complexity.

posts.author: cmaloney
posts.text:
Wouldn't combining that improvement with an optimization of PyFile_WriteString() achieve the same performance as this PR?

A single PyObject_CallMethodOneArg is cheaper than PyObject_GetAttr + PyObject_CallOneArg. For every object printed there is an additional call, and that's where the the gap opens up between the two. Calling the bound object in print_write takes less time and instructions than calling PyFile_WriteObject(obj, file, Py_PRINT_RAW) with PyObject_CallMethodOneArg inside.
I wanted to validate that so built a microbenchmark just focused on doing more and more arguments. Each argument gets a separator printed as well which doubles the difference.

        "import os; devnull = open(os.devnull, 'w')",
    )

posts.author: StanFromIreland
posts.text:
Unfortunately I don't see a way around this. We could leave the codec alone and make tarfile's path check operate on bytes. That isn't ideal in itself, and it only fixes tarfile, os.fsdecode() followed by os.fsencode() would still return different bytes on EUC-KR hosts, so os.path.realpath(), pathlib.Path.resolve(), shutil and any other str-based path check keep the same flaw. I agree the regression risk isn't zero, but it looks small, I think a potential path-escape vulnerability (which could affect those banking systems you noted) has to outweigh some breakage for a rare input.
But, I'm not all that familiar here, so maybe you have a different solution in mind?

posts.author: mangod12
posts.text:
CI for PR #160706 fails on all three macOS jobs in the new test_concurrent_queries_on_shared_connection: it segfaults inside sqlite3_prepare_v2 while threads share the connection. I pushed cf13208 to explicitly request SQLITE_OPEN_FULLMUTEX whenever the linked SQLite build has mutex support, while keeping the statement reservation fix. SQLite documents that flag as selecting serialized mode and notes sqlite3_threadsafe() alone does not report runtime mode: https://sqlite.org/threadsafe.html
The new CI run will tell us whether that addresses the macOS failure. I could not build CPython locally here because the Windows C toolchain is unavailable.

posts.author: mangod12
posts.text:
Yes it was done with help of ai. And thanks for the reply.
The issue as i understood was that concurrent execution calls on a shared connection can pick the same cached SQLite statement before sqlite3 mark it busy. Both threads can then try to use that same statement.
This fix reserves that statement with a flag ( in_use) so other cursor gets an uncached one.
Also used fullmutex so that sql lite processes on the shared connection are in order.
For regression i ran concurrent queries from 4 threads sharing connection and returned blob data were checked also that subprocesses end cleanly.
For testing i had issues initially then i installed c toolchain and ran it with help of ai.

posts.author: scrieve
posts.text:
Disclosure: this patch was prepared with AI assistance. What follows is code in the diff and output from commands run on the patch, not recollection.
The test builds a 2500-character non-BMP haystack with a 100-character needle. Those are the three thresholds adaptive_find needs (haystack of at least 2500, needle of at least 100, needle at least a third of the haystack), and non-BMP characters make PyUnicode_KIND UCS4, so the run reaches ucs4lib_adaptive_find. That instantiation was the cold one in the gcov numbers in the description: 0.00% of 39 lines, against 66.67% for UCS2 and 71.79% for UCS1. The loop body is now under with self.subTest(N=N):, from the review comment at Lib/test/test_str.py:276.
Verification: on the 3.16.0a1+dev free-threading build, running the test at head fc31458 prints Ran 1 test and OK in 0.004 s. The change is a pure addition to Lib/test/test_str.py with no production code touched, so it can only fail by returning a wrong index from the UCS4 adaptive path for a needle that is present.

posts.author: StanFromIreland
posts.text: Please reply in your own words, and don't copy from an LLM.

Please reply in your own words, and don't copy from an LLM.

The fast string search has one copy for each character width, and the tests only ever run the narrow ones. This adds a test using musical symbols to force the wide copy, then checks it finds a pattern that is there and reports one that is not. No other changes proposed.

posts.author: corona10
posts.text:
@nascheme @DinoV
The results from Tools/gcbench from Thomas show that reducing the page size from 64 KiB to 16 KiB increases GC time by 6–8%, since each collection visits four times as many pages. GC-bound pathological cases are 5–8% slower, while steady-state workloads and pyperformance show no change in total runtime.
Peak RSS is generally unchanged on these large-heap tests, although bigcollect/container shows an 11% increase. That case would be worth a separate follow-up if we decide to merge this PR.
This PR aims to reduce the memory overhead relative to the default build from the current 18% to 15%, as measured by pyperformance. I think we should also compare against the default build using the GC benchmarks to make sure both the performance and memory overheads remain within the guardrails outlined in PEP 779. If both criteria are met, I would like to propose merging this PR.
I’ll share the results once I’ve run the GC benchmarks against the default build.

However, since Donghee did extensive testing and it does seem a small win with no major regressions, this seems safe to change.  Another point: if we can port some of the GC optimizations from the default build, doing fewer heap traversals by combining passes, this would likely be a bigger win.

posts.author: pablogsal
posts.text:
I took a first look at the PR. A few ideas for this change or later PRs:

Add a small, bounded cache in the reader that maps frame IDs to immutable FrameInfo objects. Reuse these objects across samples, while each callback still receives a fresh frame list. I suspect this will reduce the CPU spent on repeated object allocation.
For long captures, avoid a whole-file preload. On Linux, remove eager page population and release pages after the reader finishes with them. On Windows, replace the whole-file buffer with reads of individual blocks. This looks useful for keeping resident memory low as captures grow.
Give each hash bucket in the writer cache room for two or four stacks. Currently, stacks that map to the same bucket replace each other, even if both recur. Keep the total number of slots unchanged. I expect fewer collisions to discard useful entries.
The reuse cache also excludes stacks encoded as changes to a previous stack. For a repeated stack, consider a full-stack record so later occurrences can use REUSE. That gives us another opportunity for compression, provided the later savings cover the larger initial record.
Base the block cutoff on decoded column size, rather than the larger temporary buffers. Keep a separate memory limit for those buffers. I think this will give us fuller blocks and less overhead per sample. The trade-off to check is whether larger flushes cause longer pauses.

There's a wider discussion about counts vs. timestamps. See the trick from #149719 but in the binary format. I think of pstats, collected and flamegraph here. Two notes: this can combine non-consensutive occurences, and maybe REUSE could identify these before even create frames. That's a general question about decode_block(): how lazy decoding (materialization) can be?
Similarly: https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/160313/changes#diff-dfdcb94821b5902e4d751f5d78e385c19c1efa6ef2ed808e358741e41fda369bR1063-R1067 maybe there's no need to decode / memset?
Maybe in build_frame_list() we can read in the reverse order, without temporary stacks in flush_stream_batch().
Each stream retains a prev_stack buffer until writer destruction. Each buffer reserves frame IDs. When a stream enters a new block, block_add_stream() resets its stack depth and timestamp. The previous block's stack contents are no longer needed. Maybe we can we keep the ID registry global, but keep stack, timestamp, and repeat state only for streams in the current block? This also avoids reset growing linearly.
Thought experiment: the stream count gives us the bit width needed for the indices. With four streams, we only need two bits instead of a byte.
Perhaps we can compare independent zstd blocks with the columnar format. Then try REUSE, repeat counts and the bit/byte planes separately. I'm curious how much comes from splitting the data into blocks, how much from each encoding. File size, write/replay CPU time, peak memory, distribution of flush times etc. I can do this if you want!

Thank you! I promise more!

posts.author: gpshead
posts.text:
Reworked to keep ob_start and avoid the extra allocation: the delete now moves ob_start and the size before the resize. A failed shrink leaves the bytes removed and the larger block in place, raising MemoryError as the non-front path already does.
... we could have a failed shrink not raise at all, since the larger block is valid? I still like the error myself. del implies someone was hoping to release memory. Silently not doing so is presumably only going to happen in a high memory pressure situation? Being silent would then just mean that something else fails soon after.

posts.author: StanFromIreland
posts.text:
This has a lot of conflicts.
I suggest deferring primes() to a follow-up. primes() is currently algorithmically the same as (p for p in itertools.count(start) if isprime(p)). And, while the C iterator saves some overhead, it a small constant factor. It also greatly complicates this PR and the implementation. As such, I simply think that the limited benefit is not worth it. I think that if we ever want a fast prime iterator it should be designed as a sieve from the start, but that should be left to a later discussion.
I'm happy to review isprime() once those points are resolved, I think it's a reasonable addition.
CC @mdickinson

finally, you probably can store the state in tls instead of making it global, this should greatly improve the free-threaded performance

posts.author: encukou
posts.text: Why not keep both? Simple typedefs have virtually no maintenance cost.

posts.author: vstinner
posts.text:
Py_UNICODE is a ghost from the past. It was only relevant when a large part of the PyUnicode C API used this type (as Py_UNICODE* strings). In Python 3.16, using Py_UNICODE is no longer relevant. Using wchar_t makes the code less Pythonic (easier to understand for people not used to Python C API).
Removing Py_UNICODE can help C extensions maintainers to discover bugs in their old code (especially if the code was written with Py_UNICODE APIs and was updated later to newer APIs)

posts.author: fedonman
posts.text: I left PY_UNICODE_TYPE out because only Py_UNICODE is on the 3.16 removal list. Unlike Py_UNICODE_WIDE, both typedefs have given a compiler deprecation warning since 3.13. I'll follow whatever you two settle on: remove one, both, or neither.

posts.author: encukou
posts.text:
Removing Py_UNICODE can help C extensions maintainers to discover bugs in their old code (especially if the code was written with Py_UNICODE APIs and was updated later to newer APIs)

That seems unlikely to me. What kinds of bugs is this likely to help discover?
Removing Py_UNICODE means that any project that uses it is forced to change code. If they find the porting instructions in the removal notice, they'll replace Py_UNICODE by wchar_t. I don't think that has much potential for finding bugs. (But, of course, each such forced trivial change is a chance for the project to re-evaluate whether Python support is worth the churn.)

posts.author: encukou
posts.text:
Does it mean that we should keep forever?

Yes, that's the current guidance in PEP-387:

If the expected maintenance overhead and security risk of the deprecated behavior is small (e.g. an old function is reimplemented in terms of a new, more general one), it can stay indefinitely (or until the situation changes).

posts.author: hugovk
posts.text:
An LLM check on the 29 projects:

Summary: one actively maintained project breaks (lxml), and the root cause is Cython. Everything else is either dead code behind Python 2 / pre-3.3 guards, already broken on 3.12+, or not C code at all.


Details

I went through Victor's list of 29 projects by downloading each sdist and checking the preprocessor guards around every Py_UNICODE match, and by compiling lxml's shipped etree.c against headers with the typedef removed.
Would break on 3.16 with this PR (compiles fine on 3.13 today)

lxml 6.1.3 (and lxml master). _setupPythonUnicode() in src/lxml/parser.pxi declares cdef Py_UNICODE *uchars. The call is guarded by PY_VERSION_HEX < 0x030C0000 at runtime, but Cython compiles the function unconditionally. The shipped etree.c compiles cleanly against current main (with two Py_UNICODE is deprecated warnings) and fails with 14 errors against headers without the typedef, all from etree.c:129077 and :129080. lxml master still has this code; its only added guard is #define Py_UNICODE wchar_t under Py_LIMITED_API, so normal builds are still affected.
Cython 3.3.0 itself. Any cdef Py_UNICODE in user code is emitted verbatim as Py_UNICODE in the generated C: CPyUnicodeIntType.sign_and_name() returns "Py_UNICODE" in 3.3.0 and on master. So this removal breaks every Cython project using the type until Cython emits wchar_t instead. lxml is one such project.
PyICU-binary 2.7.4. Seven unguarded sizeof(Py_UNICODE) == sizeof(UChar) comparisons in bases.cpp. Abandoned fork, last released September 2021. The real PyICU 2.16.2 guards every use with PY_VERSION_HEX < 0x030d0000 and is fine.

Already broken on 3.12+ regardless (they use PyUnicode_AS_UNICODE, removed in 3.12)

pyScss 1.4.0 (2022): unconditional Py_UNICODE in block_locator.c. The C speedups are optional and fall back to pure Python.
Distance 0.1.3 (2013): unconditional typedef. The C extension only builds with an explicit --with-c flag.

Not affected

Guarded to Python 2 or pre-3.3: g

Maybe these would be better suited for https://github.com/python/library-fuzzers, that way, there's more compute thrown at them?

Hm... I don't love that these are in separate locations. I feel like one of the strengths of property tests is that they scale pretty well with compute — we use them as basically test parameterization via @example, they are a useful way to sample a subset of the full space on each PR when exhaustive tests aren't reasonable and you can turn them into fuzz tests just by instrumenting them differently. I feel like we should try and make use of this property and have some way to just point fuzzers at certain tests in the normal test suite.

Done: the expected failure is removed from this PR and filed separately as #160148, with the test included in the issue text for reference. The branch now has only the infinite loop fix, its regression test, and the round-trip property (plus a comment pointing at #160148 for why the strategy avoids encoded-word look-alikes).

posts.author: serhiy-storchaka
posts.text:
Node is practically an abstract class and is not intended to be instantiated, so Node() in the test creates something which should not exist.
The addition itself is fine: it matches the other defaults on Node (parentNode, ownerDocument, prefix), and allows removing nodeValue = None from DocumentFragment, Element, DocumentType, Entity, Notation, EntityReference and Document.
But nothing changes at runtime, so there is nothing to announce in NEWS.  And the reported problem is already solved for type checkers: typeshed declares nodeValue: str | None on Node.
Please remove the test and the NEWS entry.  The redundant definitions in the subclasses also can be removed -- nodeValue in the seven classes above, and also parentNode in DocumentFragment and Document, and previousSibling and nextSibling in Document, which already repeat the defaults of Node.

posts.author: SomSamantray
posts.text:
Thanks for the review — pushed a commit that applies all three requests:

Removed testNodeValueDefaultOnBaseNode. Agreed that Node() shouldn't be instantiated directly; the base-class default is already covered by typeshed for type checkers, and by the existing suite's normal construction paths for runtime behavior.
Removed the NEWS entry, since there's no runtime behavior change.
Removed the redundant nodeValue = None from DocumentFragment, Element, DocumentType, Entity, and Notation, and from Document along with its redundant parentNode and previousSibling/nextSibling.

One note: your comment mentioned seven classes for the nodeValue cleanup including EntityReference, but I don't see an EntityReference class in Lib/xml/dom/minidom.py on this branch — only six classes actually declare a redundant nodeValue = None (listed above). Let me know if you meant something else there.
Verified by building this branch from source (the branch needs a 3.15-capable interpreter for PEP 810 lazy imports, so I couldn't just import against system Python) and running the full test_minidom suite (131 tests, all passing — one fewer than before since the removed test is gone) plus test_xml_etree, test_pyexpat, and test_sax for broader regression coverage (636 tests total, all passing). comments.author: efimov-mikhail
comments.html:
Thanks for the review, Sergey!

But I have to say that I've discovered one even more difficult case without tracing at all:

import _thread
import threading

local = _thread._local()

class ClassWithDel:
    def __del__(self):
        getattr(local, 'c', None)

def thread_func():
    local.c = ClassWithDel()

t = threading.Thread(target=thread_func)
t.start()
t.join()

There's a leak with ASAN since finalizer of local.c object recreates localsdict for this thread.

CC @mpage @colesbury @ambv as author and reviewers of #121655.

Btw, we can merge this as is and create another issue for this case if this will be clearer.

comments.author: colesbury
comments.html: This does not look like the right approach to me. I think you will end up playing whac-a-mole where each time you "fix" one leak you will introduce other bugs. You need a robust approach to dealing with finalizers like the GC has.

comments.author: efimov-mikhail
comments.html:
Thanks for the comment, @colesbury .
I'd like to stress that this PR doesn't introduce new bugs, it just doesn't fix all related issues in the current state. There's a leak with this code snippet on main.

And I'll be grateful for some piece of advice, if possible.

comments.author: colesbury
comments.html:
I think you just haven't yet found the new bugs that this PR introduces. The original bug report was only found via fuzzing. I suspect that if you keep fuzzing you will find different ones with this PR.

The problems is that we have code in the form:

Py_CLEAR(tstate->var1);
Py_CLEAR(tstate->var2);
...
Py_CLEAR(tstate->varN);

The underlying problem is that when you clear tstate->var2 you may execute Python code that re-initializes tstate->var2 or variables cleared earlier like tstate->var1. If you move around the order of clearing, you change the possible bugs.

For example, if you move tstate->threading_local_key to the end, you now have potential leaks where thread local variable destructors set things like tstate->asyncio_running_loop

comments.author: efimov-mikhail
comments.html:
In general, I agree with you, swapping clear function calls isn't good way of fixing anything.
I have some new thoughts on this topic. I'll continue to find better solution.

reviews.author: sergey-miryanov
reviews.html:
Tracer handles Python calls. If a thread's locals contain an object with a Python callback (e.g., a __del__ finalizer), then tracer will handle the call.

When our thread is finalizing, the locals are cleared, as are all objects within them. In this case, the finalizer of our object's __del__ will be called and handled by the tracer. This leads to the recreation of thread locals (threading_local_key and threading_local_sentinel), which leak because we mistakenly believe that the locals were cleared and will not be recreated.

In this PR, we clear the locals after clearing the tracers, so any callbacks from finalizers will not be handled, and the locals cannot be recreated.

     int type, code = r_byte(p);
     int flag, is_interned = 0;
     PyObject *retval = NULL;
+    bool track_tuple = false;
 
     if (code == EOF) {
         if (PyErr_ExceptionMatches(PyExc_EOFError)) {
@@ -1670,6 +1671,11 @@ r_object(RFILE *p)
         if (v == NULL)
             break;
 
+        // empty tuples are untracked, and we can check if n > 0,
+        // but using PyObject_GC_UnTrack is clearer
+        PyObject_GC_UnTrack(v);
+        track_tuple = false;
+
         for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
             v2 = r_object(p);
             if ( v2 == NULL ) {
@@ -1677,9 +1683,16 @@ r_object(RFILE *p)
                     PyErr_SetString(PyExc_TypeError,
                         "NULL object in marshal data for tuple");
                 Py_SETREF(v, NULL);
+                track_tuple = false;
                 break;
             }
             PyTuple_SET_ITEM(v, i, v2);
+            if (!track_tuple && PyObject_GC_IsTracked(v2)) {
+                track_tuple = true;
+            }
+        }
+        if (track_tuple) {
+            _PyObject_GC_TRACK(v);
         }
         retval = r_ref_insert(v, idx, flag, p);

158282.bodyHTML:
The current implementation has some problems. The eval loop and module attribute lookup repeat the code that resolves a lazy import and replaces its placeholder. These copies behave differently. We also hold the global import lock during resolution, which can deadlock with another thread importing a package.

This moves the placeholder structure and resolution code into lazyimportobject.c. One helper now resolves the import and updates the namespace where we found the name. It only replaces the value if it is still the same placeholder or the child module that the normal importer just put there. Assignments and deletions made during the import are preserved. For ordinary dicts, the check and replacement are atomic.

We also remove the global import lock around resolution. Importlib still locks modules while loading them. Each thread keeps a set of placeholders being resolved to detect cycles. Custom import hooks can now run concurrently.

This removes duplicate lookup and cleanup code. The eval loop and module attribute lookup use the same helper, so they no longer need separate implementations of these rules.

With this design, a placeholder records the module to import and where the import was declared. A name taken from that import holds a reference to the original placeholder and records the attribute to look up. When the name is first used, the resolver follows those references, imports the module and performs the attribute lookups in order. The shared helper then replaces the placeholder in the namespace where it was found, provided that binding still holds the placeholder or that child module.

In both uncollectable and collectables we would
iterate through gc items using GC_NEXT(gc).
However in the case the current item was cleaned
during iteration this would reuslt in UAF when
fetching the next step in the loop.

The fix is to move each item to a temporary seen list
before printing it, and always take the next
item from the head of the original list, so the
loop never reads from a freed item. This takes
a similar approach to finalize_garbage().

capi-workgroup/decisions#84.title: Add `PyTuple_MakeSingle()` and `PyTuple_MakePair()` functions
capi-workgroup/decisions#84.author: vstinner
capi-workgroup/decisions#84.bodyHTML:
@sergey-miryanov analyzed the Python code base for tuple creation and identified that the most common tuple sizes are 1 and 2 items. He proposes adding PyTuple_MakeSingle() and PyTuple_MakePair() functions as the new way to create these tuples.

There are already other ways to build tuples of arbitrary size:

  • PyTuple_New() + PyTuple_SET_ITEM()
  • PyTuple_New() + PyTuple_SetItem()
  • PyTuple_Pack()
  • PyTuple_FromArray() -- new in Python 3.15

Proposed functions are a little bit faster, but it's matter of nanoseconds: benchmark on Linux. Fastest to slowest method:

  • PyTuple_FromArray() -- PyTuple_MakeSingle() or PyTuple_MakePair() -- similar performance
  • PyTuple_Pack()
  • PyTuple_New() + PyTuple_SET_ITEM()
  • PyTuple_New() + PyTuple_SetItem()

The difference with PyTuple_FromArray() is that you don't have to create a temporary array on the stack to build the tuple.

    PyObject *array[2] = {key, value};
    return PyTuple_FromArray(array, 2);

versus:

    return PyTuple_MakePair(key, value);

It's more convenient and natural to build a 2-tuple like that.

It's common to have to create strong references for items when building a new tuple. Example:

    PyObject *key = new_key();
    PyObject *value = new_value();
    if (!key || !value) {
        Py_XDECREF(key);
        Py_XDECREF(value);
        return NULL;
    }

    PyObject *tuple = PyTuple_MakePair(key, value);
    Py_DECREF(key);
    Py_DECREF(value);
    return tuple;

It was also proposed to add PyTuple_MakeSingleSteal() and PyTuple_MakePairSteal() variants which transfer the items ownership. The example becomes:

    PyObject *key = new_key();
    PyObject *value = new_value();
    if (!key || !value) {
        Py_XDECREF(key);
        Py_XDECREF(value);
        return NULL;
    }

    return PyTuple_MakePairSteal(key, value);

Using Steal variant, the final DECREF is no longer needed. But these variants were put aside for now.

@kumaraditya303 added:

I would prefer to have only steal versions because there are less redundant reference counting operations. decrefs are expensive on hot paths and users can easily incref before passing to steal function as needed.

Considering that reference counting is more expensive on free-threading, I think we should encourage the use of Steal functions to avoid redundant reference counting operations.

python/typing#1994.title: Unsoundness with `typing.IO` and friends
python/typing#1994.author: JelleZijlstra
python/typing#1994.bodyHTML:
The classes typing.IO, typing.BinaryIO, and typing.TextIO look like they want to be Protocols or ABCs, but in fact they are defined as regular generic classes, both at runtime and in typeshed. However, they are meant to encompass the concrete IO classes defined in the io module, and in typeshed we implement that by having these classes inherit from typing.*IO classes, even though there is no such inheritance at runtime.

This can easily lead to unsound behavior:

import io, typing

def f(x: int | io.BytesIO) -> int:
    if isinstance(x, typing.BinaryIO):
        return x.fileno()
    return x

f(io.BytesIO()) + 1  # boom

Type checkers think BytesIO is a subclass of BinaryIO, because that's how it's defined in typeshed, but in fact it isn't at runtime.

I can see a few solutions:

  1. Special-case typing.*IO in the spec and say that type checkers should reject isinstance()/issubclass() calls involving them.
  2. Deprecate the typing.*IO classes and eventually remove them, nudging people to use their own Protocols (or the new io.Reader/io.Writer) instead. This is conceptually clean but may be annoying for a lot of users; the typing classes are nice to use in simple application code.
  3. Make these classes actually (runtime-checkable?) Protocols at runtime, though they would be unwieldily large.

Even if we do (2) or (3) type checkers might still want to do (1) since it will be a while before the relevant runtime changes take effect.

(Noticed this while looking into python/cpython#133492 .)

last.author: srittau
last.html:
I still tend towards (2), although easy protocol composition would go a long way here. Reader and Writer were originally intended to be broader to encompass most cases, but became smaller in the process (which is probably for the best). But in python/cpython#133492 I suggested that we add a fairly broad protocol to _typeshed for now, maybe that's a good first step.

I also think we should looking into deprecating BinaryIO and TextIO first, before looking into IO. BinaryIO is basically identical with IO[bytes] (except that IO[bytes].__enter__ return IO not BinaryIO). TextIO has a few more methods, but they all look highly situational.

last.author: cmaloney
last.html: For these is there any way to differentiating/expose the difference in .write() behavior between "Raw I/O" (ex. io.FileIO) vs. high level I/O (BufferedIO and TextIO)? For "Raw I/O" if the write() system call only writes part of the buffer, it isn't retried while higher level I/O will loop until either the whole buffer is written or an exception is raied (non blocking fds have extra caveats).

last.author: JelleZijlstra
last.html: I don't think so; in general typing can only cover information in the method's interface (what parameters it take and of what types, and what it returns), not more subtle aspects of behavior.

python/typeshed#14071.title: Use positional only arguments for dunder methods in collections.abc
python/typeshed#14071.author: randolf-scholz
python/typeshed#14071.bodyHTML:
Currently, some dunder methods like Sequence.__getitem__ do not use positional-only arguments, which causes errors when trying to subclass with positional-only arguments. Therefore, dunder methods, especially operators like __getitem__, that are typically not called using keyword arguments, should probably be annotated using positional only arguments in the stubs.

Code sample in pyright playground

from typing import Protocol, Self, overload, Literal

class SupportsSequenceGetitemA[T](Protocol):
    @overload
    def __getitem__(self, index: int) -> T: ...
    @overload
    def __getitem__(self, index: slice) -> "SupportsSequenceGetitemA[T]": ...

class MySequenceA[T](SupportsSequenceGetitemA[T], Protocol):
    @overload
    def __getitem__(self, index: int, /) -> T: ...
    @overload
    def __getitem__(self, index: slice, /) -> Self: ...  # ❌

class SupportsSequenceGetitemB[T](Protocol):
    @overload
    def __getitem__(self, index: int, /) -> T: ...
    @overload
    def __getitem__(self, index: slice, /) -> "SupportsSequenceGetitemB[T]": ...

class MySequenceB[T](SupportsSequenceGetitemB[T], Protocol):
    @overload
    def __getitem__(self, index: int, /) -> T: ...
    @overload
    def __getitem__(self, index: slice, /) -> Self: ...  # ✅

last.author: srittau
last.html: While I do agree that these should be positional only, this should be done in CPython first. If the Python maintainers agree that this is a good idea, we can implement it in typeshed – and I'd be okay to do this for all Python versions in typeshed.

last.author: Akuli
last.html: This is different with mypy. In mypy, dunder methods are implicitly positional-only, and your example type-checks without errors as is. I'm tempted to say that mypy is correct here, and this is a pyright problem, but I don't feel very strongly about it.

last.author: randolf-scholz
last.html:
I opened python/cpython#135312.

However, I do want to point out that the current stubs can actually lead to some false negatives. For instance, list does not allow calling __getitem__ with index as a keyword. Code sample in pyright playground

from collections.abc import Sequence

def get(x: Sequence[int], index: int) -> int:
    return x.__getitem__(index=index)

get([1,2,3], 0)  # TypeError at runtime

Also, I noticed that the stubs already use positional-only sometimes when CPython doesn't, for instance with Container.__contains__.

gpshead/cpython#24.title: gh-160863: Restore tarfile data filter's resolved destination check
gpshead/cpython#24.author: gpshead
gpshead/cpython#24.bodyHTML:
This is the minimal fix proposed in pythongh-160863, an alternative to the broader fix in #23.

python#160098 (for pythongh-160097) moved data_filter's check for link members that resolve to the destination directory into the code shared with tar_filter. A later commit in that PR made the shared check lexical: it now looks only at whether the member's normalised name is .. As a result, link members that reach the destination any other way pass filter='data', which has been the default since 3.14:

Archive members (filter='data') main today This PR
../dest → dest RecursionError OutsideDestinationError
d/, s → ., hard link s/. → d completes; the destination's own mode is changed OutsideDestinationError
first.txt, ../current → real, later.txt, extracted into an existing symlink current → real completes; current is replaced and later.txt is written outside the destination OutsideDestinationError

Change

Lib/tarfile.py: puts back the five lines that python#160098 removed from the 'data' link checks (if target_path == dest_path: raise OutsideDestinationError, with their comment). The six-line lexical check that tar_filter gained is kept. data_filter behaves exactly as it did before pythongh-160097.

Lib/test/test_tarfile.py: test_link_resolving_to_destination covers the three reproducers from the issue under filter='data'.

No doc change: the data_filter docs did not describe this check before pythongh-160097 either.

Compared with #23

This PR is smaller and only restores old behaviour, so it is the safer one to backport. It leaves two things as they were before pythongh-160097, and #23 fixes both:

  • tar_filter still has only the lexical check, so ../dest and s/. still pass filter='tar'. That is no regression: tar_filter never had this check before pythongh-160097.
  • The old false positive is back for filter='data': extracting an archive that contains self → . into the same directory a second time raises OutsideDestinationError.

Testing

Run on a Linux --with-pydebug build:

  • ./python -m test test_tarfile test_shutil -u all passes (1,032 run, 162 skipped).
  • Without the tarfile.py change, the new test fails in all three cases: one RecursionError and two "OutsideDestinationError not raised".
  • Windows and macOS have not been run.

gpshead/cpython#23.title: gh-160863: Reject links reaching destination via symlinks or ..
gpshead/cpython#23.author: gpshead
gpshead/cpython#23.bodyHTML:
Summary

Fix a security vulnerability in tarfile.tar_filter() and tarfile.data_filter() where symlink and hardlink members could reach the destination directory or existing symlinks outside it through .. components or earlier symlink members in the archive.

Changes

Core Fix (Lib/tarfile.py)

Modified the link validation logic in _get_filtered_attrs() to:

  • Judge link members by where they would actually be made, not just their name
  • Resolve only the parent directory path (not the link target itself)
  • Reject links that would be placed at the destination directory itself
  • Reject links that would replace existing symlinks outside the destination

This prevents attackers from using constructs like:

  • ../dest symlinks that reach the destination
  • s/. hardlinks where s is a symlink to ..
  • Links replacing outer symlinks that point into the destination

Tests (Lib/test/test_tarfile.py)

Added three comprehensive test cases:

  • test_link_reaching_destination(): Verifies rejection of links reaching destination via .. or symlink traversal
  • test_link_replacing_outer_symlink(): Ensures links cannot replace existing symlinks outside the destination
  • test_link_to_dot_reextracted(): Confirms symlinks to . can be re-extracted correctly

Documentation (Doc/library/tarfile.rst)

Updated documentation to clarify that:

  • Links are refused if they would be made at the destination or outside it
  • Only parent directories are resolved; links replace rather than follow their target path
  • Added version note about the security fix

Test Plan

All new tests pass with both 'tar' and 'data' filters. Existing tarfile tests continue to pass, confirming backward compatibility for legitimate use cases.

This has been around since the earliest copy of PIL I've found, from 1998 :)

HAVE_PROTOTYPES and STDC_HEADERS were set by CPython's configure script to confirm the compiler supports C89 features (function prototypes and the standard headers). But C99 is already the minimum Pillow needs:

  • #8644

openssl/openssl#33420.title: [4.1.0] Regresion or Undocumented Behavioral change in the X509_check_host
openssl/openssl#33420.author: tregubovav-dev
openssl/openssl#33420.bodyHTML:
Problem description

Starting the 4.1.0 the X509_check_host always fails when the X509 certificate contains the only subject DN with CN identifies the hostname and no SAN(s) is included. and no flags are used (flags parameter is set to 0).
The call like that X509_check_host(cert, expected_hostname, 0, 0, NULL); returns 0 in Openssl 4.1.0 and returns 1 with previous releases.

The openssl verify command clearly display the behaviour difference. The command below returns:

openssl verify -CAfile <CAFilePath> -verify_hostname <`CN entry` in the `Subject DN`> <certificate path>
  • In 4.1.0:
<Subject DN content>
error 62 at 0 depth lookup: hostname mismatch
error <certificate path>: verification failed
  • in 4.0.2 and earlier:
    <certificate path>: OK

Steps to reproduce

  • Generate the certificate with the FQDN/hostname in the Subject DN and does not contain any Subject Alternative Name fields.
  • run the command below against the 4.1.0 and earlier version(s) of openssl binaries,

last.author: idrassi
last.html:
Thanks for the certificates. I have reproduced the issue.

PR #31982 intentionally changed this behavior. The changelog documents it, but the command line manual still promises CN matching. The standard verification options don't expose a switch to enable it. For these certificates, reissuing with DNS:srv.test.tld in the SAN is the straightforward migration.

Applications that perform their own CN matching also need to be updated. OpenSSL 4.1 applies DNS constraints to the CN only with X509_CHECK_FLAG_ALWAYS_CHECK_SUBJECT set and X509_CHECK_FLAG_NEVER_CHECK_SUBJECT clear. An application can otherwise accept a CN that OpenSSL hasn't checked against the issuer's DNS constraints.

Curl is one example: it relies on OpenSSL for chain validation but performs CN fallback itself. I tested curl commit 3163ec065643, from tag curl-8_23_0, against both releases.

Only the root was trusted. The server supplied this chain beneath it:

Intermediate: critical nameConstraints, permitted DNS:allowed.test
Leaf: CN=victim.test, no subjectAltName

I requested https://victim.test over loopback using --resolve, with certificate and hostname verification enabled.

OpenSSL curl result
4.0.2 Error 60; OpenSSL error 47, permitted subtree violation
4.1.0 Exit 0; HTTP response received

Reversing the x509_vfy.c change in e7f3a42 restores rejection without restoring CN matching by default. That isolates the cause: it doesn't settle where the compatibility fix belongs. OpenSSL integrated hostname verification rejects this certificate.

For applications retaining independent CN matching, the extra checks must be enabled during chain verification. Setting ALWAYS_CHECK_SUBJECT there rejects this example in my probe. Adding it only to a later X509_check_host call won't restore those checks.

The flag isn't an exact replacement for the old behavior:

  • In OpenSSL hostname matcher, it lets a matching CN override a DNS SAN mismatch.
  • With an independent matcher, it doesn't change the application SAN precedence but can reject an otherwise acceptable certificate because an unused CN fails the additional constraint check.

@t8m The curl example shows that moving to 4.1 can weaken certificate validation in applications that retain their own CN matching. Could the project publish a prominent migration notice explaining this impact and how applications should enable the necessary CN constraint checks?

last.author: tregubovav-dev
last.html:
Thanks a lot Mounir to pointing me out the PR and changelog that missed from my eyes.
It finally confirms our approach to resolve this behavior change.

I would suggest to update the openssl tool documentation update to avoid customers' confusion.
You are free to close this issue if you are not planning do any action based on it.

last.author: idrassi
last.html:
There is still the impact I described above on certificate validation for applications like curl.
We need to communicate about it to avoid security issues on third party application that would update to 4.1. Not sure how this can be done.

checkpoint-restore/criu#3268.title: pycriu: fix getting RPC response size with Python 3.15.1
checkpoint-restore/criu#3268.author: kolyshkin
checkpoint-restore/criu#3268.bodyHTML:
To find out the size of an RPC response, pycriu peeks one byte with MSG_TRUNC, which makes recv(2) return the real message length, and relies on Python's socket.recv() growing the returned bytes object to that length (with only the first byte being valid).

Python 3.15.1 no longer does that and raises ValueError instead (see PyBytesWriter_FinishWithSize), so every RPC call fails:

PAGE_SERVER_CHLD failed with internal error: size larger than allocated size

Use socket.recv_into(), which returns the value from recv(2) as is.

This breaks the Fedora Rawhide based CI jobs (x86_64 Fedora Rawhide, VM Fedora Stable/Next based test, which all run tests in a fedora-rawhide container, now with python3-3.15.1-1.fc46), e.g. on criu-dev: https://github.com/checkpoint-restore/criu/actions/runs/40074914293

Fixes: #3251

Update: this is essentially same as #3255 modulo test; I don't think test is needed.

last.author: kolyshkin
last.html:
Some background:

  • The change in Python 3.15.1 is python/cpython@c38a347 (backport of python/cpython#157226, "gh-129813: Check size in PyBytesWriter_FinishWithSize()"). It is about the PyBytesWriter C API; socket.recv() breaking with MSG_TRUNC is a side effect. It has no NEWS entry, so it's not mentioned in the 3.15.1 changelog.
  • The behavior pycriu relied on (socket.recv(size, MSG_TRUNC) returning more than size bytes) was reported as a bug back in 2015 (by someone named AndreyWagin): python/cpython#69121 (bpo-24933), still open.
