robotframework/robotframework#5825.title: `isatty` utility does not handle streams with detached buffers correctly with Python 3.14.9 and 3.15.1
robotframework/robotframework#5825.author: pekkaklarck
robotframework/robotframework#5825.bodyHTML:
We have this utility function for checking is a stream console output or not:

def isatty(stream):
    # first check if buffer was detached
    if hasattr(stream, "buffer") and stream.buffer is None:
        return False
    if not hasattr(stream, "isatty"):
        return False
    try:
        return stream.isatty()
    except ValueError:  # Occurs if file is closed.
        return False

The check for detached buffers was added by PR #1948 that fixes issue #2003. A unit test for the fix fails on the hasattr(stream, "buffer") line with a ValueError when using the recently released Python 3.14.9 and 3.15.1. Earlier versions, including 3.14.8 and 3.15.0, work fine.

I consider hasattr failing like this a bug and will report that to Python itself, but we need to fix this in our code base as well. Good news is that fixing this requires only removing the separate detached buffer check. Calling stream.isatty() if the buffer is detached fails with a ValueError. The same error occurs also if the stream is closed and we already handle that,

python/importlib_metadata#486.title: API incompatibility with `importlib.metadata` (or at least the API is not type-safe?)
python/importlib_metadata#486.author: abravalheri
python/importlib_metadata#486.bodyHTML:
When 3rd-party MetaPathFinder are implemented using importlib.metadata, the return types in importlib_metadata are not respected, which causes the API to behave in an unexpected way (with unexpected errors).

This is an example similar to the one identified in pypa/pyproject-hooks#195 (comment) and pypa/setuptools#4338:

mkdir -p /tmp/stash/private_path/_test-0.0.1.dist-info
cat <<EOF > /tmp/stash/private_path/_test-0.0.1.dist-info/METADATA
Name: _test
Version: 0.0.1
EOF

cat <<EOF > /tmp/stash/private_path/_test-0.0.1.dist-info/entry_points.txt
[_test.importlib_metadata]
hello = world
EOF

cat <<EOF > /tmp/stash/install_finder.py
import sys
from importlib.machinery import PathFinder
from importlib.metadata import DistributionFinder, MetadataPathFinder


class _ExampleFinder:
    def __init__(self, private_path):
        self.private_path = private_path


    def find_spec(self, fullname, _path, _target=None):
        if "." in fullname:
            # Rely on importlib to find nested modules based on parent's path
            return None

        # Ignore other items in _path or sys.path and use private_path instead:
        return PathFinder.find_spec(fullname, path=self.private_path)

    def find_distributions(self, context=None):
        context = DistributionFinder.Context(path=self.private_path)
        return MetadataPathFinder.find_distributions(context=context)


sys.meta_path.insert(0, _ExampleFinder(["/tmp/stash/private_path"]))
EOF

cd /tmp/stash/
python3.8 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -U importlib-metadata
.venv/bin/python
>>> import install_finder
>>> from importlib_metadata import distribution
>>> distribution("_test").entry_points.select(group="_test.importlib_metadata")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'select'

The expected behaviour as per API documentation would be:

>>> distribution("_test").entry_points.select(group="_test.importlib_metadata")
EntryPoints((EntryPoint(name='hello', value='world', group='_test.importlib_metadata'),))

It seems that the origin of this problem is a little "lie" in the API definition:

Instead of

importlib_metadata.Distribution.discover(...) -> Iterable[importlib_metadata.Distribution]

what actually happens is:

importlib_metadata.Distribution.discover(...) -> Iterable[importlib_metadata.Distribution | importlib.metadata.Distribution]

and that propagates throughout the whole API.

I haven't tested, but there is potential for other internal errors too, if internally importlib_metadata is relying that the objects will have type importlib_metadata.Distribution to call newer APIs.

It is probably worthy to change the return type of importlib_metadata.Distribution.discover(...) to Iterable[importlib_metadata.Distribution | importlib.metadata.Distribution] and then run the type checkers on the lowest Python supported (I suppose Python 3.8), to see if everything is OK.

It also means that consumers of importlib_metadata cannot rely on the newer APIs (unless they are sure that 3r-party packages installed in their environment are not using importlib.metadata).

last.author: abravalheri
last.html:
What do you think about this proposed approach?

I think it has great potential to work, specially if we have tests that ensure that the newly defined protocols are backward compatible with the stdlib's importlib.metadata.* existing classes.

last.author: jaraco
last.html:
In the latest commits on #505, I've implemented IDistribution and IPackagePath. Along with the existing PackageMetadata, I believe this provides the necessary interfaces for downstream consumers to rely on a consistent interface across importlib_metadata and importlib.metadata.

if we have tests that ensure that the newly defined protocols are backward compatible with the stdlib's importlib.metadata.* existing classes.

At first, I was thinking the mypy checks would be sufficient to validate these interfaces, but thinking about it more, they only check that the importlib_metadata interfaces match and don't really consider stdlib. I'll explore if there's a way to have mypy (or simply Python) validate that the stdlib objects implement their respective protocols.

last.author: jaraco
last.html:
A suggestion that came out of documenting this downstream (python/cpython#160344, for python/cpython#123976): consider warning on conformance rather than on class identity.

Today localize.dist warns for any Distribution subclass whose module isn't importlib_metadata:

if dist.__class__.__module__ != 'importlib_metadata':
    warnings.warn(f"Unrecognized distribution subclass {dist.__class__}")

Now that this PR adds IDistribution, that guard could ask whether the object actually satisfies the interface instead. The difference matters for the downstream guidance. As it stands, a provider that implements IDistribution completely still warns, and the person who sees the warning is not the person who can act on it. The custom-provider example in the CPython docs is exactly this case: a DatabaseDistribution that subclasses importlib.metadata.Distribution, implements read_text and locate_file, and inherits the rest. It works correctly under the backport and it warns. So the stdlib text has to explain a warning that providers cannot clear except by depending on this package, which is the coupling #486 set out to avoid. With a conformance check, the guidance collapses to "implement the whole interface", and the warning means something is genuinely missing.

One implementation note, since it is not obvious: isinstance(dist, IDistribution) is not the way to spell it. With requires-python = ">=3.11" and IDistribution carrying property members, isinstance against a runtime-checkable protocol evaluates those properties on 3.11, so the check would read METADATA for every distribution just to decide whether to warn, and a property that raises propagates out of isinstance. Measured on a protocol with metadata and version properties:

Python properties evaluated by isinstance property that raises
3.11 metadata, version exception propagates
3.13 none no effect

Checking the type avoids that on every supported version, and can name what is missing:

_REQUIRED = (
    'read_text', 'locate_file', 'metadata', 'name',
    'version', 'entry_points', 'files', 'requires',
)

if missing := [name for name in _REQUIRED if not hasattr(type(dist), name)]:
    warnings.warn(
        f"Distribution subclass {dist.__class__} is missing {', '.join(missing)}"
    )

(issubclass is not available here: protocols with non-method members reject it.) This would also subsume the __module__ check that currently works around pytest replacing importlib_metadata, since a replaced class still conforms.

Entirely possible the identity check is deliberate and I am missing a case it protects. The stdlib text works either way; it is just longer, and asks providers to live with a warning rather than to fix something.

pre-commit/pre-commit#3766.title: envcontext restore deletes empty-valued env vars on Windows (root cause of #3245)
pre-commit/pre-commit#3766.author: frankiexo
pre-commit/pre-commit#3766.bodyHTML:
search you tried in the issue tracker

missing config value GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0 → found #3245 (closed and locked, root cause never identified). Opening a new issue with the root cause, minimal repro and a proposed fix.

describe your issue

Root-caused the missing config value GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0 failure from
#3245 on Windows. pre_commit.envcontext restores the environment after each Python-language hook with os.environ.clear(); os.environ.update(before).
Re-setting an empty-valued variable through CPython's Windows environment implementation deletes it because CPython uses the Microsoft CRT _wputenv(), where KEY= means deletion. This differs from the underlying Win32 SetEnvironmentVariableW() API, which can represent an empty-valued variable. As a result, os.environ may initially contain an inherited empty-valued variable, but round-tripping it through os.environ can remove it from the process environment. When the
lost variable is GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0 (exported empty by GitHub Desktop
and some agent runtimes as a credential-helper reset), every git
subprocess spawned afterwards exits 128 with missing config value GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0: that is what breaks the unstashed-changes
git apply in #3245, and it also makes pre-commit run --files report
a phantom "files were modified by this hook" on every hook (the
before/after diff comparison reads an empty, failed diff). Minimal
standalone repro, Win32-level evidence, and a proposed fix (restore only
patched keys instead of clear+update of the whole environment) are in the
attached analysis.

pre-commit --version

pre-commit 4.6.2

.pre-commit-config.yaml

repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
    rev: v6.0.0
    hooks:
      - id: trailing-whitespace
# any python-language hook triggers it; the standalone repro in the attachment needs no pre-commit at all.

~/.cache/pre-commit/pre-commit.log (if present)

pre-commit-issue-corrected.txt

last.author: asottile
last.html: seems like you should report this to python instead. the semantics of environ should be portable

last.author: frankiexo
last.html:
You're right — I had one important part of the Windows semantics wrong.

Microsoft's CRT does document _wputenv(L"KEY=") as deleting the variable. However, that is a CRT semantic, not a Win32 limitation: SetEnvironmentVariableW(name, L"") can create an empty-valued variable; only SetEnvironmentVariableW(name, NULL) deletes it.

There is a closely related .NET issue, dotnet/runtime#50554, covering the same distinction. .NET used to normalize an empty string to null, effectively deleting the variable, but that behavior was changed in .NET 9 so that "" now represents an empty value and only null deletes the variable:
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/compatibility/core-libraries/9.0/empty-env-variable

CPython currently uses _wputenv() deliberately. The implementation explains that _wputenv() updates both the Win32 process environment and the CRT environ / _wenviron state, whereas SetEnvironmentVariableW() updates only the Win32 environment:
https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Modules/posixmodule.c

So making os.environ preserve empty-valued variables on Windows is not fundamentally impossible, but doing so while keeping the Win32 process environment and the CRT environment in sync involves a real compatibility/design tradeoff.

Reporting this upstream to CPython is reasonable. I still think avoiding a full clear(); update(before) round-trip in envcontext would make pre-commit more robust against this class of platform-specific side effect, but my original assumption that pre-commit is the only layer where it can be fixed was incorrect.

Thanks for the pointer. In the meantime I'll use the workaround in my projects.

russfellows/s3dlio#302.title: Python 3.14: crash at exit ("PyInterpreterState_Delete: remaining threads") with get_async in flight on a daemon thread's asyncio loop
russfellows/s3dlio#302.author: russfellows
russfellows/s3dlio#302.bodyHTML:
Summary

On Python 3.14, a process crashes at interpreter exit if a daemon thread is running an asyncio event loop with an s3dlio get_async call in flight. stderr shows:

Fatal Python error: PyInterpreterState_Delete: remaining threads
double free or corruption

The exit code is 139 (SIGSEGV) or 134 (SIGABRT).

This is not #298. #298's PyO3 0.29.3 upgrade fixes the sync-call aborts on every Python version, but not this crash. It was found while building the #298 fix.

How to reproduce

The scenario is async_get in python/tests/test_exit_daemon_threads_298.py on the fix/298 branch: 8 daemon threads, each running its own asyncio loop that awaits s3dlio.get_async("file://<4 MiB file>") in a loop, while the main thread sleeps 1 s and returns.

import asyncio, os, tempfile, threading, time
import s3dlio

d = tempfile.mkdtemp(); p = os.path.join(d, "obj.bin")
open(p, "wb").write(os.urandom(4 << 20))

def worker():
    async def loop():
        while True:
            await s3dlio.get_async("file://" + p)
    asyncio.run(loop())

for _ in range(8):
    threading.Thread(target=worker, daemon=True).start()
time.sleep(1)

Results (30 runs of the scenario per row, Loki-4, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64, release wheels)

Build Python Non-zero exits
current (pyo3 0.27.2) 3.14.10 25/30
#298 fix (pyo3 0.29.3) 3.14.10 28/30
#298 fix (pyo3 0.29.3) 3.11.18, 3.12.3, 3.13.7, 3.13.18 0/30 each

On 3.14 these related scenarios are clean (0/30 each): sync calls, get_into_async, put_bytes_async, and a get_async that never completes (pending forever).

PyPI has no cp314 wheel for 0.10.0, so the 3.14 rows use locally built wheels. CI does not run Python 3.14.

Investigation so far (root cause NOT known)

  • It predates #298's fix and is not caused by the PyO3 upgrade; it happens with pyo3 0.27.2 too.
  • A pure-Python script that runs daemon-thread asyncio loops on 3.14 fails differently (executor-shutdown noise, no fatal error). So it is not simply CPython's own daemon-asyncio behaviour.
  • Builder's hypothesis (unverified):
    • a tokio thread that attached to Python (PyGILState_Ensure) to deliver a get_async result is parked or hung at finalization;
    • CPython 3.14 then finds a thread state still registered when it deletes the interpreter, and aborts;
    • the "double free or corruption" would follow from that teardown.
  • Still to do: a gdb backtrace of the crashing thread on 3.14.10, check whether CPython 3.14 changed PyInterpreterState_Delete or daemon-thread handling, and check how pyo3-async-runtimes delivers results at shutdown (it already has a delivery drain from #192).

Workarounds (today)

  • Stop daemon-thread event loops, or join() their threads, before the interpreter exits.
  • Or run the asyncio loop on the main thread or on a non-daemon thread.

Acceptance

  • Root cause identified with a backtrace.
  • The async_get scenario of test_exit_daemon_threads_298.py passes 30/30 on 3.14. It is currently xfail(strict=False) on 3.14; remove the xfail once fixed.
  • Add Python 3.14 to the CI matrix.
  • Changelog and README updated.

last.author: russfellows
last.html:
Investigation update: likely root cause found (independent review of the #298 fix)

Reproduced: on 3.14.10 the async_get scenario fails 8 of 10 runs with the #298 fix wheel (pyo3 0.29.3), exiting 139 or 134 with double free or corruption and PyInterpreterState_Delete: remaining threads. The same scenario is clean, 0 of 30, on 3.12.3 and 3.13.7.

gdb backtrace of the crashing process: a tokio worker thread is inside PyGILState_Ensure -> _PyThreadState_Attach, called from the closure of get_async_py.

Likely cause:

  • get_async_py (src/python_api/python_core_api.rs, around line 2793) builds its result inside the future that future_into_py runs on the tokio runtime. It ends with Python::attach(|py| Ok(Py::new(py, PyBytesView::new(bytes))?.into_any())), so a tokio worker attaches to the interpreter itself.
  • s3dlio's async bridge gate (src/python_api/async_bridge.rs) only covers the result-delivery spawn_blocking. These attaches inside future_into_py bodies are not gated.
  • On Python < 3.14, pyo3-ffi 0.29 guards PyGILState_Ensure and parks the thread during finalization. On 3.14, pyo3 leaves that to CPython, and this attach races CPython 3.14's interpreter teardown.
  • The frame mapping to line 2793 is inferred, because the frames are inlined.

The same ungated pattern (Python::attach on a tokio worker inside a future_into_py body) is also at python_core_api.rs lines 1253, 2700, 2720, 2813, 3993, 4015, 4135 and 5600 (base commit 5b7ddd2). Those are candidates for the same crash.

Fix idea: don't attach on the worker. Return the plain Rust value from the future and build the BytesView (or other Python object) inside the gated delivery path, so no tokio thread ever attaches to the interpreter during finalization. Root cause still to confirm with a fix plus the 30-run check on 3.14.

last.author: russfellows
last.html:
Reported upstream:

  • CPython: python/cpython#124619 (comment with a pure-C reproducer and the 3.13.8+ vs 3.14 regression analysis: 3.14.10 23/30 crashes, 3.13.18 0/30, no Rust/PyO3 involved).
  • PyO3: PyO3/pyo3#6564 (AttachGuard::try_attach checks Py_IsInitialized() before Py_IsFinalizing(), so Python::attach during finalization reaches PyGILState_Ensure).
    s3dlio's own fix (no Tokio thread attaches in async entry points; Python objects are built in the gated delivery path) is in progress and does not depend on either upstream change.

last.author: russfellows
last.html:
Fixed in 0.10.1 (PR #308). On CPython 3.14, exiting while async calls are in flight no longer crashes. The root cause was also reported upstream (python/cpython#124619, PyO3/pyo3#6564). 0.10.1 ships Python 3.14 wheels.

Release: v0.10.1 (pip install --upgrade s3dlio==0.10.1). Details: PR #308 and docs/Changelog.md, "Version 0.10.1".

qmk/qmk_cli#60.title: [Bug] Failed loading libhidapi.dylib on M1 mac due to homebrew path changed
qmk/qmk_cli#60.author: LSChyi
qmk/qmk_cli#60.bodyHTML:
Can not compile firmware even dependencies are fulfilled.

Describe the Bug

After manually installed the osx-cross/avr/avr-gcc (which installs avr-gcc@9 at the time present) and arm-none-eabi-gcc, qmk doctor passed with just a warning about the avr-gcc version, I can run the build command on my M1 Macbook Pro. However, the build failed with just saying that

ERROR: Can not run "qmk" command!

 Please run util/qmk_install.sh to install all the dependencies QMK requires.

make: *** [phoenix:default] Error 1

After digging into the code, I found that it fails at loading the dynamic library HIDAPI, which fails at the __init__.py of the hid site package. I checked my LD_LIBRARY_PATH and the libhidapi.dylib is right there.

This happens because the homebrew path changed on M1 machines into /opt/homebrew, thus the search failed. I know this may not be the issue of qmk_cli, but there are some improvements we can make:

  1. Improve the error message without just saying ERROR: Can not run "qmk" command!, at least make the error clear with different log levels such as debug.
  2. Find a workaround for fixing this:
    • Could be setting some environment variables to make the search of dynamic library successful? I am not sure about that because looks like it is using another process without passing environment variables.
    • Document the workaround such as make a soft link pointing to the old search path.

Additional Context

I have tested by manually setting the load path to

hidapi = ctypes.cdll.LoadLibrary("/opt/homebrew/lib/libhidapi.dylib")

in /opt/homebrew/Cellar/qmk/0.0.52/libexec/lib/python3.9/site-packages/hid/__init__.py and I can compile the firmware without any problem.

DataDog/dd-trace-py#19802.title: fix(profiling): safely read Python 3.14 asyncio task offsets
DataDog/dd-trace-py#19802.author: taegyunkim
DataDog/dd-trace-py#19802.bodyHTML:
Description

On Python 3.14, the profiler walks the asyncio task lists rooted at PyInterpreterState.asyncio_tasks_head and _PyThreadStateImpl.asyncio_tasks_head. Their offsets were compiled into _stack.so, but they move between 3.14 patch releases (3.14.4 and 3.14.5 both shifted them), so a wheel built against one patch release reads the wrong memory on another. Asyncio task profiles then go missing or are severely inflated.

This PR reads the offsets from CPython's AsyncioDebug table, which _asyncio publishes for out-of-process debuggers, during asyncio initialization:

  • Discovery. On Linux, section headers are read from the loaded binary's file, which must first be proven to match the loaded image (program headers, plus a GNU build ID or the table bytes). On macOS, everything is read from memory. Discovery runs only during initialization, with the GIL released, and never on the sampling thread.
  • Validation. Every table field is checked against its struct size and alignment, and the task layout must match Echion's compile-time TaskObj mirror.
  • Fallback. If no table is found and the interpreter is the exact release the extension was built against, compile-time offsets are used. Otherwise native task-list attribution is turned off.
  • Retries and reporting. A failure is retried only after binaries are loaded or unloaded. init_asyncio reports whether the lists are available, and _stack._asyncio_task_lists() reports where the offsets came from.

Testing

  • New native tests: test_asyncio_debug, test_asyncio_debug_linux (ELF parsing, binary identity, injected syscall and I/O failures), test_asyncio_debug_macos (Mach-O fixtures), and test_task_fuzz_coverage.
  • New Python test test_asyncio_task_lists.py: offsets must come from the runtime table, so the fallback cannot hide a discovery failure in CI.
  • At the current head: 134/134 native tests pass on Linux arm64 (CPython 3.14.8, GCC 14) and 80/80 on macOS arm64 (CPython 3.14.0).
  • Earlier revisions: one wheel recorded correct task stacks on official CPython 3.14.2 and 3.14.4, and an overlayfs mount on Linux 6.1 was handled.

Risks

  • The table has no cookie or version, so validation cannot rule out every incompatible layout.
  • On Linux, initialization reads binary files and can block on a slow filesystem. Neither the GIL nor the loader lock is held.
  • Discovery takes the first valid table in load order, which assumes a single CPython build carrying the table is loaded.
  • Where discovery fails and the fallback does not apply, suspended asyncio tasks are not profiled. On 3.14 the native lists are the only record of asyncio.Task instances. Running coroutines still appear in thread stacks.

Additional Notes

  • JIRA: PROF-16272
  • Optional discovery diagnostics are in the stacked PR #20270.
  • Includes a release note.

Pre-review checklist

  • The changes have been tested in real services in staging
  • The PR does not result in new crashes

last.html: I guess I found a CPython bug too.

last.author: AlexWaygood
last.html:
If we want to be maximally paranoid, we could also make this change:

--- a/src/typing_extensions.py
+++ b/src/typing_extensions.py
@@ -2954,8 +2954,10 @@ if not _PEP_696_IMPLEMENTED:
 def _has_generic_or_protocol_as_origin() -> bool:
     try:
         frame = sys._getframe(2)
-    # not all platforms have sys._getframe()
-    except AttributeError:
+    # - Catch AttributeError: not all Python implementations have sys._getframe()
+    # - Catch ValueError: maybe we're called from an unexpected module
+    #   and the call stack isn't deep enough
+    except (AttributeError, ValueError):
